findings.title: Rebasing stETH held by the PoolManager gains and loses balance outside pool accounting
findings.difference: stETH balances are recalculated on each Lido oracle report, normally daily, with no transfer. The change is positive on staking rewards and can be negative after slashing or penalties. Lido's integration guide lists Uniswap among applications that are not designed for rebasing tokens and recommends wstETH.
findings.mechanism: Pool accounting never reads token balances. Balances are read only in sync and in _settle, and the only credit from a balance is the increase between a sync and the settle that follows in the same transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). A positive rebase raises balanceOf(PoolManager) with no sync and settle around it, so the increase belongs to no pool, no position and no claim. The only outflows are take and collectProtocolFees (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57), and both debit an accounted amount, so the surplus cannot be paid out to LPs. Someone who can run sync, the rebase and settle inside one transaction would be credited the whole rebase on the PoolManager's balance. For stETH the rebase happens inside submitReportData, which only an oracle committee member or a SUBMIT_DATA_ROLE holder can call. A negative rebase lowers the balance below the sum of pool and claim accounting, and the last withdrawals of stETH revert in Currency.transfer. Transfer rounding is safe for the PoolManager: a take debits the full amount while stETH moves at most that amount, and settle credits what arrived.
findings.impact: The PoolManager holds 80.4539 stETH at block 26470360. LPs in stETH pools earn no staking yield on it; the yield accumulates as an unclaimable surplus. After a negative rebase the shortfall falls on whoever withdraws stETH last. wstETH (2,295 held) is not affected because its balances do not rebase.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use stETH or another elastic supply token as a currency. The loss case needs a negative Lido report. Capturing the positive rebase needs an oracle committee member acting through a contract or an EIP-7702 delegated account. I derived the rounding argument from the share formula in the Lido guide and did not test it on chain. I did not compute how much of the 80.4539 stETH is surplus.
findings.mitigations: Use wstETH in pools. Interfaces can warn on pools whose currency is stETH or another rebasing token. A hook cannot fix this because the surplus is not reachable through any delta.

verification.factCheck: The Lido integration guide says stETH balances are recalculated when the oracle reports, normally daily, that a rebase can be negative after slashing or penalties, that transfers can move 1 to 2 wei less than requested, and that Maker, UniSwap and SushiSwap are not designed for rebasable tokens so holders there may not receive their daily rewards. The same guide says daily rebases had never been negative at the time of writing. The accounting oracle page says submitReportData reverts with SenderNotAllowed unless the caller holds SUBMIT_DATA_ROLE or is a consensus member, and that this call triggers the rebase. On chain at block 26470974 stETH.balanceOf(PoolManager) was 80.468369861 and sharesOf was 64.380487063, which is 1.2498875596 stETH per share. The researcher recorded 80.453883612 and 64.372946869 at block 26470380, which is 1.2498089263 per share. The rate rose by 0.0063 percent between the two readings. That matches one daily report at about 2.3 percent a year and added about 0.005 stETH to the PoolManager's balance on the earlier shares with no transfer. The public RPC refused archive calls, so I could not read the earlier block myself. The earlier figures are the researcher's.
verification.codeCheck: balanceOfSelf is called only in sync (src/PoolManager.sol:285) and in _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:359). currency.transfer is called only in take (src/PoolManager.sol:295) and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). take debits the caller's delta by the full amount, and collection is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued with a checked subtraction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-55). A balance increase that has no sync before it and no settle after it therefore reaches no delta and cannot be paid out. A caller who runs sync, then the rebase, then settle in one transaction is credited the whole increase on the PoolManager's balance (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364), and sync needs no unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:279). For stETH only an oracle member or a SUBMIT_DATA_ROLE holder can place the rebase inside such a transaction. After a negative rebase the balance is below the sum of deltas that pools and claims can produce, and the last take reverts in Currency.transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). I checked the rounding argument from the share formula: a transfer moves floor(amount * totalShares / totalPooledEther) shares, so the sender's balance falls by at most the amount that take debited. I did not test it on chain. No test in test/ models a rebasing token.
verification.corrections: I raise the severity from low to medium. Low is for hazards with no direct loss path. Here the staking yield on stETH held by the PoolManager is stranded for good, the increase is visible on chain, and the loss is limited to stETH pools and claims, which is the medium definition. The effect is closer to a permanent freeze of the yield than to degrade. The principal shortfall case needs a negative report, which the Lido guide says had not happened when it was written. The same sync, trigger, settle sequence applies to any token whose balance at the PoolManager a third party can raise inside one transaction, which is recorded as a lead.

findings.title: A take to a recipient whose receive policy rejects the PoolManager succeeds and strands the funds in ReceivePolicyGuard
findings.difference: Since T6 any Tempo account can set a receive policy in the TIP-403 registry: a sender list, a token filter and a recovery authority. When a TIP-20 transfer fails the recipient's receive policy, the transfer does not revert. The token credits ReceivePolicyGuard at 0xB10C000000000000000000000000000000000000, records a receipt and returns true. Only the recovery authority captured in the receipt can claim the amount. With recovery authority address(0) the claimer is the originator, which is the from address of the transfer. An ERC-20 transfer on Ethereum either credits the recipient or reverts.
findings.mechanism: 1. A user or a router calls take(currency, to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The caller's delta is debited and the PoolManager calls transfer(to, amount) on the TIP-20 (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). 2. The recipient to has a receive policy that rejects the PoolManager as sender, or filters out the token. The TIP-20 precompile moves the amount from the PoolManager to ReceivePolicyGuard with the PoolManager as originator and returns true. 3. The return value is 32 bytes of 1, so the success test at src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 passes and take completes. The recipient's balance is unchanged. 4. If the recipient's recovery authority is its own address or a third party, that party can claim. If it is address(0), only the originator can claim. The originator is the PoolManager, which has no function that calls the guard, so the receipt can never be claimed. 5. PoolManager accounting stays consistent, because the delta was debited and the balance fell by the same amount. The loss is the withdrawing party's.
findings.impact: The amount of each affected take is lost for good when the recipient's recovery authority is address(0), and delayed until a claim otherwise. This hits LP withdrawals and swap outputs sent to accounts that restrict senders, for example custodial deposit accounts with a sender whitelist. Pool reserves and other users are not affected.
findings.preconditions: The recipient must have set a receive policy that rejects the PoolManager address or the token, and must have chosen address(0) as recovery authority for the loss to be permanent. The party that names the recipient in take must not check the policy first. An attacker cannot set a policy for someone else. receivePolicy(PoolManager) is unset on chain, and the PoolManager cannot set one, so payments into the PoolManager are not redirected.
findings.mitigations: Routers and interfaces on Tempo should call validateReceivePolicy(token, PoolManager, recipient) before a take and refuse or warn when it would block. Account owners who use sender whitelists should add the PoolManager address or set themselves as recovery authority. The deployer can document that withdrawals originate from the PoolManager address.

verification.factCheck: The receive policies page states that a blocked inbound TIP-20 transfer still succeeds, that delivery goes to ReceivePolicyGuard at 0xB10C000000000000000000000000000000000000, and that with recovery authority address(0) only the transfer originator may claim. The TIP-20 specification says a receiver policy rejection must not revert the transfer. In the client source, transfer returns Ok(true) when validate_transfer reports a blocked inbound, validate_inbound_or_block moves the amount from the originator to the guard, and for transfer the originator is msg.sender. claim in the guard reverts with unauthorized_claimer unless msg.sender equals the recovery authority resolved from the receipt. I tested it on chain. I read the ReceivePolicyUpdated logs of the registry over the last 30,000,000 blocks and found 19 events. Two accounts, 0xec0eca588024e2d0091e74bd9034ff581111ea7f and 0x5bfa9123fa9dc6448d24ebbdb59e98f237de70c3, have sender policy 0, which rejects every sender. validateReceivePolicy(OUSD, PoolManager, account) returns 2 for both. An eth_simulateV1 of OUSD.transfer(account, 1) from the PoolManager address returns true and emits Transfer from the PoolManager to the guard and TransferBlocked from the guard. Afterwards the guard's balance is up by 1, the recipient's balance is unchanged and the PoolManager's balance is down by 1. The guard's functions are claim(address,bytes) with selector 0xbb1757cf, balanceOf(bytes) and burnBlockedReceipt(bytes). eth_call from the PoolManager address to the guard with transfer(address,uint256) and balanceOf(address) reverts with an unknown selector error.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller's delta and calls transfer(to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The success test accepts a 32 byte return value of 1 (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), which is what the TIP-20 returns for a redirected transfer, so take completes. Nothing in take reads the recipient's balance. The debit and the balance drop are equal, so PoolManager accounting stays whole and the loss falls on the party that named the recipient. The PoolManager makes outbound calls with four kinds of selector only: transfer(address,uint256) at src/types/Currency.sol:60-73, balanceOf(address) at src/types/Currency.sol:94, unlockCallback(bytes) to its caller at src/PoolManager.sol:110, and hook selectors to addresses with flag bits (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-134). The guard address has no flag bits and none of these selectors is claim, so a receipt whose originator is the PoolManager cannot be claimed. The tests have no token that returns true without crediting the recipient.
verification.corrections: The mechanism holds as written. Two points on reach. First, both accounts that reject all senders today name themselves as recovery authority, so they could claim a redirected amount. Three accounts have chosen address(0) as recovery authority, and all three currently allow every sender and every token. I found no account that is in the permanent loss configuration today. Second, a router that takes to itself and then forwards becomes the originator, and a router has no claim function either. The Universal Router and PositionManager on Tempo were not read. The severity stays medium. No third party can trigger the loss, pool reserves are not in reach, and the amount is limited to takes sent to accounts that set such a policy.

findings.title: Any account can book a balance increase it triggers at the PoolManager as its own payment, and EIP-7702 removes the origin check that guards Ampleforth's public rebase
findings.difference: Mainnet is the reference chain, so the difference is one that arrived after the Dencun rules the build targets. Since Pectra (EIP-7702) an EOA can run code and still satisfy msg.sender == tx.origin. The Ampleforth Orchestrator on mainnet uses that check as its only guard on the public rebase() function, and its source says the guard exists to protect liquidity providers from flash loan attacks. Mainnet also has reward contracts that pay a holder when any third party asks, such as Compound's claimComp(holder).
findings.mechanism: sync has no lock check and records balanceOf(PoolManager) for any currency (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). _settle credits the named recipient with the whole rise in that balance since the sync (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). Pool accounting never reads balances, so a rise that comes from a rebase or a reward payment belongs to no pool, position or claim until someone settles it. The steps for AMPL are these. The attacker is an EOA that has delegated to its own contract code and sends a transaction to itself. Its code calls unlock, and the PoolManager calls unlockCallback on the same EOA (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). Inside the callback the code calls sync(AMPL), then Orchestrator.rebase(), which passes the origin check because the caller is the transaction sender. When the day's supply change is positive, the AMPL balance of every holder grows, including the PoolManager's. The code then calls settle, which credits the attacker with the growth on the PoolManager's entire AMPL balance, and take(AMPL, attacker, growth), which pays it out (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). All deltas are zero and unlock returns. The attacker paid gas only. The same bracket works for any token where an ordinary account can cause a transfer or a balance increase to the PoolManager: a reward claim on behalf of a holder, an airdrop claim that pays a named account, or a rebase with a public trigger. A negative rebase is never bracketed, so liquidity providers keep the losses and lose the gains. This is the unprivileged form of the stETH finding from cycle 1, where the trigger needs an oracle member.
findings.impact: The gain of each positive rebase or reward payment on the full balance the PoolManager holds in that token, across all pools, claims and accrued protocol fees. The existing mainnet PoolManager holds 16 base units of AMPL, and the public triggers I simulated moved nothing at block 26471590 (0 COMP from claimComp, no sOHM change), so the amount at risk today is close to zero. The new deployment starts empty. The exposure grows with any pool that lists a token of this kind. Without an attacker the same increase stays in the PoolManager as a surplus that core has no function to pay out, so liquidity providers do not receive it in either case; the attacker turns a stranded amount into a taken one.
findings.preconditions: A pool or claim balance in a token whose balanceOf(PoolManager) an ordinary account can raise without paying the same amount: AMPL when a positive rebase is due and the attacker is first in the rebase window, or a token with a public reward or airdrop push to holders. For AMPL the attacker needs an EIP-7702 delegation, which any EOA can set. The rebase window is 1,200 seconds per day (offset 7,200 seconds into each 86,400), and the policy reported inRebaseWindow() = 0 at block 26471631, so my simulated rebase() call reverted. I did not execute the full sequence and did not simulate a delegated EOA; the origin check claim rests on the EIP text and the verified source. I checked 12 rebasing or reward-bearing tokens out of 66,554 token rows the explorer lists for the PoolManager.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers and interfaces can avoid or flag pools in elastic supply and reward-pushing tokens and use wrapped, non-rebasing forms. A keeper or a hook can run the same bracket first and pass the proceeds to the pool with donate (src/PoolManager.sol:256-276), which returns the increase to in-range liquidity providers. Token projects cannot rely on msg.sender == tx.origin to keep contracts out. The deployer cannot close this in core without tracking reserves per currency.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the Sourcify record for 0x6fb00a180781e75f87e2b690af0196baa77c7e7c on 22 November 2026. It reports a full creation and runtime match, contract name Orchestrator, solc 0.4.24. rebase() is external, its first statement is require(msg.sender == tx.origin), it then calls policy.rebase() and runs a list of downstream calls, and it reverts if one of them fails. The comment above it says contracts are guarded from calling to avoid flash loan attacks on liquidity providers. On chain at block 26472347 through the RPC in networks.json (reth v2.11.0): AMPL.monetaryPolicy() is 0x1b228a749077b8e307c5856ce62ef35d96dca2ea, policy.orchestrator() is the Orchestrator and Orchestrator.policy() points back, AMPL.balanceOf(PoolManager) is 16 base units, totalSupply is 1527834484102092 base units (9 decimals), inRebaseWindow() is 0, lastRebaseTimestampSec is 1795312800, the interval, offset and window length are 86400, 7200 and 1200 seconds, epoch is 2695 and the Orchestrator holds 4 downstream calls. eth_config reports fork id 0x07c9462e with activation time 1767747671. All of this matches the finding. The finding says it did not simulate a delegated account. I did, with eth_simulateV1 on the latest block (26472347 or a few blocks later) and a block time override of 1795399230, which lies inside the next rebase window. A call to rebase() from an account without code succeeded with 11 logs and 343,310 gas. The same call routed through a 51 byte forwarding contract placed by state override reverted after 24,029 gas with empty data, which is the origin check. An account whose code was overridden to the EIP-7702 designator 0xef0100 followed by the forwarder address then sent a transaction to itself. Its delegated code called rebase() and the call succeeded with the same 11 logs and 345,901 gas. Without the time override the plain account and the delegated account both reverted deeper in the call (43,028 and 45,618 gas) and the forwarder contract still stopped at 24,029 gas. A delegated account therefore passes the guard while it runs code, on the node that serves mainnet today. EIP-7702 (status Final) says in the section on self-sponsoring, lines 299 to 319, that the EIP breaks the invariant that msg.sender == tx.origin only happens in the topmost execution frame, and that the protection against atomic sandwich attacks such as flash loans would be broken. Lines 554 to 559 repeat this. The amount is zero today. In my simulated rebase the total supply and the PoolManager balance of 16 base units did not change. The last real rebase, at block 26467574, logged a supply change of 0 at a market rate of 1.2473 against a target of 1.2708. I reran the other triggers the finding names: Comptroller.claimComp(PoolManager) from an unrelated account succeeded and left the COMP balance at 5422.05, and Olympus staking rebase() succeeded and left the sOHM balance at 249.389779689, with epoch() reporting nothing to distribute. The Blockscout token list for the PoolManager had 66,563 rows at my fetch and shows the AMPL row with value 16. I found no primary source that contradicts the finding. I did not rerun the CometRewards claim and I did not read the source of the deployed monetary policy, which emits a newer rebase event than the policy code bundled with the Orchestrator source.
verification.codeCheck: sync has no modifier. For a non-zero currency it reads balanceOf(PoolManager) and stores the currency and that value in transient storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). _settle reads the synced currency, rejects msg.value for a non-zero currency (line 356), computes paid as the current balance minus the stored value with checked subtraction (358-360), clears the synced currency (361) and credits the named recipient with paid (364). Nothing ties the rise to a transfer made by the settler. take debits msg.sender and then transfers (291-297). unlock calls unlockCallback on msg.sender and afterwards requires the count of open deltas to be zero (104-114). A credit of g from settle and a debit of g from take under the same currency and account cancel in _accountDelta (368-378), so the count check passes. I looked for a guard that would stop the sequence and found none. The msg.value check does not apply because no value is sent. The synced currency check in collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52) only limits the fee controller. The int128 cast in settle and take (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59) limits an amount to 2^127 - 1, far above the AMPL supply. AMPL returns true from transfer, so the return data check in Currency.transfer passes (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). A search of the non-test sources shows that balanceOfSelf is called only at PoolManager.sol:285 and 359, so pool, position and claim accounting never see a rebase, and a positive one is credited to whoever brackets it. A negative rebase makes line 360 revert, so only gains can be booked. donate debits the donor and raises fee growth for in-range liquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:256-276, src/libraries/Pool.sol:466-480), so the mitigation described is available. sync is not the only route. take lets the caller hold the whole pooled AMPL balance for a nominal debit (291-297). If the rebase runs while the caller holds the tokens, the caller repays the nominal amount through sync, transfer and settle and keeps the growth. The result is the same as the bracket in the finding.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged is right: every step is open to any account, and the pooled token and the pool are not made by the attacker. The assumptions should also list A5, because a take of the pooled balance before the rebase followed by a nominal repayment gives the same gain without a sync before the rebase. A change that only restricted sync would leave that route open. The supports text for the EIP source says the broken invariant is that msg.sender == tx.origin implies an account without code. The EIP words it as the check being true only in the topmost execution frame, and it says the use of the check to ensure that msg.sender is an EOA is unaffected. The conclusion for the Orchestrator guard is the same. The preconditions should say that recent rebases changed supply by zero (block 26467574, and my simulation of the next window), so a gain needs a market rate outside the policy's deviation band as well as a pool that holds AMPL. With 16 base units held, the gain rounds to zero today. The Blockscout row count was 66,563 at my fetch. Severity stays medium on the scale: the loss is limited to pools that hold an elastic supply or reward pushing token, and no such pool holds a material balance today.

findings.title: Anyone can run the staking rebase of five Olympus forks on Polygon and BNB Smart Chain, and on Polygon bots already book each sLGNS and sATH rebase on the PoolManager balance as ERC-6909 claims
findings.difference: The cause is a token design, and Polygon and BNB Smart Chain are where pools hold such tokens. Staked Longinus (sLGNS), Staked Aegis (sATH) and Staked Klima (sKLIMA) on Polygon, and Staked NovaBank (sNVB) and sShadowsClaw (sSAC) on BNB Smart Chain, raise every holder's balance when their staking contract runs rebase(). That function has no caller check and takes effect once per epoch. F-041 recorded this class on Ethereum for AMPL, where an origin check stands in the way. These five tokens have no such check, and the Polygon PoolManager shows the path in use since May 2026.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync has no lock check and stores balanceOf(PoolManager) for any currency (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289). _settle credits the caller with the whole rise of that balance since the sync (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365). Pool accounting never reads balances, so a rise that comes from a rebase is booked as a payment by whoever brackets it. 2. The Longinus staking contract 0x1964ca90474b11ffd08af387b110ba6c96251bfc exposes rebase() to any caller. When epoch.endBlock <= block.number it calls sLGNS.rebase(epoch.distribute, epoch.number), which raises the total supply and lowers the gons per fragment, so every balance grows inside that call (Staking source lines 672 to 693, sLGNS source lines 1068 to 1090 and 1121 to 1123). 3. Observed on chain: transaction 0xfe645530665d1f424807e4ef99fc8cd3569d3fbaab75af4dca893749098eae11 in Polygon block 97,799,112, the block in which epoch 3018 became due, at transaction index 0. An externally owned account calls a contract of 851 bytes. The trace shows unlock, then inside unlockCallback sync(sLGNS), Staking.rebase(), settle() and mint(). The PoolManager emitted an ERC-6909 Transfer from the zero address with the sLGNS id for 9.015568747 sLGNS. The sender paid 3.39 POL at 5,250 gwei to be first in the block. 4. The same gain needs no settle credit: a caller can take the whole pooled balance (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), call rebase() while holding it, pay the principal back and keep the growth. 5. Read-only tests through Multicall3 with the call list balanceOf(PoolManager), rebase(), balanceOf(PoolManager): KlimaStaking.rebase() raised the PoolManager's sKLIMA balance by 1,276,529 base units at the latest block, with about 1,232 epochs outstanding. The NovaBank StakingV2.rebase() raised its sNVB balance by 82,488,131 base units on BNB Smart Chain. The same call for sLGNS, sATH and sSAC succeeded and changed nothing, because their epoch was not yet due at the time of the call; the sATH and sSAC staking contracts contain the rebase() selector.
findings.impact: sLGNS: the PoolManager held 36,908.56 sLGNS, about 5,900 USD at 0.16 USD, in 267 pools of which 265 have no hook. An epoch is 14,400 blocks and the next rebase adds 8.78 sLGNS on that balance, four times a day. From block 87,258,312 (22 May 2026) to block 97,799,112, 661 ERC-6909 mints with the sLGNS id went to six recipients for 20,418.69 sLGNS in total, about 3,300 USD at today's price, and every one of them sits in a block where an epoch became due. In the one day window the sLGNS balance rose 36.92 beyond its Transfer logs. sATH: 150 mints for 328.86 sATH to two recipients against a balance of 389.04. sKLIMA: 8 mints for 0.0102 sKLIMA against a balance of 247.67. BNB Smart Chain: the PoolManager holds 38,313.74 sNVB and 2,287.62 sSAC; the endpoint returned no claim mint for either id in the last 1,344,000 blocks, and a payout through take would not appear in that search. Who loses: liquidity providers in these pools would have earned this growth by holding the token outside the pool. Inside the PoolManager the growth belongs to no pool, position or claim, and core has no function that pays it to them. The amount taken was therefore never an accounted balance of any user, and principal is not reduced. The balance does not fall back afterwards.
findings.preconditions: A pool or claim balance in a token whose rebase any account can start. The taker must be the first caller after the epoch becomes due. No role, no hook and no token of the taker's making is needed. I did not run the sequence. The call order comes from debug_traceTransaction of one of the 661 transactions; the other 660 were checked by their mint logs and block numbers only. The sLGNS price is the figure the DexScreener API returned for the LGNS and sLGNS pairs. The sATH, sNVB and sSAC staking sources are not on Sourcify and I read their selectors from bytecode.
findings.mitigations: Core cannot tell a rebase from a payment and keeps no total of what is owed per currency, so it cannot compute or redirect the surplus. Liquidity providers should pool a wrapped form with a fixed balance where the project offers one. Interfaces and routers should warn on or hide pools whose currency changes balance without transfers; reconcile.py in the work directory finds them from chain data. A deployer who wants the growth to reach liquidity providers needs a wrapper or a vault held by a hook around the token, outside core.

verification.codeCheck: sync has no modifier and stores balanceOf(PoolManager) for the named currency in transient storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). settle requires the unlocked state (src/PoolManager.sol:300-302). _settle reads the synced currency, rejects msg.value for an ERC-20 (line 356), computes paid as the balance now minus the synced balance with a checked subtraction (lines 358-360), resets the synced currency (line 361) and credits the recipient (line 364). mint debits the caller by the same amount and writes the ERC-6909 balance (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329, src/ERC6909.sol:79-83). After settle and mint the caller's delta in that currency is zero, so the count check at src/PoolManager.sol:112 passes. I looked for a guard that would stop this and found none: nothing in src/ compares a token balance with pool accounting, and the only other balance read is the one in sync. The variant in step 4 also holds: take debits the caller and transfers first (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), the rebase then grows the tokens while the caller holds them, and a sync followed by a transfer of the principal and a settle clears the debit. For sLGNS a transfer moves value times gonsPerFragment gons, so the PoolManager balance falls by exactly the amount that take debited, and the rebase only raises supply. The credited amount is the rise of the whole PoolManager balance, so it was never part of a pool's or a claim holder's accounted amount. The observed trace matches this path call for call.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged is right: the sender needs no role, no hook and no token of its own, and the pools involved have no hook. Three details need correction. First, the preconditions say the sNVB staking source is not on Sourcify, while the sources list cites the verified StakingV2 record at 0x6bcd1273eba684ff62614e41eff87123113112d1; I fetched it, Sourcify reports a match, and rebase() is public at line 716. Only the sATH staking contract 0x98d21b8e6bf0c1d2dfb0e3fcb82035095dcdd7de and the sSAC staking contract 0x99954eb0b159514d608f64c89a2c5bbe9f42120b were read from bytecode. Second, the sATH epoch is counted in seconds: epoch() returned length 28,800 and an end value of 1795417200, which is a timestamp. Third, balanceOf(PoolManager) for sLGNS was 34,658.405133592 at block 97,804,424, below the 36,908.56 in the finding, so the next rebase adds about 8.24 sLGNS on today's balance. The finding states the scope limit correctly: the cause is the token design and would be the same on any network, the amount taken is unaccounted surplus, and no accounted balance of a liquidity provider or claim holder falls. This is a second and third token for the class in F-041 with live use, and it is unrelated to any difference between Polygon or BNB Smart Chain and Ethereum.

findings.title: Interest Protocol lets any caller accrue interest, which raised the PoolManager's USDI balance by 399,373 in one transaction and can raise it again today
findings.difference: This is a second token for the class in F-041 and it needs no EIP-7702 delegation. USDI at 0x2a54ba2964c8cd459dc568853f79813a60761b58 is a rebasing token. Its VaultController at 0x4aae9823fb4c70490f1d802fc697f3fff8d5cbe3 has calculateInterest(), which any contract can call and which distributes accrued interest to all holders by raising their balances.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync, settle and take work as in F-041 (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 349-365). 2. Transaction 0xad36440ffe69062fe8b57599f3d5e77ae69f38b81bf19667c2e39957464ebc4d in block 26,469,396 was sent through Multicall3 by an ordinary account. It made the VaultController donate 874,691 USDI of interest, which moved the supply from about 1.53 million to 2.40 million. The sender took 158,347 USDI out of a v2 style pair in the same transaction and sold 118,000 USDI through v4 pools. 3. In that block the PoolManager's USDI balance rose from 697,167.03 to 1,214,540.56. Of the rise 118,000 arrived by Transfer and 399,373.53 came from the rebase. The sender did not bracket the rebase with sync and settle, so the 399,373.53 USDI stayed in the PoolManager and belongs to no pool. 4. Read-only test through Multicall3 with balanceOf(PoolManager), calculateInterest(), balanceOf(PoolManager): at block 26,469,395 the balance rises by 399,373.08, and at the latest block it rises by 4,636.71. A caller who runs sync before and settle after that call, or who takes the pooled USDI, makes the call and pays the principal back, is credited that amount.
findings.impact: The PoolManager holds 1,214,540.56 USDI, which is 47.5 percent of the supply, in six pools without a hook. Any account can book 4,636.71 USDI today and more as interest accrues. The market value is small: the 118,000 USDI sold through v4 pools in the observed transaction returned 9.04 USDC. Liquidity providers do not receive this growth in either case, because core has no function that pays out an unaccounted balance. The amount was never an accounted balance of any user. The balance does not fall back afterwards.
findings.preconditions: A pool or claim balance in USDI and interest that has accrued since the last call. The VaultController implementation at 0xffc8c49c5b38bc9bafd0bb0f5f189eecd35e35e2 is not on Sourcify, so the statement that anyone may call calculateInterest() rests on the two simulations from Multicall3 and on the observed transaction, which also came from Multicall3. I did not run the bracket.
findings.mitigations: Same as for the Polygon finding. Core cannot separate this growth from a payment. Liquidity providers should not pool USDI, and interfaces should warn on currencies whose balance changes without transfers.

verification.codeCheck: The path is the one in finding 0 and in F-041. sync stores the balance with no lock check (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). _settle credits the rise since the sync after a checked subtraction and the msg.value check (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). take pays out before anything is paid in (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), and the delta count check at src/PoolManager.sol:112 is met when the credit is taken or minted. No line in src/ ties a balance rise to a pool, so the interest that calculateInterest() adds between a sync and a settle is credited to the settler. Without a bracket the rise stays in the balance and no function pays it out: take and burn debit accounted amounts, and collectProtocolFees is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56).

The severity medium follows F-041 as a class rating; by value this instance is negligible. No accounted balance of a liquidity provider or claim holder is reduced.

findings.title: ViciCoin on Polygon counts every PoolManager transfer against a daily net flow limit of 6 VCNT, and the PoolManager is not exempt
findings.difference: No chain rule is involved. ViciCoin (VCNT, 0x8a16d4bf8a0a716017e8d2262c4ac32927797a2f) is a pooled token on Polygon whose owner installed the plugin TransferLimitHybridPluginV04 at 0xf58fed40fba1ab7aa7ffc160b863bedd998386a7. The plugin runs before every transfer and keeps one signed running total per address and per day. A transfer out lowers the total of the sender and a transfer in raises the total of the recipient. A transfer reverts with TransferTooLarge() when the sender total would fall below minus the limit or the recipient total would rise above the limit. On chain the limit is 6 VCNT (about 109 USD at 18.12 USD per VCNT), the period is 86,400 seconds counted from the Unix epoch, 57 addresses are exempt, and the PoolManager 0x67366782805870060151383f4bbff9dab53e5cd6 is not one of them. The source comment of the plugin says that DeFi contracts must be added as exemptions and that otherwise the limit restricts total volume.
findings.mechanism: 1. take(VCNT, to, amount) makes the PoolManager call VCNT.transfer(to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). The plugin subtracts the amount from dailyTotals[PoolManager][day] and reverts when the result is below minus 6 VCNT. The revert reaches the caller as ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). 2. A payment of VCNT into the PoolManager before settle adds to the same total and reverts when the result is above plus 6 VCNT, so settle cannot be reached with that payment (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). 3. A take that is repaid in the same unlock moves the total down and back up by the same amount. I simulated it: after the round trip transferLimitAmountUsed(PoolManager) and transferLimitAmountRemaining(PoolManager) were unchanged. The free round trip therefore does not use up the limit. 4. A net outflow does. At block 97,801,741 the PoolManager had a total of plus 0.1256 VCNT and transferLimitAmountRemaining returned 6.1256 VCNT. In simulation, after transfers of 6 VCNT and 0.1256 VCNT to two recipients the view returned 0, and a further transfer of 0.01 VCNT and of 1 base unit reverted with 0x1b97a875 (TransferTooLarge). A payment of 1 VCNT into the PoolManager reopened exactly 1 VCNT. 5. An account that holds about 6.13 VCNT of ERC-6909 claims or of pool liquidity can burn or remove it at the start of a UTC day (src/PoolManager.sol:331-336 and 291-297). From then on every take of VCNT by any other user reverts until someone pays VCNT in or the day ends. The account can pay the same VCNT back in at the end of the day, when the total returns to zero, and repeat the next day. A buy of the same size through a swap has the same effect and costs the swap fee. 6. The recipient is limited as well, so one take of more than 6 VCNT to a recipient that is not exempt reverts even when the PoolManager has room. A take of zero VCNT reverts with the string invalid transfer.
findings.impact: Withdrawals of VCNT from every v4 pool on Polygon share one allowance of 6 VCNT of net outflow per UTC day. The PoolManager held 11.35 VCNT (about 206 USD) at block 97,801,699, so the liquidity providers of these pools cannot withdraw all of it in one day without matching inflows, and one account can keep the allowance at zero for the cost of gas and about 111 USD of VCNT that it keeps. No funds are taken. The amount at risk today is small. The hazard grows with the VCNT that pools hold, because the cap does not grow with it.
findings.preconditions: The PoolManager stays outside the exemption list of the plugin. The blocking account needs about 6.13 VCNT of net outflow per day, which means it holds VCNT claims, VCNT liquidity or the other currency to buy with. It needs no role. A round trip without capital does not trip the limit.
findings.mitigations: The token owner can add the PoolManager with transferLimitAddExemption, as the plugin source asks for DeFi contracts. Until then liquidity providers should treat VCNT in v4 pools on Polygon as withdrawable at 6 VCNT per day at most, and interfaces can read transferLimitAmountRemaining(PoolManager) before building a take. Pool creators should check any token for a transfer limit plugin and for its exemption list before pairing it.

verification.factCheck: Every chain fact held under my own queries on 2026-11-23. Source: I fetched the Sourcify record of 0xf58fed40fba1ab7aa7ffc160b863bedd998386a7 (match, TransferLimitHybridPluginV04) and read checkTransfer at lines 438 to 489 of TransferLimitHybridPluginV04.sol. For a sender that is not exempt it computes dailyTotals[from][timestamp / timeBlockSize] minus the amount and reverts with TransferTooLarge when the result is below minus the user limit. For a recipient that is not exempt it adds the amount and reverts when the result is above the limit, unless the sender is the zero address. The header comment at lines 23 and 24 says DeFi contracts must be exemptions and that a Uniswap pool outside the exemptions makes the limit restrict total volume. TransferValidationHybridPlugin routes transfer, transferFrom and transferAndCall into checkTransfer. Chain, https://polygon.drpc.org at blocks 97,804,497 to 97,804,523: transferLimit() = 6e18, getTransferLimitForUser(PoolManager) = 6e18, masterTransferLimitOverride() = 0, transferLimitAmountUsed(PoolManager) = 125,605,912,695,548,320, transferLimitAmountRemaining(PoolManager) = 6,125,605,912,695,548,320, getExemptionCount() = 57, balanceOf(PoolManager) = 11,350,331,586,494,174,070, decimals 18. introspect(VCNT) on the plugin returns timeBlockSize 86,400, limit 6e18 and 57 exemptions. I read all 57 with getExemptionAtIndex. The PoolManager 0x67366782805870060151383f4bbff9dab53e5cd6, the v4 PositionManager, the three Universal Router addresses of networks.json and Permit2 are absent. The list holds the v3 routers and the v3 position manager. Behaviour, eth_call with from set to the PoolManager: transfer of 1 VCNT returns true, 7 VCNT reverts with 0x1b97a875, and a zero amount reverts with the string invalid transfer. I computed 0x1b97a875 locally as the selector of TransferTooLarge(). With the Multicall3 runtime code placed at the PoolManager address by state override, transfers of 6 VCNT and of the remaining 0.1256 VCNT to two fresh recipients succeeded, transferLimitAmountRemaining then returned 0 and transferLimitAmountUsed returned minus 6e18, and transfers of 0.01 VCNT and of 1 base unit reverted with 0x1b97a875. A transfer of 5 VCNT out and back in one call left both views at their starting values, so a repaid take does not consume the allowance. Victim side: eth_getLogs on https://polygon-bor-rpc.publicnode.com for blocks 97,364,523 to 97,804,523 shows 15 VCNT transfers that touch the PoolManager, each between 0.009 and 0.127 VCNT, 9 out and 6 in. Two receipts I opened carry a Swap event of the PoolManager for pool id 0x7d4853d263223b620af200c3b281036f267f9fc1b309660300df0ca274af4a3f. I recomputed that id locally as keccak256 of (WETH 0x7ceb23fd6bc0add59e62ac25578270cff1b9f619, VCNT, fee 3000, tick spacing 60, hooks address zero). The pool has no hook and pairs VCNT with WETH, so its liquidity providers match the victim definition. The same token address has no code on the other 20 networks. Not confirmed: the price of 18.12 USD and the DEX reserve figure. The GeckoTerminal API answered 429 on three attempts. The last sale in the v4 pool traded 0.1256 VCNT for 0.001324 WETH. I did not repeat the storage slot reads or the debug_traceCall of the finding. The view calls and the plugin introspection give the same values.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller and then calls currency.transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). CurrencyLibrary.transfer sends transfer(address,uint256) with all gas and treats a reverted call as failure (src/types/Currency.sol:55-75), then reverts through CustomRevert.bubbleUpAndRevertWith with the token address, the transfer selector, the bubbled reason and ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). There is no try path and no alternative payout, so a TransferTooLarge revert in the token makes the whole take revert. burn credits the caller and take pays out, so a claim holder reaches the same transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336). modifyLiquidity with a negative delta gives a positive delta that the provider collects by take (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184). On the way in, _settle credits only the rise of balanceOf since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364), and the token transfer that produces the rise is made by the payer. When it reverts, no credit exists and the unlock ends with CurrencyNotSettled (src/PoolManager.sol:112). No guard in core changes this. The msg.value check at src/PoolManager.sol:356 and the delta count check at line 112 are unrelated, and the int128 cast at line 294 does not bind at these amounts. A user can still end an unlock with mint in place of take (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), so a liquidity provider can leave the pool, take the WETH side and keep the VCNT side as an ERC-6909 claim. The freeze applies to the token payout, and the claim stays subject to the same daily allowance later.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged stands. Any account can bring the allowance to zero, and the victims use a hookless WETH and VCNT pool that the attacker did not create. The cause is an issuer setting, and the issuer can end it with one exemption. Three refinements. First, at the start of a UTC day the running total is zero, so the amount needed is exactly 6 VCNT of net outflow. The figure 6.13 applies on a day that already had 0.1256 VCNT of inflow. Each recipient that is not exempt can receive at most 6 VCNT on that day, so an outflow above 6 VCNT needs two recipients or an exempt one. Second, the cost is not fixed at the value of 6 VCNT held overnight. An account can also buy the VCNT in the pool and sell it on a venue whose contracts are exempt, which costs fees and price impact. I did not measure the depth of either venue. Third, the limit binds without any hostile account. Net withdrawals of all v4 pools together cannot exceed 6 VCNT per UTC day plus the inflows of that day, and the same holds in the other direction for payments in. Blocked users can leave with ERC-6909 claims. This hazard is a token setting on Polygon. It does not come from a difference between Polygon and Ethereum, and it gives no path to take funds. The amount exposed today is 11.35 VCNT. The severity is medium on the scale because liquidity operations are blocked without loss.

findings.title: QANX and seventeen tokens of one generator family count locked units in balanceOf and let any holder assign them, so the PoolManager's transferable balance can be swapped for units it can never send
findings.difference: The cause is a token design and the three networks are where pools hold such tokens today. Two contracts named QANX (0xaaa7a10a8ee237ea61e8ac46c50a8db8bcc1baaa on Ethereum, 0xaaa9214f675316182eaa21c85f0ca99160cc3aaa on Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain) return _balances plus the locked amount from balanceOf, and their transferLocked function lets any holder send an amount to any recipient under a lock whose end date the sender chooses. Seventeen tokens built with one token generator (contract name MainToken with FreezableToken: WOZX, IZI, RKME, EXO, EAT, MNTO, ZITI, LED, GHD, YF4 and DXF on Ethereum, ELV on BNB Smart Chain, CARR, WELT, BLITZ, ALGB and HITT on Polygon) return the plain balance plus freezingBalance from balanceOf, and their freezeTo function lets any holder move its own tokens into the frozen balance of any address. In both designs transfer spends the unlocked part only. The trial sweep of this unit found no such token on the other eighteen networks.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync stores balanceOf(PoolManager) for the currency without any lock check (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). _settle credits the caller with balanceOf now minus the stored figure (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364). take pays out with a plain transfer call (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). The credit is therefore counted in units of balanceOf and the payout is made in transferable units. 2. Inside one unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114) a caller takes an amount X of the token, which the PoolManager pays from its transferable balance, then calls sync, then calls transferLocked(PoolManager, X, far date, far date, 0) on QANX or freezeTo(PoolManager, X, far date) on a generator token, then calls settle. balanceOf(PoolManager) is back at its old value, so settle credits X and the debt from the take is cleared. All deltas are zero and unlock returns. The caller needs no tokens of its own and pays gas only. X can be the whole transferable balance. 3. After that the PoolManager reports the same balance and can send X less. Every take of that currency beyond the remaining transferable balance reverts with the wrapped ERC20TransferFailed error, for every pool, every ERC-6909 claim and the protocol fees of that currency, because all of them share one holder address. 4. How long it lasts. In the generator tokens only the holder can release frozen units (releaseOnce and releaseAll act on msg.sender, MainToken.sol lines 479 to 516 in the WOZX source), and the PoolManager has no function that calls them, so the units stay frozen whatever date was chosen. In the old QANX contract unlock(account) can be called by anyone after hardLockUntil, a uint32 the sender chooses, so the lock can run to the year 2106. In the newer QANX contract the dates are uint64. 5. Read-only test. I placed a measuring stub at the PoolManager address by state override and ran one eth_call per token: the PoolManager address sends an amount to an ordinary account A, A calls the function with the PoolManager as recipient, and the stub then reads balances and tries two transfers. Old QANX on Ethereum at block 26,476,590 with the whole balance of 21,210,277.639 QANX: balanceOf(PoolManager) is 21,210,277.639 after the call, A holds 0, a transfer of the full balance is refused and the reported balance stays in place. With one third of the balance the transfer of balance minus amount is accepted and the transfer of the full balance is refused. The newer QANX gave the same result with 3,512.31 QANX on Ethereum and 10,297.83 QANX on BNB Smart Chain (block 135,237,759). freezeTo gave the same result on DXF, WOZX and ZITI on Ethereum, on ELV on BNB Smart Chain and on all five Polygon tokens. The other eight Ethereum generator tokens share the selector set of WOZX and were not run one by one. I did not send the sequence through the PoolManager itself.
findings.impact: Liquidity providers and claim holders of every pool in the affected token lose access to the amount that was swapped for locked units, up to the whole pooled balance, and nobody gains it. Amounts today: 21,210,277.64 old QANX at the Ethereum PoolManager in pools from 6 Initialize logs. coins.llama.fi values that at about 204,500 USD because it gives both QANX contracts the price 0.00964 USD, and this figure should not be relied on: QANplatform replaced the old contract after the bridge wallet attack of 11 October 2022, distributed the new token by a snapshot of that date and states that only the new token is supported, and DexScreener lists no pair for the old contract. The old balance is therefore worth little or nothing. Newer QANX: 3,512.31 on Ethereum (about 34 USD) and 10,297.83 on BNB Smart Chain (about 99 USD), in pools from 21 Initialize logs on Ethereum. Generator tokens: 2,158,038.8 EXO (about 182 USD at the DexScreener price), 2,297,431 CARR (about 70 USD at the coins.llama.fi price), 3,062.3 YF4, which is 10.2 percent of that token's supply, and fourteen others without a price. The freezingBalanceOf(PoolManager) and lockedBalanceOf(PoolManager) readings are zero for all of them today, so nobody has done this yet. The new deployment starts empty and the same exposure appears as soon as a pool lists a token of this kind.
findings.preconditions: A pool or claim balance in a token whose balanceOf includes units that transfer cannot move and whose lock function is open to any holder. No role, hook or attacker made token is needed. For the old QANX contract the recipient must have no lock yet, because the contract allows one lock per address. Link I could not confirm: the behaviour of the eight Ethereum generator tokens that were covered by their family representative only. The search used function names from a public signature database, which named 85,092 of 137,912 selectors, and a fixed set of argument patterns, so a lock function with an unlisted name or unusual arguments would have been missed.
findings.mitigations: Core cannot tell locked units from transferable ones, because it reads balanceOf only (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). Interfaces and routers should refuse or flag currencies that expose transferLocked, freezeTo, freezingBalanceOf, lockedBalanceOf or actualBalanceOf. Liquidity providers should not pool these tokens. For the old QANX contract anyone can protect the PoolManager by sending it a lock of one base unit with a far end date, since a second lock on the same address is refused while the first exists. The newer QANX contract adds to an existing lock and has no such protection. A hook cannot prevent the sequence, because take, sync and settle do not call hooks.

verification.codeCheck: sync has no modifier and stores balanceOf(PoolManager) (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). take debits the caller and pays with a plain transfer call (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). _settle credits reservesNow minus reservesBefore to the recipient (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364). With the order take, sync, lock transfer, settle the two deltas of the caller cancel, NonzeroDeltaCount is zero and unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). I looked for a guard and found none: nothing compares the synced currency with a take that ran before the sync, the int128 cast only caps the amount, the msg.value check at line 356 does not apply to a token, and the synced-currency check in src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52 concerns fee collection only. After the sequence every take above the remaining transferable balance reverts through the wrapped ERC20TransferFailed error (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86), and a position holder can still convert the stuck side into an ERC-6909 claim (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329). verification.corrections: The statement that nobody gains is incomplete for both QANX contracts. transferLocked lets a sender whose unlocked balance is too small pay from its own locked balance when the new lock is the same or stricter and allowedHops is lower (old QANX lines 471 to 495, newer QANX _transferLocked). A holder of locked QANX with allowedHops of at least 1 can therefore send locked units to the PoolManager between sync and settle and take liquid units for them, which is a gain for that holder at the expense of the pools. I read this in the source and did not search for holders with such locks. The WOZX balance at the PoolManager is 4,364 base units, which is dust. The cause is a token design and has no link to a network difference, so this entry does not answer the question about a network specific weakness. Severity high is kept because an ordinary account can freeze accounted funds for good in pools that exist; the amounts at risk today are a few hundred USD.

findings.title: Two pooled tokens on Ethereum let any holder grant revocable vesting tokens to the PoolManager, book the grant as a payment and then revoke it, which removes pooled tokens without a debit
findings.difference: The cause is a token design. The old AdEx token ADX (0x4470bb87d77b963a013db939be332f927f2b992e, contract ADXToken, 4 decimals) and CDT (0x177d39ac676ed1c67a2b268ad7f1e58826e5b0af, contract CDTToken) inherit an early library contract named VestedToken. grantVestedTokens is public: it records a grant for the recipient and transfers the amount to it. The grant can be made revocable, and revokeTokenGrant lets the granter take the unvested part back out of the recipient's balance. This is a balance that an ordinary account can raise for the PoolManager and later pull back. District0x DNT and ESCB carry the same function names and reject the call from an ordinary account, ESCB through a whitelist in its source.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync, settle and take work as described in the QANX finding (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 349-365). 2. Inside one unlock a caller takes X of the token from the PoolManager, calls sync, then calls grantVestedTokens(PoolManager, X, start, cliff, vesting, revokable = true, burnsOnRevoke = false) with dates in the future. The token transfers X to the PoolManager (ADXToken.sol lines 275 to 307), so balanceOf(PoolManager) is back at its old value and settle credits X, which clears the debt of the take. 3. Still inside the callback, or in any later transaction, the caller calls revokeTokenGrant(PoolManager, grantId). The token adds the unvested amount, which is all of X before the cliff, to the caller and subtracts it from the PoolManager (lines 314 to 338). Core records nothing, because no PoolManager function runs. 4. The caller now holds X and owes nothing. The PoolManager balance is lower by X while pools, claims and protocol fees still record the old amounts. X can be the whole pooled balance. 5. Read-only test at Ethereum blocks 26,476,597 to 26,476,600 with a measuring stub at the PoolManager address. ADX with the whole balance of 165,963 base units: after the grant alone balanceOf(PoolManager) is 165,963, the full transfer is refused and the account holds 0; after grant and revoke in one call balanceOf(PoolManager) is 0 and the account holds 165,963. CDT with half of 310.02 CDT: after the grant alone the balance is back at 310.02 and the full transfer is refused; after grant and revoke the PoolManager holds 155.01 and the account 155.01. tokenGrantsCount(PoolManager) is 0 on both today. I did not send the sequence through the PoolManager itself.
findings.impact: The whole pooled balance of the token, taken from liquidity providers, claim holders and accrued protocol fees of every pool in it. Today that is 16.5963 old ADX and 310.02 CDT, both without a market price that I could find, so the loss available now is negligible. The size follows the token: any pool that lists a token with open revocable grants can be emptied of that token by anyone, and the new deployment has the same exposure once such a pool exists. If the caller does not revoke, the result is the freeze of the QANX finding, because granted tokens are not transferable before they vest.
findings.preconditions: A pool or claim balance in a token with a public grant function whose grants the granter can revoke. The recipient may hold at most 20 grants in this library, which does not hinder a single grant. No role, hook or attacker made token is needed. I searched by function name and by trial, so a clawback function under another name (revoke, cancelVesting, reclaim) on a token that the trial arguments did not fit would have been missed.
findings.mitigations: None in core, which cannot see that a balance increase carries a revocation right. Interfaces should refuse or flag currencies that expose grantVestedTokens, revokeTokenGrant or transferableTokens. Liquidity providers should not pool such tokens.

sources.supports: _settle credits the rise of balanceOf(PoolManager) since sync to the caller, with no view of how the rise came about.

findings.severityNote: Rated high by the verifier. The review rates it medium, in line with F-041 and F-066: the loss is limited to pools of two tokens, and 16.6 ADX and 310 CDT are at risk today.

verification.factCheck: I fetched both Sourcify records. ADXToken.sol (match): grantVestedTokens is public, pushes a grant whose granter is msg.sender when revokable is true and then calls transfer(_to, _value) (lines 275 to 307). revokeTokenGrant requires grant.revokable and grant.granter == msg.sender, computes the non vested amount, adds it to the granter and subtracts it from the holder (lines 314 to 338). transferableTokens subtracts non vested grants from the balance and the canTransfer modifier enforces it on transfer (lines 210 to 222, 347 to 364). transfer returns no value. CDTToken.sol has the same two functions (lines 265 to 328). I repeated the test with eth_simulateV1 and no stub. A revoke by a third account reverts. A revoke by the granter succeeds, after which balanceOf(PoolManager) is 0, the granter holds 165,963 and can transfer them on. CDT at block 26,477,487 with half of 310020428424547839288: the balance is back at the full figure after the grant, the full transfer fails, and after the revoke the PoolManager and the account hold 155010214212273919644 each. tokenGrantsCount(PoolManager) is 0 on both. The same grant call reverts on DNT and ESCB. coins.llama.fi returned no price for either token. I did not read the ESCB source line that the finding cites.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller and transfers first (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The transfer of these two tokens returns no data, which src/types/Currency.sol:68 accepts. sync stores the lowered balance (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). The grant raises balanceOf(PoolManager) by X through an ordinary token transfer, and _settle credits X (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364), so the caller's delta is zero and unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). The revoke is a call to the token alone. No PoolManager function runs, so pool state, claims and protocolFeesAccrued keep their figures while the token balance is lower by X. I found no guard that sees the revocation right. The order matters: the take must come before the sync, which nothing in the code prevents.
verification.corrections: No error found in the mechanism. The amounts at risk today are 16.5963 old ADX and 310.02 CDT with no price at coins.llama.fi, so the loss available now is negligible. The cause is a token design and has no link to a network difference. Severity high is kept on the ground that an ordinary account can remove accounted funds of pools that exist; the rating describes the class and not the value at stake today.

findings.title: The deployed PositionManager refuses to mint claims, so a position with one currency that cannot leave the PoolManager closes only by forfeiting that side or by placing it in a new position, and the published SDK builds neither call
findings.difference: Several of the 21 networks hold pooled tokens that refuse a transfer from the PoolManager address under a rule that Ethereum pools rarely meet. ViciCoin on Polygon counts every PoolManager transfer against a daily net outflow limit that any account can use up (F-072). G$ on Celo blocks the PoolManager as sender (F-056). Ten wrapped stock tokens on Monad can be paused by a two signature Safe (F-061). TIP-20 tokens on Tempo carry transfer policies set by their issuers. The PoolManager core can still pay such a currency out as an ERC-6909 claim, but the PositionManager that holds the positions of ordinary users does not expose that route on any of the 21 networks.
findings.mechanism: 1. A position made through the PositionManager belongs to the PositionManager inside the PoolManager, so its owner can act only through PositionManager.modifyLiquidities and the action list of _handleAction. 2. A removal creates a positive delta in both currencies for the PositionManager. Every delta must be zero when unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). 3. TAKE, TAKE_PAIR and CLOSE_CURRENCY end in PoolManager.take, which calls transfer on the token (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). When the token refuses, the whole call reverts and the other currency stays in the pool as well. 4. Core offers mint(to, id, amount) to turn a positive delta into a claim without touching the token (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329). The PositionManager does not handle action 0x17 (MINT_6909) or 0x18 (BURN_6909). A read-only modifyLiquidities call with action 0x17 reverts with UnsupportedAction(0x17), data 0x5cda29d7 followed by 0x17, on all 21 networks. SWEEP does not help because the tokens never reach the PositionManager. 5. Two sequences succeed in simulation from the position owner. Sequence A is DECREASE_LIQUIDITY or BURN_POSITION, TAKE of the other currency, then CLEAR_OR_TAKE of the blocked currency with amountMax set to the maximum uint256. That calls PoolManager.clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319), which erases the delta. The tokens stay in the PoolManager balance with no delta and no claim behind them, so the provider loses that side for good. Sequence B is DECREASE_LIQUIDITY, TAKE of the other currency, MINT_POSITION_FROM_DELTAS (action 0x05) into a range on the side of the current price that holds only the blocked currency, then CLEAR_OR_TAKE for the rounding remainder. The provider leaves with the other currency and a new position that holds the blocked currency. No sequence leaves the provider with an ERC-6909 claim. 6. The v4 SDK that Uniswap publishes for building these calls ends every removal and every fee collection with TAKE_PAIR, and its Actions enum has the lines for MINT_POSITION_FROM_DELTAS and CLEAR_OR_TAKE commented out, so a front end built on it cannot produce sequence A or B. Simulations: Celo position 178 (G$ and cUSD) at block 83,530,712 and Polygon position 60652 (WETH and VCNT) at block 97,817,338 with the tokens as they are today, Monad position 651334 at block 124,698,657 and Arc position 333954 at block 32,722,324 with one currency replaced by reverting code through an eth_call state override. In all four the six sequences that pay or close the blocked side revert, MINT_6909 reverts with UnsupportedAction, and sequences A and B succeed.
findings.impact: For a user who relies on a front end, a block on one token of a pool also locks the other currency of every position in that pool, although core could release it. On Polygon an ordinary account can cause this at will: F-072 shows that one account can keep the shared ViciCoin allowance of 6 VCNT per day at zero, and 8 of the 15 ViciCoin pools have an open position held through the PositionManager. On Celo 5 of 8 G$ pools have such a position and the standard removal reverts today. On Monad a pause of the wrapped stock tokens would put the USDC side of about 7.9 million dollars of pools (figure from F-061) in the same state. A provider who learns of sequence A loses the blocked side. A provider who uses sequence B keeps it as a range position that converts to the other currency if the price crosses the range. No funds move to the attacker.
findings.preconditions: A pooled token refuses transfers from the PoolManager. On Polygon any account can bring this about for VCNT by using up the daily allowance. On the other networks it needs the token issuer or its transfer policy. The provider holds the position through the PositionManager and uses a front end that builds removals with TAKE_PAIR. Not confirmed: which calls the hosted Uniswap web application sends for a removal. I read the published SDK, and the application may build its transactions through a server interface whose output I did not capture.
findings.mitigations: Add MINT_6909 and BURN_6909 handling with the caller as recipient and payer to the PositionManager that ships with this deployment, or publish a documented exit that uses MINT_POSITION_FROM_DELTAS. Front ends can fall back to sequence B when a simulation of TAKE_PAIR fails, and should warn before sequence A. Providers in pools with a token that has issuer controls or a transfer quota can hold positions through their own contract that calls PoolManager.mint for a side that cannot be paid.

sources.supports: Verified source of the Ethereum PositionManager (match). src/PositionManager.sol:197-286 lists the handled actions: 0x00 to 0x05, SETTLE_PAIR, TAKE_PAIR, SETTLE, TAKE, CLOSE_CURRENCY, CLEAR_OR_TAKE, SWEEP, WRAP, UNWRAP. Lines 474-484 show _clearOrTake calling poolManager.clear when the credit is at most amountMax. The Actions library defines MINT_6909 as 0x17 and BURN_6909 as 0x18 and the handler has no branch for them.
removeCallParameters (lines 334-391) encodes BURN_POSITION or DECREASE_LIQUIDITY and then addTakePair. collectCallParameters (lines 413-423) encodes a decrease by zero and addTakePair.
The Actions enum (lines 30-66) has MINT_POSITION_FROM_DELTAS = 0x05 and CLEAR_OR_TAKE = 0x13 as comments only and has no entry for 0x17 or 0x18.

verification.factCheck: PositionManager source. I fetched the Sourcify record of 0xbD216513d74C8cf14cf4747E6AaA6420FF64ee9e on Ethereum (creation and runtime match, solc 0.8.26). In src/PositionManager.sol, _handleAction (lines 197 to 286) has branches for INCREASE_LIQUIDITY, INCREASE_LIQUIDITY_FROM_DELTAS, DECREASE_LIQUIDITY, MINT_POSITION, MINT_POSITION_FROM_DELTAS, BURN_POSITION, SETTLE_PAIR, TAKE_PAIR, SETTLE, TAKE, CLOSE_CURRENCY, CLEAR_OR_TAKE, SWEEP, WRAP and UNWRAP and ends with revert UnsupportedAction(action). _clearOrTake (lines 474 to 484) calls poolManager.clear when the credit is at most amountMax. src/libraries/Actions.sol defines MINT_6909 as 0x17 and BURN_6909 as 0x18 under the comment that they are not supported in the position manager or router. Chain. On 2026-11-23 I sent eth_call of modifyLiquidities with the single action 0x17 from an unrelated account to the PositionManager of each of the 21 networks, using the endpoints in networks.json. All 21 revert with 0x5cda29d7 followed by 0x17. I computed 0x5cda29d7 as the selector of UnsupportedAction(uint256). Action 0x18 gives the same error with 0x18 on 20 networks. The Avalanche endpoint rate limited that one call. eth_getCode returns 23,877 bytes on 19 networks and 19,965 bytes on Elysium and HyperEVM. Simulations from the position owner, built with my own encoder. Celo, https://forno.celo.org, blocks 83,532,678 and 83,533,160, position 178 (G$ and cUSD, owner 0xf18f712b760732cde4d1835673b98b2c7978b3a8): decrease with TAKE_PAIR, with TAKE of each side and with CLOSE_CURRENCY all revert with 0x90bfb865 carrying the G$ address and selector a9059cbb. MINT_6909 reverts with UnsupportedAction(0x17). Leaving the G$ delta open reverts with 0x5212cba1. Decrease or burn, TAKE of cUSD and CLEAR_OR_TAKE of G$ with the maximum amount return without error. Decrease, TAKE of cUSD, MINT_POSITION_FROM_DELTAS into ticks -106690 to 887270 and CLEAR_OR_TAKE return without error, and a multicall that reads the result shows new token 605 with liquidity 100,918,514,712,628,699,620 owned by the same account and the old token at zero. The same calls from an unrelated account revert with NotApproved. Polygon, https://polygon.drpc.org, blocks 97,818,649 to 97,818,969, position 60652 (WETH and VCNT): the full removal shows the same pattern, and sequence B leaves new token 159444 with liquidity 1,034,117,479,046,245,712. transferLimitAmountRemaining(PoolManager) was 6.1256 VCNT at that time, so nobody had used up the allowance. Removals of 50, 10 and 2 percent of position 60652 with TAKE_PAIR succeed today, and position 14963 exits in full. The full removal of 60652 fails today because its VCNT side is larger than the allowance. I then found the storage slot of the daily total of the PoolManager in the plugin 0xf58fed40fba1ab7aa7ffc160b863bedd998386a7 with a prestate trace of a 1 VCNT transfer (slot 0x177da5a421dc5b34775004a7c8f5481d6125d6eba1e5f5ef95b99364e3e7eb64) and set it to minus 6 VCNT by state override. With that override transferLimitAmountRemaining returns 0, a transfer of one base unit from the PoolManager reverts with 0x1b97a875, a 2 percent removal of 60652 and the full removal of 14963 with TAKE_PAIR revert, and sequences A and B still succeed. That state is the one F-072 shows an ordinary account can produce with about 6.13 VCNT of net outflow per day. Monad, https://rpc.monad.xyz, block 124,707,777, position 651334 with the code of 0xe7cd86e13ac4309349f30b3435a9d337750fc82d replaced by 0x5f5ffd: same pattern. SDK. I fetched PositionManager.ts and utils/v4Planner.ts from the main branch of Uniswap/sdks. removeCallParameters (lines 334 to 399) adds a burn or a decrease and then addTakePair. collectCallParameters (lines 407 to 430) adds a decrease by zero and addTakePair. The Actions enum (lines 30 to 66) has INCREASE_LIQUIDITY_FROM_DELTAS, MINT_POSITION_FROM_DELTAS, CLEAR_OR_TAKE and WRAP as comments and no entry for 0x17 or 0x18. Not rechecked: the counts of ViciCoin and G$ pools with PositionManager positions (8 of 15 and 5 of 8), the 7.9 million dollar figure taken from F-061, the Arc simulation, and which calldata the hosted Uniswap web application sends for a removal.
verification.codeCheck: I traced the path in this repository. modifyLiquidity records the position under msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161) and credits the removal to msg.sender (line 183), so a position made through a periphery contract can be closed only by that contract. unlock reverts with CurrencyNotSettled when any delta is left (src/PoolManager.sol:112), which matches the 0x5212cba1 revert seen when the blocked side is left open. take debits the caller and then calls currency.transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The ERC-20 branch makes the call at src/types/Currency.sol:64-73 and reverts with the wrapped error when the token call fails or returns anything other than nothing or a 32 byte true (lines 82-86). The wrapped error carries the token address and selector a9059cbb, which is the revert data seen on Celo, Polygon and Monad. One failed take reverts the whole modifyLiquidities call, so the other currency stays in the pool too. clear requires the amount to equal the caller's positive delta and then erases it with no token call and no claim (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319). mint debits the caller's delta and calls _mint with no token call (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329, src/ERC6909.sol:79-83), so core can pay a blocked currency as a claim. I looked for a guard that changes this and found none: the msg.value check in _settle (line 356), the synced currency check in collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52) and the int128 casts (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59) play no part in a removal. Core behaves as written. The missing route is in the PositionManager, which is outside src/.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged is right for Polygon (chain 137) alone, where F-072 lets any account use up the ViciCoin allowance. On the other 20 networks in chainIds a token must first refuse transfers from the PoolManager, and that needs the token issuer (G$ on Celo, the wrapped stock tokens on Monad, TIP-20 policies on Tempo). The chainIds list should be read as where the PositionManager lacks the action, and the unprivileged trigger exists on one network. The Polygon evidence needs one change. Position 60652 fails to close in full today because its VCNT side exceeds the 6 VCNT daily allowance, with 6.1256 VCNT of allowance still open. Removals of 50, 10 and 2 percent succeed with TAKE_PAIR, which the SDK can build through liquidityPercentage. The block for every size appears only after the allowance is used up, which I reproduced with a state override. The freeze applies to providers who rely on interface-built calldata. An owner who sends modifyLiquidities by hand can leave with the other currency through sequence B at any time, or by INCREASE_LIQUIDITY_FROM_DELTAS into another position of the same pool. No funds reach the attacker. The amounts under the unprivileged trigger are small: the PoolManager on Polygon held 11.35 VCNT, about 206 USD. The finding is about periphery code and a third party token rule. It does not follow from a difference between a network and Ethereum, and the same PositionManager behaviour exists on Ethereum. It overlaps F-072, F-056 and F-061 and adds to them the fact that the paired currency is locked for interface users. SDK line numbers: removeCallParameters ends at line 399 and collectCallParameters spans lines 407 to 430 in the file I fetched. Unconfirmed link: what the hosted Uniswap interface sends for a removal.
