findings.title: The Klik fee hooks keep one pending fee amount per token and burn it in the currency of whichever pool of that token swaps next, and they accept a pool of the token against any currency from any account
findings.difference: None. The behaviour does not depend on the network. It comes from one family of third party fee hooks (VERSION strings klik-multichain-1 and klik-anypair-1) that launch pads deployed on nine of the 21 networks. The PoolManager code behaves as written.
findings.mechanism: 1. The hook charges a fee on swaps of a launched token and holds it as ERC-6909 claims at the PoolManager. It records the amount in pendingClaims(token), one number per token. In Tempo transaction 0x36bf56c18219aeb53b5f8a04f6f2fa4c062ccf81c67c1966c202635fc7073fbc the hook mints 0x2d5067 claims of pathUSD to itself inside beforeSwap. 2. At the next swap the hook pays the pending amount out. In Tempo transaction 0xa23224d5f477539161486a82ab2430469d6c08ec74e56ae67800d949595f913d beforeSwap calls PoolManager.burn(hook, pathUSD, 0x2d5067), then take(pathUSD, hook, 0x2d5067), then transfers 60 percent to the platform treasury and calls transfer for the rest to the factory. The trace marks that last inner call as out of gas and the swap continues. 3. The currency of that burn is read from the PoolKey of the swap. I called beforeSwap from the PoolManager address with a PoolKey that pairs a launched token with the codeless address 0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111112 and traced it with debug_traceCall. On six deployments the hook calls PoolManager.burn(hook, 0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111112, amount), and the amount equals pendingClaims(token), which was accrued in another currency: 23876031656686502 and 2079850173284467176091326 on the two Ethereum hooks, 143394835225437444 on Unichain, 333714925697516922 on Robinhood Chain, 54489710721685566614 on Monad and 230765 on Tempo. The afterSwap fee is minted in the same way: on Tempo the trace shows mint(hook, 0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111112, 10000000000000000). 4. The hook does not restrict who creates pools. PoolManager.initialize accepts any PoolKey that names the hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142) and calls beforeInitialize (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-182). An eth_call of initialize from an ordinary account with a launched token and the foreign currency succeeds on all eleven hook addresses listed under sources. The hooks have no liquidity flags, so anyone can add liquidity to such a pool. 5. First consequence, a swap freeze that exists today. When a token has pools against two currencies, fees accrued in the first are looked for in the second. If the hook holds fewer claims of the second currency than the pending amount, burn reverts on the checked subtraction (src/ERC6909.sol:85-87, src/PoolManager.sol:332-336) and beforeSwap reverts, so every swap of that pool reverts. The deployed Quoter on Ethereum returns the PoolManager error wrapped around Panic(0x11) from beforeSwap for seven pools: 0x227260acd3c0fa351a1360f11e8408f5fca8f099ce3b34e0dd8d886f61fdc228, 0x02ae580f824b1e9407c9063e08e7d2e29262a73917db4da9ac9acc23155403e8, 0x2256de11213c69f6a404cd2b973d79782e5a888114ef86b932768c99deb288e6, 0x9415295f90547e1b1ec7bed8e5396158003ca5889ad0fc9687a1014171d1fb29 and 0x1dc6439eb8e3e653d053533fd0a14c5a67b9aae60369885807cc0a8f5e2971a8 on hook 0x1d06faa7ff674ccfd8a5736c0c0973cb0a8fa0cc, and 0x1d3f06543054f9035578cf564802fd565fd424c1812dba91d841f61d0098246b and 0x8699a47da36461ce75bff3cdf0e6370bfb054203d1ebc7aae1a858f784b264fe on hook 0x6d01769ab90674d0d56b155f57003284e1b460cc. For the last one the token 0xe07befffcc37771dd3a5250fdd3b9a0798e415cc has 39205855192377918360 pending, the hook holds 39205855192377928360 claims of currency 0x29ef66e020e391aad7a8b1b5897af599251893b5 from the token's other pool, and only 2551319276869624230 claims of WLFI, the currency of the pool that fails. The same Quoter call succeeds for 63 other pools of the two hooks, and five pools without liquidity fail with the Quoter's own NotEnoughLiquidity or price limit errors. 6. Second consequence, which I derived from the traces and did not run. An account that creates a pool of token T against a currency it issues can grow pendingClaims(T) by any amount at no cost, because the fee is a share of its own swap in its own currency. A later swap in a pool of T against a valuable currency then burns that amount from claims the hook holds for the pending fees of other tokens and pays it to the platform treasury and to the fee receiver of T through the factory. The other tokens keep their pendingClaims entries, the hook no longer holds the claims, and their pools fail as in step 5. In the opposite direction, a swap in a pool of T against a worthless currency after the hook was given that many worthless claims (PoolManager.mint accepts any recipient, src/PoolManager.sol:322-329) clears pendingClaims(T) and pays T's receivers in the worthless currency. 7. The books already disagree on two hooks. On Ethereum hook 0x1d06faa7ff674ccfd8a5736c0c0973cb0a8fa0cc the pending amounts of tokens whose pool uses SPCXon (0xc9eef266834730340a55b6cc24621b31baf55581) sum to 79607629840677756 and the hook holds 7798353546842757 claims of it. On Unichain the pending amounts in UNI sum to 272597197961328745 against 262597197961328745 claims. I did not trace which transactions caused the difference.
findings.impact: Fees that the hooks hold as ERC-6909 claims for token creators and platforms, and the ability to swap in the affected pools. The claims are small today: about 16 USD and 17 USD at DexScreener prices on the two Ethereum hooks (44 and 23 tokens with pending fees), 0.26 UNI on Unichain, claims in 14 tokenised stock currencies on Robinhood Chain worth about 12 USD for the six that have a price, 54.49 MON on Monad and 0.230765 pathUSD on Tempo, where the factory holds a further 2.946234 pathUSD of creator fees. Seven Ethereum pools cannot be swapped today. Three of the five on the first hook have liquidity (153845604096252485200300 units each), the other two have none, and the liquidity of the two on the second hook was not read. Liquidity providers are not locked in, because the hooks have no liquidity callbacks and removal does not call them. Holders of the launched tokens lose the route through the frozen pool. The hooks serve 83 and 59 pools on Ethereum, 46 on Base, 30 on Unichain, 14 on Ink, 7 on Arbitrum One, 34 on Robinhood Chain, 11 on Avalanche, 15 on Monad and 2 on Tempo.
findings.preconditions: None for the freeze: it follows from a second pool of a token against another currency, which any account can create with initialize, and it has already happened on Ethereum. To gain from the payout the account must be the fee receiver of a token launched through the same factory. On Tempo launchEnabled() is true, but I did not confirm that launch has no caller restriction, and the path from creditCreatorFee to collectFees in the factory was read from selectors only. The burn was traced on Ethereum, Unichain, Robinhood Chain, Monad and Tempo. On Base, Ink, Arbitrum One and Avalanche no token of the sampled pools had pending fees, so only the open initialize was confirmed there. The Base hook 0x5b0a864213d49f23ed2a6635cc42b3b4fe7720cc has the code length of the traced Ethereum hook (8082 bytes, 232 bytes differ), and the Ink, Arbitrum One and Avalanche hooks have the code length of the traced Unichain and Monad hooks (9123 bytes). The newer Ethereum hook 0xcba49142a75da64a679f32a159f4316f11a7e0cc (klik-anypair-direct-dividends-2, 254 pools) reverts a foreign initialize with "only factory initializes" and returned a zero delta for the foreign PoolKey.
findings.mitigations: The PoolManager deployer cannot change this, and the PoolManager code is not at fault. The hook author can record pending fees per pool id or per token and currency, burn only in the recorded currency, and reject initialize from any caller other than the factory, as the newer hook does. A frozen pool swaps again once someone mints the missing claims to the hook. Interfaces should not route through a second pool of a Klik token. Liquidity providers can withdraw at any time.

verification.codeCheck: initialize has no caller check and calls beforeInitialize with the caller and the caller's PoolKey (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-182), so the hook alone decides whether a second pool of a token exists. Flags 0x20cc are beforeInitialize, beforeSwap, afterSwap and the two swap return delta flags (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:29-45). No liquidity flag is set, so modifyLiquidity never calls the hook (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:195-206 and 209-245) and anyone can add or remove liquidity in any of these pools. swap calls the hook before the pool is touched (src/PoolManager.sol:202, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:248-282) and a hook revert is bubbled up (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:137), so a failing burn in beforeSwap blocks every swap of that pool. burn credits the caller and then subtracts the claim balance with checked arithmetic (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22, src/ERC6909.sol:85-87). A burn above the balance reverts with Panic(0x11), which is the error the Quoter returns. burn followed by take of the same amount nets the hook's delta to zero (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), so the count check at the end of unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:112) does not stop the payout. mint accepts any recipient and debits the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), so any account can give the hook claims of a currency it issues, which lets the burn in a foreign pool succeed. No guard in src/ was missed: the PoolManager has no notion of which pool a claim balance of a hook was earned in, and none of the checks named in the task (msg.value in _settle, synced currency in collectProtocolFees, int128 casts, hook return data length) lies on this path. The PoolManager behaves as written. The fault is in the hook, which was read through traces and bytecode comparison because no verified source was fetched.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged is right: every step (public factory launch, initialize, mint of claims to the hook, swap) was done by an ordinary account in the transactions cited, and the affected pools use a hook and tokens the attacker did not write. Severity medium is right on the SCHEMA scale: the loss is confined to the fee claims and the swaps of one hook family, the claims are worth tens of USD, and liquidity removal does not call the hook. Corrections. (1) Step 6 is no longer a derivation. It ran on Ethereum in transaction 0xd903d0ad at block 26330140 and moved 85325615158209763 SPCXon claims (about 11 USD) that backed the pending fees of other tokens. Evidence for that step is primary. (2) Step 7 can name the cause: that transaction explains the whole Ethereum shortfall, and transaction 0x2b6aab13 explains the 0.01 UNI on Unichain. (3) The three frozen Ethereum pools that hold liquidity (0x227260ac, 0x02ae580f, 0x9415295f on the first hook) are frozen as a result of that transaction, because they share the SPCXon claim balance it drained. (4) The two frozen pools on the second Ethereum hook have zero liquidity (StateView getLiquidity returns 0 for 0x1d3f0654 and 0x8699a47d). They were initialized inside contract creation transactions sent by 0x02dcd01d534477b5e76628a7284e7fa71c7a7ed7 and 0x3a15cf422307e922645d671cb247e76e8b1ec50d, so no user funds sit in them. (5) The preconditions understate the freeze. An account does not need liquidity or a token of its own launch to freeze the pool of another creator's token T: it initializes a pool of T against a currency it issues, mints that currency's claims to the hook for the current pendingClaims(T), and swaps there with a large specified amount. pendingClaims(T) then exceeds the hook's claims in the real quote currency and the real pool reverts with Panic(0x11) until someone mints the missing claims to the hook or resets the entry through another pool. I did not simulate this sequence end to end. Each step is shown separately by the transactions above. (6) The doubt about launch on Tempo can be narrowed: on Ethereum the launch function is called by many unrelated senders. The Tempo factory was not tested. (7) The Base hook 0x64746dca (b20-stock-1) should stay marked as open initialize only.

findings.title: Any holder of 1,000,000 DEAD can take the PoolManager's whole DEAD balance on Base after 90 days without a payout, and one account did so on 17 November 2026
findings.difference: The cause is a token rule, and Base is where the token and its pools are. DeadToken at 0xf0197f10ea542a67914ecc0ec5304dc9df1faf6f lets any caller who holds 1,000,000 DEAD call claimIdleTokens(target) and move the whole balance of an address that has sent no DEAD for 90 days: half to the caller, 40 percent burned and 10 percent to three platform addresses. The token keeps a whitelist of pool addresses that are exempt, and the Uniswap v4 PoolManager is not on it. Earlier cycles recorded balances that rise through a public trigger (F-041, F-066, F-067). This is a public trigger that lowers a balance that pools have recorded.
findings.mechanism: 1. Core keeps no per currency total. A pool's reserves are numbers in pool state, and the only place the token balance is read is sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-365). When the balance falls without a take, every later take of that currency draws on less than pools record, and the transfer in take reverts once the balance is too low (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). 2. DeadToken updates lastTransferTime only for the sender of a transfer, and for a receiver whose balance was zero (verified source Dead.sol lines 563 to 578). The PoolManager is a sender only when a take pays DEAD out. A quiet period of 90 days without a DEAD payout makes the whole pooled balance claimable (lines 388 to 420: balance check of the caller at 390, whitelist check at 394, idle check at 398, 50 percent to the caller at 405 and 413, 40 percent burned at 406 and 414). 3. Observed: transaction 0xc32384b25be1e5d29cd5e978fc5f531359ddd8dcae67a1ff89204e98c27d0d2b in Base block 58,594,779 (17 November 2026, 09:55:31 UTC) is a contract creation by 0x5f21bfbe94a4774fc6fb88ac84d47538422f7976. The new contract 0x25bead0f62a7c234e89691e4519ca5e74079cf3f receives 1,000,000 DEAD from the pair 0x098a1a39a006ea83c86fd8da991c0e7134eaf68c, emits three TokensClaimed logs (targets 0x50ddc37e9060fda26cc5fe2f521fe9d01bc29810 for 18,583.25 DEAD, the PoolManager for 14,899.78 DEAD and 0xaa2e244d93fd4d0d8a6c6d525de06468d77be7b3 for 13,444.75 DEAD) and returns 1,003,009.03 DEAD to the pair. The PoolManager emitted no log in that transaction. Its DEAD balance was 14,899.783090229956530365 at block 58,594,778 and 0 at block 58,594,779. lastTransferTime(PoolManager) one block earlier was 1784165391, which is 10,743,940 seconds (124 days) before the block. 4. The PoolManager took no part in the call. No sync, settle, take or unlock is needed, so no check in core can see it. 5. The balance does not come back. Three later swaps paid 88.41, 699.16 and 872.46 DEAD into the PoolManager, which holds 1,660.03 DEAD today. Those tokens are recorded by pools as well, so the gap of 14,899.78 DEAD stays.
findings.impact: 14,899.78 DEAD left the PoolManager: 7,449.89 to the claimer, 5,959.91 burned and 1,489.98 to the three platform addresses. I found no price source for DEAD and did not value it. The liquidity of the pools on the routes of the DEAD swaps before and after the claim is unchanged across the claim block (for example pool id 0x18fca1729428c26f554c4f431a551e05404b0d6b8ae9ae518966e5a9e9371121 holds liquidity 319,322,205,084,229 at block 58,594,778 and today), so pools still record the DEAD that was taken. Liquidity providers and buyers in the DEAD pools lose: a swap or a removal that must pay out more DEAD than the PoolManager holds reverts. The loss is limited to currency DEAD, because deltas, takes and settles are kept per currency (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378). Pools in other tokens are not touched. The token saw 136 TokensClaimed logs since block 56,000,000, so claiming idle holders is routine for this token.
findings.preconditions: A DEAD balance of 1,000,000 for the length of one call, which the observed account borrowed from a pair inside its creation transaction. No DEAD payout from the PoolManager for 90 days. The PoolManager stays off the token's pool whitelist (whiteListedPool(PoolManager) returns 0 and getPoolWhitelistStatus(PoolManager) returns false, false and 0). After the claim the timer restarted when the PoolManager received DEAD into a zero balance at timestamp 1795149430 (20 November 2026), and getTimeUntilClaimable(PoolManager) returned 7,502,995 seconds at my read, so the balance becomes claimable again on about 18 February 2027 unless a take pays DEAD out before then. I did not read the PoolKey of the DEAD pools (the Base log endpoint serves 1,000 blocks per request), so the list of pools comes from the Swap logs of the transactions that moved DEAD, and I did not send any transaction.
findings.mitigations: The token admin can put the PoolManager on the pool whitelist with setWhiteListPool, which takes effect after a 60 minute timelock (Dead.sol lines 315 to 324 and 355 to 382). Any account can restart the timer by causing a DEAD payout from the PoolManager, for example a swap that buys a small amount of DEAD. Liquidity providers should not pool a token that lets third parties move idle balances. Interfaces can find such tokens with the search of this unit: an ERC-20 Transfer log with the PoolManager as sender in a transaction where the PoolManager emitted no log. Core cannot prevent it, because the token moves the balance without calling the PoolManager.

verification.factCheck: All chain facts were re-run on 23 November 2026 against https://mainnet.base.org/ and https://base.gateway.tenderly.co. Token source: the Sourcify record for 0xf0197f10ea542a67914ecc0ec5304dc9df1faf6f is an exact match for DeadToken (solc 0.8.30). Dead.sol line 58 sets IDLE_PERIOD to 7,776,000 seconds and line 61 sets MIN_CLAIMER_BALANCE to 1,000,000 tokens of 18 decimals. claimIdleTokens (lines 388 to 420) checks the caller's balance, the pool whitelist and the idle period, then moves 50 percent of the target's balance to the caller, burns 40 percent and sends 10 percent to three platform addresses. _update (lines 563 to 578) sets lastTransferTime for the sender, and for a receiver only when its balance was zero. Transaction: the receipt of 0xc32384b25be1e5d29cd5e978fc5f531359ddd8dcae67a1ff89204e98c27d0d2b (block 58,594,779, timestamp 1794909331, status 1, 78 logs) shows 1,000,000 DEAD sent by pair 0x098a1a39a006ea83c86fd8da991c0e7134eaf68c to 0x25bead0f62a7c234e89691e4519ca5e74079cf3f, five Transfer logs with the PoolManager as sender (7,449.89 to the claimer, 5,959.91 to the zero address, 744.99, 446.99 and 298.00 to the platform addresses), a TokensClaimed log with target PoolManager and amount 14,899.783090229956530365, and no log of the PoolManager. balanceOf(PoolManager) is 14,899.783090229956 at block 58,594,778 and 0 at block 58,594,779 on both endpoints, and 1,660.03 at the latest block. lastTransferTime(PoolManager) was 1784165391 one block before the claim and is 1795149430 now. whiteListedPool(PoolManager) and pendingPoolWhitelist(PoolManager) are 0 at both blocks. Read-only test of the call itself at block 58,594,778: claimIdleTokens(PoolManager) from an address without DEAD reverts with InsufficientBalanceToClaim (0xb347e4bf), and from the pair, which holds more than 1,000,000 DEAD, it succeeds. At the latest block the same call reverts with TokensNotIdleLongEnough (0x22ba57ac) and getTimeUntilClaimable(PoolManager) returns 7,493,182 seconds. The link the finding left open is now closed. The pools that hold DEAD are three pools of USDC and DEAD without a hook, with static fees of 25, 60 and 70 percent: 0x18fca1729428c26f554c4f431a551e05404b0d6b8ae9ae518966e5a9e9371121, 0x625f17175b0939fcc2a97f35335877998f53d7c43beddd4c9c0ae733237e7bdb and 0xa20d780775626e7ae792654039daf1d3dc44da5099b4d582da277b1392994cfa. I read their parameters from PositionManager.poolKeys and their state from StateView. A read-only Quoter call that sells 1,000,000 USDC into each pool returns the DEAD the pool would pay out: 11,091.73, 83.85 and 195.27 DEAD at block 58,594,778, the same three figures at block 58,594,779 when the PoolManager held 0 DEAD, and 12,223.30, 97.47 and 229.93 DEAD at the latest block. The three pools therefore record at least 12,550.71 DEAD payable to swappers today while the PoolManager holds 1,660.03 DEAD. Value: the 25 percent pool stood at tick 358,751 before the claim, which is about 3,800 DEAD per USDC, so the 14,899.78 DEAD were worth about 4 USD.
verification.codeCheck: The path needs no call into the PoolManager, so no guard in src/ can act on it. The token balance is read in two places only: sync (src/PoolManager.sol:285) and _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:359), both through balanceOfSelf (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). No per currency total exists in storage; pool amounts are numbers in pool state and protocol fees are a counter (src/ProtocolFees.sol:21, 66-70). take debits the caller and then calls transfer on the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), and Currency.transfer reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the token call fails or returns false (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74, 82-86). DeadToken is an OpenZeppelin ERC-20 and reverts on a short balance, so a take of more DEAD than the PoolManager holds reverts, and with it the swap or liquidity removal that needs it. collectProtocolFees pays with the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). Deltas are stored per target and currency (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16, src/PoolManager.sol:368-378), so the shortfall cannot be drawn from another currency. A caller with a positive DEAD delta can still close it with mint or clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329). The checks named in the task do not apply: the msg.value check, the synced currency check in collectProtocolFees and the delta count check at the end of unlock all run inside PoolManager calls, and this balance change happens in a call from a third contract to the token.
verification.corrections: Actor unprivileged is right: the claimer needs 1,000,000 DEAD for one call, borrowed it from a pair inside one transaction, and is neither the token owner 0x485f77d6362f5922fcb63a40aaa4fd79d26ec905 nor the admin 0x6f8b4f05434df0f1af51f3e27a34b36dc8fbbac3. Four points need fixing. First, the contract created by the transaction is 0x120df14514851c4fbec63d374703b0b7ef7fd71e according to the receipt; the claimer 0x25bead0f62a7c234e89691e4519ca5e74079cf3f is a second contract deployed inside the same transaction. Second, the nine pool ids in the raw file and the pool named in the impact text are the pools on the swap routes, and five of them do not hold DEAD according to PositionManager.poolKeys (0x9f6013f1 pairs USDC with 0xc1a36ca099c37ded68f0d6be608fb00767238aa4, 0x90333bb0 and 0xec746b81 pair WETH with USDC, 0xbd976d4c and 0x24662c76 pair USDC with two other tokens); a sixth, 0xcfd23695, has no PositionManager record and I could not read its currencies. The DEAD pools are the three listed in the fact check, and 0x18fca172 is one of them, so the conclusion holds. Third, the finding gives no value. At the pool price the amount taken is about 4 USD, and the shortfall against what the three pools would pay out is about 10,900 DEAD today, under 3 USD. Fourth, the 136 TokensClaimed logs come from two transactions by two claimers (3 logs in block 58,594,779 and 133 logs in block 58,617,833), so the word routine overstates it. The title says the claimer takes the whole balance; the claimer receives half and the whole balance leaves the PoolManager. The cause is a rule of one token and has nothing to do with how Base differs from Ethereum, as the finding says. Medium stands because the loss is confined to the pools of one token and the path is closed until about 18 February 2027 unless no DEAD payout happens before then.

findings.title: Any account can call claimFor on Alpaca ibBUSD for the PoolManager on BNB Smart Chain, which burns the whole pooled ibBUSD balance and stakes the replacement where the PoolManager cannot reach it
findings.difference: ibBUSD 0x7c9e73d4c71dae564d41f78d56439bb4ba87592f is the share token of the Alpaca Finance BUSD vault on BNB Smart Chain (proxy, implementation 0xf19c0106fad0892b6d9f5db0ae1c9a2cfd14635b). Alpaca converted the BUSD of that vault to USDT under its proposal AIP-29 and told holders in February 2024 to claim the converted assets. Its function with selector 0xddeae033, claimFor(address), converts the ibBUSD of any holder, and the caller does not have to be that holder. The token is not attacker made and the PoolManager holds it for 16 hookless pools.
findings.mechanism: 1. The PoolManager keeps no total per currency. It reads the token balance only in sync and settle and pays with transfer in take (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 349-365, src/types/Currency.sol:60-80). A balance that a third party removes stays recorded in pool state. 2. An eth_call of claimFor(PoolManager) from the unrelated address 0x00000000000000000000000000000000000a11ce returns success on three endpoints at blocks 135,293,814 to 135,293,817. The same call for an address without shares reverts with the text no shares. 3. The call trace shows what the function does for the PoolManager: ibBUSD logs Transfer(PoolManager, zero address, 56658476151267410600), which is the whole balance. It then approves 55.48 units of the token 0x90476bfef61f190b54a439e2e98f8e43fb9b4a45 (symbol ibUSDT) to 0xd20b887654db8dc476007bdca83d22fa51e93407, and that contract deposits them into 0x4579587ae043131999ce3d9c66199726972e3fb7 with the PoolManager as the account and pool number 5 (selector 0x0efe6a8b). 4. After the call the PoolManager holds no ibBUSD and no ibUSDT. The ibUSDT sits in a staking contract under the PoolManager address. The PoolManager can only call transfer and balanceOf on a currency, the hook selectors on a hook and unlockCallback on its caller, so it has no way to withdraw that position. 5. I did not read the source of the staking contract and did not test whether a third party can withdraw the position for the PoolManager.
findings.impact: 56.658476151267410600 ibBUSD, about 56 USD at the coins.llama.fi price, held for 16 pools that were created between blocks 48,048,145 and 133,218,725. Nine of them pair ibBUSD with USDT, and their LP fees lie between 88 and 99.9996 percent. Once any account sends the call, every take of ibBUSD reverts in the transfer and the liquidity providers of those pools cannot withdraw that side. The amount is small. The class is the same as the DEAD case on Base (F-085): an ordinary account empties the PoolManager balance of a token that the victims did not get from the attacker.
findings.preconditions: None beyond gas. The call has not been sent yet: the PoolManager balance was 188.70 ibBUSD at block 60,000,000, 18.87 at block 120,000,000 and is 56.66 today.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should withdraw ibBUSD from v4 pools now. Interfaces should stop listing ibBUSD pools. The assigned balance sweep tests one token per selector family, so vault tokens with a conversion or migration function that names the holder as an argument should be listed per token on every network.

verification.factCheck: I ran the calls myself on 23 November 2026. balanceOf(PoolManager) on ibBUSD 0x7c9e73d4c71dae564d41f78d56439bb4ba87592f returned 56658476151267410600 on bsc-dataseed1.bnbchain.org, bsc.api.pocket.network, bsc.rpc.sentio.xyz and bsc-rpc.publicnode.com. An eth_call of selector 0xddeae033 (claimFor(address), selector recomputed) with the PoolManager as argument from 0x00000000000000000000000000000000000a11ce returned success on all four endpoints, and the same call for an address without shares reverted with the text no shares. I then ran one eth_simulateV1 request on bsc-rpc.publicnode.com at block 135,297,578 without any state override: balance reads, claimFor(PoolManager) from the unrelated account, balance reads, and a transfer of one base unit of ibBUSD from the PoolManager. The claim emitted ten logs: Transfer(PoolManager, zero address, 56658476151267410600) on ibBUSD, an approval and transfer of 55476046033883265769 ibUSDT 0x90476bfef61f190b54a439e2e98f8e43fb9b4a45 from ibBUSD to 0xd20b887654db8dc476007bdca83d22fa51e93407, a transfer of the same amount from there to 0x4579587ae043131999ce3d9c66199726972e3fb7, and a deposit log of that contract with caller 0xd20b..., account PoolManager and pool 5. Afterwards the PoolManager held 0 ibBUSD and 0 ibUSDT, and the transfer of one base unit reverted with ERC20: transfer amount exceeds balance. The link the researcher left open is closed as far as sources allow. The proxy 0x4579... points to implementation 0x15474b03710187eb9de4401d99e75680ed240b27, which Sourcify lists as an exact match for the Alpaca MiniFL contract. In that source deposit and withdraw both carry onlyWhitelisted, and withdraw only lets the calling funder take back what it funded and pays the tokens to the caller (MiniFL.sol lines 252 to 356). The funder is 0xd20b..., whose implementation 0x86bc51819b8c2dde261d3b706b5d8cab0a5204f7 is not verified. Its 30 selectors resolve at the openchain signature database to the Alpaca account manager functions. The only exits are unstakeAndWithdraw(address,uint256) and unstakeAndWithdrawETH(uint256), which take no account argument, so the position can be closed only by a call from the PoolManager address, which the PoolManager cannot make. This last step rests on selector names, since no source is published. The Alpaca recap of 8 March 2024 states that the BUSD migration under AIP-29 is complete and that depositors may claim their assets converted into USDT. coins.llama.fi prices ibBUSD at 1.0007 USD, so the balance is worth 56.70 USD. The Initialize list in the work directory holds 16 ibBUSD pools without a hook, with LP fees from 88 to 99.9996 percent, and I recomputed all 16 pool ids from the listed parameters. StateView.getLiquidity is above zero for five of them today. I did not recheck the balances quoted for blocks 60,000,000 and 120,000,000.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller and then calls transfer on the token, and a failed transfer reverts with the wrapped ERC20TransferFailed error (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). The token balance is read only in sync and in _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-365), and _accountDelta works on per caller deltas (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378), so nothing in core notices that the balance is gone. No guard stands in the way: the claim is a call to the token by a third party and never enters the PoolManager. After it every take of ibBUSD reverts for all pools, claims and protocol fees of that currency, because they share one holder address.
verification.corrections: The actor and the effect are right. Two details to add: only five of the 16 pools show liquidity in range today, and the pool fees of 88 to 99.9996 percent suggest bait pools more than ordinary liquidity, so the 56.70 USD at stake may belong to very few parties. The claim that the staked ibUSDT is out of reach is now supported by the verified MiniFL source and by the selector list of the unverified account manager.

findings.title: The sSAC rebase on the PoolManager balance has been paid out to ordinary accounts on BNB Smart Chain in 119 transactions since block 115,986,214, and on Polygon the sLGNS and sATH rebases were booked 193 times in 30 days
findings.difference: The staked tokens of these Olympus forks raise every balance at a rebase that any account can start. Ethereum pools of the main assets hold no token whose balance an ordinary caller can raise at will.
findings.mechanism: 1. settle credits the caller with balanceOf(PoolManager) now minus the balance stored by sync (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-365). 2. I read every log with topic 0x917acfbe39be6509ccf7fecb66a7e42ce2be1083c2d7dd3b9b7491dabddb8da4 that sSAC 0x0ae7cd10f94fd16a6f9a29a372708718144c46f8 emitted from block 104,200,000 (the PoolManager balance is zero before block 104,200,560) to block 135,290,559: 191 rebase transactions, epochs 45 to 367. 3. Each of them was classified with one rule from its receipt and its call trace. 119 are payouts: the trace shows sync(sSAC), the rebase call 0xaf14052c on the staking contract 0x99954eb0b159514d608f64c89a2c5bbe9f42120b, settle returning more than was transferred in, and take or mint of that amount. The other 72 rebase transactions hold no call from the PoolManager to sSAC. 4. The payouts sum to 210.068614 sSAC (9 decimals). 119 were taken out as tokens and 0 were minted as claims. The senders: 0x2d68a551e7c8ecf7312ee083a16e736dce2347d5 through 0x0b675fb382e0c986d724fd6cbb51837b3ae30e8a in 117; 0x00000000004ef5098c6a84d085a2e9d69e332b2f through 0x0000000000be226afde21672a5e4adc45692e69d in 1; 0x000000000062b66705d912df5940ffacbbec6a82 through 0x0000000000be226afde21672a5e4adc45692e69d in 1. 5. The list with transaction hash, block, epoch, amount, sender and called contract is in the work directory. 6. Polygon, 30 day census: 109 sLGNS bookings that sum to 1,349.946362 sLGNS and 84 sATH bookings that sum to 78.935549 sATH, each a claim mint after sync, rebase and settle with no transfer in.
findings.impact: The amounts are the rebase on the tokens that pools hold. Pool accounting never records them, so no pool becomes short. The liquidity providers lose the rebase that their staked tokens earned: about 0.11 percent of the pooled sSAC per epoch on BNB Smart Chain, where the PoolManager holds 2,287 sSAC. The loss repeats every epoch for as long as the tokens sit in the PoolManager.
findings.preconditions: A rebase that is due and that any account can start. The taker needs no funds.
findings.mitigations: Holders of rebasing staked tokens should pool the wrapped, non rebasing form. Interfaces should mark pools whose currency balance grows without transfers.

sources.supports: eth_getLogs for the sSAC rebase topic in windows of 5,000 blocks from block 104,200,000, then eth_getTransactionReceipt and debug_traceTransaction with callTracer for each of the 191 transactions. Old balances were read through https://bsc.rpc.sentio.xyz.
One entry per payout: transaction, block, epoch, credited amount, sender, called contract and the calls made between sync and settle.
Census of blocks 96,099,090 to 97,827,090 on Polygon and debug_traceTransaction of every flagged row: the sLGNS and sATH rows show sync, the rebase call 0xaf14052c, settle and a claim mint.
The credit is the balance rise since sync, whoever caused it.

verification.factCheck: The mechanism and the listed transactions hold, and the count for BNB Smart Chain is too low. I fetched the receipt of every one of the 119 listed transactions. Each succeeded, each holds the sSAC rebase log, an sSAC Transfer from the PoolManager equal to the credited amount, no sSAC Transfer to the PoolManager and no PoolManager log, and the amounts sum to 210.068614491 sSAC. The senders are 0x2d68a551e7c8ecf7312ee083a16e736dce2347d5 in 117 and two other accounts in one each, and 0x2d68... has no code. For three of them I read balanceOf(PoolManager) one block before and at the block: the balance is the same (41.82, 1,597.81 and 2,287.62 sSAC), so the rebase rise left in the same transaction. No endpoint I reached served a trace, so the order sync, rebase, settle, take rests on the receipts and balances here and on the traces of the cycle 5 verifier. The rebase log file has 191 rows for epochs 45 to 367, and the staking contract 0x99954eb0b159514d608f64c89a2c5bbe9f42120b reports an epoch length of 96,000 blocks at blocks 104,400,000, 116,000,000 and today, so there are 323 epochs and 132 logs are missing. The cause is the log source: the same eth_getLogs request for the block of epoch 169 on bsc.api.pocket.network returned one log in 12 of 18 tries and an empty list without an error in 6. I located all 132 missing rebase transactions, 35 by log windows and 97 by a binary search on epoch() at old blocks followed by a single block log query, and read their receipts. 69 of them are payouts of the same form: sender 0x2d68..., called contract 0x0b675fb382e0c986d724fd6cbb51837b3ae30e8a, an sSAC Transfer out of the PoolManager, none in, no PoolManager log. They sum to 61.853007741 sSAC and lie between blocks 115,890,216 (epoch 165) and 128,466,212 (epoch 296). The corrected figures are 188 payout transactions among 323 rebase transactions, 271.921622232 sSAC, first payout at block 115,890,216. The 63 missing rows that are no payout went to other contracts and hold no sSAC transfer of the PoolManager. coins.llama.fi has no price for sSAC. Polygon: eth_getLogs on polygon.gateway.tenderly.co for ERC-6909 Transfer logs of the PoolManager with from zero in blocks 96,099,090 to 97,827,090 returned 109 logs for the sLGNS id that sum to 1,349.946361641 sLGNS, all to one recipient, and 84 logs for id 0x2f712578fbd1c42c3459b67dd2b9035e994bbc93 that sum to 78.935548641, which match the finding. I did not trace the Polygon rows again.
verification.codeCheck: sync has no modifier and stores balanceOf(PoolManager) (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). _settle credits the recipient with the balance now minus the stored balance, whoever caused the rise, and the subtraction is checked (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365). take pays the credited amount out and mint books it as a claim (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 322-329). unlock only requires that the count of nonzero deltas is zero at the end (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). No guard ties a credit to a transfer by the settler.
verification.corrections: The BNB Smart Chain count is 188 payout transactions and 271.921622232 sSAC, where the finding has 119 and 210.068614. The first payout is in block 115,890,216, which is 95,998 blocks before the one named. 135 of 323 rebase transactions hold no PoolManager transfer, where the finding has 72 of 191. The log scan through bsc.api.pocket.network silently lost 132 of 323 logs, so every other whole history scan through that endpoint needs a second source. The 69 missed payouts are saved in theme-currency-lists.work/raw/ssac_rebase_missed_verifier.json. The value taken is rebase surplus that no pool records, so the effect is lost yield for liquidity providers, as the finding says.

findings.title: WHITE on Ethereum and ARGUS on Arc charge the sender on top of a transfer to a listed pair, so a take that names such a recipient costs the PoolManager more than the caller is debited
findings.difference: Both tokens keep a list of trading pairs. A transfer to a listed address moves the amount to the recipient and a further share from the sender to a tax address: 10 percent for WHITE 0x9cdf242ef7975d8c68d5c1f5b6905801699b1940 (to 0x287ecebd1223e235b929217fe596c905a11752ae) and 1 percent for ARGUS 0xece5ca8bf9220718e5727754026757512212cb3c (to the token contract). The main assets of Ethereum pools take nothing from the sender beyond the amount.
findings.mechanism: 1. take debits the caller by amount and then calls transfer(to, amount) on the token (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-80). Core assumes that the call lowers its balance by amount. 2. The census flagged these rows because the logged outflow exceeds the Swap amounts of the transaction. Ethereum transaction 0x36869e0c74164dfaf399507b77a3d4398d90bb3b0f53d3bb52f47085f381c3fc: the trace shows one transfer call from the PoolManager for 27,819.93 WHITE to 0x6ec94f50cadcc79984463688de42a0ca696ec2db, and the receipt shows a second Transfer log from the PoolManager for 2,781.99 WHITE to the tax address. Arc transaction 0xaf96d29fbbc703117f44d34945c9e8b04fc768ed235c2cd93d66bd0c4289ff4c: 176.74 ARGUS to the pair 0x6a3bacaa6493734c1ac221ebf42cf530a96c1e02 and 1.767 ARGUS to the token contract. 3. Simulation with a measuring stub at the PoolManager address (state override, eth_call): a transfer of one third of the balance to the listed pair lowers the PoolManager balance by 110.0000 percent of the amount for WHITE and 101.0000 percent for ARGUS. The same transfer to an address without code lowers it by the amount only. A transfer from the WHITE pair to the PoolManager arrives in full, and one from the ARGUS pair arrives at 99 percent. 4. Whole history of Transfer logs from the PoolManager to the tax address: 766 transfers that sum to 6,129,406.68 WHITE between blocks 23,150,160 and 26,459,964, and 1,295 transfers that sum to 188,007.27 ARGUS between blocks 21,078,826 and 32,673,463. 5. The recipient of take is chosen by the caller, so any account can make the PoolManager pay the charge on any amount it takes to a listed pair. The caller owes only the amount. I did not test whether the caller can get the amount back out of the pair, so the cost of doing this on purpose is unknown. 6. BNB Smart Chain shows the same pattern once in the 3 day census: in transaction 0x82b6ad131efc04d9ee34211e458f107a1a94f9d093fd679e1554edcf7ebfaf06 the pool owed 212,712.18 units of the token with symbol T 0x4ef42e4cf51cd779e9947db65b629ecd8c92b1da and the PoolManager paid a further 6,381.37 units, 3 percent, to 0xfe34d3505cc8a835f7efe54bf8ff4d680d2bd6b5. I did not simulate that token.
findings.impact: The pools of these two tokens together record 6,129,406.68 WHITE and 188,007.27 ARGUS more than the PoolManager holds, assuming no other flow outside pool accounting. The PoolManager holds 48,265,470.02 WHITE and 46,697,370.97 ARGUS. DexScreener prices WHITE at 0.0000303 USD, so the WHITE shortfall is about 186 USD. I found no price for ARGUS. The last liquidity providers to withdraw bear the shortfall, and it grows with every routed sale into a listed pair. The same test on the new lists found 13 currencies on BNB Smart Chain, 12 on Base and 2 on X Layer where the PoolManager loses more than the amount it sends. The priced ones are receipt tokens of lending markets that lose between 1 and 537 base units by rounding.
findings.preconditions: A pool of such a token and a route or a caller that names a listed pair as the recipient of take. The list is set by the token owner.
findings.mitigations: Routers should take such tokens to their own address first. Interfaces should flag tokens whose transfer lowers the sender balance by more than the amount. Liquidity providers in WHITE and ARGUS pools should expect a shortfall.

Ethereum: the receipt of 0x36869e0c74164dfaf399507b77a3d4398d90bb3b0f53d3bb52f47085f381c3fc (block 26,387,568) shows two WHITE Transfer logs from the PoolManager, 27,819.929136657607 to 0x6ec94f50cadcc79984463688de42a0ca696ec2db and 2,781.9929136657606 to 0x287ecebd1223e235b929217fe596c905a11752ae. owner() of WHITE returns that second address, which has no code, so the charge goes to the token owner. 0x6ec94f... is a Uniswap v2 pair of WHITE and USDC (factory 0x5c69bee701ef814a2b6a3edd4b1652cb9cc5aa6f). eth_getLogs on mainnet.gateway.tenderly.co from block 21,688,329 to 26,478,880 returned 766 WHITE transfers from the PoolManager to the owner address that sum to 6,129,406.680924483 WHITE, first block 23,150,160, last block 26,459,964. In my simulation a transfer to its PancakeSwap pair costs the PoolManager 103 percent of the amount and a skim back leaves it 8.9 percent short, with a settle credit of 94.1 percent, so the caller would have to add 5.9 percent of its own.
verification.codeCheck: take books minus amount on the caller and calls transfer(to, amount) on the token (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The transfer routine checks only that the call did not revert and returned nothing or true (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). Nothing compares the fall of the PoolManager balance with the amount. sync is callable while unlocked and stores the balance after the take (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). When the pair then pays the amount back to the PoolManager, _settle credits the full amount (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365), the caller's delta is zero and unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). The 10 percent charge stays outside all accounting. The recipient of take is a free argument, so every step is open to any account.
verification.corrections: Severity rises from low to medium. For WHITE the cost of doing this on purpose is gas only: one unlock with take to the v2 pair, sync, skim to the PoolManager and settle moves 10 percent of the taken amount from the pooled balance to the token owner, and repeating it empties the PoolManager balance of WHITE. The caller gains nothing unless it is the token owner, so for an ordinary account the effect is a loss and freeze for the liquidity providers of the hookless WHITE pools, and for the owner 0x287ecebd1223e235b929217fe596c905a11752ae it is a siphon. The actor unprivileged is right. For ARGUS and for T the round trip is not free on the pairs I tried, so they stay at the level the finding describes. I did not rerun the count of 13, 12 and 2 currencies on the other lists.

findings.title: The Klik factories pay creator fees in a token's listed pair currency whatever currency the hook delivered, and two Ethereum transactions used this to take the fees of other creators
findings.difference: None. The behaviour does not depend on the network. It comes from the Klik launch pad contracts (KlikLauncher, AnyLauncher, KlikHook, AnyHook) that third parties deployed on nine of the 21 networks. The PoolManager behaves as written.
findings.mechanism: This answers lead L-378 and adds a direct gain to the finding. 1. Verified source of KlikLauncher 0xb6da931df2ed2c80db47923d4eb46fd913ee01c3 on Ethereum: launch (lines 310 to 328) has no caller check. _launch (lines 362 to 404) requires launchEnabled and an enabled pair, deploys a new KlikToken, and records creatorOf[token] = msg.sender and pairOf[token] = pair. An eth_call of launch from an ordinary account returns a token address on Ethereum and on the unverified Tempo factory 0x20839c453a0ed8bcab1095ea068669469098297c. 2. creditCreatorFee(token, amount) (lines 559 to 564) is callable by the hook and only adds amount to creatorFees[token]. It takes no currency argument. collectFees(token) (lines 566 to 574) lets the creator withdraw creatorFees[token] and pays it with _safeTransfer(pairOf[token], creator, amount), that is in the pair recorded at launch. AnyLauncher 0x95e0da371711502eed78bcc3f17856b4415120ca has the same two functions (lines 596 to 609). Its launch has no caller list either, and it needs a price quote signed by the platform priceSigner (_verifyQuote, lines 296 to 301). 3. Verified source of KlikHook 0x1d06faa7ff674ccfd8a5736c0c0973cb0a8fa0cc: _tokenOf (lines 373 to 378) takes the token from currency1 of the PoolKey when the factory knows it, and takes the pair from currency0 of the PoolKey, without comparing it with pairOf(token). _beforeSwap (lines 446 to 485) mints the buy fee as claims of currency0 and adds it to pendingClaims[token], pendingPlatform[token] and pendingCreator[token]. At the next swap _flushClaims (lines 245 to 266) burns pendingClaims[token] in currency0 of that PoolKey, takes the currency, sends the platform share to the treasury and the creator share to the factory in that currency, and calls creditCreatorFee(token, share). 4. PoolManager.initialize has no access control (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142) and these hooks accept any caller, so an account that launched token T can open a pool that pairs T with a currency X it issues. A swap there accrues a fee in X at no cost. The next swap makes the hook send X to the factory and credit creatorFees[T] by the same number. collectFees(T) then pays that number of units of the real pair from the factory balance, which is the uncollected fee money of every creator who launched against that pair. 5. This has run on Ethereum. Transaction 0xe91af1e1dfb2e1bc9d8026fa275275b16f40c94512207eb3b6936b52b12a9a11 (block 26078723, sender 0x690193287a9f3e0095adae116f4260818332ce0a through contract 0xdb9b1e94b5b69df7e401ddbede43491141047db3): the hook mints and burns 2439181612486875092 claims of currency 0x8b74867835f2207cd61710fc3fd7ffdc6c5d1ca8 for token 0xec2d248beff7f0424fd5d6c602dfd3e6a11c8ce6, whose listed pair is SPCXon. The factory logs a credit of 975672644994750037 and then transfers 975672644994750037 SPCXon to the token creator 0x1ec0e76d1a7f023995cf603dc2802863e5821ec3, which forwards 975770212259253512 SPCXon to the sender. No SPCXon enters the factory in that transaction. Transaction 0x341ecc661e5a52595f908573ae1d560ae8964990ea7c57ab229fc93b8504ceb9 (block 26151960, sender 0x888ddf6a86fd6e6da39395cd3f333ecba55ff364 through contract 0x6730d584c0e5f84b6af8698a16a11d6f82089b1e) repeats it for seven tokens created by that contract. The fees arrive at the factory in token 0x43c6b27489139debfdb71463f83552cc7264968b, which is minted from the zero address in the same transaction, and the factory pays out 36032480969017805 units of 0x2d1f7226bd1f780af6b9a49dcc0ae00e8df4bdee, 15311085289905665 of 0xf6b1117ec07684d3958cad8beb1b302bfd21103f, 8548104401245769 SPCXon, 6797353818778040 of 0xba47214edd2bb43099611b208f75e4b42fdcfedc, 4284309310775460 of 0xfedc5f4a6c38211c1338aa411018dfaf26612c08, 2836402531014289 of 0x14c3abf95cb9c93a8b82c1cdcb76d72cb87b2d4c and 470446068834558 of 0x59644165402b611b350645555b50afb581c71eb2. 6. The factory books no longer match its holdings. For the 16 tokens launched against SPCXon the factory logged credits of 2873155228010260120, the hook sent it 1888836911349760839 SPCXon, and the difference of 984318316660499281 is exactly the two transactions above. Creators collected 1884499543919557792, creatorFees still records 988655684090702328, and the factory holds 4337367430203047 SPCXon. In an eth_simulateV1 run collectFees for token 0xe413ebda258f05cd12aea2aaf9348b1045a136e4 from its creator, with 752539572571985445 recorded, reverts with "transfer failed". The pairs 0xf6b1117e, 0xfedc5f4a, 0x59644165 and 0xba47214e show owed amounts equal to what the second transaction took, against a factory balance of zero. 7. On Tempo an eth_simulateV1 run of creditCreatorFee(DUCK, 100000) from the hook address followed by collectFees(DUCK) from the creator makes the factory transfer 2946234 pathUSD, its whole balance, where creatorFees(DUCK) was 2846234 before.
findings.impact: Creator fees that the Klik factories hold between collection calls, and the ability of honest creators to collect. On Ethereum about 0.984 SPCXon (about 130 USD at the 132 USD price recorded in cycle 5) and small amounts of six other pair tokens were taken, and at least 0.9887 SPCXon of recorded creator fees can no longer be paid. What the factories hold today is small: 0.0043 SPCXon, 0.0040 AAPLon, 0.0050 NVDAon and two other tokens at 0xb6da931df2ed2c80db47923d4eb46fd913ee01c3 (about 3 USD), about 2 USD of tokens at 0x95e0da371711502eed78bcc3f17856b4415120ca, 2.946234 pathUSD on Tempo, 0.212 UNI on Unichain, 20.65 MON on Monad, about 5 USD of stock tokens on Robinhood Chain, 0.0012 ETH on Ink, 0.2868 AVAX on Avalanche and 14.99 units of one token on Base. Every later fee payment into these factories is exposed in the same way. No liquidity in the PoolManager is touched by this step. The swap freeze of the earlier finding still applies.
findings.preconditions: None beyond what any account has: launch a token through the factory (open on Ethereum and Tempo by eth_call), initialize a second pool, swap twice, call collectFees. The source was read for the two Ethereum factories and the Ethereum and Unichain hooks. The Tempo factory is unverified and was tested by simulation. The factories on Base, Ink, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Avalanche and Monad were not read. launchEnabled() returns 1 on every one of them, including the Avalanche factory 0x5e91ca49f5e94319755634539bd9a1d2f15467a2, which holds 0.2868 AVAX. On Robinhood Chain a launch call from an ordinary account fails only with "pair not enabled" for the pair I chose. The AnyLauncher factories (second Ethereum factory, Unichain, and by the hook version string also Base, Ink, Arbitrum One, Avalanche and Monad) need the signed price quote for a launch. I did not examine who can obtain such a quote, so open launch is unconfirmed there. The newer Ethereum hook 0xcba49142a75da64a679f32a159f4316f11a7e0cc rejects a foreign initialize, and its factory 0xfe4a23bbe27be16955f4d8599c73bac88ef647d1 (0.118 ETH and about 480 USD of tokens) was not read.
findings.mitigations: The PoolManager deployer cannot change this. The factory author can record the currency with each credit and pay each credit in the currency received, and the hook author can compare currency0 with pairOf(token) and reject initialize from any caller other than the factory. Creators should collect often. Interfaces should treat a second pool of a Klik token as hostile.

AnyLauncher has the same two fee functions (596 to 611) and its _launch calls _verifyQuote (433, 296 to 302). On chain at Ethereum block 26478686 (ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com): launchEnabled() is 1, all 30 listed pairs are enabled, and an eth_call of launch from 0x00000000000000000000000000000000c0ffee77 with pair SPCXon and no dev buy returns a token address for salts 2 and 7. collectFees(0xe413ebda258f05cd12aea2aaf9348b1045a136e4) from its creator 0xc28eba2b0551267f4016ad0dc2324b2b6a770cbf reverts with "transfer failed", with 752539572571985445 recorded and 4337367430203047 SPCXon in the factory. I fetched the receipts of both cited transactions from eth.drpc.org. They show what the finding says: in 0xe91af1e1 the factory logs a credit of 975672644994750037 for token 0xec2d248b and sends that amount of SPCXon to 0x1ec0e76d with no SPCXon entering the factory, and in 0x341ecc66 seven credits arrive in token 0x43c6b274 and seven different pair tokens leave. I then ran my own reconciliation: all 2412 factory logs and 2341 token transfers into the factory from block 25901000 to 26478695, matching each CreatorFeeCredited log to a transfer of the same amount in the same transaction. 2233 credits are backed in the listed pair. The unbacked credits sit in four transactions, two more than the finding names. On Tempo at block 50448312 launch from an ordinary account returns a token address, and eth_simulateV1 of creditCreatorFee(DUCK, 100000) from the hook followed by collectFees(DUCK) from the creator emits a pathUSD transfer of 2946234 from the factory.
verification.codeCheck: The PoolManager side is as cited. initialize has only noDelegateCall and the currency order, tick spacing and hook address checks (src/PoolManager.sol:117-126), so any account can open a second pool of a launched token on a hook whose beforeInitialize accepts it (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-182). mint debits the hook in the currency id it names and burn credits it (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336), take debits the caller and transfers (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), and the fee the hook returns from beforeSwap is charged to the swapper in the PoolKey currency (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:266-279, src/PoolManager.sol:220-226). The check at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:276 holds because the fee is below the input. No guard in src/ stands in the way, and none should: every delta in the foreign currency nets to zero at src/PoolManager.sol:112, and the loss happens in the factory after the tokens have left the PoolManager. Actor check: launch, initialize, two swaps and collectFees are open to any account on the Ethereum KlikLauncher and on Tempo, and the four Ethereum transactions came from two ordinary senders. The victims are creators who used the launch pad as intended.

The shortfall per pair at block 26478691, summed over the 71 tokens of the factory, is 984318316660499281 SPCXon, 225793904152729682 NVDAon, 149040397478561157 AAPLon, 15311085289905665 of 0xf6b1117e, 6797353818778040 of 0xba47214e, 4284309310775460 of 0xfedc5f4a and 470446068834558 of 0x59644165. findings.title: A sale of WHITE or ARGUS that pays the listed pool through take leaves the sell charge to the PoolManager, the Arc PoolManager holds about 107,000 USD of ARGUS, and no other priced currency on the 21 networks charges the sender
findings.difference: The cause is the token contract in both cases. Neither Ethereum nor Arc adds a network property. WHITE 0x9cdf242ef7975d8c68d5c1f5b6905801699b1940 on Ethereum debits the sender 10 percent on top of the amount when the recipient is its Uniswap v2 pair with USDC 0x6ec94f50cadcc79984463688de42a0ca696ec2db or its Uniswap v3 pool with WETH 0xf8f6191561997010870056fc265d0f7ddaf105bf (fee 0.3 percent). The v3 pool is a second charged recipient that F-092 did not list. ARGUS 0xece5ca8bf9220718e5727754026757512212cb3c on Arc debits the sender 1 percent on top when the recipient is its mainPool() 0x6a3bacaa6493734c1ac221ebf42cf530a96c1e02, a Uniswap v3 pool with USDC at fee 1 percent. ARGUS reports currentTaxes() = (100, 100) basis points, taxExpiry() = 0 and isExempt(PoolManager) = false.
findings.mechanism: 1. take debits the caller by amount and then calls transfer(to, amount) on the token (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The transfer routine checks only that the call did not revert and returned nothing or true (src/types/Currency.sol:60-88). No line compares the fall of the PoolManager balance with the amount. 2. Sweep of this cycle: a measuring stub placed at the PoolManager address by state override (eth_call only) sent one third of the balance of every priced currency to every candidate recipient and read the balances before and after. 13,001 priced currencies on 21 networks, 12,751 with a balance of at least 3 base units, 128,687 recipient trials, 127,554 accepted, 43,808 of them to a v2 style pair, a v3 style pool or a pair listed by DexScreener. Recipients came from getPair and getPool of 83 factories (v2 style, Solidly style and v3 style, each verified on chain) against up to 13 base tokens per network, from every address that a zero argument call of any selector of the token returns, from DexScreener pair lists for currencies above 50 USD, and from four fixed recipients (a plain account, the token itself, the dead address, the wrapped native contract). 3. Result: the PoolManager balance fell by more than the amount for 86 currencies. For 84 of them the excess is 1 to 536 base units (Aave and Compound receipt tokens and valTUSD), which is rounding. The two others are WHITE and ARGUS. 4. WHITE at Ethereum block 26,479,738 on two endpoints: a transfer of 16,088,490.01 WHITE from the PoolManager to the v2 pair lowers its balance by 17,697,339.01 (110.0000 percent) and the pair receives 100 percent. skim(PoolManager) on the pair then returns 16,088,490.01 in full, so the net loss is 1,608,849.00 WHITE. The same transfer to the v3 pool also costs 110.0000 percent. A transfer from either pool to the PoolManager arrives in full, and a transfer from a plain holder to the PoolManager carries no charge. 5. ARGUS at Arc block 32,779,722 on two endpoints: a transfer of 15,539,568.77 ARGUS to the v3 pool lowers the PoolManager balance by 101.0000 percent of the amount. The pool has no skim. A transfer from the pool to the PoolManager arrives at 99.0000 percent. A transfer from a plain holder to the PoolManager carries no charge. 6. Who gains. A holder that sells into the listed pool from its own address pays the amount plus the charge: in the trial a plain holder that sent WHITE to either pool paid 110.0000 percent of the amount, and one that sent ARGUS to its pool paid 101.0000 percent. A caller that pays the amount into the PoolManager, or buys it in a v4 pool, and names the listed pool as recipient of take owes the PoolManager the amount only, and the token takes the charge from the pooled balance. The caller keeps the charge it would have paid: 10 percent of a WHITE sale and 1 percent of an ARGUS sale. Arc transaction 0x471fafc3a4761f749412e3856fac067b8f95e73d1d7bf6240dee396e9fc3e9fb (block 32,766,474) shows the pattern: the contract 0x4d680e3a362f64005b4f71004fdfebe203b0ea59 swaps in v4, the PoolManager sends 3,161.80 ARGUS to the v3 pool and 31.62 ARGUS to the token contract, and the pool pays 7.200687 USDC to the PoolManager. 7. Cost of doing it without a real sale. WHITE: take to the v2 pair, sync, skim to the PoolManager and settle costs gas only and moves 10 percent of the taken amount to the token owner 0x287ecebd1223e235b929217fe596c905a11752ae. One round can take at most 10/11 of the balance, so each round removes at most 1/11 of it and 48 rounds leave about 1 percent ((10/11)^48 = 0.0103). The caller gains nothing from this unless it is the token owner. ARGUS: the return leg loses 1 percent to the buy charge and each v3 swap pays the 1 percent pool fee, so a round trip costs the caller about 3 percent of the amount to remove 1 percent from the PoolManager. 8. History. The cycle 6 scan counted 766 charge transfers and 6,129,406.68 WHITE up to block 26,459,964. No charge transfer followed up to block 26,479,742 (eth_getLogs on one endpoint; the second endpoint refused the range), and balanceOf(PoolManager) is still 48,265,470.022830203421280226 WHITE, the value cycle 6 recorded. For ARGUS two more charge transfers of 59.24 ARGUS in total followed between blocks 32,673,464 and 32,779,791 on two endpoints, which brings the total to 1,297 transfers and 188,066.52 ARGUS.
findings.impact: ARGUS: the PoolManager holds 46,618,706.31 ARGUS, about 107,300 USD at the DefiLlama price of 0.002302 USD (DexScreener: 0.002293 USD, 222,906 USD of liquidity in the listed v3 pool, 53,316 USD of volume in 24 hours). The v4 pools of ARGUS, among them the hookless pool 0xb3f441e8871840ecfcb284e5cbb5b9c21a50e961e1c50109bdced25e429f00cc (USDC and ARGUS, fee 0.985 percent, tick spacing 99, no hook, 90,823 USD of liquidity at DexScreener), together record 188,066.52 ARGUS (about 433 USD) more than the PoolManager holds, assuming no other flow outside pool accounting, and the gap grows by 1 percent of every amount taken straight to the listed pool. The gain goes to the caller of each such route as a saved charge, and the loss falls on the liquidity providers who withdraw last. WHITE: the PoolManager holds 48,265,470.02 WHITE, about 1,495 USD at the DefiLlama price of 0.00003098 USD. Any account can move nearly all of it to the token owner at the cost of gas, and any seller into the two listed pools can let the PoolManager pay the 10 percent charge. Nothing else was found: 19 networks have no priced currency with a sender charge above rounding. The sweep covers priced currencies only. The unpriced token T on BNB Smart Chain that F-092 mentions was not retested.
findings.preconditions: A v4 pool of the token with a balance at the PoolManager, and a caller that names a listed pool as recipient of take. Both hold today. The lists of charged recipients are set by the token owners. I did not check which deployed routers pass a pool address as the recipient of take on their own.
findings.mitigations: Routers and interfaces should take these two tokens to their own address and pay the pool from there, so that the sender of the sale carries the charge. Interfaces should flag a currency when a simulated transfer from the PoolManager to one of its pools lowers the PoolManager balance by more than the amount. Liquidity providers in WHITE and ARGUS pools should expect a shortfall on withdrawal. The deployer cannot close this in core without a balance check around the transfer in take.

findings.title: Polygon system token at 0x1010 mirrors the PoolManager native balance and cannot be paid out by take
findings.difference: Polygon has a genesis contract at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 that presents native POL as a token. Its balanceOf returns the native balance of the account. Its transfer is payable and returns false unless msg.value equals the amount. Ethereum has no ERC-20 face of ETH at the protocol level.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync(0x1010) stores balanceOf(PoolManager) as reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286, src/types/Currency.sol:94). That value is the full native POL balance of the PoolManager, which already backs pools that use address(0). 2. settle with 0x1010 synced credits the caller with any rise in that native balance since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). msg.value is rejected at src/PoolManager.sol:356 and the PoolManager has no receive function, so the balance can rise only through a forced transfer such as SELFDESTRUCT. 3. take(0x1010, to, amount) calls transfer on 0x1010 with zero value (src/types/Currency.sol:73). The token returns a 32 byte zero. The success test at src/types/Currency.sol:68 fails and the call reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86. collectProtocolFees for this currency reverts the same way (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). 4. A positive delta in currency 0x1010 can therefore only be cleared, minted as an ERC-6909 claim, or swapped. The POL that paid for it stays in the PoolManager native balance and no account holds a native delta to take it. 5. Double credit was checked and is not possible. A native settle while 0x1010 is synced reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:356, and sync(address(0)) clears the synced currency (src/PoolManager.sol:281-283), so one POL is never credited under both currencies.
findings.impact: POL that a contract pays into a pool or claim denominated in 0x1010 cannot leave the PoolManager as that currency and is not claimable as native POL either. Pools that hold POL under address(0) are not affected. The PoolManager held about 3.1 million native POL at the time of the query. Protocol fees accrued in currency 0x1010 would also be stuck.
findings.preconditions: Someone initializes a pool with 0x1010 as a currency, and a custom contract forces POL into the PoolManager between sync and settle. Standard periphery cannot do this because approve and transferFrom on 0x1010 revert. The actor loses its own funds. No path was found that takes funds from other users.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces, routers and pool indexers on Polygon should refuse 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 as a pool currency and direct users to address(0) or WPOL. Block explorers label 0x1010 as the POL token, so the warning should be explicit in deployment notes.

verification.codeCheck: sync(0x1010) stores the native balance as reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286, src/types/Currency.sol:94). _settle rejects msg.value while 0x1010 is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356) and credits balance minus reserves with a checked subtraction (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). settle and settleFor are the only payable functions (src/PoolManager.sol:300, src/PoolManager.sol:305) and the contract has no receive or fallback function, so only a forced transfer can raise the balance inside the window. take(0x1010) calls transfer with zero value (src/types/Currency.sol:73), receives a zero word, fails the test at src/types/Currency.sol:68 and reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86. collectProtocolFees reverts the same way for this currency (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). I tried to turn the mirror into a double credit. A caller can take native POL, sync 0x1010, force the same POL back and receive a 0x1010 credit. The native debit from the take remains (src/PoolManager.sol:294). It can be cleared only with msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354) or by a swap against a pool that other users funded with 0x1010, and those users could fund it only by forcing in their own POL. Operations on a pool the caller funds alone conserve each currency, so the 0x1010 credit never becomes native credit for free. test/Sync.t.sol:255-274 covers the rejected native settle with the NativeERC20 model from src/test/NativeERC20.sol. No test covers a token whose transfer returns false for the PoolManager.
verification.corrections: Nothing wrong in the mechanism. One detail to add: a take of amount zero on 0x1010 would see transfer return true, and it changes nothing because a zero delta is ignored (src/PoolManager.sol:369). findings.title: Three more recipients on HyperEVM accept a PoolManager payout and strand it: the L1 block number precompile, the ERC-4337 EntryPoints and a system address reached through the stHYPE contract
findings.difference: HyperEVM has a precompile at 0x0809 that answers any call, with or without value, with the L1 block number. The ERC-4337 EntryPoints v0.6 and v0.7 are deployed and book incoming value as a deposit of the sender. HyperCore credits an ERC-20 sent to a token's system address only from the Transfer log of the linked contract, and for STHYPE the linked contract is wstHYPE, one of two contracts that move the same balance.
findings.mechanism: take debits the caller and then pays (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). Read-only calls from the PoolManager address show what three recipients do with the payout. A native payout of 1 wei to 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000809 returns success, so by the EVM's call rules the value is then held by a precompile address that cannot send it on (src/types/Currency.sol:44-53). A native payout to either EntryPoint succeeds and is booked as the PoolManager's deposit, which only the PoolManager could withdraw. Both EntryPoints answer balanceOf(PoolManager) with that deposit. A caller can therefore sync the EntryPoint address, make the payout and call settle, and is credited the same amount under the EntryPoint address as currency id (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365). That credit can be minted as an ERC-6909 claim and can never be paid out, because the EntryPoints revert on transfer(address,uint256). The caller still owes the native amount. A take of stHYPE to 0x2000000000000000000000000000000000000077 moves shares to the STHYPE system address while the linked contract, wstHYPE, emits no Transfer log, so by the documented rule HyperCore credits nobody. A take of wstHYPE to the same address is credited to the PoolManager's HyperCore account, as F-021 describes. In each case the caller pays the full amount and no other user loses anything.
findings.impact: The loss falls on the caller who chose the recipient, or on the user of a router that lets the user name any recipient. Pool reserves stay whole. Claims under an EntryPoint id are worthless and cannot affect another currency.
findings.preconditions: A caller or a router that passes one of these addresses as recipient. The stHYPE case needs stHYPE in the PoolManager, which holds none today, and the statement that HyperCore credits nothing rests on the docs and was not tested.
findings.mitigations: Routers and interfaces on HyperEVM should refuse recipients in 0x0800 to 0x08ff, the EntryPoint addresses, 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 and addresses that start with 0x20 followed by zeros, unless the payer chose them knowingly. The 0x settler contracts added a similar rule for HyperCore system addresses.

verification.factCheck: I reran the calls with the PoolManager as sender on 2026-11-22. 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000809 has no code and a zero balance, and it answers empty calldata with 1 wei of value, empty calldata without value, the transfer shape and the balanceOf shape with one 32 byte word that holds the L1 block number (0x495e7718 and following). A value call that succeeds leaves the value at that address. EntryPoint v0.7 (16,035 bytes) and v0.6 (23,689 bytes) both accept empty calldata with 1 wei from the PoolManager, answer balanceOf(PoolManager) with a 32 byte zero and revert on transfer(address,uint256). spotMeta lists STHYPE at index 119 with evmContract 0x94e8396e0869c9f2200760af0621afd240e1cf38, the wstHYPE contract, and the transfers page states that an EVM to HyperCore credit is taken from the Transfer log of the linked contract. In the verified source an stHYPE transfer emits Transfer from the stHYPE contract only (stHYPE.sol lines 244 to 256), while a wstHYPE transfer emits one log from each contract (wstHYPE.sol line 112 and stHYPE.sol line 285). The 0x settler changelog has the entry that payouts naming a HyperCore system address revert on HyperEVM unless the payer funds the transfer. That HyperCore credits nobody for an stHYPE transfer to 0x2000000000000000000000000000000000000077 follows from the documented rule and was not observed on chain.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller before the payout (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295). The native payout is a call with empty calldata and all gas whose only test is the success flag (src/types/Currency.sol:44-53), so a recipient that accepts value ends the matter for the PoolManager. For the EntryPoint id, sync stores balanceOf(PoolManager) (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286), settle credits the rise (lines 358-364), and a take under that id reverts because the EntryPoint reverts on transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). The credit therefore exists only as a delta or a claim under the EntryPoint address, and deltas and claims of one address cannot pay a debt under another (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16). The caller still owes the native amount when unlock checks the delta count (src/PoolManager.sol:112). I looked for a way to turn any of these into a gain at the cost of others and found none: anyone can raise the PoolManager's EntryPoint deposit through depositTo, and the result is the same worthless credit paid for in full.
verification.corrections: The stHYPE part is a consequence of the documented crediting rule and needs stHYPE in the PoolManager, which holds none. The actor value unprivileged is right in the sense that any caller can do it, and the loser is that caller or the user of a router that passes the recipient through. No other user loses funds.

findings.title: The OP Stack wrapped native predeploy on Celo calls itself Wrapped Ether and WETH but wraps CELO
findings.difference: On OP Stack chains that use ETH for gas, 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000006 is canonical WETH. On Celo the same address is a live wrapper of the native asset, which is CELO, and it still returns name 'Wrapped Ether' and symbol 'WETH' because the L2 L1Block predeploy reports the gas token as Ether. The bridged ETH token on Celo is a different contract at 0xD221812de1BD094f35587EE8E174B07B6167D9Af.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager accepts any address as a currency and reads no metadata (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). It learns balances only through balanceOf (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). Anyone can obtain the predeploy token one for one by depositing CELO. A pool, hook, router table or price source that treats this address as ETH backed WETH values a CELO backed token at the ETH price. Liquidity placed against it at that price is bought with tokens that cost one CELO each, and the paired asset leaves the PoolManager through ordinary swaps. Swappers who buy the token in such a pool receive a claim on CELO.
findings.impact: Funds of LPs and swappers in pools that list 0x4200...0006 as a currency, and integrations that map that address to WETH across OP Stack chains. Pools on the bridged WETH or on CELO are not affected. The PoolManager holds none of this token today, and its total supply is 0.143 CELO.
findings.preconditions: Someone must create or join a pool with the predeploy as a currency while pricing it as ETH, or an integration must hardcode the address as WETH. Any account can do the rest.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces and token lists for Celo should hide or relabel 0x4200...0006 and point to 0xD221...D9Af for ETH. Deployment scripts and routers should take the wrapped native address from Celo specific configuration. Pool creators should check that remoteToken() on a WETH candidate returns the Ethereum WETH address.

PositionManager.WETH9() returns the CELO token 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438. The runtime code of the PositionManager and of the first Universal Router contains the CELO token address. None of the PositionManager, the three routers or the PositionDescriptor contains the predeploy address or the bridged WETH address.

findings.title: Aave aTokens held by the Arbitrum One PoolManager grow outside pool accounting and the growth cannot be claimed
findings.difference: This is the rebasing token case that the Ethereum unit recorded for stETH, found here for Aave aTokens. No chain rule is involved. An aToken balance is a stored scaled amount multiplied by the reserve's liquidity index, so balanceOf(PoolManager) rises with time without any transfer.
findings.mechanism: Step 1: a liquidity provider adds liquidity in a pool whose currency is an aToken. The pool records a fixed amount and the PoolManager receives the aTokens. Step 2: the index grows with time and balanceOf(PoolManager) grows with it. For aArbUSDT the PoolManager has a scaled balance of 1,214.98 and a balance of 1,504.61. Step 3: a credit exists only for a balance increase between a sync and a settle in the same transaction (PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 358-360). The index does not move inside a transaction as far as I could establish: interest accrues with time and the Aave pool sends the whole flash loan premium to the protocol. I checked the premium setting on chain and did not read the Aave pool code for other paths. A sync therefore always includes the interest accrued so far in the reserve figure, and no settle is ever credited for it. Step 4: take, burn and fee collection pay out only recorded amounts, so the accrued interest stays in the PoolManager balance and belongs to no pool, claim or fee. The provider gets back the recorded amount and the pool fees. I found no way for an ordinary account to collect the surplus, and none to reduce the balance below the recorded amounts.
findings.impact: Liquidity providers in aToken pools lose the lending interest on their deposit for as long as it stays in the pool. Balances today are small: 1,504.6 aArbUSDT, 443.3 aArbUSDCn, 34.9 aArbUSDC and 0.41 aArbWETH. Principal is not affected.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use an aToken or another token whose balance rises without transfers. Nobody has to act. If a future Aave version again added value to the supplier index inside a transaction, an account that calls sync before it and settle after it would be credited the PoolManager's share of that addition.
findings.mitigations: Use a non-rebasing wrapper of the aToken as the pool currency. Interfaces can warn when a pool currency reports a scaled balance that differs from its balance.
