verification.factCheck: The chain facts hold. crates/hardfork/src/constants.rs at commit 697ea97 sets SSTORE_CREATE_COST to 250,000, TEMPO_T1_GENERAL_GAS_LIMIT to 30,000,000 and TEMPO_T1_TX_GAS_LIMIT_CAP to 30,000,000, and tips/tip-1000.md at the same commit gives 252,100 gas for a cold write to an empty slot and says the transaction gas cap is 30M. The endpoint reports tempo/v1.19.0-697ea97. Block 50,378,538 has gasLimit 500,000,000, mainBlockGeneralGasLimit 30,000,000 and baseFeePerGas 600,000,000. I ran a gas probe with eth_estimateGas and override code at an unused address: a call that stops at once costs 274,318 gas, one SSTORE from 0 to 1 costs 530,642, two such writes cost 784,951, and a write over a nonzero slot costs 279,364. A fresh slot therefore costs 256,324 gas for the first and 254,309 for the second, and a rewrite costs 5,046. Two fresh slots per crossing give about 510,000 gas, which agrees with the 504,684 of the finding. crates/precompiles/src/storage_credits/accounting.rs charges 245,000 gas up front for each creation in the default Refund mode on top of the 5,000 residual, so the gas limit must cover the full amount. crates/payload/builder/src/lib.rs lines 561 to 604 defer a transaction that is no payment when the general gas already used plus min(gas limit, cap) exceeds the general limit. The test uses the gas limit of the transaction, so a swap sent with a 30,000,000 limit is admitted only while no general gas has been used in that block. The fee document gives a floor of 600 million and a cap of 12 billion attodollars per gas and a general limit of 30M gas per block. The cost figures follow: 30,000,000 gas is 0.018 USD at the floor and 0.36 USD at the cap, and 540,000 gas is 0.0003 USD at the floor. I listed the 167 Initialize logs of the PoolManager and read slot0, both fee growth globals and liquidity of every pool with extsload. 70 of the 147 pools without a hook have both globals nonzero, so the precondition holds on live pools. I did not repeat the harness simulation that plants positions and swaps. The per crossing figure rests on the slot probe above and on the source.
verification.codeCheck: Pool.updateTick writes the two fee growth outside values only when the tick is at or below the current tick (src/libraries/Pool.sol:533-538), so a tick first used above the price keeps both at zero. Pool.crossTick writes global minus outside to both slots with no condition (src/libraries/Pool.sol:606-609), and the swap loop calls it for every initialized tick it reaches (src/libraries/Pool.sol:413-428). For a price raising swap the first argument is the stored feeGrowthGlobal0X128 and the second is the running value for currency1 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:416-418), so both writes create a slot when both globals are nonzero. modifyLiquidity has no owner or allowlist check and takes msg.sender as position owner (src/PoolManager.sol:145-168). A range above the price owes currency0 only (src/libraries/Pool.sol:209-217). The swap loop has no bound on the number of crossings other than the price limit and the amount (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344), and a revert from lack of gas undoes the whole swap. Liquidity removal has no loop over ticks. It updates two tick slots, at most two bitmap words, the position slots and the pool liquidity (src/libraries/Pool.sol:159-203, src/libraries/Position.sol:76-102), so it stays far below the cap. take and mint add one TIP-20 transfer or one claim balance write each (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 322-329). I found no guard that the finding missed. The actor is right: the planter needs no role and the victims use a pool without a hook and with ordinary tokens. No funds move to the planter and no withdrawal is blocked, which fits low.
verification.corrections: The pathUSD and USDC.e pool with fee 375 and spacing 4 (id 0x2fafb8d5...297d) is initialized and empty on chain: liquidity, feeGrowthGlobal0X128 and feeGrowthGlobal1X128 all read zero. The measured figures therefore describe a state that the harness built by override, and the finding should say so. The count of 58 crossings ignores the 63/64 rule. The swap runs at least two call frames below the transaction, so the count is a little lower. The statement that price lowering swaps are not affected is too wide. A tick at or below the price that was initialized while a global was zero starts with an empty slot, and a downward crossing writes zero when the global equals the stored value, after which the next upward crossing creates the slot again. The cost figures are upper bounds. The PoolManager account holds 13 storage credits (balanceOf on 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000), removals that clear tick or position slots mint more, and settle_storage_credit_refunds returns 245,000 gas per credit at the end of a transaction that created slots in PoolManager storage. The refund lowers the fee and leaves the needed gas limit unchanged. Because the builder admits by gas limit, any earlier transaction of the general lane with a higher tip defers a swap that carries a 30,000,000 limit in that block. This strengthens the degrade effect for large swaps and does not touch withdrawals, whose gas limits are small.

findings.title: Interest bearing receipt tokens and time indexed tokens grow in the PoolManager on thirteen networks and the growth can be neither claimed nor captured
findings.difference: F-037 recorded four Aave aTokens on Arbitrum One. The sweep finds the same class on eleven more networks and in more protocols: Aave v2 and v3, Spark, Radiant, Seamless, Moola, Neverland, Horizon, DeltaPrime, ExtraFi, Compound III and Wildcat. It also finds tokens with a pure time index: 666, EXPT and EXPT2 on Robinhood Chain and two test tokens on Arbitrum One.
findings.mechanism: balanceOf of these tokens is a stored amount times an index that is computed from block.timestamp at read time. Inside one transaction the timestamp is constant, so a sync and a settle in the same transaction see the same index and no caller is credited (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289, 349-365). The growth between transactions stays in the PoolManager balance and belongs to no pool. 666 at 0x73eb4a9db8d8c7539ba5701cf1cdd3452038970b has DAILY_GROWTH 1.33e18, MAX_DAYS 200 and a start time 4.3 days before the read, and the PoolManager balance rose from 1,936,719 to 2,595,372 in 93,084 seconds while one Transfer of 34,778 went out. Two side observations. First, when someone supplies to Aave v3 on behalf of the PoolManager, the aToken logs a Transfer for the supplied amount plus the interest accrued since the PoolManager's last index update, so the logs overstate what arrived; this explains the negative differences on aEthDAI, aEthUSDT, aAvaUSDT, aAstarASTR and aBnbUSDT. Second, Compound III lets anyone call CometRewards.claim for a third party; simulated for the PoolManager on Ethereum, Arbitrum One and Optimism it moved no reward token, with 0.000016 COMP owed on Ethereum and nothing on the other two.
findings.impact: Liquidity providers in these pools forgo the interest or the index growth for as long as the tokens stay pooled. Largest balances: 3,410.66 aEthUSDC, 2,268.28 aEthUSDT and 4,565.90 USPD on Ethereum, 60,244 rzRDNT and 1,504.67 aArbUSDT on Arbitrum One, 24,696 nWMON on Monad, 2,786.51 aBasUSDC on Base, 2,501.34 aASTR on Soneium, 548.71 aBnbUSDT on BNB Smart Chain, 845.05 aOptUSDC on Optimism. 666: the PoolManager holds 2,595,372 tokens, 37.9 percent of the supply, and its balance grows by about a third per day. Principal is not affected and no ordinary account can collect the surplus.
findings.preconditions: A pool in such a token. Nobody has to act. I did not test whether a flash loan premium or another call can move an Aave style index inside one transaction on these networks; F-037 checked that for Arbitrum One only. A caller who paid such a premium would be credited only the PoolManager's share of it, which is below 1 percent of supply for every receipt token found except rzRDNT at 3.8 percent.
findings.mitigations: Pool the wrapped form with a fixed balance, for example the static or wrapped aToken, or accept that the yield is lost. Interfaces should mark these currencies.

verification.factCheck: I sampled the class on five networks. Two Multicall3 reads 24 to 27 seconds apart, each stamped with the block timestamp, show balanceOf(PoolManager) growing with no transaction of mine in between: aEthUSDC 3,410.687144 to 3,410.687210, aEthUSDT by 51 base units and aDAI by 83,765,025,440 base units on Ethereum; aArbUSDT by 28 base units and rzRDNT by 19,962,354,109,229 base units on Arbitrum One; nWMON by 851,920,932,989,994 base units on Monad; aOptUSDC by 2 base units and exOptOP by 459,244,053,601 base units on Optimism. These balances follow the block timestamp at read time. On Robinhood Chain 666 grew by 54 tokens in 6 seconds, and index(), DAILY_GROWTH(), MAX_DAYS(), startTime() and totalSupply() return 3.53e18, 1.33e18, 200, 1795033136 and 7,017,240. EXPT and EXPT2 did not move in those 6 seconds. Their balance rose in steps over the last 800,000 blocks, their bytecode holds EPOCH(), currentEpoch(), rebaseIndex() and startTime() as views, and the only state changing functions are transfer, transferFrom and approve, so the step comes from the timestamp and no caller can trigger it. The PoolManager holds the whole EXPT supply of 713,731,483.6. The researcher's classification of the 177 lending rows is by symbol pattern (classify.py, the LEND expression), so only the tokens I sampled and those the researcher read one by one are confirmed as time indexed. One exception to the statement that nothing moves inside a transaction: the Aave v2 pool on Ethereum returns FLASHLOAN_PREMIUM_TOTAL 9 and is not paused, and in Aave v2 the flash loan premium is added to the supplier index. I did not read the Aave v2 pool source in this session; the on-chain setting is the evidence. I did not rerun the CometRewards simulation.
verification.codeCheck: sync records the balance at the time of the call and _settle credits the balance now minus that record (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). Both run in one transaction with one timestamp, so growth that depends only on the timestamp is inside the record and produces no credit. The growth between transactions belongs to no delta, and take, burn and collectProtocolFees pay accounted amounts only (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 332-336, src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). Where a caller can raise the index inside a transaction by paying a premium, the credit is the premium times the PoolManager's share of the token supply, which is 50.49 of 8,146,003 aDAI and 60,244 of 1,568,330 rzRDNT, so the caller pays more than the credit. A supply on behalf of the PoolManager is a payment by the caller and settle credits the real rise, whatever the Transfer log says.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged is acceptable only in the sense that no privilege is needed. No account acts and no account gains, nothing leaves the PoolManager and nothing is frozen, so this is lost yield for providers who pool a rebasing receipt token and it lies outside the goal of the review. The title says the growth can be neither claimed nor captured. That holds for growth that comes from time. For Aave v2 and its forks a flash loan premium moves the index inside a transaction and a bracket would capture the PoolManager's share of it at a net loss to the caller; the finding says this in its preconditions and the title should be read with that limit. The 177 rows were classed by symbol, and a token with a stored index that a public call updates would belong to the class of finding 0. I found none in my sample.

findings.title: A sync left earlier in a shared transaction makes a later native payment revert for routers that settle value without their own sync
findings.difference: Ethereum has the same code path. The networks differ in how often one transaction carries the operations of several users. Among the most recent transactions that hold a PoolManager Swap event, 342 of 463 on World Chain, 300 of 600 on Soneium and 62 of 600 on Base were ERC-4337 handleOps calls, and bundles with two or three user operations occur on all three. On Ethereum the count was 7 of 600. EntryPoint v0.6 to v0.9, Multicall3 and the public Simple7702Account hold code on all 21 networks, and senders with an EIP-7702 delegation were among the sampled swap senders on 13 of them. Tempo is left out of the chain list because no transaction there can carry native value (cleared in an earlier cycle), so the path has no target.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync has no lock check and no caller check. For a token it stores the currency and balanceOf(PoolManager) in two transient slots and returns (src/PoolManager.sol:279-289, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). Nothing clears the currency slot when the call ends. Only a later sync or a later ERC-20 settle changes it (src/PoolManager.sol:283, 286, 361). 2. unlock returns with the lock flag false and reverts unless every delta is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). The synced currency and its reserves are therefore the only PoolManager values that one party can leave for the next party inside one transaction. 3. _settle reads the synced currency first. When it is nonzero and msg.value is above zero the call reverts with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:349-356). The comment at src/PoolManager.sol:348 tells integrators to call sync before a native settle. 4. The attacker needs one call, sync(X) for any token X, that runs before the victim's operation in the same transaction. Carriers: an earlier user operation in a handleOps bundle, the validation step of any operation in the bundle (all four EntryPoint versions run every validation before the first execution), a pre hook of a CoW order, a call in a relayer or delegated account batch. 5. Test, read only. For recent swaps the original call was replayed at its parent block by eth_call. The sender address received the code of the public Simple7702Account by state override and ran executeBatch of [original call] as control and of [PoolManager.sync(token), original call] as test. Of the replays whose control succeeded, 209 native value replays and 193 token input replays gave the same result, and 9 and 7 reverted in the test only. The revert data was ExecuteError(1, NonzeroNativeValue) in 15 of the 16 cases and a router specific error 0x81ceff30 in one (Elysium, cause not decoded). 6. Contracts that reverted: Ethereum 0x3e8282bd1bfabd23249701e978e9db3df3d7073a (unverified, 187,745 transactions). Soneium LiFiDiamond 0x864b314d4c5a0399368609581d3e8933a63b9232 on routes through EisenDiamond 0x7e36665858d17fd1cbfd4fd464d2a3da49aa3b9d, whose facet 0x0b20601669dbce7e14210e24ca2b748cfb6dfc08 is unverified; EisenDiamond was the swap sender in 18.1 percent of 4,082 recent Soneium Swap events. Avalanche AvaxHookRouterV2 0xc8b2b67a1e286f74648a705617d54a0415fc651a (verified source line 103 calls settle with value and no sync), SwapHelper 0xde9d7290959b6060860b983b32f2d65b2701ebc2 and 0xfe807eb087439ec6e59ed5f93fad011223cb50f9. Arc 0x944fe8becf9a02a3e9378b4cadde1b14ef8d2ed9. BNB Smart Chain 0xdc0e98fd40ccd1c1d7084de9f254d7853846cc6e and 0x95337791024b5f0480b353fbafd2882b4d8e99c8. Monad 0x7db99f225af7a1a21b7b6468ed28f4bc60fbe937. Robinhood Chain 0x29d8d0a5c38716ebb4ae1786a46cf0ab74d480db, the sender of 11.0 percent of 5,624 recent Swap events. Zora 0xdb2e211c43ee4ac4665c44e8ae6723adfd62a07f. Elysium 0xa834e70303322d86e5dae95ee47e9c6a073d9812. 7. By source reading only, without a replay: the verified NodeRouter implementation 0x893f30424f8e6064b1d7284e5415be8413901c0d on World Chain (4.3 percent of sampled swaps there) calls settle with value and no sync at line 1127, as do the verified Bot 0xe41698520e4817b55c1841859a36847d50f0c82f (line 1014) and Router 0xeff6cb8b614999d130e537751ee99724d01aa167 (line 836) on Ethereum. 8. Inside a real bundle: three Base handleOps transactions replayed through eth_simulateV1 with a sync placed before handleOps kept UserOperationEvent.success true and lost their PoolManager swaps (5 to 4, 1 to 0 and 2 to 0 Swap events). The account behind them, with swap sender 0x5c40d83c6361aef9604c3d9a20d8452d496035eb, catches the failed leg and ends without trading. 9. No wrong credit follows from the leftover state. A payer that calls sync itself replaces both slots (src/PoolManager.sol:286). A payer that sends value without sync reverts at line 356. A zero value settle against the leftover credits its own caller with the balance rise since the stale sync, which is the attacker's own donation, or reverts on the checked subtraction at line 360 when the balance fell.
findings.impact: No funds move to the attacker and none are locked. The victim's native input swap reverts and the victim pays the gas of the failed operation. In an ERC-4337 bundle that fee still goes to the bundler. Accounts that catch the failure end the operation without the trade. The attacker can repeat this in every transaction it shares with the victim. Users of the canonical Universal Router, the PositionManager and the 0x Settler are unaffected. The largest exposed public paths found are LI.FI routes through Eisen on Soneium, where half of the sampled swap transactions travel in bundles, the NodeRouter on World Chain, where three quarters do, and launchpad routers on Avalanche.
findings.preconditions: The victim's call and the attacker's sync run in one transaction with no sync and no ERC-20 settle by anyone in between. The victim pays native value through a contract that does not call sync before settle. The attacker holds no role. It needs a place ahead of the victim in the same transaction: its own operation in the same bundle, or a bundle that it submits itself, since handleOps accepts any caller. A sync costs 27,891 to 35,717 gas as a standalone transaction on seven networks by eth_estimateGas, and less inside a bundle, plus the overhead of one user operation. Not confirmed: how often an outsider's operation lands directly ahead of a given victim in the bundles of World Chain, Soneium and Base, and whether the listed unverified contracts are open to the public or are single operator bots.
findings.mitigations: Router authors: call sync(address(0)) immediately before every settle that carries value, as the canonical routers and the 0x Settler do. Smart account users: place a sync(address(0)) call first in the same batch when a route pays native value through another router. Deployer: the state cannot be removed without a code change. A change that clears the synced currency when unlock begins would remove it and would break callers that sync before unlock. Publishing the rule at src/PoolManager.sol:348 for integrators on bundle heavy networks costs nothing.

(on https://robinhood.drpc.org), Monad 0x230fc6a1..., and Ethereum 0xfd340225... (on https://mainnet.gateway.tenderly.co; the endpoint in networks.json refused the block as archive state). The revert data was ExecuteError(1, 0xb0ec849e) in six of them. On Soneium the payload is a router error 0x9eea691b that wraps 0xb0ec849e. My own Keccak gives 0xb0ec849e for NonzeroNativeValue(). The third run shows that the synced slot is the only cause and that a sync(address(0)) before the payment removes the revert. eth_simulateV1 on https://mainnet.base.org/ for the handleOps transactions 0xb5e34489... and 0x8e445f70... (EntryPoint v0.6, bundler code overridden in the same way): the control produced 1 and 5 PoolManager Swap events, the test with a preceding sync produced 0 and 4, and UserOperationEvent.success stayed true in all four runs. A Multicall3.aggregate3 probe that I ran on all 21 endpoints returned a zero currency slot, lock and delta count at the start, the token address in the currency slot after sync(token), a reserves slot equal to balanceOf(PoolManager), ManagerLocked (0x54e3ca0d) for a settle outside unlock, and a zero currency slot after sync(address(0)). eth_getCode shows code of equal length on all 21 networks for EntryPoint v0.6 (23,689 bytes), v0.7 (16,035), v0.8 (21,738), v0.9 (22,425), Multicall3 (3,808) and Simple7702Account (3,639). Verified sources fetched from Sourcify: EntryPoint v0.7 runs the validation loop at lines 182 to 194 and the execution loop at lines 199 to 201; v0.6 has handleOps at line 92 and the execution loop at 108; v0.8 calls _iterateValidationPhase at line 65 and executes at 71; v0.9 does the same at lines 85 and 91. Routescan returns AvaxHookRouterV2.sol with settle{value: paid}() at line 103 and no sync before it, and sync at line 106 before the token settle at 108. Sourcify returns NodeRouter (exact match, World Chain) with settle{value: amountToPay}() at line 1127 and sync at line 1132 before the token settle at 1138. World Chain 50 of 81, four bundles with more than one operation, the largest held four. Ethereum 1 of 120. The shares are of the same order as the ones in the finding. eth_estimateGas for sync(token) gave 27,891 on World Chain, 33,309 on Arc, about 35,400 to 35,500 on Ethereum, Base, Soneium and Avalanche, and 35,813 on Arbitrum One. Tempo answers an eth_call that carries value 1 with 'value transfer not allowed', which supports leaving Tempo out. Not repeated by me: the replays on BNB Smart Chain, Zora and Elysium, the third Base bundle, the sender shares of EisenDiamond and of the Robinhood Chain contract, the source lines of the Ethereum Bot and Router, the transaction count of 0x3e8282bd..., the count of EIP-7702 senders, and the CoW hooks page. I found no primary source that contradicts the claim.
verification.codeCheck: sync has no modifier and no caller check (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). For a token it writes the currency and balanceOf(PoolManager) to two transient slots (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32). For address(0) it writes zero to the currency slot only (src/PoolManager.sol:283, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-25). The currency slot is written at three places in src/: the two branches of sync and the reset in the token branch of _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:361). unlock does not touch it at entry or exit (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), so a value set by one party stays for the next party in the same transaction. _settle reads the slot first (line 350). When it is nonzero and msg.value is above zero it reverts with NonzeroNativeValue at line 356, before any accounting. settle and settleFor are the only payable entry points and both end there (lines 300-307). The comment at line 348 asks integrators to sync before a native settle. Guards I looked for that could change the result: none clears the slot for the victim. The subtraction at line 360 is checked, so a balance below the stale reserves reverts and cannot credit. The credited currency (line 364) and the measured balance (line 359) come from the same slot, so a stale sync cannot turn a payment in one currency into a credit in another. The int128 cast at line 364 and the delta count check at line 112 work as usual. The only other reader of the slot is collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52), which reverts for the stale currency and concerns the fee controller alone. A caller that runs sync itself overwrites both slots (line 286) or zeroes the currency (line 283), which is why the canonical routers pass. A liquidity removal produces credits that leave through take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and never calls settle with value, so this path cannot block a withdrawal. The code path is as the finding states: a repeatable revert for payers of native value that skip sync, and no movement of funds. Actor check: sync is open to any account, so unprivileged is right. The victims are users of third party routers that skip the sync asked for at line 348; users of the canonical routers are outside it. Severity check: no loss path and no blocked withdrawal, which is the low level of the scale.
verification.corrections: The mechanism and the actor stand. Six points need adjusting. 1. Ref: F-014 already records that a stale sync makes a later native settle revert at src/PoolManager.sol:356. This entry extends F-014 with carriers and exposed routers and should carry that id. 2. Soneium: the revert data is ExecuteError(1, 0x9eea691b(bytes)) with 0xb0ec849e inside the inner payload, where the finding quotes ExecuteError(1, 0xb0ec849e). 3. Carriers: the statement that handleOps accepts any caller holds for EntryPoint v0.6, v0.7 and v0.8. The verified v0.9 source requires tx.origin == msg.sender and a caller without code (lines 68 to 75), so on v0.9 a sync cannot be placed in front of handleOps inside one transaction, and the carrier must be an operation inside the bundle. 4. Carriers: a sync made in the validation step works only in a bundle that the attacker submits itself. ERC-7562 treats TSTORE like SSTORE (OP-070) and limits validation to the account's own or associated storage, so a bundler that follows it rejects such an operation. A sync in the execution step of an earlier operation is under no such rule. 5. Preconditions: top level value is not needed. The Monad and Robinhood Chain transactions carry zero value at the top level and still end in NonzeroNativeValue, so routers that pay native value from their own balance are exposed too. 6. Reach: an exposed router or account was shown on 11 of the 20 listed networks (Ethereum, Base, Zora, World Chain by source only, Soneium, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, Arc). On the other nine the path exists in the code and no exposed integration was shown. Also: every replay ran against the PoolManagers deployed today, which are other bytecode than a build of this checkout. For this build the finding rests on the source lines, which I read. The position of the attacker ahead of the victim inside a third party bundle remains unconfirmed, as the finding says. The finding is outside the review's stated goal: it takes no funds held by the PoolManager and blocks no withdrawal.

findings.title: One Polygon pool already uses the native token contract 0x1010 as a currency, it holds no liquidity, and the inner frame tests leave the finding unchanged
findings.difference: Polygon has a genesis contract at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 whose balanceOf returns the native POL balance of an account and whose transfer returns false unless msg.value equals the amount. Ethereum has no ERC-20 face of its native asset in the protocol.
findings.mechanism: 1. The precondition that someone initializes a pool with 0x1010 has been met once. Pool 0x79d1ed6dc35a3472253c1a5f4b13edfc1481e3b4bd70189c481cbf04b34cbf73 pairs 0x1010 with the token 0x5eb10e40c4969dba42f344eb0cc2cd1a4bb3ad21 since block 70,895,654. It has zero liquidity, the PoolManager holds none of the other token, and no protocol fee accrued under 0x1010. 2. From a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address, called by another account, 0x1010 answered transfer of 0 with true, transfer of 1 with false, balanceOf under STATICCALL with the native balance, and reverted on value calls, on the ten hook selectors and on unlockCallback. This equals the top level results of cycles 1 and 2, so take of a non-zero amount still fails the success test at src/types/Currency.sol:64-74. 3. Among all 6,772 currencies that the PoolManager holds, 0x1010 is the only one whose balanceOf equals the native balance, so no second address measures POL. 4. Walk across the two ids. sync(0x1010) records the native balance. A native settle with value then reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:356. sync(address(0)) clears the synced currency (src/PoolManager.sol:281-283), and a later sync(0x1010) reads the balance again, so the stored reserve is never older than the last native credit. A native take or a native fee collection between sync(0x1010) and settle lowers the balance and makes settle revert at src/PoolManager.sol:360. A credit under 0x1010 therefore still needs POL that reached the PoolManager without a call, and it still cannot be paid out.
findings.impact: Unchanged. POL forced into the PoolManager and booked under 0x1010 cannot leave as that currency. The one existing pool holds nothing. Pools that hold POL under address(0) are not affected.
findings.preconditions: A custom contract must force POL into the PoolManager between sync and settle. The actor loses its own funds. No path takes funds of other users.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces and indexers on Polygon should refuse 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 as a pool currency and should flag the existing pool. The probe of 0x1010 should be repeated after every Bor fork, because forks can replace genesis contract code and recent forks were distributed privately.

verification.factCheck: The Initialize logs of the Polygon PoolManager name 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 exactly once: transaction 0xc379c9cb2f0c0b51fd792c8983c2b6ec091f7a23c3d85ba11bd077415886e443 at block 70,895,654, pool id 0x79d1ed6dc35a3472253c1a5f4b13edfc1481e3b4bd70189c481cbf04b34cbf73, currency1 0x5eb10e40c4969dba42f344eb0cc2cd1a4bb3ad21, fee 3000, tick spacing 60, no hook. StateView reports zero liquidity for it, the PoolManager holds none of the other token, and protocolFeesAccrued for 0x1010 is zero. At block 97,816,608 eth_getBalance(PoolManager) and balanceOf(PoolManager) on 0x1010 both return 3,064,824.134955069793283705 POL. Called from the PoolManager address at the top level, and again as an inner frame with Multicall3 code placed at the PoolManager address and another account as sender, transfer of 0 returns a 32 byte true, transfer of 1 and of 1 POL return a 32 byte zero, balanceOf is unchanged, and the unlockCallback selector and empty calldata revert. A 1 wei call with empty calldata to the PoolManager reverts, and 0x1010.transfer(PoolManager, 1) with value 1 reverts, so 0x1010 cannot push POL into the PoolManager. sync(0x1010) on the deployed PoolManager succeeds. I rebuilt the currency list from all 20,316 Initialize logs: 7,457 token addresses, of which 6,772 have a non-zero PoolManager balance at block 97,817,048. 0x1010 is the only one whose balance equals the native balance. I repeated eight of the sixteen call shapes of the stub sweep and did not repeat the ten hook selectors.
verification.codeCheck: sync(0x1010) stores the native balance as the reserve (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286, src/types/Currency.sol:94). While 0x1010 is synced, _settle rejects any msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:356) and credits balance minus reserve with a checked subtraction (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). settle and settleFor are the only payable functions (src/PoolManager.sol:300, src/PoolManager.sol:305) and src/ has no receive or fallback function, so inside the window the native balance can rise only through a forced transfer. sync(address(0)) clears only the synced currency (src/PoolManager.sol:281-283, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:17-21), and the next sync(0x1010) reads the balance again, so a native payment is never inside a 0x1010 window. take(0x1010, to, amount) calls transfer with zero value (src/types/Currency.sol:73), the token answers a zero word for any non-zero amount, the test at src/types/Currency.sol:68 fails and the call reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86. I tried to turn the mirror into a gain. A native take, then sync(0x1010), then a forced return of the same POL gives a 0x1010 credit and leaves the native debit, which only msg.value can clear. A native fee collection between sync(0x1010) and settle is not stopped by the address comparison at src/ProtocolFees.sol:49, and it lowers the balance so that the settle reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:360 unless the settler adds its own POL. A 0x1010 credit can be cleared, minted as a claim or swapped in a pool that nobody else has funded, and it cannot be paid out. Native settlement never reads a balance (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354), so the 3.06 million POL held for address(0) pools are not reachable through the second id.
verification.corrections: Nothing wrong in the mechanism. The figure 6,772 is the number of pooled currencies with a non-zero balance, out of 7,457 token addresses. The actor value unprivileged is formally right because any account can do every step, and the only party that can lose is the account that forces its own POL in. No user who did nothing unusual is exposed, so this entry is not a path to funds of others.

findings.title: TITHE on Robinhood Chain pays accrued holder rewards to the PoolManager when any account calls claimFor, and 10,002.56 TITHE can be booked through sync and settle today
findings.difference: This is a further token for the class recorded for Ethereum, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche, found on Robinhood Chain with an amount that is due now. TITHE 0x3751b9250a90342e47173bd3a7c7de4f297c060a is a dividend paying token (functions magnifiedRewardPerShare, withdrawableRewardOf, excludedFromRewards, claimFor(address[])). The PoolManager is not excluded from rewards and claimFor has no caller check.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync, settle and take work as in the earlier findings of this class (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 349-365). 2. A caller runs sync(TITHE), then TITHE.claimFor([PoolManager]), then settle inside one unlock. The token transfers the accrued reward to the PoolManager, settle credits the rise to the caller, and take pays it out. 3. Read-only test at block 121,278,927 with a measuring stub at the PoolManager address: claimFor([PoolManager]) called by an ordinary account succeeds and raises balanceOf(PoolManager) by 10,002.5557 TITHE, from 97,123.82 to 107,126.38 after one third of the balance had been moved out for the test. The caller's own balance does not change. The source is not on Sourcify, so the reading of the functions rests on selector names and on this simulation.
findings.impact: 10,002.56 TITHE today, 6.9 percent of the 145,685.74 TITHE that the PoolManager holds, plus whatever accrues later. I found no price for TITHE. Without a caller the reward stays outside pool accounting, so liquidity providers do not receive it in either case. Four sampled tokens on Robinhood Chain share this selector set.
findings.preconditions: A pool or claim balance in a token that pays holder rewards on a call anyone can make. The other tokens with claimFor or similar functions that the sweep tried on the 21 networks changed nothing at the time of the call, which shows only that no amount was due then.
findings.mitigations: None in core. A hook or keeper can run the same bracket and donate the proceeds to the pool (src/PoolManager.sol:256-276).

Reply 404, no verified source for TITHE.
Names of the selectors found in the TITHE code: claimFor(address[]), withdrawableRewardOf(address), magnifiedRewardPerShare(), excludedFromRewards(address).

verification.factCheck: Queries on https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com (client nitro v3.13.0-rc.9) at block 121,368,672. TITHE 0x3751b925... has symbol TITHE and 18 decimals, balanceOf(PoolManager) is 145685737169972676053750, withdrawableRewardOf(PoolManager) is 10002555720378059060354 and excludedFromRewards(PoolManager) is 0. eth_simulateV1 without any override: claimFor([PoolManager]) sent from an ordinary account returns 10002555720378059060354 and emits a Transfer of that amount from the token contract to the PoolManager. balanceOf(PoolManager) rises to 155688292890350735114104, the caller's balance stays 0, withdrawableRewardOf(PoolManager) falls to 0, and the PoolManager address can then send out its old balance and a further 10,000 TITHE. The amount is the same as at the researcher's block 121,278,927, so no new reward was distributed in between. I did not check the price, the pools that hold TITHE or the three other tokens said to share the selector set. The token source is not verified, so the reading rests on the simulation.
verification.codeCheck: sync(TITHE) stores the balance, the claim raises it by a transfer from the token contract, and _settle credits the rise to whoever calls settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-364). The caller can take that amount or mint a claim (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 322-329). The reward was never recorded for a pool, a position or a claim, so no accounted balance falls. Without a caller the reward stays at the token contract, and after a claim outside a sync window it sits in the PoolManager as surplus that the next sync and settle cannot credit.
verification.corrections: Nothing wrong in the mechanism. This is one more token of the class in F-041, F-060, F-066 and F-067 and should be filed as a variant of that class. What is taken is unaccounted surplus, and the token has no price that I found.

findings.title: Any account can lower the PoolManager balance of XAMP through a public negative rebase, and 37 unpriced pooled tokens expose burn or transfer functions without a caller check
findings.difference: Token designs again. XAMP 0xf911a7ec46a2c6fa49193212fe4a2a9b95851c27 on Ethereum has an owner contract 0x8ceb211a7567cf399e1ee01e6974bf4a13b64c04 whose rebase() any account can call and which cuts every balance. The other tokens have burn(address,uint256), burnFrom without an allowance check, or transfer functions that move another holder's balance, open to any caller.
findings.mechanism: 1. A balance that falls without a take leaves pools recording more than the PoolManager holds, and the last holders to withdraw cannot be paid (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297 pays from one shared balance). A fall between sync and settle makes the subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 revert, so it cannot be turned into credit. 2. XAMP: in a read-only trial at block 26,476,665 an ordinary account called rebase() on the owner contract and balanceOf(PoolManager) fell by 1.0 percent, and the account's own balance fell by the same share. 3. The trial sweep found tokens where a call by an ordinary account lowered the PoolManager balance with no fee involved: 10 on Ethereum (for example directTransfer on 0x1d4214081985ad20aa3ca93a2206ae792635cbec and a public _transfer on 0x28c78083f81818e151d84f1103c1c34598281c55, which moved the amount to the caller, and burnFrom on 0x1a7ebb948e9d2a93f7117c693b35003a929c9d84), 9 on Unichain, 7 on Arbitrum One, 5 on Polygon, 3 on Robinhood Chain and 1 each on Monad, Arc and HyperEVM. Most are test tokens with an open burn(address,uint256).
findings.impact: 647.02 XAMP at the PoolManager, without a price. None of the 37 other tokens has a price at coins.llama.fi. Holders of these tokens can lose them at any address, so the PoolManager adds nothing to the hazard. The entry is recorded so that the class is not searched again.
findings.preconditions: A pool in such a token. The flaw sits in the token and its author chose it or missed it.
findings.mitigations: None in core. Interfaces can flag tokens whose balance a third party can lower.

XAMP 0xf911a7ec... has 9 decimals and owner 0x8ceb211a.... rebase() on that owner contract, sent from an ordinary account, succeeds with three logs and balanceOf(PoolManager) falls from 647017555174 to 640547379622, which is 1.0 percent. A second rebase() in the same block reverts, so the cut is limited per period. I ran the three named examples. directTransfer(PoolManager, caller, amount) on 0x1d4214... (symbol PNDX) moved the whole PoolManager balance of 3221609151992631643015 to the ordinary caller. _transfer(PoolManager, caller, amount) on 0x28c780... (symbol HPNE) moved 951380006741755555889104 to the caller. burnFrom(PoolManager, amount) on 0x1a7ebb... burned the PoolManager balance of 23935. coins.llama.fi has no price for these three and returns 0.0009 USD for XAMP with confidence 0.94, which makes the 647.02 XAMP worth less than one dollar. The code has no step that would let the PoolManager add to the loss or prevent it.

Any account can call rebase() on the XAMP owner contract and the open burn and transfer functions of the other tokens, and the attacker does not need to be the author of the token, which is what the schema asks for pool-creator. The finding also says XAMP has no price, while coins.llama.fi now returns 0.0009 USD. For PNDX and HPNE the caller receives the tokens of the PoolManager, so the effect for those two is a removal and not only a degradation. Severity low stays: the same call empties any other holder of these tokens, the PoolManager code plays no part, and none of the tokens has a market value that I could find.

findings.title: FACTR and TC on BNB Smart Chain join the tokens that count locked units in balanceOf and let any holder assign them to the PoolManager
findings.difference: FACTR 0xdefac16715671b7b6aeefe012125f1e19ee4b7d7 has transferAndLock(address,uint256,uint32,uint32,uint16) and TC 0x659049786cb66e4486b8c0e0ccc90a5929a21162 has freezeTo(address,uint256,uint64). Both let a holder send units that the recipient cannot move until a release time, and balanceOf counts them.
findings.mechanism: 1. settle credits the rise of balanceOf(PoolManager) since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-365). 2. Trial by eth_call with state overrides: the PoolManager address hands an ordinary account A one third of its balance, A calls the function with the PoolManager as recipient, and the stub then tries to send the full balance and the balance minus the amount. For both tokens the balance rose by the amount, the full transfer was refused and the transfer of the balance minus the amount passed. 3. A caller can therefore book locked units as a payment through sync and settle and take the same number of free units out, as described in F-078. 4. Ten tokens gave this result on the new list: FACTR, TC and eight without a price. The test ran on one token per selector family, and TC stands for a family of 5 tokens.
findings.impact: The PoolManager holds FACTR worth 78 USD and TC worth 1 USD at coins.llama.fi prices. The liquidity providers of those pools can be left with units that cannot be paid out until the lock ends.
findings.preconditions: The caller holds the token. No role is needed.
findings.mitigations: As for F-078: interfaces should hide pools of tokens whose balanceOf counts locked units that third parties can assign.

sources.supports: Trial sweep by eth_call with state overrides on the BNB Smart Chain list, rows of class locked-assign for FACTR and TC.

verification.factCheck: I repeated both trials with eth_simulateV1 on bsc-rpc.publicnode.com and no stub code. findings.title: Three route hooks on Arbitrum One pay swaps from their own token balance whatever currencies the pool names, so a pool against a worthless token empties them
findings.difference: None. The behaviour does not depend on the network. Three third party hooks on Arbitrum One (CamelotHook proxies 0x9b21e1cdd975e58f714fd1bd5a803198d5520088 and 0x157af7a18e040b9c8dc409c13140873d5bb24088, and GoldenGateFeeHook 0x195b3936afeae0f9ada52473bb34d67466a4c0c8) route swaps to an external exchange and hold working balances. The PoolManager behaves as written.
findings.mechanism: 1. The hooks have the flags beforeSwap and beforeSwapReturnDelta and no initialize flag, so PoolManager.initialize accepts any PoolKey that names them from any account (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-182). An eth_call of initialize from an ordinary account succeeded for all seven PoolKey variants on each hook. 2. Verified source of the CamelotHook implementation 0x57ea4782fbdb6cd8256aae28075ce3a0e7e13f0f, _beforeSwap lines 71 to 176: for an exact input swap the hook calls poolManager.take(sourceCurrency, hook, amount) where sourceCurrency is the input currency of the PoolKey, then swaps on the Algebra pool 0xB1026b8e7276e7AC75410F1fcbbe21796e8f7526 with hardcoded WETH and USDC. In algebraSwapCallback (lines 178 to 207) it pays that pool with IERC20(WETH).transfer or IERC20(USDC).transfer from its own balance. It then settles the bought amount in the output currency of the PoolKey and returns a delta of plus the input and minus the output. Nothing compares the currencies of the PoolKey with WETH and USDC. 3. In a pool that pairs a token W the attacker issues with USDC, a swap of W for USDC therefore takes W from the PoolManager, sells the hook's own WETH and hands the USDC to the swapper. The hook ends with W. Its deltas net to zero: the take debits it W (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297), the returned delta credits it W and debits it the output (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:287-311, src/PoolManager.sol:216-217), and its settle credits the output (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). The unlock therefore completes once the swapper has paid W. The mirror pool, WETH against a token W2 with the swap going from W2 to WETH, sells the hook's USDC. 4. Test inside a real unlock, without sending anything: debug_traceCall of the deployed Quoter 0x8928074CA1b241D8Ec02815881c1Af11E8bC5219 from an unrelated address, with a state override that writes slot0 of the foreign pool id in the PoolManager as initialize would. For 0x9b21e1cd, pool (codeless W, USDC), input 1650159984937101: the trace shows take(W, hook, 1650159984937101), WETH.transfer(Algebra pool, 1649829952940113) from the hook, sync(USDC), USDC.transfer(PoolManager, 2840657), settle, and the Quoter returns 2840657. For pool (WETH, codeless W2), input 64130252: USDC.transfer(Algebra pool, 64117425) from the hook and WETH.transfer(PoolManager, 37171745553261727), Quoter returns 37171745553261727. For 0x157af7a1 the same two runs return 14148521 USDC for its 8221214982138125 WETH and 20257073477671002 WETH for its 34923926 USDC. For GoldenGateFeeHook the runs return 3759006195674900 WETH for its 10843 units of WBTC and 1851 units of WBTC for its 659454474487714 WETH, through pool 0x03a3be7ab4aa263d42d63b6cc594f4fb3d3f3951. 5. The exact output branch of CamelotHook takes real WETH or USDC from the PoolManager in the callback (lines 193 and 203) and is credited in the pool currency. In a foreign pool that leaves the hook with an open WETH or USDC debt, so the unlock reverts with CurrencyNotSettled (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). PoolManager funds are not reachable through it.
findings.impact: The token balances of the three hooks: 64.130252 USDC and 0.00165 WETH at 0x9b21e1cd, 34.923926 USDC and 0.00822 WETH at 0x157af7a1, 0.00010843 WBTC and 0.00066 WETH at 0x195b3936, about 124 USD together at block 526824360. The balances belong to the hook operators. No funds held by the PoolManager for other pools are involved, and the pools of these hooks (five, one and one) keep working after the balances are gone because the normal path pays the exchange with the tokens it just took. The amount grows with whatever the operators leave on the hooks.
findings.preconditions: None. Any account can deploy a token, initialize the pool, add no liquidity and swap. The cost is gas. The runs above used a codeless address as the foreign currency, which works for the take because a transfer call to an address without code succeeds (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). A real run needs a token contract so that the swapper can settle its input. I did not send a transaction. Proxy 0x157af7a1 points at the unverified implementation 0xe43403ad1f3b53d1a59d31756bdb1b28b45631e7 and was judged from its traces, which match the verified one call for call.
findings.mitigations: The PoolManager deployer cannot change this. The hook owner can add a beforeInitialize check or compare the PoolKey currencies with the hardcoded tokens in beforeSwap, and can sweep the balances with the owner only multicall function. Until then the owners should keep no balance on the hooks.

sources.supports: Verified CamelotHook source: _beforeSwap takes the PoolKey input currency and trades hardcoded WETH and USDC (lines 71 to 176), algebraSwapCallback pays from the hook balance (178 to 207), owner only setFee, multicall and setEnabled (209 to 221).

debug_traceCall of Quoter.quoteExactInputSingle with a state override of the pool slot0, from 0x00000000000000000000000000000000c0ffee03: the call sequences and returned amounts quoted in the mechanism for the three hooks.

Blocks 526821824 to 526824360: EIP-1967 implementation slots of the two proxies, WETH, USDC and WBTC balances of the three hooks, eth_call of PoolManager.initialize from an ordinary account with seven PoolKey variants succeeding on each hook.
GoldenGateFeeHook is verified. Its source was fetched and scanned for value moves. The behaviour was established by trace.

ETH at 1721 USD on 23 November 2026, used for the USD estimates of this unit. Token prices in the ranking come from the same endpoint per network, pair with the most liquidity, position capped at half that liquidity.
take debits the caller in the currency it names and transfers that currency.
The hook delta returned from beforeSwap is accounted in the two currencies of the PoolKey.

findings.severityNote: Rated medium by the verifier. Filed as low because the balances at risk sit in the hooks themselves, outside the PoolManager, and the parties that lose are the hook operators and not pool users.

verification.factCheck: Sourcify holds CamelotHook 0x57ea4782fbdb6cd8256aae28075ce3a0e7e13f0f (match) and GoldenGateFeeHook 0x195b3936afeae0f9ada52473bb34d67466a4c0c8 (exact match). CamelotHook _beforeSwap (71 to 176) takes the PoolKey input currency, swaps hardcoded WETH and USDC on 0xB1026b8e7276e7AC75410F1fcbbe21796e8f7526 and pays that pool from its own balance in algebraSwapCallback (178 to 207). Nothing compares the PoolKey currencies with WETH and USDC. On chain at Arbitrum One block 526844458 (arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc): the two proxies have flags 0x88 and EIP-1967 implementations 0x57ea4782 and 0xe43403ad, GoldenGateFeeHook has flags 0xc8, and the balances are 1650159984937101 WETH and 64130252 USDC, 8221214982138125 WETH and 34923926 USDC, and 659454474487714 WETH and 10843 WBTC units. An eth_call of PoolManager.initialize from 0x00000000000000000000000000000000c0ffee77 succeeds for a pool of a codeless currency with USDC and for one with WETH on both proxies, and for pools with WETH and with WBTC at fee 0x800000 on GoldenGateFeeHook. I repeated the Quoter test with a state override of slot0 for the foreign pool id. For 0x9b21e1cd the quote for 1650159984937101 units of the codeless currency returns 2945354 USDC and the mirror pool returns 35737211665487918 WETH for 64130252 units. For 0x157af7a1 the results are 14661595 USDC and 19501592155717823 WETH. For GoldenGateFeeHook with fee 0x800000 the results are 3759111254671993 WETH for 10843 units and 1851 WBTC units for 659454474487714 units. A debug_traceCall on arbitrum.drpc.org shows the sequence the finding describes: take of the codeless currency, a transfer of WETH or WBTC from the hook to the exchange pool, sync, a transfer of the output from the hook to the PoolManager, settle.
verification.codeCheck: initialize accepts the PoolKey because the hooks have no initialize flag (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-182). take debits the hook in the currency it names and a transfer call to an address without code counts as success (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). The returned delta credits the hook the input and debits it the output in the PoolKey currencies (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:266-279 and 295-313, src/PoolManager.sol:220-226), and settle credits the output the hook transferred (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). The swap amount becomes zero after the hook delta, which passes the check at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:276 and makes Pool.swap return a zero delta (src/libraries/Pool.sol:320). The hook ends with no open delta, the swapper owes the worthless input and is owed the real output, and the count check at src/PoolManager.sol:112 passes once the swapper settles. I found no guard in src/ that stops this. The PoolManager loses nothing: every unit it pays out was transferred in by the hook in the same call. The exact output branch leaves the hook with a WETH or USDC debt from the callback take (CamelotHook 193 and 203) and reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:112, as the finding says.
verification.corrections: 1. The mechanism cites src/PoolManager.sol:216-217 for the hook delta. The lines are 220-226. 2. GoldenGateFeeHook routes only when the PoolKey fee is 0x800000 (source line 263). 3. GoldenGateFeeHook has a shorter route that the finding did not see. When hookData is 20 bytes long the hook uses it as the exchange pool address without comparing it with referencePools (lines 284 to 285), stores it as _activePool (313), and uniswapV3SwapCallback sends WBTC and WETH from the hook balance to that address in the amounts the caller states (365 to 380). A swap in the real pool of the hook with a caller made pool address therefore reaches the same balances. I read this in the source and did not run it. 4. Scope: the balances are the fee float of the hook operators (CamelotHook keeps 0.02 percent through ratio 9998, GoldenGateFeeHook keeps its fee until harvest). The victims are those operators. They are outside the victim class of the threat model, the funds are outside the PoolManager, and the fault does not depend on the network. The actor value is still unprivileged because any account can do every step. 5. The quotes differ from the finding by a few percent because the exchange price moved between the two blocks.

findings.title: SpawnerHook on Base keeps one pending ETH fee bucket for every spawn token and pays it to the creator of whichever token is sold when the threshold is crossed
findings.difference: None. The behaviour does not depend on the network. SpawnerHook 0xb476c448da4453208df4e371fee26f4e630d3044 is a third party hook with 15,249 pools in the Base census.
findings.mechanism: Verified source, _afterSwap lines 234 to 310. The hook charges its fee in the unspecified currency of the swap. For an exact input sale of a spawn token the fee currency is native ETH, and the pending amount is kept in spawnerFeesBalance[feeToken] with feeToken equal to the zero address (line 290), so one number serves all pools. When the number reaches minimumFeeDistribution the hook resets it and calls _distributeFees(spawnToken, creator, total) for the token of the current swap (lines 295 to 297): a quarter goes to the Spawner owner, half buys tokens that are sent to that creator, a quarter is deposited for that creator (lines 320 to 360). Fees taken in a spawn token are converted and stored under that token, so only the ETH side is shared. beforeInitialize accepts any caller for a pool of native ETH against a spawn token (lines 188 to 198), and every swap through a whitelisted router calls spawner.createSpawn(swapper, spawnToken) (line 303), which makes the swapper the creator of a new spawn token, so an account can become a creator and sell its token when the bucket is close to the threshold. I did not read Spawner.createSpawn in full.
findings.impact: ETH fees pending for other tokens, at most the distribution threshold per round. spawnerFeesBalance(address(0)) was 945018262798261 wei (about 1.6 USD) at block 61256529. The hook holds 0.5627 ETH in total. The rest of that balance is not tracked by this ledger and I found no function that pays it out to a caller.
findings.preconditions: The sale must go through a router on the hook whitelist. minimumFeeDistribution is not public and was not read. Not simulated.
findings.mitigations: The hook author can keep the pending ETH per pool id. The PoolManager deployer cannot change this.

sources.supports: Verified SpawnerHook source: _beforeInitialize (188 to 198), _afterSwap with spawnerFeesBalance[feeToken] (234 to 310), _distributeFees (320 to 360).

Block 61256529: spawnerFeesBalance(address(0)) is 945018262798261, totalCreatorFees() is 26132431268132716624, native balance 562744349885641100 wei. The in unlock test with foreign PoolKeys ends in revert 0xb76b08ae from afterSwap.

verification.factCheck: Sourcify holds SpawnerHook 0xb476c448da4453208df4e371fee26f4e630d3044 as an exact match. _afterSwap (234 to 310) takes the fee in the unspecified currency, keeps the pending amount in spawnerFeesBalance[feeToken], and when the amount reaches minimumFeeDistribution it calls _distributeFees for the token and creator of the current swap (290 to 300). For an ETH fee the mapping slot is address(0), so one number serves every pool. Spawner.createSpawn(swapper, spawnToken) at line 303 makes the swapper the creator of a new spawn token (Spawner.sol 218 to 227, Spawn.sol 66). On chain at Base block 61285777 (mainnet.base.org): spawnerFeesBalance(address(0)) is 945018262798261, totalCreatorFees() is 26132431268132716624, the native balance is 562744349885641146 wei, storage slot 3 holds 0.01 ether, which is minimumFeeDistribution, and slot 4 holds 10. The Spawner is 0x95fe5bc073763fed6e8572e33db9e0e1c06bc78e (read from the immutables in the hook code), isKilled() is false and totalSpawnCount() is 15241. The pending amount and the fee total are the same as at the finding's block 29,000 blocks earlier.
verification.codeCheck: The hook takes its fee with take and returns it as the afterSwap delta, so the swapper pays it (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:298-313, src/PoolManager.sol:220-226). The PoolManager accounting is unaffected. The shared number lives in the hook, and the ETH it pays out is the hook's own native balance. swap, modifyLiquidity and donate check that the pool is initialized before they call a hook (src/PoolManager.sol:154, 196 and 264), so the callbacks run only for pools that passed the hook's beforeInitialize.
verification.corrections: 1. The fee is ETH in two cases: an exact input sale of the spawn token and an exact output purchase (line 255). The finding names the first only. 2. minimumFeeDistribution is 0.01 ETH, read from slot 3. The finding left it unread. 3. The gain is small and conditional. The account that crosses the threshold receives 75 percent of the bucket (half as tokens bought for it, a quarter as a deposit) and 25 percent goes to the Spawner owner. With B pending from others and f paid by the account itself the net is 0.75 B minus 0.25 f, at most about 0.0075 ETH per round, and it is negative today because B is 0.000945 ETH and f would have to be about 0.009 ETH. Effect degrade describes this better than siphon. 4. Nobody ran the path. I did not find the whitelisted routers and did not simulate a sale, so the profit side rests on the source alone and the evidence for it is inferred. 5. Scope: the ETH is held by the hook, outside the PoolManager, and the behaviour does not depend on the network.

findings.title: Any account can burn the PoolManager's whole Imperium balance on Polygon today through scanAndClean, and two more pooled tokens carry the same kind of rule
findings.difference: The cause is a token rule, and Polygon is where the token and its pools are. ImperiumToken (IMP) at 0xf236d2b542eadf2246b307bb1278eafb94fadda6 has a function scanAndClean(address[] targets) without any caller check. For each target that has received no IMP for 90 days it sets the balance to zero, lowers totalSupply by the amount and credits 5 percent to the token owner. The token records lastActivity only for the receiver of a transfer, so an address that only pays out is idle by this rule. This is the class of the DeadToken finding on Base (F-085). It differs in two points: the caller needs no token balance, and nobody but the token owner receives anything, so the caller gains nothing and the pools lose the amount. The same selector search found BankToken (symbol USD.M) at 0x718102f857b91eb573b78c41c654af2db05dd0b1 on Ethereum with reclaimInactive(address), and a second deployment of the DeadToken code at 0x720f29e57cda0a987b7ff37ace02b7021aacbc0c on Polygon. The PoolManager holds dust of those two (800 base units and 1 base unit).
findings.mechanism: 1. Core keeps no total per currency. Pools record their reserves in pool state, and the token balance is read only in sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-365). A take pays with a plain transfer call and reverts when the token refuses (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-87). When the balance falls without a take, pools record more than the PoolManager holds. 2. ImperiumToken._transfer writes lastActivity[to] = block.timestamp and nothing for the sender (verified source, lines 88 to 101). scanAndClean (lines 202 to 215) checks block.timestamp - lastActivity[target] >= burnInactiveAfter and balanceOf[target] > 0, then sets the balance to zero, subtracts the amount from totalSupply and adds amount * protocolFee / 10000 to the owner. burnInactiveAfter is the constant 90 days (line 18) and protocolFee reads 500. 3. State today: lastActivity(PoolManager) is 1753576517 (27 July 2025), which is 484 days before Polygon block 97,824,929 (timestamp 1795442866). balanceOf(PoolManager) is 3,029.036932838782921101 IMP. 4. Read-only trial at block 97,824,929: with a measuring stub at the PoolManager address (state override) an account without code and without IMP called scanAndClean([PoolManager]). The call succeeded and balanceOf(PoolManager) went from 3,029.036932838782921101 to 0. A plain eth_call of scanAndClean([PoolManager]) from an address with no code and no tokens, without any override, also returns without revert. The same result came back with the block time moved forward by 8 hours, 91 days and 400 days. 5. The PoolManager takes no part in the call. No unlock, sync, settle or take is involved, so nothing in core can see or stop it. 6. The balance does not come back. Later payments into the PoolManager restart the timer for 90 days and are recorded by pools as well. 7. BankToken.reclaimInactive(account) has no caller check either. When the owner set autoAction to 1 it burns the whole balance of an account that is past INACTIVITY_PERIOD, and with 2 it sends the balance to the treasury or the owner. In the trial with the block time moved forward by 91 days and by 400 days the PoolManager balance of 800 base units fell to 0, and it stayed at the current time and at 8 hours. 8. The second DeadToken deployment answers getTimeUntilClaimable(PoolManager) with 0 and whiteListedPool(PoolManager) with 0, so the PoolManager is a valid target there now. Its balance has been 1 base unit at every sample since Polygon block 79,980,384. I found no verified source for this address and identified it by its selectors (claimIdleTokens, getTimeUntilClaimable, lastTransferTime).
findings.impact: Liquidity providers and claim holders of the IMP pools lose the pooled IMP: 3,029.04 IMP, of which 2,877.59 vanish and 151.45 go to the token owner 0xe77e6c411f2ee01f1cfbcccb1c418c80f1a534fe. The Initialize logs read in cycle 4 show two pools with IMP as a currency. GeckoTerminal reports a total reserve of about 1.57 USD for the token and no price, and coins.llama.fi and DexScreener have no entry, so the amount at stake today is negligible. The loss stays inside currency IMP because deltas are kept per currency (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378). The finding matters as a pattern: a pool in any token with such a rule can be emptied by an account that holds nothing, and the PoolManager is idle by a receiver based timer whenever a pool sees no inflow for the period. The step 2 trials found no token with a market price above 1,000 USD at a PoolManager that has such a rule, on the lists available (see the leads for the networks where the list is incomplete).
findings.preconditions: A pool or claim balance in a token that lets any caller remove the balance of an idle holder. For IMP: no IMP received by the PoolManager for 90 days, which holds since 25 October 2025. No role, hook, token balance or attacker made token is needed. I did not send any transaction and did not read the fee and hook settings of the two pools.
findings.mitigations: None in core. The token owner cannot exempt an address from scanAndClean in this source (excludeFromFee covers the fee only). Liquidity providers should leave IMP pools. Interfaces and routers should refuse or flag currencies whose code holds scanAndClean, reclaimInactive, sweepInactive or claimIdleTokens selectors, and a deployment that lists tokens should test each token with a call from a stranger at a shifted block time before it is shown to users.

_settle reads the token balance and credits the rise since sync. No other place compares pool records with the balance.
A take is a plain transfer call that reverts when the token refuses, which is what happens once the balance is gone.

findings.severityNote: Rated medium by the verifier. Filed as low because the verifier found that the only liquidity provider of the two Imperium pools is the token owner and that the other side of the pools is worth less than one cent, so no third party funds are at risk today.

verification.codeCheck: The path holds. The only reads of a token balance in src/ are sync (src/PoolManager.sol:285) and _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:359), both through balanceOfSelf (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). No persistent per currency total exists: CurrencyReserves keeps the synced currency and reserves in transient storage only (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:15-38). A fall of the token balance outside a take is therefore seen by no check. take debits the caller and then calls transfer on the token (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). When the token refuses, the call reverts with the wrapped ERC20TransferFailed error (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86), and Imperium refuses with Insufficient balance once the balance is gone (ImperiumToken.sol line 90). The same transfer is used by collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). Guards I looked for and did not find in the way: the call to scanAndClean never enters the PoolManager, so the lock, the delta count at the end of unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:112) and the synced currency check in collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52) play no part. The burn gives the caller nothing inside core either: a sync before the burn and a settle after it reverts on the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360, so no credit can be booked. Deltas are kept per currency (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378), so the shortfall stays inside currency IMP. Pool state read through extsload with the layout of this repository (the _pools mapping at slot 6, liquidity at offset 3 of Pool.State, src/libraries/Pool.sol:83-91): pool 0x5d1dd78d9934a3db691919cc020e75512a38a952e7c17502fc28d945464e1985 (native POL and IMP, fee 3000, tick spacing 60, no hook) records liquidity 12489942943046485015 at tick 109762, and pool 0x9356106411a79af20fc90e7ec5d5608dce68857e91f5ce531e1a7ec8ad79a48c (USDT and IMP, fee 3000, tick spacing 60, no hook) records liquidity 21599229951. From these figures the two full range positions record about 3,019.2 IMP and 1.18 IMP, and the rest of the 3,029.04 IMP is swap fee owed to the first position. Pools therefore record IMP that the PoolManager would no longer hold after the call.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged is right for the mechanism: the caller needs no role, no token balance and no contract, and both pools have no hook. The impact text needs three corrections. First, no claim holder exists. The PoolManager has emitted no ERC-6909 Transfer log with id IMP, and protocolFeesAccrued for IMP is 0. Second, the only liquidity provider is the token owner. Each pool has one ModifyLiquidity log, made through the PositionManager 0x1ec2ebf4f37e7363fdfe3551602425af0b3ceef9 with IMP paid in by 0xe77e6c411f2ee01f1cfbcccb1c418c80f1a534fe, and ownerOf for position tokens 33811 and 33815 returns that address today. The party that loses the pooled IMP is the party that wrote the rule and that receives the 5 percent. No third party funds are at risk in these two pools today. Third, the other side of the pools is about 0.052 POL and 396 base units of USDT, so the value that a failed removal could strand is below one cent. The PoolManager received IMP in four transfers (155.9987, 2861.8602, 10 and 1.1781 IMP in blocks 74,452,496 to 74,452,887) and has never paid IMP out. For BankToken the finding leaves out that autoAction reads 2, so the 800 base units would go to the treasury, which is the owner, and that the period is 365 days: the rule first applies to the PoolManager on about 26 December 2026 unless it sends or receives the token before then. For the DeadToken copy the caller needs a DEAD balance, as on Base; the threshold was not read because the source is not verified. The finding is of the class of F-085 and adds no network property: the cause is the token in all three cases, so it does not answer the question of a weakness that follows from how a network differs from Ethereum. I kept medium in line with F-085 and F-079 (loss limited to pools of particular tokens, negligible amounts today). I could not read the two liquidity transactions by hash on the public endpoints, so the sender of those transactions rests on the Transfer logs and on ownerOf.

findings.title: Any account can set the starting price of a pool or move the price of an empty pool for free, and core takes no price or amount bound on the first deposit (OpenZeppelin M-03, acknowledged and not resolved)
findings.difference: None in the code path, which is the same on Ethereum. Networks differ in who can see a pending transaction, and I fetched no source on that for the 21 networks in this session. The variant that initializes a predictable PoolKey ahead of its creator needs no view of pending transactions.
findings.mechanism: 1. initialize accepts any caller and stores the caller's price (src/PoolManager.sol:117-134, src/libraries/Pool.sol:100-107). The price is not part of the pool id (src/types/PoolId.sol:11-15), and a second initialize reverts (Pool.sol:101). Whoever is first sets the price. 2. swap has no check for liquidity. With zero liquidity in range each step returns zero amounts and moves the price to the next tick or to the limit (Pool.sol:344-437, src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-106), so any account can move the price of a pool without in range liquidity to any value inside the bounds for a zero delta. 3. modifyLiquidity computes the two amounts from the stored price (Pool.sol:206-236) and accepts no minimum or maximum from the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184). 4. A provider that adds liquidity after the price was set away from the market deposits at that price, and the attacker then swaps against the position at the off market price. 5. Nothing in src closes this. The report records the team's answer that peripheral contracts add slippage protection. I did not read the periphery. 6. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers an eth_call of initialize from an arbitrary account for an unused PoolKey returned ticks 0, 138162, -887272 and 887271 for four prices of my choice.
findings.impact: The first liquidity provider of a pool who adds through code without amount bounds can lose part of the deposit, up to most of its value, to the account that set the price. Pools that already hold in range liquidity are not affected, because moving their price costs the swap amounts.
findings.preconditions: A pool that is not yet initialized or has no in range liquidity, and a provider that adds liquidity without checking the pool price or bounding the amounts. The attacker needs no role.
findings.mitigations: Initialize and add liquidity in one transaction with amount bounds, as the report's update says the periphery does. Integrations that call modifyLiquidity themselves should read slot0 and compare the price before they add.

findings.title: A donation is shared by whoever holds in-range liquidity at the instant of the call, and core has no statement that keeps liquidity added moments earlier from collecting it
findings.difference: None in the code path, which is the same on every network. What differs per network is how easily an ordinary account can place its own calls directly around another party's donation: inside one transaction when the donation can be triggered by any caller, or in neighbouring transactions where pending transactions are visible and ordering can be bought. This unit did not establish the ordering rules of the 21 networks and names that as an open lead.
findings.mechanism: 1. donate(key, amount0, amount1) debits the caller and raises feeGrowthGlobal by amount * 2^128 / liquidity, where liquidity is the pool's active liquidity at slot0.tick when the call runs (src/PoolManager.sol:256-276, src/libraries/Pool.sol:466-480). There is no minimum holding time, no snapshot and no vesting. 2. A position added before the call earns its share liquidity / total through the ordinary fee growth path when it is next touched (Pool.sol:184-192, Position.sol:92-97) and can be removed right after. Adding and removing liquidity is open to any account and costs only the rounding of the amounts. 3. A second effect makes the set of recipients movable. When a zeroForOne swap ends exactly on the price of an initialized tick n, the tick is crossed and slot0.tick becomes n - 1 while the price is that of n (Pool.sol:413-432). A swap with sqrtPriceLimitX96 equal to the price of tick n does this on purpose. A donation made in that state goes to positions that cover tick n - 1, and positions whose lower bound is n receive nothing. 4. Spearbit 5.1.1 and Certora M-02 describe these two effects, both at medium. The recorded responses are comments (IPoolManager.sol:150-155, Pool.sol:409-412, Pool.sol:80-82). No statement in src closes either one. 5. Read-only log queries show donate in use: 108 Donate events in 5,000 blocks on Ethereum, 138 in 100,000 blocks on Robinhood Chain, 304 on Elysium and 7 on Arbitrum One. In the four transactions I opened, one per network, the donor is a contract and the same transaction also swaps through the pool that receives the donation.
findings.impact: The donor's funds reach other accounts than the liquidity providers they were meant for, and the long standing providers of that pool lose the share. The amount at risk is one donation at a time. The sampled donations are small: 8.0e12 units of currency0 on Ethereum, 11,230 units of currency1 on Arbitrum One, 5.11e18 units of an 18 decimal currency on Robinhood Chain. A donation that is funded by the swap that triggers it gives a caller who triggers it only its own money back, so the loss arises where the donated amount was accrued earlier or where another party's swap can be bracketed. I did not find a donor contract that pays out an earlier accrued balance on a public call, and I did not look for one beyond the four samples.
findings.preconditions: Some party donates to a pool. The attacker holds or can borrow both currencies for the length of the capture and can run its liquidity change directly before the donation: in the same transaction when the donating call is open to any caller, otherwise through transaction ordering on that network.
findings.mitigations: Donors should not donate amounts that are worth capturing in one call. A hook that distributes fees can pay them over time or require that liquidity was present before the block of the donation, and can check both slot0.tick and the price before donating, as the comment at Pool.sol:409-412 advises. Core could not close this without storing per position time data, which the reports do not ask for.

I did not open the Elysium sample again. I read both audit passages in the PDF files of this repository. Spearbit 5.1.1 is rated medium, describes the three transaction sandwich with liquidity added before and removed after the donation, and records the response that comments were added in PR 851, marked verified. Certora M-02 is rated medium, states that donate may pay the wrong tick when the price sits exactly on an initializable tick, and records the response acknowledged, will not be fixed, comments added in PR 851. No source contradicts the finding. The finding names no difference between a network and Ethereum, and I found none: the path is plain contract logic.
verification.codeCheck: donate carries onlyWhenUnlocked and noDelegateCall and has no condition on who holds liquidity or since when (src/PoolManager.sol:256-276). Pool.donate reads state.liquidity, reverts when it is zero, and adds amount * 2^128 / liquidity to the global fee growth of each currency (src/libraries/Pool.sol:466-480). The donor is debited the full amounts at PoolManager.sol:270, so the gift is paid by the donor and no reserve of another pool or position is touched. modifyLiquidity is open to any caller during an unlock and records msg.sender as the owner (PoolManager.sol:145-184). A position that is in range collects global growth minus the two outside values (Pool.sol:488-510) times its liquidity when it is next touched (src/libraries/Position.sol:91-97, Pool.sol:184-192). I looked for a snapshot, a minimum holding time or a per position start block and the text has none. The tick effect also holds: when a step ends on the price of the next tick the tick is crossed if it is initialized and result.tick is set to tickNext - 1 for zeroForOne (Pool.sol:413-432), the loop stops when the price equals the limit (Pool.sol:344), and the stored liquidity is the value after the crossing (Pool.sol:442). A position whose lower bound is that tick then falls in the first branch of getFeeGrowthInside (Pool.sol:498-500) and receives nothing from a donation made in that state. The interface comment at src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:149-155 and the comment at Pool.sol:409-412 warn about both effects and add no check.
verification.corrections: The actor value unprivileged stands for the mechanism: adding and removing liquidity around a call needs no role. Four points need correction or a limit. First, the effect is narrower than siphon suggests. The only funds that move are the donated amounts, which the donor gives up at PoolManager.sol:270. Principal and earlier fees of other providers cannot be reached through this path. Second, in all three receipts that I read the donation is made by a contract inside a transaction that also swaps through the same pool, so a caller who triggers it funds it. Capture then needs ordering around another user's swap, which is the same position a just in time provider has toward ordinary swap fees. The finding says this and I agree that it keeps the rating at low. Spearbit rates the mechanism medium, and medium would apply under SCHEMA.md once a donor is found that pays out a balance accrued earlier on a call open to anyone. None is known. Third, the remark on senders is slightly off: the most frequent Ethereum sender in the window is 0x3f8262ed65fdd4d46c0d008a49e938769bb22488 with 15 events, whose address ends in 488, and the next five end in 888. Fourth, the unit's raw file has no log count for Base, World Chain, X Layer, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche and Monad, because those queries failed, so four networks with donations is a lower bound. I queried second endpoints: BNB Smart Chain shows 22 Donate events in blocks 135,322,108 to 135,327,108 (13 from 0x8c7852bb503b4579c28a6fa2bcf112c7657a6488), and Base (61,353,982 to 61,358,982), Polygon (97,832,805 to 97,837,805), Avalanche (101,187,597 to 101,192,597), X Layer (1,000 blocks) and Monad (1,000 blocks) show none in those short windows. World Chain could not be queried. The hazard does not follow from any network difference, so it is not the planted weakness the review is looking for.
