findings.title: X Layer voids blacklisted L1 deposits at the execution layer, so forced inclusion is no guaranteed exit from the PoolManager
findings.difference: On Ethereum nobody can stop a valid transaction from executing once it is in a block. On a standard OP Stack chain a deposit sent through the OptimismPortal on Ethereum must be executed on L2 as written, which gives users an exit that the sequencer cannot refuse. The X Layer execution client adds a consensus rule: before it runs a user deposit it asks the TxBlacklist contract at 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 whether the deposit's source hash is listed, and a listed deposit is recorded as a failed deposit without running its call. The contract is an upgradeable proxy. Its owner and the owner of its proxy admin are one account without code, 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa.
findings.mechanism: 1. Every pool's funds leave the PoolManager through take inside unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 291-297), and a liquidity position belongs to the msg.sender that created it (src/PoolManager.sol:159-167). An exit is therefore a transaction that must execute on X Layer from the position owner's address. 2. Cycle 1 recorded that the X Layer block builder can leave out sequencer submitted transactions through a risk control filter, and that an L1 deposit remained as the exit. 3. In the client source at tag xlayer/v0.1.7, OpEvm::transact_raw calls intercept_blacklisted_deposit before it executes a transaction. For a deposit that is not a system transaction and does not come from the L1 attributes depositor, it makes an uncommitted system call isBlacklisted(sourceHash) from 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe to the address that the source fixes for chain id 196. 4. When the call returns true, the client builds the result through the handler's failed deposit path: every change of the transaction is reverted, the sender nonce is bumped, the mint is kept and the call to the target is never made. The deposit is included in the block and has no effect. 5. A source hash is known from the moment the deposit event is emitted on Ethereum. User deposits are executed in the first L2 block of the epoch whose origin is that Ethereum block, and the sequencer builds this block after the Ethereum block exists and may lag behind it inside the sequencing window. The party that controls the blacklist therefore has time to list the hash before the deposit is executed. 6. On chain, addToBlacklist(bytes32) reverts for an arbitrary sender, for the owner and for the PoolManager. The implementation has an operators(address) mapping and the setOperator(address,bool) selector, so the owner appoints the accounts that can list hashes. The same owner can replace the implementation through the proxy admin. 7. A liquidity provider whose ordinary transactions are filtered by the builder and whose deposits are listed has no remaining way to call the PoolManager. The code in src/ has no path that works without transaction execution.
findings.impact: Funds of any chosen liquidity provider, swapper or claim holder on X Layer can be held in the PoolManager for as long as the operator keeps filtering and listing. This covers 307.9 OKB and 5,889,016 USDT0 at the time of the query. Nothing is taken: the code has no time dependence, so the funds are intact when the block is lifted. The rule is part of the state transition that every X Layer node applies. The release notes say the same Rust stack is used for proof generation, so a proof would be expected to accept a voided deposit as correct. I did not read the proof program to confirm this.
findings.preconditions: The holder of 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa, or an operator that this account appoints, must list each deposit's source hash before the deposit is executed, and the sequencer must also keep the same user's ordinary transactions out of blocks. An ordinary account cannot list a hash. Whether any hash has been listed could not be read, because the public endpoint limits log queries to 100 blocks. The tag xlayer/v0.1.7 is the op-node release that operators had to run by 10 November 2026. The exact submodule commit that the mainnet sequencer runs was not confirmed, and the blacklist file is also present at tag xlayer/v0.1.6.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should treat X Layer positions as dependent on one operator account and should not rely on L1 forced inclusion as an exit. The deployer can ask OKX to publish the conditions under which deposits are listed and to move ownership of the blacklist and its proxy admin to a multisignature account with a delay. Integrators can monitor the blacklist contract for operator changes and new entries.

sources.supports: The mainnet blacklist address is fixed to 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 for chain id 196. isBlacklisted(sourceHash) is called with transact_system_call from SYSTEM_ADDRESS. Only user deposits are eligible: system transactions and the L1 attributes depositor are excluded.

transact_raw calls intercept_blacklisted_deposit before executing. On a hit it passes an invalid transaction error with the text 'deposit blacklisted' to the handler's catch_error and returns that result with the finalized state.
catch_error for a deposit reverts to the first journal checkpoint, bumps the caller nonce, adds the mint, commits and returns the FailedDeposit halt.

User deposited transactions are placed in the first L2 block of an epoch and are derived from the receipts of the L1 origin block. An L2 block timestamp is at or after the timestamp of its L1 origin, and the L2 blocks of an epoch are derived from the sequencing window that starts at that origin.
The block builder screens each transaction against rules from an external risk control service and excludes transactions with a deny verdict.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the three client files at tag xlayer/v0.1.7 of okx/optimism. xlayer_blacklist_contract.rs maps chain id 196 to 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727, calls isBlacklisted(sourceHash) through transact_system_call from the EIP-4788 system address, treats a revert or a malformed answer as false, and exempts system deposits and the L1 attributes depositor. In lib.rs, transact_raw calls intercept_blacklisted_deposit for every transaction, with no fork or flag condition. The function returns early for anything that is not a user deposit, and on a hit it passes an InvalidTransaction error with the text 'deposit blacklisted' to OpHandler::catch_error and returns the finalized state. In op-revm handler.rs, catch_error for a deposit reverts to the first journal checkpoint, bumps the caller nonce, adds the mint and commits. The same two files are present with the same mainnet address at the okx/optimism ref xlayer-dep/a492b62bbecbdcf3be90719e042c9abca47c8cc6 and on main. The release page for xlayer/v0.1.6 lists 'feat(rcs): intercept blacklisted L1 deposits before execution (51ce81a)' and says that release was for testnet only. The release pages for xlayer/v0.1.7 and xlayer-reth v0.0.7.3 say operators must run both by November 10, 2026, and neither page names the blacklist. Cargo.toml of xlayer-reth at tag v0.0.7.3 takes alloy-op-evm and op-revm from the path deps/optimism/rust, and .gitmodules points that path at okx/optimism. On chain at X Layer block 76,601,162 on 2026-11-22: the endpoint reports reth/v2.3.0-f60420a with the suffix xlayer/v0.0.7. The blacklist address holds 1,059 bytes of code, its EIP-1967 implementation slot holds 0xe44bfef30cfd8ecbfb917d78fa2ac215b3397f8e (3,516 bytes) and its admin slot holds 0x57ffb399eb2d8fb1831001ba893483bc13bd8c2f. owner() on the proxy and on the admin both return 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa, which has no code and account nonce 2,098. pendingOwner() is zero. The implementation bytecode contains the selectors of isBlacklisted(bytes32), blacklisted(bytes32), addToBlacklist(bytes32), removeFromBlacklist(bytes32), batchAddToBlacklist(bytes32[]), batchRemoveFromBlacklist(bytes32[]), operators(address) and setOperator(address,bool). addToBlacklist reverts with 0x7c214f04, the selector of NotOperator(), for an arbitrary sender and for the owner. setOperator(address,bool) succeeds in simulation from the owner and reverts with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount for another sender. isBlacklisted returns false for a test hash when called from 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe. eth_getLogs for the contract over the last 100 blocks returned nothing. The OP Stack derivation specification says user deposits are placed in the first L2 block of an epoch, before sequenced transactions, and that an L2 block may keep an L1 origin whose timestamp is up to max_sequencer_drift older than its own. A hash therefore has to be listed in an L2 block that precedes the block of the deposit, and the sequencer chooses when it advances to the L1 origin that holds the deposit. One link is backed by release documents and not by direct observation: I could not read the submodule pointer of xlayer-reth v0.0.7.3, and I found no deposit that was voided on mainnet.
verification.codeCheck: Funds leave the PoolManager through take, which carries onlyWhenUnlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 96-99), and unlock hands control to msg.sender and requires all deltas to be zero on return (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). A liquidity position is stored under msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161), so only that account can reduce it. ERC-6909 claims are burned from an account by that account, by its operator or by a spender with allowance (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22), and each of these still needs a transaction on X Layer. collectProtocolFees pays out accrued protocol fees only and needs the controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). No function in src/ depends on block time or lets a third party withdraw for an owner without the owner's earlier approval. A user whose transactions are never executed therefore cannot move funds out. I found no guard in src/ that the finding missed, and none could exist, because the hazard sits below the contract.
verification.corrections: The actor value operator is right: an ordinary account cannot list a hash and cannot make the sequencer filter a transaction. The balances moved since the research query. The PoolManager held 300.77 OKB and 5,945,282 USDT0 at block 76,601,162. Step 7 of the mechanism holds only while every transaction that could move the position is stopped. An account that already holds an ERC-6909 operator approval, an allowance or a PositionManager approval from the owner can act for the owner from a different sender, and the operator would have to filter or list that transaction as well. The finding says the rule is active by construction for chain id 196. That statement is true of the source at the release tag. Whether the running sequencer build pins that commit is unconfirmed, as the finding itself notes. Severity high follows the scale, since a freeze needs a privileged chain-level actor, and it matches the Robinhood Chain filter finding F-001.

findings.title: The GoodDollar owner has blocked the PoolManager address on Celo, so 550 million G$ held for pools cannot leave
findings.difference: G$ on Celo is a Superfluid Super Token with an owner controlled list of accounts that can neither send nor receive it, and with an owner function that burns from any account. After the Superfluid incident of September 2026 the owner put the Uniswap v4 PoolManager on that list and has not removed it. Ethereum's PoolManager holds no token in this state.
findings.mechanism: 1. On 11 September 2026 at 13:48:08 UTC (Celo block 77,233,730, transaction 0x22cd34a5f179dfa342fd3659d029e4d40469ca8fa02abd032145f162b0b8dd4d, sent by 0x6823a04a6fd4148167567d5ef6dcca1f34db0494 to the contract 0xa2521e8f5a990903fdd8afa6570c52526e7e0d5e) the token emitted BlockedUpdated with value true for eleven addresses, one of which is the PoolManager 0x288dc841A52FCA2707c6947B3A777c5E56cd87BC. setBlocked is restricted to the owner role. isBlocked(PoolManager) returned true at block 83,475,285 on 22 November 2026. 2. Every ERC-20, ERC-677 and ERC-777 movement of G$ runs _processFees, which reverts with SUPER_GOODDOLLAR_BLOCKED (0xe7d0c09e) when the sender or the recipient is blocked. An eth_call of transfer from the PoolManager reverts with that selector for amounts 1 and 0. A transfer of 1 unit from the owner account to the PoolManager reverts the same way, and the same transfer to another address returns true. 3. take debits the caller and then calls transfer on the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). A failed transfer makes take revert (src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). Every take of G$ therefore reverts, including a take of zero. The PoolManager's 550,022,104.456 G$ stay where they are. 4. A position owner who removes liquidity from a G$ pool receives a positive G$ delta. The owner can take the other currency. For the G$ side the remaining choices are mint, which turns the delta into an ERC-6909 claim (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), and clear, which gives it up (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319). A swap that buys G$ ends the same way. 5. A payment of G$ into the PoolManager by transfer reverts as well, so a seller needs a G$ claim to burn (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336). The token source says a blocked account can still be credited through Superfluid agreements. Such a credit would raise balanceOf(PoolManager), and sync followed by settle would credit it to the settler (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364). I did not simulate that path. 6. The owner can also call adminBurn(account, amount), which skips allowance, hooks, pause and the block list. A burn of the PoolManager's balance would leave pool liquidity and G$ claims without tokens behind them. Superfluid's report says 544 million G$ was burned elsewhere during the recovery.
findings.impact: 550,022,104 G$, which is 13.7 percent of the G$ supply and about 60,000 USD at the price Blockscout shows (0.00010924 USD). GoodDollar names one position holder with two wallets as the depositor. Because all pools share one address, the block also covers every other G$ pool in this PoolManager, every G$ claim and any protocol fee accrued in G$. The paired currencies of those pools can still be withdrawn.
findings.preconditions: None remain. The block is in force. It ends when an account with the G$ owner role calls setBlocked with false for the PoolManager. owner() returns 0x495d133b938596c9984d462f007b676bdc57ecec. GoodDollar states it will do so once the position holder contacts Good Labs or moves the position to the Good Labs Safe.
findings.mitigations: The deployer cannot lift the block. Interfaces should stop routing through G$ pools on Celo and should show G$ positions as withdrawable only as claims. Liquidity providers can remove liquidity, take the paired currency and mint the G$ side as a claim. Integrations should not value G$ claims or G$ pool liquidity at the market price while the block and the admin burn function exist. New deployments should treat any token with a per address block list as able to freeze every pool of that token at once.

verification.factCheck: I repeated the chain reads on https://forno.celo.org at block 83,491,539 on 2026-11-23. isBlocked(PoolManager) on G$ 0x62B8B11039FcfE5aB0C56E502b1C372A3d2a9c7A returns true. balanceOf(PoolManager) is 550,022,104.456 G$ of a supply of 4,020,965,252 G$, which is 13.68 percent. An eth_call of transfer(address,uint256) with from set to the PoolManager reverts with 0xe7d0c09e for amounts 1 and 0. I computed that selector myself: it is the first four bytes of keccak256 of SUPER_GOODDOLLAR_BLOCKED(). A transfer of 1 unit from the owner account 0x495d133b938596c9984d462f007b676bdc57ecec to the PoolManager reverts with the same selector, and the same transfer to an unrelated address returns true. eth_getLogs for block 77,233,730 and topic 0x148a8679 (keccak256 of BlockedUpdated(address,bool), also computed here) returns 11 logs with value true in transaction 0x22cd34a5f179dfa342fd3659d029e4d40469ca8fa02abd032145f162b0b8dd4d. One of the 11 accounts is the PoolManager. The block timestamp is 2026-09-11 13:48:08 UTC, the sender is 0x6823a04a6fd4148167567d5ef6dcca1f34db0494 and the target is 0xa2521e8f5a990903fdd8afa6570c52526e7e0d5e. The endpoint limits log queries to 5,000 blocks, so I did not scan for a later unblock event. The current value of isBlocked answers that question. The ERC-1967 slot and getCodeAddress() of the G$ proxy both hold 0xb4419A3Df33b9aa6fbE452Df8816389E599C29eF. Blockscout returns verified source for that address under the name SuperGoodDollar. I read it: isBlocked is a public mapping (line 48), setBlocked(address[],bool) and adminBurn(address,uint256) call _onlyOwner (lines 365 to 391), transfer, transferFrom, send and transferAndCall all pass through _processFees, and _processFees calls _onlyNotBlocked for the sender and for the recipient (lines 434 to 470). The comment on setBlocked says a blocked account can still be credited by agreements. The library SuperGoodDollarFlows rejects, for a blocked account, a higher CFA deposit, a higher GDA buffer, a lower GDA balance and every IDA write. The GoodDollar post of 20 October 2026 says all liquidity pools were unblocked on 28 September except the Celo Uniswap V4 pool, which holds 550M G$, and that it stays blocked until the position holder contacts Good Labs or moves the position to the Safe 0x4e31993d9F13F940828bf9eC2f643A7E55B21e8C. The Superfluid technical report of 2 October 2026 gives 2,801,252,167 unbacked G$, the 900 KB callback return data, the 30 million block gas limit, the host upgrade of 4 September and 544 million G$ burned. Blockscout shows a G$ price of 0.00011464 USD today, which values the balance at about 63,000 USD. Not confirmed: that a Superfluid agreement can still credit the blocked PoolManager in practice. I read the guard code and it lets a balance increase pass, and I did not simulate a distribution or a stream.
verification.codeCheck: take is at src/PoolManager.sol:291-297. It debits the caller at line 294 and calls currency.transfer at line 295. For an ERC-20 the call is at src/types/Currency.sol:73, and a reverting token gives success zero, so lines 82 to 85 revert through CustomRevert.bubbleUpAndRevertWith (src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). The whole take reverts, including the debit, for every amount including zero, because the token checks the block list before it looks at the amount. There is no other function in src/ that moves an ERC-20 out of the PoolManager except collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57), which uses the same transfer. A positive G$ delta can be closed by mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), which only writes an ERC-6909 balance, or by clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319), which gives the amount up. unlock reverts while any delta is open (src/PoolManager.sol:112). An inbound payment needs the token balance to rise between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364), and an ERC-20 transfer to the blocked PoolManager reverts, so a seller needs a claim to burn (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336) or a credit through an agreement. I found no guard that the finding missed. The freeze follows from one address holding all pools (assumption A6) and from core having no reaction to a failing transfer.
verification.corrections: The actor value issuer is right. The block was set by the G$ owner role, an ordinary account can neither set nor lift it, and no step lets an ordinary account take funds. The mitigation that tells liquidity providers to mint the G$ side as a claim does not hold for positions held through the PositionManager. In core the position owner is the msg.sender of modifyLiquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:161), so only the contract that opened a position can remove it. The runtime code of the Celo PositionManager 0xf7965f3981e4d5bc383bfbcb61501763e9068ca9 (23,877 bytes) contains the selectors of take, clear, settle, sync, modifyLiquidity and unlock and does not contain the selector of mint(address,uint256,uint256) (0x156e29f6) or of burn(address,uint256,uint256) (0xf5298aca). A holder of such a position who removes liquidity must close the G$ delta with take, which reverts, or with clear, which forfeits the G$. I did not establish whether the PositionManager can move the G$ delta into another position inside the same unlock. setBlocked takes an array of accounts. At today's Blockscout price the balance is worth about 63,000 USD. The statement that no later unblock event exists was not checked by a full log scan here.

findings.title: Issuers of the tokens that make up most pool value on Celo and X Layer can pause, block, burn or upgrade the PoolManager's balance
findings.difference: The pooled value on these two networks sits in issuer controlled tokens that are small or new: wBRL and wARS on Celo, and USDT0, USDG, two USDC contracts and tokenized stocks on X Layer. On Celo the PoolManager holds 83.7 percent of all wBRL and 59.0 percent of all wARS. Each of these tokens has roles that act on a single holder address.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools keep a currency in one balance at the PoolManager address, and that balance leaves only through transfer inside take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). A role that stops transfers for that one address stops every pool of the token. 2. wBRL and wARS are proxies of LatamStable. Its compliance role can switch the blocklist on and block the PoolManager, after which _update reverts for it as sender and as recipient. Its pauser role stops all transfers. Its upgrader role can replace the implementation through UUPS and with it the balance logic. The blocklist is switched off today and neither token is paused. 3. On X Layer USDT0 has addToBlockedList and destroyBlockedFunds, USDG has freeze and wipeFrozenAddress, both USDC contracts have a blacklister and a pause, and xETH has a deny list and a pause. A wipe or a destroy sets the PoolManager balance to zero while pool accounting and ERC-6909 claims still count the tokens. 4. BMNRx and ANTx report balanceOf as shares times a multiplier that a multiplier updater role sets, and a fee per period can lower the multiplier over time. A lower multiplier lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) without a take, which leaves pools with less than their accounting says (assumption A2). A higher multiplier adds tokens that no settle credits. The multiplier is 1.0 and the fee is 0 today. 5. On Celo the owner of USDm, which is Celo Governance, can name operators and burners that move or burn the balance of any account. 6. core has no function that reacts to any of these actions. Liquidity providers who exit first after a partial loss take the remaining tokens, and later exits revert when the balance runs out.
findings.impact: On Celo about 522,000 USD of wBRL and 129,000 USD of wARS at the prices Blockscout shows, plus the USDC paired with them. On X Layer about 5.97 million USDT0, 459,000 USDG and 97,700 USDC, plus the 4.67 million USDe that trade against USDT0 in the largest pool. USDe itself has no block or pause function in its code. A freeze stops withdrawals of the affected token for every pool. A wipe, burn or lower multiplier is a loss shared by all liquidity providers and claim holders of that token.
findings.preconditions: An action by a role holder of the token: compliance, pauser or upgrader for wBRL and wARS, the owner of USDT0 (0x4dff9b5b0143e642a3f63a5bcf2d1c328e600bf8), the asset protection role of USDG, the blacklister or pauser of each USDC contract, the multiplier updater or owner of the stock tokens, and the owner of USDm, which is Celo Governance (0xD533Ca259b330c7A88f74E000a3FaEa2d63B7972). No such flag is set for the PoolManager on either chain at blocks 83,476,610 (Celo) and 76,608,329 (X Layer).
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should size positions in these tokens with the issuer roles in mind, and pool interfaces should show them. Monitoring should watch the PoolManager address in each token's block, freeze and pause state and the stock token multiplier. Pools in rebasing stock tokens should use the wrapped ERC-4626 versions, which keep a fixed balance. The deployer cannot remove any of these roles.

findings.title: A two signature Safe can pause ten wrapped stock tokens or list the PoolManager as sanctioned, which would stop pools that hold 7.9 million dollars on Monad
findings.difference: On Monad the second largest asset class at the PoolManager is a set of wrapped stock tokens (wSPYx, wSPCXx, wTSLAx, wQQQx, wEWYx, wSMHx, wNVDAx, wSKHYx, wMUx, wANTx). The PoolManager holds between 89.4 and 99.8 percent of the supply of each. Every transfer of these tokens checks a pause flag and a sanctions list that the issuer controls. cbBTC on Monad adds freeze, pause and burn roles. The exposure comes from the tokens that make up the pooled value on this network. The Monad client plays no part in it.
findings.mechanism: 1. All pools of a currency share one balance at the PoolManager address, and take pays out with currency.transfer and reverts when the token call fails (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). 2. The wrapper's transfer hook requires that isPaused is false and that neither sender nor recipient is on the sanctions list of the underlying stock token (WrappedBackedTokenImplementation.sol lines 178 to 193). 3. setPause can be called by the pauser, a Safe with threshold 2 of 4. The sanctions list at 0x615dd3b9445a94334c1579f68115042d77cc7c44 has addToSanctionsList and is owned by a Safe with threshold 2 of 3, which also owns the wrappers and the proxy admin and can replace the wrapper code. 4. If the pauser pauses a wrapper, or the owner lists the PoolManager address, every take of that wrapper reverts, so no liquidity removal and no swap that pays out the wrapper can settle in any pool of that token. Transfers into the PoolManager revert as well, so settle cannot be funded. 5. isPaused is false for all ten wrappers and isSanctioned(PoolManager) is false today. 6. cbBTC (40.0 coins at the PoolManager, 43 percent of supply) has freeze(address), pause() and burn(address,uint256) behind FREEZER_ROLE, PAUSER_ROLE and BURNER_ROLE. A freeze of the PoolManager or a pause has the same effect, and a burn would leave pool accounting above the balance. 7. A live example of this class exists at small size. Curvance has paused the market manager 0xbc4cd7bbd8d38027a88838b88ba04561fa778c35, and a transfer of cWBTC or ceBTC from the PoolManager reverts today with MarketManager__Paused(). Five pools use each of the two tokens, and the PoolManager holds about 83 dollars of each. 8. No ordinary account can trigger any of these steps. A third party cannot move the PoolManager's wrapper shares, because redeem and withdraw spend an allowance of the owner (lines 265 to 273) and delegatedTransfer needs an ECDSA signature that recovers to the owner address (lines 112 to 131).
findings.impact: A pause or a sanctions entry freezes about 7.9 million dollars of wrapped stock tokens together with the other side of those pools while it lasts, for every liquidity provider in them. A freeze or pause of cbBTC does the same for about 2.5 million dollars of cbBTC. A burn of the PoolManager's cbBTC would leave the last providers unpaid. The Curvance pause already locks about 170 dollars.
findings.preconditions: Two signers of the pauser Safe or of the owner Safe act, or the holder of a cbBTC role acts. No action by an ordinary account leads there.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should treat the issuer's pause and sanctions rights as a condition of these pools. The deployer can list these tokens in user documentation as issuer controlled. Core cannot route around a token that rejects transfers from the PoolManager.

verification.factCheck: The chain facts hold. I fetched WrappedBackedTokenImplementation.sol from the Backed repository. _beforeTokenTransfer requires isPaused to be false and asks the sanctions list of the underlying token about the sender and the recipient (lines 178 to 194). setPause accepts only the pauser (lines 142 to 146). A withdraw or redeem by another account spends the owner's allowance (lines 265 to 274), and delegatedTransfer requires that ECDSA recovery returns the owner address (lines 112 to 132). On Monad at block 124,634,156 I read eight of the ten wrappers: wSPYx 0xe7e553cd128f0011777323a0b44a7b96ea1cb540, wTSLAx 0xc3fdbe3a68ee5de461d30415a8165cf9aefe1171, wSPCXx 0x8e2eed8b8b5e13ea7bf38e50d7821d2c57309072, wQQQx 0x4c1ae29c159838fc1b224636e28e086eb69101f7, wSMHx 0x23c4bddea5e7e284fb4027c6050bc5e6f7fae23f, wSKHYx 0x6215a58ed045d71f2561aaabe54f4c885c522998, wANTx 0xabec6aeab037b77c09a2a99264f9c81a35b02649 and wMUx 0xe2047ee3bddb5c99ae428ab83df63f8730698e30. Each has implementation slot 0x76c6851ea0b2741eedcbbed240715e8817e85583, owner 0x49754062e35f7591b93cc4f9915965be89643a65, pauser 0x8768cda7a463dae1baa6b2500efb025ebd7ffc50 and isPaused false. The PoolManager holds between 89.2 percent (wANTx) and 99.8 percent (wTSLAx) of the supply of each. For wSPYx and wMUx I also read the admin slot, which is 0x312063009e74142339edc92bcff6cfcfaa958bfa, and the owner of that contract is the same Safe 0x4975. The underlying token of wSPYx (0x90a2a4c76b5d8c0bc892a69ea28aa775a8f2dd48, SP500 xStock) names sanctions list 0x615dd3b9445a94334c1579f68115042d77cc7c44. The owner of the list is the Safe 0x4975 and isSanctioned(PoolManager) is false. getThreshold and getOwners give 2 of 3 for Safe 0x4975 and 2 of 4 for Safe 0x8768, both Safe version 1.3.0. The implementation bytecode (11,606 bytes) contains 46 function selectors. They equal the 46 selectors I derived from the source file and its OpenZeppelin parents, with none missing and none extra. Simulations with eth_call: setPause(true) from an arbitrary account reverts with Only pauser and succeeds from the pauser Safe. addToSanctionsList with the PoolManager address reverts for an arbitrary account with the Ownable message and succeeds from the owner Safe. A prestate trace of the simulated setPause shows that it writes slot 0x132 of the wrapper. With that slot set by state override, transfer from the PoolManager address reverts with token transfer while paused, and a transfer to the PoolManager reverts with the same message. With the code of the sanctions list replaced by a stub that answers true, transfer from the PoolManager reverts with sender is sanctioned. Without overrides a transfer from the PoolManager address succeeds for all eight wrappers. From an arbitrary account, redeem, withdraw and transferFrom with the PoolManager as owner revert with insufficient allowance, and delegatedTransfer and permit with an arbitrary signature revert with invalid signature. GeckoTerminal prices give 5.68 million dollars for the seven wrappers I priced, and each of the seven is within one percent of the figure in the research file. I could not find the addresses of wNVDAx and wEWYx, so 1.54 million dollars of the 7.92 million total were not read again. cbBTC (0xd18b7ec58cdf4876f6afebd3ed1730e4ce10414b) is a proxy over 0xd1611e6e93ec512bfbd2b6428a26c463c1dce6f9. The PoolManager holds 39.92 of 93.26 coins, which is 42.8 percent. paused() is false and isFrozen(PoolManager) is false. The implementation bytecode contains the selectors of freeze(address), unfreeze(address), pause(), burn(address,uint256), FREEZER_ROLE(), PAUSER_ROLE() and BURNER_ROLE(). freeze, burn and pause from an arbitrary account revert with error 0xe2517d3f, which carries the caller and the missing role. cWBTC and ceBTC both name market manager 0xbc4cd7bbd8d38027a88838b88ba04561fa778c35. A transfer of half the balance from the PoolManager address reverts with 0xf47323f4 for both, and I computed that value as the selector of MarketManager__Paused(). The PoolManager holds 0.00134 units of each.
verification.codeCheck: take is open to any caller inside an unlock. It debits the caller and then calls currency.transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). For an ERC-20 the library calls transfer on the token and reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the call fails or returns anything other than no data or a 32 byte true (src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). CustomRevert.bubbleUpAndRevertWith always reverts (src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). The code has no custody per pool, so one balance serves every pool of a currency, and a token that rejects transfers from the PoolManager address makes every take of that currency revert. collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). settle credits only the rise of balanceOf between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364), so a token that rejects transfers to the PoolManager cannot be paid in. Actor check in the code: the PoolManager calls a currency address only with transfer and balanceOf (src/types/Currency.sol:60-73, 94), sends native value with empty calldata (src/types/Currency.sol:48), calls unlockCallback on the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:110) and calls hook addresses with the IHooks selectors (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). None of the ten hook selectors and not unlockCallback occurs in the wrapper or cbBTC implementation bytecode. No caller can therefore make the PoolManager approve, redeem, pause or sign anything on these tokens, and the issuer rights are the only way to the freeze. One guard the finding leaves out: mint, burn and clear do not call the token (src/PoolManager.sol:310-336, src/ERC6909.sol:79-89). While a token is paused, a caller who is owed that token can still close the delta by minting ERC-6909 claims for it, and can take the other currency of the pool as usual.
verification.corrections: The actor value issuer is right and the severity high fits the scale. The impact statement is too wide at one point. A pause or sanctions entry does not freeze the other side of those pools at the level of the PoolManager. A liquidity provider who can call the PoolManager directly can remove liquidity, take the other currency and mint ERC-6909 claims for the blocked wrapper (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), and a swap that pays out the wrapper can be closed the same way. What is frozen is the wrapper itself: no take and no settle of it works until the issuer lifts the block. Whether providers who hold positions through the deployed PositionManager can use this route depends on that contract, which is outside this repository and was not read. Two of the ten wrappers (wNVDAx and wEWYx) were not located by me, so the statement that all ten share the roles rests on eight read here and on the research file for the other two. The burn right on cbBTC was confirmed as a selector and a role check only. I did not read which accounts hold the cbBTC roles.

findings.title: A TIP-20 issuer has already frozen a pooled token on Tempo by setting the always reject transfer policy
findings.difference: A TIP-20 token carries a transfer policy id that its admin can change at any time. Policy 0 is built in and rejects every sender and recipient.
findings.mechanism: 1. GABAGOOL at 0x20c000000000000000000000030a4c7f7b8f3586 was used as a currency in two pools of the PoolManager, which still holds 600,000 base units (0.6 tokens). 2. transferPolicyId() on the token now returns 0, and isAuthorized(0, PoolManager) is false. 3. take calls transfer on the token (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). The precompile reverts with PolicyForbids and the take reverts with the wrapped ERC20TransferFailed error. I simulated a take of 1 unit and of the full balance. Both revert. 4. A holder of a position in those pools can still remove liquidity, take the other currency and turn the GABAGOOL delta into an ERC-6909 claim or clear it (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329). The GABAGOOL itself cannot leave. 5. Of the 73 currencies that Tempo pools name, this is the only one where a take of the PoolManager balance fails today.
findings.impact: This instance concerns 0.6 tokens of a token with a supply of 310.6. It shows that the issuer control described in F-031 is used in practice on this network. The same single call by the policy admin of OUSD or pathUSD would stop takes of 406,692 OUSD and 19,629 pathUSD.
findings.preconditions: The admin of the token calls changeTransferPolicyId, or the admin of the policy changes its lists. No action by an ordinary account produces this state.
findings.mitigations: List the transfer policy id and its admin for each pooled TIP-20 in the deployment notes and monitor changes. Liquidity providers should treat TIP-20 tokens with an active admin as revocable.

verification.factCheck: I repeated the reads on https://rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz near block 50,378,600. On 0x20c000000000000000000000030a4c7f7b8f3586 symbol() returns GABAGOOL, decimals() 6, totalSupply() 310,600,000 base units, transferPolicyId() 0 and balanceOf(PoolManager) 600,000. isAuthorized(0, PoolManager) on 0x403c000000000000000000000000000000000000 returns false and isAuthorized(1, PoolManager) returns true. An eth_call with the PoolManager as sender to transfer(address,uint256) reverts with 0x54cfe659 for amounts 0, 1 and 600,000. My own Keccak gives 0x54cfe659 for PolicyForbids(). The token emitted one TransferPolicyUpdate log in its whole history: block 43,401,478, updater 0x3b387f83c0b46a544050eaa307e185f701c21871, new policy 0, transaction 0x7e0b7b5e33ce3b867fce2f5b4ae0eeca38d9a68642bb2d0c155e4e39b290023a. The two pools that name the token were initialized at blocks 43,299,165 and 43,299,232, so the policy changed after the pools existed. crates/precompiles/src/tip20/mod.rs lines 280 to 304 let a holder of DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE set any existing policy id. The same transfer of 1 unit from the PoolManager returns true on pathUSD, OUSD and USDC.e. pathUSD and OUSD both report transfer policy 2, and policyData(2) returns type 1 (BLACKLIST) with admin 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246. The PoolManager holds 19,633 pathUSD and 408,832 OUSD at this block. I did not repeat the take test on the other 69 currencies, so the statement that GABAGOOL is the only failing one rests on the research run.
verification.codeCheck: take debits the caller and then calls currency.transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). For a token the library calls transfer(address,uint256) and treats a revert as failure (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), then reverts with the wrapped ERC20TransferFailed error (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). No other function of the PoolManager moves a token out except collectProtocolFees, which uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:55). A positive GABAGOOL delta can still be closed without a transfer through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329) or clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-319), so the other currency of a position can leave. The actor is right for the hazard class: the state needs the admin of the token or of its policy, and no step is open to an ordinary account. High fits the scale because the freeze needs a token issuer. The live instance itself is 0.6 tokens.
verification.corrections: Both GABAGOOL pools carry the hook 0x55aeb9ebfa15c28ff9d9a675e8574a5bbe186aa8 (21,648 bytes of code). Its address has the beforeInitialize, beforeAddLiquidity, beforeRemoveLiquidity, beforeSwap, beforeDonate and beforeSwapReturnsDelta flags, so step 4 of the mechanism also depends on that hook accepting the removal (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:195-206). The finding does not mention the hook. TIP20Factory.create_token has no role check (crates/precompiles/src/tip20_factory/mod.rs lines 98 to 149), so the admin of GABAGOOL is whoever created it. For a token that an attacker issues and that victims then choose to pool, the schema class is pool-creator. The class issuer stays right for pathUSD, OUSD and the other stablecoins. The cited registry file holds the interface only. The checks that a transfer runs and the admin check for a policy change are in crates/precompiles/src/tip20/mod.rs. pathUSD and OUSD share policy 2, a blacklist with one admin, so one entry for the PoolManager stops takes of both tokens at once. The OUSD balance is 408,832 at my block, where the finding has 406,692.

findings.title: Three issuers have blocked the Ethereum PoolManager address and two pooled tokens are paused, so yUSD, yETH, xSolvBTC, KITE and NTX held for pools cannot leave today
findings.difference: This is an observed state of the hazard that the stablecoin findings describe for Ethereum. The full balance transfer test of this unit ran over 60,024 currencies of the Ethereum PoolManager and 1,119 refused. Six of the refusals carry a price above 100,000 USD at coins.llama.fi. Five of them have an issuer cause, a block on the PoolManager address or a pause of the token. The sixth, VIBESTR 0xd0cc2b0efb168bfe1f94a948d8df70fa10257196 (about 150,000 USD), rejects every nonzero transfer made outside its own trading flow, which belongs to the author gated class recorded in earlier cycles.
findings.mechanism: 1. take pays with transfer from the single PoolManager address (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). 2. eth_call with from set to the PoolManager at block 26,476,678. yUSD 0x19ebd191f7a24ece672ba13a302212b5ef7f35cb and yETH 0x8464f6ecae1ea58ec816c13f964030eab8ec123a revert with the message blacklisted for every amount including zero, in both directions, while a zero transfer between two other accounts succeeds. xSolvBTC 0xd9d920aa40f578ab794426f5c90f6c731d159def reverts with error 0xbb70159d carrying the PoolManager address, and isBlacklisted(PoolManager) returns true while it returns false for another account. KITE 0x904567252d8f48555b7447c67dca23f0372e16be reverts with EnforcedPause (0xd93c0665) and NTX 0xf0d33beda4d734c72684b5f9abbebf715d0a7935 with the message ERC20Pausable: token transfer while paused, for every sender. 3. Every take of these five currencies reverts, and for the three blocked tokens a payment into the PoolManager reverts as well, so settle cannot complete. A position holder can still remove liquidity and turn the delta of the stuck currency into an ERC-6909 claim (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329) and take the other currency.
findings.impact: Balances at the Ethereum PoolManager and their value at coins.llama.fi prices: 677,988 yUSD (about 677,000 USD), 62.69 yETH (about 102,000 USD), 3.2104 xSolvBTC (about 197,000 USD), 3,755,211 KITE (about 530,000 USD) and 95,177,682 NTX (about 163,000 USD). The sum is about 1.67 million USD that liquidity providers and claim holders of these pools cannot withdraw until the issuer lifts the block or the pause. I did not check since when each state holds or how many pools are affected.
findings.preconditions: An issuer or token admin decision. No unprivileged party can cause or lift it. Whether the yUSD and yETH block is an entry for the PoolManager address or a rule that covers a class of addresses is not confirmed, because the tokens answer none of the usual list getters. The prices come from one service and were not cross checked.
findings.mitigations: None in core. Interfaces should mark pools whose currency rejects transfers from the PoolManager. The new deployment has a new address, so these blocks do not carry over, and the same issuers can block it in the same way.

findings.title: Issuer controls on USDG and Dinari USD+ cover 2.78M more in the Arbitrum One PoolManager, and the USD+ operator can lower the pooled balance by a rebase
findings.difference: F-036 lists USDC, USDT0, PYUSD and cbBTC. A ranking of all priced pool currencies shows two more issuer controlled tokens among the six largest positions. Global Dollar (USDG) has a freeze list and a pause. Dinari USD+ keeps balances as shares times an index, checks every transfer against a restrictor contract, and lets the holder of its operator role raise or lower the index.
findings.mechanism: USDG: the issuer freezes the PoolManager address or pauses the token. transfer then fails with the PoolManager as sender, Currency.transfer reverts, and every take and every fee collection in USDG reverts, as F-036 describes for the other tokens. USD+: step 1, the owner of the restrictor 0x2ed5c85d5105abe5d13586c5c3a8f99a837942b4 lists the PoolManager. checkTransferRestricted runs before every transfer, so payouts and payments in USD+ revert. Step 2, separately, the operator calls rebaseSub. balanceOf(PoolManager) is sharesOf(PoolManager) times balancePerShare, so it falls in proportion while pools, claims and accrued fees keep their recorded amounts. The last withdrawers find less USD+ than the pools record. Step 3, in the other direction rebaseAdd raises the balance. The index stands at 1.0707, so about 70,678 USD+ of the 1,070,678 held came from index growth after deposit, on the assumption that the 999,999.89 shares were deposited near an index of 1. No settle is credited for that growth, because a sync and a settle in one transaction read the same index, and the rebase functions revert for an ordinary account. The surplus belongs to no pool. I read rebaseSub in the public Dinari repository, whose current version takes one argument. The deployed version 6.0.0 takes a second bytes32 argument and rejects ordinary callers with AC: unauthorized. The implementation 0xff5bff8081eaee966bd74e9c0c059949df2345e1 is not verified on Sourcify and the Blockscout API was not reachable, so the deployed body of rebaseSub is unconfirmed.
findings.impact: All pools and claims in USDG and USD+. The PoolManager holds 1,712,030.85 USDG and 1,070,677.64 USD+, which is 34.4 percent of the USD+ supply. A freeze stops withdrawals in the token. A downward rebase takes a share of the pooled USD+ from the last liquidity providers to withdraw.
findings.preconditions: The Paxos asset protection role for USDG. For USD+ the owner of the transfer restrictor (0x269e944ad9140fc6e21794e8ea71ce1afbfe38c8) or the holder of the operator role of the token. No ordinary account can act.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should treat a USD+ pool as exposed to the issuer's index and restrictor. Interfaces can label both tokens as issuer controlled. The deployer cannot remove the exposure in core, because one address holds every pool's balance.

verification.factCheck: USDG. eth_call on https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc at block 526,831,684: 0x004b506865409877c9fa29bfb1eba929984b9bbc reports name Global Dollar, 6 decimals, total supply 65,785,893.96, isFrozen(PoolManager) false, paused false in globalTransferSettings(), owner 0x6c9e821ade9efc1bcda763f9942dd7822d6e86b4 and payoutGroupIdOf(PoolManager) 0. balanceOf(PoolManager) is 1,685,060.10, which is 27,000 less than the finding quotes and moves with trading. The Paxos documentation lists this address as USDG on Arbitrum. The implementation 0x031610e2d186d78d3defbf907f56d1eac843d9de is an exact match on Sourcify. Its transfer carries whenNotPaused and _transfer reverts with AddressFrozen when the sender or the recipient is frozen (PaxosTokenClaimableRewards.sol line 142, ClaimableRewardsBase.sol line 476). From an ordinary account freeze, unfreeze, freezeBatch and wipeFrozenAddress revert for a missing role 0xe3e4f9d7..., which is the hash of ASSET_PROTECTION_ROLE, and pause reverts for a missing PAUSE_ROLE. A transfer of 1 unit sent from the PoolManager address succeeds today. USD+. 0xfc90518d5136585ba45e34ed5e1d108bd3950cfa has implementation slot 0xff5bff8081eaee966bd74e9c0c059949df2345e1, publicVersion 6.0.0, total supply 3,113,037.91, balancePerShare 1.0706777538e18, sharesOf(PoolManager) 999,999.892917 and balanceOf(PoolManager) 1,070,677.639195, which is 34.4 percent of supply. I overrode the storage slot 0x5317...bb02 that holds the index in an eth_call: with the index at 1.0, 0.5 and 2.0 the PoolManager balance reads 999,999.89, 499,999.95 and 1,999,999.79. The deployed code therefore computes the balance as shares times that slot. rebaseAdd(uint128,bytes32) and rebaseSub(uint128,bytes32) exist and revert with AC: unauthorized for an ordinary account, the one argument forms revert with empty data, mint reverts, and burn(address,uint256) reverts for want of an allowance. transferRestrictor() is 0x2ed5c85d5105abe5d13586c5c3a8f99a837942b4, its owner and default admin is 0x269e944ad9140fc6e21794e8ea71ce1afbfe38c8, and restrict(address) reverts for an ordinary account for a missing RESTRICTOR_ROLE. The public Dinari source is version 2 and differs from the deployed version 6, as the finding says. The downward move of the index is no longer hypothetical. An archive node (https://arb-pokt.nodies.app, eth_getStorageAt) shows the index slot at 1.0706777538e18 up to block 425,966,863, at exactly 1.0707e18 from block 425,966,864, and back at 1.0706777538e18 from block 426,017,089 (2026-01-28, 02:42 and 06:11 UTC). The PoolManager received its USD+ in one transfer of 1,070,700.000000 at block 425,967,321, 457 blocks after the rise, which gave it exactly 1,000,000 shares. The fall 3.5 hours later cut its balance by 22.25 USD+. Neither move emitted BalancePerShareSet, and neither used rebaseAdd or rebaseSub. Both were made by transactions 0x16f245ef068749c80ba697e5b14962b48e2173410b59c0d80736a4c388a76903 and 0xef84fb3eb1d357044c6f0dabccca656f41641c218bda362a82eaf006ee039837, sent by the account 0x4d0d668410c765cdee19c0ef2f0523fc231e879f to Multicall3, which called 0xb7541f225385104347539397a4e01abc1d4ea8bd with selector 0x4348352c, the token address, an ECDSA signature and an inner call 0x8078438b that names one storage slot of the token, its expected old value and its new value. USD+ accepts selector 0x8078438b when the caller is 0xb7541f... (eth_call with that sender returns without revert today) and rejects it from any other sender I tried.
verification.codeCheck: One address holds every pool's balance of a currency, and each payout is a plain transfer from it. take debits the caller and calls currency.transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). For an ERC-20 the call must succeed and return nothing or a 32 byte true, otherwise the function reverts with the wrapped error (src/types/Currency.sol:60-74 and 82-86). collectProtocolFees uses the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). A frozen or paused USDG and a restricted USD+ revert inside transfer, so every take and fee collection in that token reverts. No guard in src/ offers another exit: mint moves a claim and leaves the token where it is (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329). For the index: sync stores balanceOf(PoolManager) (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96) and _settle credits reservesNow minus reservesBefore (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364). The subtraction at line 360 is checked, so a fall of the balance between sync and settle reverts the settle and credits nothing. A rise between the two is credited to the settler. Pool accounting never reads the token balance again, so after a downward move the pools record more USD+ than the PoolManager holds and the last take for the difference fails in the token. I read these lines in this checkout and found no guard that the finding missed. The live PoolManager is other bytecode than a build of this checkout, so the on-chain reads describe the tokens and the deployed manager.
verification.corrections: The actor is right: every lever needs a Paxos role, the Dinari restrictor role, or a signature that 0xb7541f225385104347539397a4e01abc1d4ea8bd accepts. Four statements need correcting. First, the mechanism says about 70,678 USD+ of the pooled balance is index growth that belongs to no pool. That is wrong. The whole balance arrived in one transfer at block 425,967,321, after the last BalancePerShareSet event (block 425,539,068). Transfer logs give a net inflow of 1,070,699.885347 and the balance is 1,070,677.639195, so the PoolManager is 22.25 USD+ short of what the pools were credited, and there is no surplus. Second, the lever that moved the index is a raw storage write to the token, authorised by an off-chain signature and submitted through a public contract. It can write the index slot and, by its shape, any other slot named in the call. The finding describes only the role gated rebase functions, and the statement that the index did not move rests on an event that this route does not emit. The call is open to any sender: an eth_call of the first transaction's calldata from an unrelated address at block 425,966,863 succeeds, both through Multicall3 and directly. A tampered signature or payload reverts, a zero signature reverts with ECDSAInvalidSignature, and both used calls revert from every sender after their first execution, so they cannot be replayed. I could not read the contract (no verified source for 0xb7541f..., its implementation 0x1b5a16e81ab8154559ec2f457fa61062a6b8876f or the token implementation), so the signer, the digest format and its other functions are unconfirmed. Third, USDG on Arbitrum One is the Paxos claimable rewards build, and the asset protection role also holds wipeFrozenAddress, so the issuer can burn a frozen balance as well as block it. On the restrictor, restrict(address) needs RESTRICTOR_ROLE, which the admin 0x269e... grants. Fourth, the value of the USD+ position is face value. All of it sits in one hookless USDC/USD+ pool (id 0x12d6df73..., fee 0.3 percent), in one position of the account 0xcd04ccbf1cd5d18c9735b59f5e41f03a2941ebad between ticks 1080 and 3540, and the pool price is at tick 3539, which is 0.70 USDC per USD+. The title's 2.78M is 1.69M USDG plus 1.07M USD+ at par today.

findings.title: The block lists that gate OUSD and AMDc transfers on Base are each administered by one externally owned account
findings.difference: B20 tokens on Base check up to three policies of the chain's policy registry on every transfer: executor, sender and receiver. A policy is changed by its admin alone. Ethereum has no registry of this kind in the protocol.
findings.mechanism: A take of a B20 token is a transfer with the PoolManager as executor and sender (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75), and a payment before settle is a transfer with the PoolManager as receiver. OUSD binds its sender scope to block list 0x7a, whose admin is 0x251d2711ebeb0a09fdb8992f5506f3d949175246. AMDc binds sender, receiver, executor and mint receiver to block list 5, whose admin is 0xec0f05c174e54fbf0fe16ad930a8afebce612812. Both admins are accounts without code. One updateBlocklist call from such an account that names the PoolManager makes every later take of that token revert with PolicyForbids, and for AMDc every payment into the PoolManager as well. The same call from an account that is not the admin reverts with Unauthorized, and no path in the registry source lets another account become admin without a stageUpdateAdmin call of the current admin.
findings.impact: The PoolManager held 5,319,114.88 OUSD (6 decimals) and 32.15 AMDc (8 decimals) at block 61,314,282. After a block list entry none of it can leave by take, for any pool or claim holder.
findings.preconditions: The policy admin, or whoever holds the private signing secret of that one account, sends one transaction. No token role is needed, because the policy admin is separate from the roles of the token.
findings.mitigations: Issuers can move policy administration to a multi-signature account with stageUpdateAdmin and finalizeUpdateAdmin. Liquidity providers should treat the policy admin of each bound policy as a party that can freeze the pooled balance, next to the token roles recorded in F-027.

verification.codeCheck: take calls currency.transfer(to, amount) with the PoolManager as msg.sender, so the PoolManager is both executor and sender of the B20 transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). A reverting transfer makes the take revert through the wrapped error (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). The only other outbound token call in src/ is the transfer in collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56), which fails the same way. A payment is a transfer to the PoolManager by the payer between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-365), so a receiver policy that names the PoolManager stops payments in that token. Nothing in src/ can route around a token that refuses the PoolManager as sender, and all pools and claims share the one balance, so after a block list entry no liquidity provider or claim holder can take OUSD or AMDc out. For AMDc the sender check is skipped because the executor and sender scopes hold the same policy and the caller is the source, so the revert names the executor scope. The outcome is the same.

findings.title: One USDC blocklist entry for the PoolManager on Arc stops native USDC in both directions, the token face and the bridged WETH token
findings.difference: On Arc the USDC blocklist lives in the Native Coin Control precompile and the EVM checks it on every value-bearing call, so a listed address can neither send nor receive the native asset. The ERC-20 face of USDC moves the same balance and fails the same check. The bridged WETH token of the CrossChainTokenService asks the same list on every transfer through an adapter contract. On Ethereum a USDC blacklist entry stops USDC only, and ETH and WETH keep moving.
findings.mechanism: 1. The USDC blacklister (0x2a2b7ff330f15f9a8c52af5fec27d775f5138467) lists the PoolManager address. In the simulation this is one storage entry of 0x1800000000000000000000000000000000000001, the entry for the PoolManager address in the mapping at slot 2, set to 1 by state override. 2. A native payout, which take performs as a value call from the PoolManager (src/types/Currency.sol:44-52), reverts with 'Blocked address', so take of address(0) reverts, and collectProtocolFees for address(0) uses the same call (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). 3. USDC.transfer from the PoolManager reverts, so take of 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 reverts (src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). 4. findings.title: A Stylus program used as a hook or token stops answering calls on expiry or a Stylus version change, and activation is blocked
findings.difference: On Ethereum, code at an address keeps answering calls. On Arbitrum One a contract can be a Stylus WASM program. A call to it fails unless the program was activated at the current Stylus version and its last activation or keepalive is less than 365 days old. ArbOS 61, active since 2026-08-20, moved the Stylus version from 2 to 3. On chain, ArbWasm.activationGas() is 2^64-1, which makes activateProgram fail for everyone, so a program that has expired or needs the new version cannot be brought back by its users.
findings.mechanism: Hook path: the PoolManager calls the hook with call() and reverts the whole action when the call fails. For a hook address with the before or after remove liquidity flag, modifyLiquidity with a negative delta calls the hook, so a hook that no longer answers blocks every liquidity removal in its pools. Hooks with swap or donate flags block those actions the same way. Token path: transfer and balanceOf on a Stylus token that no longer answers revert, so take, sync and settle revert for that currency in every pool. Step 1: a pool is created with a Stylus hook or a Stylus token while the program is active. Step 2: the program reaches 365 days without a keepalive, or an ArbOS upgrade changes the Stylus version. getActiveProgram returns ProgramExpired or ProgramNeedsUpgrade and the call fails. Step 3: anyone who tries activateProgram is charged activationGas first, which exceeds any gas limit, so the call fails. Keepalive works only while the program is still active and at least 31 days old. ArbOS 61 also removed WASM multi-value support, so a program that relies on it cannot be reactivated even when activation reopens. I did not enumerate which pools on Arbitrum One use a Stylus hook or token, and I did not establish the date on which activation gas was raised, so I cannot say how many programs missed the move to version 3.
findings.impact: LP principal and fees in pools whose hook gates liquidity removal are stuck for as long as activation stays closed. For a Stylus token, every balance of that token in the PoolManager is stuck. No funds move to an attacker. Pools without Stylus hooks or tokens are unaffected.
findings.preconditions: A pool must use a Stylus program as its hook or as one of its currencies. Then either nobody pays for keepalive within the 365 day window, or governance ships a Stylus version change. No attacker action is required and none can speed it up. The Arbitrum Foundation or Security Council can reopen activation.
findings.mitigations: Pool creators on Arbitrum One should prefer EVM hooks. LPs in a pool with a Stylus hook should check ArbWasm.programVersion and programTimeLeft for the hook and for each token, and anyone can pay codehashKeepalive once the program is 31 days old. A hook author can leave the remove liquidity flags unset so that removals never depend on the hook.

verification.factCheck: I read arbos/programs/programs.go at Nitro v3.11.3. CallProgram calls getActiveProgram, which returns ProgramNeedsUpgrade when the program version differs from the Stylus version and ProgramExpired when the age exceeds ExpiryDays. ProgramKeepalive needs an active program that is at least KeepaliveDays old. I read arbos/arbosState/arbosstate.go and arbos/programs/params.go. The ArbOS 59 step calls UpgradeToVersion(3), which sets the Stylus version from 2 to 3. I read precompiles/ArbWasm.go. ActivateProgram burns the stored activation gas first. CodehashKeepalive does not. On chain at Arbitrum One block 526,514,058 on 2026-11-22: stylusVersion() is 3, expiryDays() is 365, keepaliveDays() is 31 and activationGas() is 2^64-1. A simulated activateProgram with 30,000,000 gas reverts. I tested the effect directly. ProgramActivated logs of ArbWasm around block 496,578,581, the first block at or after the ArbOS 61 activation time, show version 2 before it and version 3 after it. The program 0x2e5d89a229cbd17efb0a731d26232f88c3746aa9, activated at version 2 in block 495,363,914 and not reactivated, now fails every eth_call with the error ProgramNeedsUpgrade(2, 3). The program 0xaff2f129d2bcba4649a54fb516be0cc78288898d was reactivated at version 3 in block 496,871,745 and answers calls. The finding did not establish when activation was closed. The Security Council report gives the date: on 2026-10-02 the council called ArbOwner.setWasmActivationGas(2^64 - 1) on Arbitrum One and Nova. ArbOS 61 activated on 2026-08-20 at 17:00 UTC, so programs had 43 days to move to version 3. The pause notice, the ArbOS 61 release notes, the Stylus introduction and the forum proposal say what the finding reports. The last post of the forum thread, by the authors on 2026-11-18, says they will integrate feedback before taking the proposal further, and the first post says protocol-level activation controls and the ability to deactivate a Stylus contract are planned for a later ArbOS proposal. I also measured exposure. The PoolManager on Arbitrum One emitted 28,689 Initialize events from block 290,000,000 to block 526,516,712, with 923 distinct hook addresses and 9,417 distinct currency addresses. None of them has code that starts with the Stylus prefix 0xeff0. No pool therefore has a Stylus program as its direct hook or currency today. This check reads the code at the hook or token address only. It does not see an EVM contract that forwards to a Stylus program.
verification.codeCheck: callHook makes a plain call with all gas and reverts with HookCallFailed when the call fails. A call that succeeds with fewer than 32 bytes also reverts with InvalidHookResponse (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). For a negative or zero liquidityDelta, beforeModifyLiquidity calls the hook when the address has the before remove liquidity flag, and afterModifyLiquidity does so for the after remove liquidity flag (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:195-206, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:209-245). Both run inside modifyLiquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:156, src/PoolManager.sol:178). The only bypass is noSelfCall, which skips the hook when the hook itself is the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:217). A program that cannot run cannot be the caller. Permissions come from the address bits (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:337-339) and the hook address is part of the pool identifier, so an LP cannot route around it. For a token, balanceOfSelf is a high-level call that reverts when the call fails (src/types/Currency.sol:90-96), and transfer reverts with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:54-87). sync, the ERC-20 branch of _settle and take all revert for that currency (src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). Claims in that currency can still be minted, burned and transferred. test/PoolManager.t.sol and test/DynamicFees.t.sol cover a hook that reverts or returns a bad response. No test covers a hook or token whose code stops answering after pool creation.
verification.corrections: The mechanism and the chain facts hold. The scope needs two changes. First, no pool on Arbitrum One has a Stylus program as its direct hook or currency today, so no funds are frozen through the direct path at present. Indirect use through an EVM proxy or an EVM hook that calls a Stylus program was not checked. Second, the date the finding could not establish is 2026-10-02, 43 days after the version change. The same mechanism reaches Robinhood Chain. Its ArbWasm precompile emitted 26 ProgramActivated events between 2026-07-25 and 2026-10-02, all at version 3, and activation gas there is also 2^64-1. Those programs expire from 2027-07-25 unless someone pays keepalive, and a Stylus version change would stop them at once. On Robinhood Chain the PoolManager emitted 1,169,661 Initialize events up to block 120.6M. 411,764 of them name a hook, across 32,935 distinct hook addresses and 745,518 distinct currency addresses. None of the 26 activated program addresses is a hook or a currency of any pool. I read the code of the 1,500 most used hook addresses, which cover 377,624 of the hooked pools, and none starts with 0xeff0. I did not read the code of the remaining hooks or of the currencies, so a contract that shares its code hash with an activated program is not excluded there. The severity stays medium because the freeze is limited to pools that depend on a Stylus program and needs either a missed keepalive or a governance upgrade.

findings.title: A pool's hook can block or reprice every liquidity removal in that pool, and core has no path that skips the hook
findings.difference: None. The code path is the same on every network. Networks where the code behind an address can change after pool creation (A7) add ways for a hook that was harmless at creation to start doing this.
findings.mechanism: modifyLiquidity calls the hook library's beforeModifyLiquidity before it touches the pool (src/PoolManager.sol:156). For liquidityDelta <= 0 the library calls beforeRemoveLiquidity when address bit 9 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-204). callHook reverts the whole call when the hook reverts (Hooks.sol:134-137) and when the return data is shorter than 32 bytes or carries the wrong selector (Hooks.sol:152-154). A hook address with no code returns empty data, so it also reverts. After the pool update, afterModifyLiquidity calls afterRemoveLiquidity when bit 8 is set, and when bit 0 is also set it reads a BalanceDelta from the return data, subtracts it from the caller's delta without any bound and credits it to the hook (Hooks.sol:232-243, src/PoolManager.sol:177-183). The hook call is skipped only when msg.sender is the hook itself (Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). No other function removes liquidity. The swap path has the same shape: beforeSwap and afterSwap deltas move value between swapper and hook (Hooks.sol:248-315), and the hook of a dynamic fee pool can set the LP fee to 100 percent (src/PoolManager.sol:339-346, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:25, 37-45).
findings.impact: Principal and uncollected fees of every position in the affected pool. A reverting hook freezes them. A hook with the return delta bit can take part or all of what a removal would pay out, up to what the LP's router accepts. Funds in other pools are not reachable this way, because the caller delta plus the hook delta always equals the pool delta (Hooks.sol:230, 242, 312) and each party must net to zero before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112).
findings.preconditions: The pool's hook address has bit 9 (0x200) or bit 8 (0x100) set, and for taking funds also bit 0. The hook code reverts, returns a bad selector, returns a hostile delta, or is replaced or removed after LPs deposit. LPs must have chosen that pool. This is how the hook design works; I list it because it is a path to a freeze or loss that the text of core does not limit.
findings.mitigations: LPs and position managers can read the low 14 bits of the hook address before depositing and treat bits 9, 8 and 0 as custody risk unless the hook code is immutable and reviewed. Routers should enforce minimum amounts on removal so a hostile return delta reverts. The deployer cannot change this without adding a removal path that skips hooks.

verification.factCheck: The finding claims no network difference, so the chain facts to check are its remark that code behind a hook address can change after pool creation and whether the repository expects the behaviour. I fetched EIP-7702, status Final. It says each authorization writes the delegation indicator 0xef0100 || address into the authorizing account's code, that a later authorization can point elsewhere or clear the code, and that code executing operations load the code the delegation points to. An externally owned account whose low 14 bits carry hook flags can therefore act as a hook, and its owner can replace or remove the logic later. I fetched EIP-6780, which limits account deletion by SELFDESTRUCT to the transaction that created the contract. On chain, eth_getCode on Arbitrum One for 0xa853180523bd16fa6a9c449ab050e108da642488 returned 0xef01001947e2c7b5ca44f2db6236cf5ac3e23457e8a488, which is a delegation indicator at an address whose low bits set beforeInitialize, afterAddLiquidity, beforeSwap and beforeSwapReturnsDelta. I did not confirm that an initialized pool uses that address, and it does not carry the removal bits 9 or 8. The repository's own tests expect the behaviour the finding describes. test/PoolManager.t.sol:272-287 expects a removal to revert with InvalidHookResponse when the hook returns a wrong selector. test/CustomAccounting.t.sol:297-322 expects a hook to receive 5.43 percent of a withdrawal through the afterRemoveLiquidity return delta.
verification.codeCheck: modifyLiquidity is the only function that changes a position (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184). It calls beforeModifyLiquidity before the pool update (src/PoolManager.sol:156). For liquidityDelta <= 0 with bit 9 set the library calls beforeRemoveLiquidity (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:203-204). callHook reverts when the call fails (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134-137) and when the return data is shorter than 32 bytes or the selector differs (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154). A call to an address without code succeeds with empty return data and then fails the length check. After the pool update, afterModifyLiquidity calls afterRemoveLiquidity when bit 8 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:233-241), requires exactly 64 bytes of return data when bit 0 is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:166) and subtracts the returned delta from the caller's delta (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:242). The subtraction is bounded only by the int128 range (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:34-46). The hook delta is credited to the hook address and the remainder to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:181-183). The only bypass is a call where msg.sender is the hook (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). I looked for a guard the finding missed and found none: there is no removal path without the hook call and no cap on the return delta. The caller delta and the hook delta always sum to the pool delta, and unlock reverts unless every delta is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:112), so funds of other pools are out of reach, and a return delta larger than the payout succeeds only when the LP's own unlock callback pays the shortfall. The swap path matches the description (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:248-315), and updateDynamicLPFee accepts any fee up to 1,000,000 from the hook of a dynamic fee pool (src/PoolManager.sol:339-346, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:25, 37-45).
verification.corrections: The difference field presents changing code as a property of some networks. EIP-7702 delegation and upgradeable proxy hooks make it possible on every network that has activated EIP-7702, Ethereum included, so the exposure does not depend on the network. The freeze case needs nothing from the LP. The taking case needs the LP's router to accept the reduced amount, as the finding says. The add liquidity path has the same shape through bits 11, 10 and 1, which can block or surcharge deposits and cannot hold existing funds. Severity stays medium because the loss is limited to pools whose LPs chose that hook address, and the tests show this is the intended trust model.

findings.title: Uncollected fees above the int128 maximum make every later update of a liquidity position revert
findings.difference: None. The condition is the same on every network. It needs a token whose supply in base units is larger than 2^127 - 1, about 1.7e38. The comment at src/libraries/Pool.sol:403 says the code assumes token supply stays within uint128.
findings.mechanism: Every modifyLiquidity call, including a zero delta poke and a removal, runs Position.update and then casts both fee amounts with feesOwed0.toInt128() and feesOwed1.toInt128() (src/libraries/Pool.sol:184-192). Position.update computes the fee as (feeGrowthInside - feeGrowthInsideLast) * liquidity / 2^128 for the whole position (src/libraries/Position.sol:92-97). SafeCast.toInt128(uint256) reverts for values of 2^127 or more (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). Because the whole call reverts, the position's fee checkpoint is never updated. The amount owed therefore never goes down, and every later call for that position reverts the same way, whatever liquidityDelta is used. Fees reach a position through swaps (Pool.sol:401-407) and through donate (Pool.sol:466-480). Each single donate or swap is capped at int128, so the threshold is crossed over two or more calls. I confirmed the arithmetic with a Python transcription of Pool, Position and SafeCast: after two donations of 2^126 + 10 units to a range with one position, updates with delta 0, -1, -1e18 and +1 all revert.
findings.impact: The principal in both currencies and the uncollected fees of that one position stay in the PoolManager with no way out. Other positions in the pool and other pools are not affected.
findings.preconditions: One position must be owed 2^127 base units or more of one currency in fees that it has not yet collected. Fees owed are real tokens paid by swappers or donors, so the token's supply in base units must exceed 1.7e38 and a payer must give up that amount. For a token with a supply below that bound the state cannot be reached. A party that controls such a token's supply can already drain the other side of the pool by selling, so this adds a way to freeze but no extra profit.
findings.mitigations: LPs can avoid pools with a token whose base unit supply exceeds 2^127, and can collect fees with a zero delta call before the amount owed gets near the bound. Pool creators can check totalSupply and decimals. A code change that caps or splits the fee credit would remove the condition.

verification.factCheck: The finding states no network difference and I found none, because the path uses no chain feature. No external source applies, so the facts are in the repository. I recomputed the arithmetic on my own. Two donations of 2^126 + 10 base units into a range with one position give a fee growth for which Position.update returns 2^127 + 19 or 2^127 + 20 for position liquidity of 1, 1e6, 1e18 and about 2^100. Each value is at or above the bound where SafeCast.toInt128 reverts. No test covers the case. test/PoolManager.t.sol:908-915 bounds a single donation to the int128 maximum, and test/libraries/Position.t.sol:26-70 fuzzes Position.update without the cast that follows it in Pool. Two links are unconfirmed. I could not confirm whether any token held by a deployed PoolManager has a base unit supply above 2^127 - 1, which is the researcher's open lead. I did not exercise the path on the deployed contracts, because it needs an unlock callback and a read only call cannot reach it.
verification.codeCheck: Pool.modifyLiquidity calls Position.update for every liquidityDelta, including zero and negative values, and then casts both fee amounts with toInt128 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:183-193). Position.update computes fees on the full liquidity held before the update (src/libraries/Position.sol:82, 92-97). SafeCast.toInt128(uint256) reverts at 2^127 (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). The revert undoes the checkpoint write at src/libraries/Position.sol:100-101, so the amount owed can stay or grow and cannot shrink. The ticks of a position that holds liquidity keep a nonzero liquidityGross, so their feeGrowthOutside values are set once and are cleared only when the last position leaves (src/libraries/Pool.sol:533-539, 196-203). Fee growth inside the range can therefore not be lowered by anyone. Wrapping the growth difference past 2^256 would take further real payments of roughly 2^128 times the position liquidity less the amount already owed, which for any realistic liquidity is far more than a uint128 supply. Pool.donate caps one donation below 2^127 (src/libraries/Pool.sol:471) and the casts on the swap delta cap one swap (src/libraries/Pool.sol:454-460), so the bound is crossed over two or more payments. The owed fees are backed by tokens: a donor who shares the range receives only its own pro rata share back, so the victim's share has to be paid in. There is no partial fee collection and no other exit, so the principal of that position in both currencies stays in the PoolManager.
verification.corrections: Severity raised from low to medium. The scale reserves low for hazards with no direct loss path, and this is a direct and permanent freeze of a position, limited to pools with a token whose base unit supply exceeds 2^127 - 1. The actor is any holder of 2^127 base units who gives them up as a donation or as swap fees, or ordinary swap volume against a passive position that never collects. The bound is 2^127, half of the uint128 supply that the comment at src/libraries/Pool.sol:403 names as the assumption, so a token inside the stated assumption with a supply between 2^127 and 2^128 can still reach it. The finding's point that an issuer with unlimited supply can already empty the pool by selling holds, and it does not cover a third party token with a large fixed supply, where the attacker gains nothing and the LP still loses access to both currencies of the position.
