findings.title: Scheduled Jenner fork adds protocol-native tokens whose issuer can seize, pause or block the PoolManager balance
findings.difference: BNB Smart Chain has scheduled the Jenner fork for 2026-12-08 02:30 UTC. It ships BEP-702, a token standard named CAS20 that runs as native code behind addresses starting with 0xCA52. Every CAS20 token has a role that can reassign a holder's balance (seizeWithMemo), a per-feature pause, and transfer policies that read shared allowlists and blocklists. BEP-703 lets governance list these tokens as payment assets with reserved block space. Ethereum has no token logic in the protocol.
findings.mechanism: 1. The PoolManager keeps every pool's reserves, all ERC-6909 claims and accrued protocol fees for a currency in one balance, read by balanceOf at src/types/Currency.sol:94 and paid out by transfer at src/types/Currency.sol:60-75. 2. A CAS20 token keeps the transfer and balanceOf selectors, so pools can be initialized with it. initialize makes no call to the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). 3. The token admin points SEIZE_HOLDER_POLICY at a blocklist that contains the PoolManager address. An account with SEIZE_ROLE then calls seizeWithMemo(PoolManager, to, value). The balance moves without any take, and no delta is recorded. Pool accounting still shows the old reserves, so the last liquidity providers and claim holders to exit find transfer failing for lack of balance. 4. If TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY stops authorizing the PoolManager, or the TRANSFER feature is paused, the token reverts every transfer from the PoolManager. Currency.transfer then reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, so take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56) fail for every pool that uses the token. 5. If TRANSFER_RECEIVER_POLICY stops authorizing the PoolManager, nobody can pay the token in, and settle credits nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). 6. The Asset variant multiplier does not change balanceOf, so it creates no rebase at the PoolManager. That part was checked and is safe.
findings.impact: All reserves, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees held in the affected CAS20 token across every pool. Seizure is a loss for liquidity providers of those pools. A policy change or pause is a freeze that lasts until the issuer reverses it. Liquidity providers can still remove liquidity, take the counter-asset and hold the affected token as an ERC-6909 claim through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), because mint makes no token call.
findings.preconditions: Jenner activates as scheduled, chain governance opens CAS20 creation through the ActivationRegistry, a CAS20 token is created, and pools holding it exist on the PoolManager. The issuer roles of that token must then act. An unprivileged attacker can do this only with a token it issued itself, which harms only those who pool against that token. None of these conditions hold today. The factory and registry addresses have no code at the time of the query. The BEP is still marked Draft and the client implementation was not read, so the final behaviour could differ from the text.
findings.mitigations: Treat CAS20 tokens as issuer-controlled assets in interfaces and routing. Before listing a CAS20 pool, read the token's six policy ids, its pause mask and the holders of SEIZE_ROLE and the admin role. Prefer tokens whose role membership is frozen with no seizer. Liquidity providers should size positions on the assumption that the issuer can take or freeze the pooled balance. After the fork, re-test take and settle against a CAS20 token on a fork node.

verification.factCheck: BEP-702 was fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com. Its status is Draft and it was created on 2026-07-16. Section 3.3 reserves every address that starts with 0xCA52 followed by eight zero bytes. Section 3.6 says seizeWithMemo reassigns the balance of the from account without an allowance and without the transfer policies, and that the account is seizable only when the holder policy does not authorize it. Section 3.8 lists six policy scopes and says each starts at policy 0 (ALWAYS_ALLOW), so no account is seizable on an unconfigured token. Section 3.9 says pause(TRANSFER) halts transfers and leaves seizeWithMemo callable. Section 3.12 says balanceOf returns the raw balance. BEP-718 lists BEP-702, BEP-703 and BEP-706 for Jenner and says token creation is opened by a governance-appointed activation switch. The BSC CHANGELOG entry for v1.8.2 schedules mainnet Jenner for 2026-12-08 02:30:00 UTC (1796697000), and params/config.go on master sets the mainnet JennerTime to 1796697000. BEP-703 names BEP-702 native tokens as eligible payment contracts. I also read the client, which the finding did not. core/vm/evm.go on master resolves any address with the CAS20 prefix to native code once IsJenner is true. core/vm/cas20_token.go implements transfer: it reverts with ContractPaused when TRANSFER is paused, reverts with PolicyForbids when the sender policy or the receiver policy does not authorize the account, and returns a 32 byte true on success. core/vm/cas20_admin.go implements seizeWithMemo: it requires SEIZE_ROLE, skips the transfer policies and moves the balance when the seize policy does not authorize the holder. On chain at BSC block 135,080,406 on 2026-11-22: the block timestamp is 1795351088, which is 15.6 days before JennerTime, and eth_getCode is empty at 0xCA5F000000000000000000000000000000000000, 0x7020000000000000000000000000000000000001, 0x7020000000000000000000000000000000000002, 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000002007 and two addresses in the token range. A revert from the token reaches src/types/Currency.sol:82-86 and reverts the take. collectProtocolFees ends in the same transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). A CAS20 transfer returns 32 bytes holding 1, which passes the success test at src/types/Currency.sol:68. initialize makes no call to either currency (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142), so a pool can be created for any CAS20 address. A seizure lowers balanceOf(PoolManager) and writes no delta. No function in src/ reconciles pool accounting with the real balance, so takes fail with InsufficientBalance once the sum requested exceeds what is left. A seizure that lands between sync and settle makes the checked subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 revert for that settle. With the receiver policy closed, no token can reach the PoolManager and settle credits zero (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). mint and burn make no token call (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336) and modifyLiquidity makes none (src/PoolManager.sol:145-184), so liquidity providers can leave with the counter-asset and an ERC-6909 claim on the frozen token, as the finding says. findings.title: EIP-7702 lets the code behind a hook address be replaced or removed after a pool is created
findings.difference: Since Pectra (EIP-7702) an EOA can point its code at any contract through a delegation indicator, repoint it in a later transaction, or clear it. Since Dencun (EIP-6780) an ordinary contract cannot delete its code after the creation transaction. On mainnet today a delegated EOA is therefore the one kind of account whose code can change or vanish at a fixed address without a proxy pattern in its bytecode.
findings.mechanism: initialize accepts a hook address on its low 14 bits alone and never looks at code (src/PoolManager.sol:126, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127). An EOA whose address ends in chosen flag bits is cheap to find because only 14 bits must match. While the EOA delegates to honest hook code the pool behaves normally. If the account holder clears the delegation, a call to the hook succeeds with empty return data, and callHook reverts with InvalidHookResponse because the result is shorter than 32 bytes (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). With the before or after remove liquidity flag set, every liquidity removal by anyone other than the hook address then reverts (src/PoolManager.sol:156, 178; src/libraries/Hooks.sol:195-206, 232-243), so LPs cannot withdraw until the holder delegates again. If the holder repoints the delegation to hostile code and the address carries a returns-delta flag, the new code can assign itself part of each withdrawal or swap, because the hook delta is credited to the hook and subtracted from the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:233-243, 298-313; src/PoolManager.sol:181-183, 224-226). The hook address is skipped when it is itself the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175, 217, 253, 293), and a delegated EOA can originate transactions. The holder can therefore delegate to code that answers the unlock callback for its own calls and returns invalid data to hook calls made for everyone else.
findings.impact: Funds of LPs and swappers in pools that use such a hook. Other pools are not affected because pool math never reads another pool's state. The same outcome is already possible with an upgradeable proxy hook; the change is that inspecting the code at the hook address at one point in time no longer shows it.
findings.preconditions: The attacker creates the pool with a delegated EOA as hook and LPs deposit into it. I did not scan mainnet for existing pools whose hook is a delegated account.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces, routers and LPs can read the code at the hook address and reject hooks whose code is the 23 byte delegation indicator starting with 0xef0100, or that have no code. The deployer could add a code check in initialize, but the same account could delegate afterwards, so the check belongs in periphery and off-chain listing.

findings.mechanism: 1. Unchanged from cycle 7: if HyperCore recorded the PoolManager as the address to rebalance from, the node would send transfer calls on that token with the PoolManager as msg.sender. The token would move the balance while pool state, ERC-6909 balances and protocol fee counters keep recording the tokens as owed, because the PoolManager reads a balance only between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365). The last takes in that token would then revert inside the transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:55-87). 2. New in this cycle. The census of 3,000 recent blocks finds 1,030 system transactions, 435 sent in the name of the CoreDepositWallet contract and 195 in the name of the treasury address 0xc20699185c15D0a2fD65779BB5d69f5b0B113c00, and none names the PoolManager; its nonce is still 1. HyperCore spot metadata links no token to the PoolManager and exposes no field that names an AQAv2 treasury, so the record behind step 1 still cannot be read. 3. An ordinary account cannot create that record: the documentation ties AQAv2 activation to two deployers that each stake 500,000 HYPE and to a validator vote, and the link of a spot token to a contract needs the contract's CREATE deployer or a finalizer stored in slot 0 or in the slot keccak256("HyperCore deployer"), which for the PoolManager only the owner contract could arrange (cleared in cycle 4).
findings.impact: All pools and ERC-6909 claims in a token for which HyperCore named the PoolManager as the rebalancing address. Nothing is exposed today: no system transaction has named the PoolManager and its nonce is 1.
findings.preconditions: The validator set, or whatever privileged record names an AQAv2 treasury, must name the PoolManager. An ordinary account cannot.
findings.mitigations: Watch the PoolManager's account nonce, which rises with the first transaction sent in its name, and the from field of system transactions. Ask the Hyperliquid team whether the node refuses an address with code as AQAv2 treasury.

findings.title: PoolManager ownership on Celo and X Layer rests on the upgradeable L2CrossDomainMessenger, and on X Layer a 2 of 3 Safe of EOAs can upgrade it
findings.difference: On Ethereum the owner is the governance timelock itself. On both chains the owner is a cross-chain account contract that accepts a call when msg.sender is the L2CrossDomainMessenger predeploy and that predeploy reports the Ethereum timelock as the cross-domain sender. The predeploy is a proxy. On Celo its admin is controlled by the alias of an L1 2 of 2 Safe of two 6 of 8 Safes. On X Layer its admin is controlled by a Safe on X Layer with threshold 2 and three EOA owners.
findings.mechanism: Whoever controls the messenger implementation can make it call the owner contract while reporting the timelock as sender. The owner contract then forwards a call to the PoolManager as owner. The only owner function in src/ is setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). The Owned base contract is missing from this checkout because lib/solmate is empty, so its ownership transfer functions could not be read. A controller chosen this way can set a protocol fee of at most 1000 pips per direction on any pool (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8 and 25-32) and can withdraw accrued protocol fees to any recipient (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). The fee is taken from swap input before the LP fee (src/libraries/Pool.sol:385-396). collectProtocolFees subtracts from protocolFeesAccrued with checked arithmetic, so it cannot pay out more than was accrued.
findings.impact: Up to 0.1 percent of swap input per direction on every pool for as long as the hostile controller stays, paid by swappers, plus any accrued protocol fees. Both are zero today because no controller is set. Pool reserves, ERC-6909 claims and LP principal are not reachable through the owner or the controller role.
findings.preconditions: On X Layer two of the three Safe owners must sign an upgrade of the messenger predeploy. On Celo both 6 of 8 Safes must sign. Uniswap governance can undo the controller change only through the same messenger.
findings.mitigations: Monitor ProtocolFeeControllerUpdated and ProtocolFeeUpdated on both chains and Upgraded events on the messenger proxy. The 0.1 percent cap in the code bounds the loss.

verification.factCheck: On both chains owner() of the PoolManager returns 0x044aAF330d7fD6AE683EEc5c1C1d1fFf5196B6b7, which has 1,488 bytes of code with the same hash on Celo and X Layer. Its l1Owner() is 0x1a9C8182C09F50C8318d769245beA52c32BE35BC and its messenger() is 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000007. Celo Blockscout serves verified source for it: forward requires msg.sender to be the messenger and xDomainMessageSender() to equal l1Owner, then calls the target. protocolFeeController() is the zero address on both chains. The EIP-1967 admin slot of the messenger predeploy holds 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000018 on both chains and the implementation slot is set. On X Layer the ProxyAdmin owner is 0xC290be56089bCC83C6993583ce2cF51a7951D45A, a Safe with threshold 2 and three owners that have no code. On Celo the ProxyAdmin owner is 0x51a3a77bAF58FEf0309452ceacB09221E556F223, which has no code and unaliases to the Ethereum Safe 0x4092A77bAF58fef0309452cEaCb09221e556E112 with threshold 2 and two owners, each a 6 of 8 Safe. The Upgrade 19 notice describes the L2 Contract Manager as a consensus layer mechanism for predeploy upgrades. An eth_call with the CLZ opcode fails as not activated on both chains, so the Osaka rules that come with Karst are not active on either.
verification.codeCheck: setProtocolFeeController is owner only (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32) and no other function in src/ uses onlyOwner. setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees accept only the controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:36 and 48). isValidProtocolFee caps each direction at 1,000 pips (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8 and 25-32), and Slot0 masks the stored value to 24 bits (src/types/Slot0.sol:78-86). Pool.swap takes the protocol share out of the fee the swapper paid in each step (src/libraries/Pool.sol:385-398), with the step fee computed in src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-105, so the share cannot exceed the fee paid. protocolFeesAccrued grows only in _swap (src/PoolManager.sol:238, src/ProtocolFees.sol:66-70) and collectProtocolFees subtracts with checked arithmetic before the transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). The owner and the controller reach accrued protocol fees and a levy of at most 0.1 percent per direction on later swaps. They do not reach pool reserves or ERC-6909 claims. lib/solmate is empty in this checkout, so Owned could not be read here. I tested the deployed contracts instead: an eth_call of transferOwnership(address) from the owner contract returns on both chains and the same call from another sender reverts with UNAUTHORIZED, as does setProtocolFeeController. The synced currency guard is covered by test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1039.
verification.corrections: 1. Severity raised from low to medium. Low requires that no direct loss path was found. This finding has one: whoever controls the messenger can appoint a controller, add up to 0.1 percent per direction to every later swap and take what accrues. The actor is a chain level upgrade authority and the reach is capped at protocol fees. The same finding on the ETH gas OP Stack chains was set to medium in this cycle. 2. The owner role includes transferOwnership on the deployed contracts. A forged message can move ownership to another address, after which Uniswap governance cannot undo the change through the messenger. The finding says governance can undo it. 3. The guard in collectProtocolFees checks the synced currency and skips address(0). It does not check the lock state (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49). On Celo a native fee collection is therefore allowed while the CELO token is synced, which the research file already lists as a lead. 4. The same signers hold wider powers than the finding covers. On X Layer the proxy admin of the L1 OptimismPortal is owned by a Safe at the same address on Ethereum with threshold 2 and the same three owners, and the SystemConfig owner is one of those three accounts acting alone. On Celo the Security Council in the governance hotfix path is the same aliased Safe that owns the ProxyAdmin. The portal route is listed as a lead. 5. Accrued fees were checked for native CELO and the CELO token on Celo, where both are zero. Other currencies and X Layer were not checked.

findings.title: PoolManager ownership rests on an upgradeable messenger predeploy on five chains and on the portal alias on two, and a takeover reaches protocol fees only
findings.difference: On Ethereum the owner is a contract that acts directly. On OP Mainnet, Base, Zora, World Chain and Soneium the owner is a CrossChainAccount that accepts a call only when msg.sender is L2CrossDomainMessenger at 0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000007 and xDomainMessageSender() equals the Ethereum timelock 0x1a9C8182C09F50C8318d769245beA52c32BE35BC. The messenger is a proxy whose admin is the ProxyAdmin predeploy, owned by an aliased L1 upgrade multisig, and since Karst predeploys are also upgraded by network upgrade deposits at fork activation. On Unichain and Ink the owner is the bare alias 0x2bad8182c09f50c8318d769245bea52c32be46cd, which only a deposit from the timelock through that chain's OptimismPortal can produce.
findings.mechanism: 1. Whoever controls the messenger implementation can make xDomainMessageSender() return the timelock address and call CrossChainAccount.forward, which then calls the PoolManager as owner. On the alias chains the same result needs a change to deposit derivation or to the portal. 2. The owner can call setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). 3. The controller can call setProtocolFee for any pool, limited to 1,000 pips per direction by isValidProtocolFee (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32), and can call collectProtocolFees to any recipient. 4. collectProtocolFees subtracts the amount from protocolFeesAccrued[currency] with checked arithmetic before the transfer (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56), so it cannot pay out more than the fees accrued for that currency. Pool reserves and ERC-6909 claims are out of reach of the owner and the controller. 5. On OP Mainnet and Base the current controller forwards collections to a fixed token jar and lets anyone trigger collect, so the present setup does not let a caller redirect fees.
findings.impact: Accrued protocol fees, about 0.030 ETH of native fees on OP Mainnet and 0.034 ETH on Base at read time, plus whatever has accrued in ERC-20 currencies, which was not read, and up to 0.1 percent per direction of future swap volume on every pool of the chain. No LP principal. On the five chains without a controller nothing has accrued.
findings.preconditions: Control of the chain's L2 predeploy upgrade path: the aliased ProxyAdmin owner, a hard fork upgrade bundle, or a compromise of the L1 timelock itself. Each of these parties can already do more damage to bridged assets than to the PoolManager.
findings.mitigations: Uniswap governance can monitor ProtocolFeeControllerUpdated and OwnershipTransferred events on each chain. Swappers and LPs can read the protocol fee of a pool from slot0 before trading. No code change in core is needed because the owner's reach is already capped by src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56.

verification.corrections: 1. Severity raised from low to medium. The definition of low requires that no direct loss path was found. This finding has one: a party that controls the predeploy upgrade path or a fork bundle can appoint itself controller, take accrued fees and add up to 0.1 percent per direction to every later swap. The actor is chain governance, which would place it at high, and the reach is capped at protocol fees, so medium fits. 2. The list of actors is incomplete. Network upgrade deposits are written by the fork authors and can carry any sender. The Ecotone and Isthmus specifications define upgrade deposits sent from the zero address. findings.title: stHYPE and wstHYPE are two currency ids over one share balance, so a loss in the rebasing face is paid from the shares of pools in the other face
findings.difference: The StakedHYPE liquid staking token on HyperEVM has two ERC-20 contracts that read and write the same storage. stHYPE at 0xfFaa4a3D97fE9107Cef8a3F48c069F577Ff76cC1 stores shares with 24 decimals and reports shares times totalSupply divided by totalShares. wstHYPE at 0x94e8396e0869c9F2200760aF0621aFd240E1CF38 keeps no balances: its balanceOf returns stHYPE.sharesOf divided by 1e6 and its transfer calls stHYPE.transferShares. Every holder has both balances at once, and a transfer through either contract changes both. The issuer's docs describe this and warn that multi entry point tokens have caused losses elsewhere. The stHYPE figure rises every second, because totalSupply is interpolated over an interval of 82,800 seconds, and a rebase to a lower supply applies in the same transaction. On Ethereum, stETH and wstETH are separate tokens with separate balances.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager treats the two addresses as unrelated currencies. Deltas, pool reserves and ERC-6909 claims are recorded per currency address in that currency's unit (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41, src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). A take under either id calls transfer on that contract and moves shares out of the single balance the PoolManager holds (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-87). Let S be the shares the PoolManager holds, W the amount owed under the wstHYPE id in shares, T the amount owed under the stHYPE id in stHYPE units, and r the stHYPE per share rate. The PoolManager can pay everyone while S is at least W plus T divided by r. I first checked what an ordinary account can do. A credit under either id needs a rise of that contract's balanceOf between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365). Both balances rise only when shares arrive, since r depends on block.timestamp and is constant inside one transaction (stHYPE.sol lines 495 to 513) and Overseer.rebase reverts for a caller without REBASER_ROLE. One deposit therefore cannot be credited under both ids, and no account can move r inside its own sync window. Rounding between the two units is at most one base unit per settle. Three effects remain. First, T is a fixed number while r grows, so the staking yield on the shares that back stHYPE pools and claims stays in the PoolManager and no pool or claim can withdraw it. Second, when the rebaser reports a lower supply, r falls at once (stHYPE.sol lines 400 to 404). T does not change, so paying T now takes more shares than were paid in. If the PoolManager also holds shares for wstHYPE pools, those takes succeed by using them, and the wstHYPE pools end up short by T times the difference of 1/r after and 1/r before. An account that sees the slash coming (the Overseer exposes pendingSlashExists) can deposit under the stHYPE id before the rebase and withdraw after it, and gains that difference on its deposit. Third, pauseTransfer on stHYPE blocks transfer and transferShares, so one pause stops take under both ids.
findings.impact: No funds are exposed today: sharesOf(PoolManager) is zero. If pools or claims exist under both ids, a slash of x percent moves about x percent of the amount owed under the stHYPE id from the LPs of wstHYPE pools to the accounts that withdraw stHYPE first. LPs of stHYPE pools lose the staking yield on their stHYPE, about 2 percent a year at the current rate. A pause freezes every pool that uses either id.
findings.preconditions: Liquidity or claims under both ids in the PoolManager. The loss needs a rebase to a lower supply, which only a holder of REBASER_ROLE can send and which follows a validator slash; Hyperliquid has no automatic slashing at present. The yield loss needs no actor. I did not read the Overseer implementation at 0x2b8698dd4b8addf7ddcabc46c6aedafe5a70b11c, which is not verified on Sourcify. That no public function other than rebase starts a rebase rests on the simulated revert of rebase for an unprivileged caller and on the last rebase transaction.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces and routers on HyperEVM should offer wstHYPE pools only and refuse pools whose currencies include the stHYPE address. LPs should not provide stHYPE through the rebasing contract. The PoolManager cannot call setSelfDisableTransfer on stHYPE with any of its call shapes, so excluding the stHYPE face needs a change in core or a refusal at the interface level. Monitoring should watch stHYPE for Rebase events whose new supply is below the current supply and for TransferPaused.

verification.factCheck: I read the two verified implementations on Sourcify (exact match for both) and reran the chain reads on 2026-11-22 near block 51,966,500. The EIP-1967 slot of stHYPE (0xfFaa4a3D97fE9107Cef8a3F48c069F577Ff76cC1) holds 0xe71caf5c1fe56d8897c7b604295d23968049e057 and that of wstHYPE (0x94e8396e0869c9F2200760aF0621aFd240E1CF38) holds 0x104324863cfb2220756c60384efa9bb67a57aaf7. wstHYPE.sol keeps no balances: balanceOf returns sthype.sharesOf(who) / 1e6 (line 149) and _transfer calls sthype.transferShares(from, to, amount * 1e6) (line 110). stHYPE.sol stores shares, converts with totalSupplyRaw over totalShares (lines 442 to 459), interpolates the supply over syncStart to syncEnd (lines 495 to 513), applies a lower supply at once in syncSupply (lines 400 to 404), restricts syncSupply to REBASER_ROLE (line 394) and blocks transfer and transferShares while transferPaused is set (lines 264 to 288). On chain: stHYPE totalSupply 2,275,416.78, wstHYPE totalSupply 2,192,579.21, ratio 1.03778, balancePerShare 1.037780935902397401, syncEnd minus syncStart 82,800 seconds, rewardsToSync 123.556 HYPE, transferPaused false. sharesOf(PoolManager) and both balanceOf(PoolManager) are zero. rebase() on the Overseer 0xB96f07367e69e86d6e9C3F29215885104813eeAE reverts with AccessControlUnauthorizedAccount (0xe2517d3f) for role 0x5fde63b5...0b75 from an unrelated address and from the PoolManager, and that role value equals keccak256 of REBASER_ROLE. pendingSlashExists() exists and returns false. The issuer page states that the two tokens are two interfaces to the same data, that a transfer of one performs the same action for the other, and warns about multi entry point tokens. The Hyperliquid staking page states that no automatic slashing is implemented at present. I also ran one creation style eth_call that reads stHYPE.balanceOf of a third holder, calls Overseer.mint(address) with 1 HYPE, reads again, calls burnAndRedeemIfPossible and reads again. Both calls succeeded and the holder balance stayed at 106401669038400087184 in all three reads, so a public mint or burn does not move the rate inside one execution. I did not simulate Overseer.redeem(uint256) and the Overseer implementation 0x2b8698dd4b8addf7ddcabc46c6aedafe5a70b11c is not verified, so the statement that only the rebaser can move the rate rests on these simulations and on the role gate in stHYPE.
verification.codeCheck: The PoolManager keys every delta on the pair of caller and currency address (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16 and 28-41) and every claim on uint160 of the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336, src/types/Currency.sol:110-118), so the two token addresses are two unrelated ids. take debits the id it names and calls transfer on that contract (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-87); both contracts return a 32 byte true to the PoolManager for a zero amount transfer, which the success test at Currency.sol:64-74 accepts. A credit is the rise of one balanceOf between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-365), the subtraction at line 360 is checked, and one transient slot holds the synced currency (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32), so one deposit of shares gives one credit. I looked for a guard that would stop the loss shift and found none: nothing in src compares the shares held with the sum owed under both ids, and no function reconciles pool state with a token balance. I also looked for an unprivileged variant. The rate is a function of block.timestamp and four storage fields that only syncSupply, mint and burn write, mint and burn keep the rate (stHYPE.sol lines 244 to 256 with the conversion at 442 to 447), and my simulation agrees. The three effects in the finding follow: a fixed stHYPE amount owed while the rate grows leaves yield in the PoolManager, a lower supply makes the same stHYPE amount cost more shares, which a take under the stHYPE id draws from the common share balance, and a pause stops transferShares, which stops wstHYPE transfers as well.
verification.corrections: The actor issuer is correct for the loss shift and for the freeze, since both need a call by a holder of REBASER_ROLE or PAUSER_ROLE, and the slash that would lead to a lower supply is not available to an ordinary account. An ordinary account that deposits under the stHYPE id before such a rebase gains only if that rebase happens. Medium fits because the PoolManager holds neither token today and the loss needs pools or claims under both ids. The statement about slashing is backed by the Hyperliquid staking page, which the finding did not cite.

findings.title: Activated Stylus programs exist on Robinhood Chain as well, and a copy of an activated program runs without a new activation
findings.difference: Nitro chains run WASM contracts next to EVM contracts. A WASM contract answers calls only while its code hash is recorded as activated at the current Stylus version and the record is younger than the expiry period. Ethereum has no contract whose callability ends with time or with a protocol version. Cycle 1 recorded this for Arbitrum One and cleared Robinhood Chain on the ground that activation is closed there, without checking for earlier activations. Robinhood Chain has 26 activated code hashes, and the activation record is per code hash on both chains.
findings.mechanism: The client looks a program up under the code hash of the called contract and fails the call when the record is missing, expired or at another Stylus version. Activation costs activationGas, which is 2^64-1 on both chains, so no new code hash can be activated and an expired one cannot be reactivated. A record can be extended with codehashKeepalive once it is 31 days old, by any account. An ordinary account can still deploy a new contract with the bytecode of one of the activated programs, at an address whose low 14 bits form a valid hook flag set, and name it as the hook or a currency of a pool. When the record of that code hash expires after 365 days without a keepalive, or when a later ArbOS release raises the Stylus version, every call to the contract fails. A failed hook call makes callHook revert, so each pool action that reaches the hook reverts, including liquidity removal when the address carries a remove flag. A failed transfer call makes take revert for that currency.
findings.impact: Funds in pools that use a Stylus program as hook or token. Liquidity providers cannot remove liquidity through a hook that no longer answers, and nobody can take a token that no longer answers. Pools without such a hook or token are not affected. On Robinhood Chain the 26 programs were activated between 2026-07-25 and 2026-10-02, so the first records expire in July 2027 unless someone extends them. I did not check whether any of the 26 programs or a copy of them is used by a pool.
findings.preconditions: The pool creator must choose a Stylus program, or a copy of an activated one, as hook or currency, and the victims must use that pool. The freeze then needs the record to lapse or the Stylus version to change, which needs time or a chain upgrade.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should avoid pools whose hook or token is a Stylus program while activation is closed. Interfaces can read ArbWasm.programVersion and programTimeLeft for a hook or token address and warn when the answer is a live program. Anyone can call codehashKeepalive to extend a record that pools depend on.

verification.factCheck: I repeated the on-chain queries on 2026-11-22. On Robinhood Chain I fetched every log of ArbWasm (0x71) from block 0 to the head near block 120,983,000 in ranges of 5,000,000 blocks. There are 26 logs, all ProgramActivated, with 26 distinct code hashes, all at version 3. The first is in block 18,864,425 (timestamp 1784967900, 2026-07-25) and the last in block 78,438,208 (timestamp 1790964946, 2026-10-02). stylusVersion() is 3, expiryDays() is 365, keepaliveDays() is 31 and activationGas() is 2^64-1 on Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain and Elysium. programTimeLeft returns 21,111,176 seconds for the oldest program 0xabce50d4038d9cfa6bc85ff8768d7b1e8149b2e5 and 27,108,774 seconds for the newest 0x3e65dfc1f7863f11ba0e12870bfb5fdf5913a34e, so the oldest record lapses near 2027-07-24. I tested the copy claim directly on Robinhood Chain. With the code of three activated programs placed at an unused address by state override, every call returned the same result as the call to the original, and ArbWasm.programVersion and programTimeLeft answered for the copy. With one byte of the code changed, the same call failed with ProgramNotActivated(). A simulated activateProgram with 30,000,000 gas reverted. A simulated codehashKeepalive for the oldest code hash from an unrelated account succeeded. On Arbitrum One the program 0x2e5d89a229cbd17efb0a731d26232f88c3746aa9, still at version 2, fails with ProgramNeedsUpgrade(2, 3). With a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address, transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(PoolManager) and a hook selector sent to it as inner calls all returned failure, while the version 3 program 0xaff2f129d2bcba4649a54fb516be0cc78288898d answered transfer and balanceOf. Source at Nitro v3.12.4: CallProgram takes contract.CodeHash and calls getActiveProgram (arbos/programs/programs.go lines 206 to 218), which fails for version 0, for a version other than the current one and for an age above ExpiryDays (lines 559 to 579). ProgramKeepalive needs an active program of at least KeepaliveDays and has no caller check (lines 603 to 624). ArbWasm.ActivateProgram burns the stored activation gas before anything else (precompiles/ArbWasm.go lines 41 to 48). The GitHub tree page of v3.12.4 shows the go-ethereum submodule at 0e44603, and at that commit initNewContract accepts deployed code with the Stylus prefix (core/vm/evm.go lines 727 to 732), so a new contract with the bytes of an activated program can be created while activation is closed. The pause notice says that new and expired programs cannot be activated, that active ones run until they expire and that keepalive renews them. The Security Council report dates the change to 2026-10-02 and names the call ArbOwner.setWasmActivationGas(2^64 - 1). Both documents name Arbitrum One and Nova only.
verification.codeCheck: callHook makes a call with all gas and reverts with HookCallFailed when the call fails (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-137). A call that succeeds with fewer than 32 bytes or with another selector reverts with InvalidHookResponse (Hooks.sol:152-154). beforeModifyLiquidity calls the hook for a zero or negative liquidityDelta when the address has the before remove flag (Hooks.sol:203-204), and afterModifyLiquidity does so for the after remove flag (Hooks.sol:233-243). Both run inside modifyLiquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:156 and 178). The only bypass is the hook itself as caller (Hooks.sol:171-175 and 217), and a program that cannot run cannot be the caller. Permissions are bits of the address (Hooks.sol:337-339), and initialize accepts any address whose bits pass isValidHookAddress (Hooks.sol:109-127, PoolManager.sol:126). The swap and donate hooks fail the same way (Hooks.sol:255-256, 298-302, 322-323 and 332-333). For a token, take debits the caller and then calls transfer, and a failed call reverts with ERC20TransferFailed (PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:64-86). sync and the ERC-20 branch of _settle call balanceOf and revert with it (PoolManager.sol:285 and 359, Currency.sol:94). I found no guard that changes this path. One limit on the token case: modifyLiquidity makes no token call, and mint writes a delta and a claim balance only (PoolManager.sol:322-329). A liquidity provider in a pool whose token stopped answering can still remove liquidity, mint claims for the dead token and take the other currency. What stays locked is the balance of the dead token.
verification.corrections: The actor and the severity stand. The actor is pool-creator because the victims must use a pool whose hook or currency the creator chose. The creator cannot bring about the lapse at will: it needs 365 days without a keepalive, which any account can pay while the record is live, or a Stylus version change by chain governance. Four additions. First, the two Arbitrum documents cover Arbitrum One and Nova. For Robinhood Chain the closed activation rests on the on-chain value of activationGas() and on the date of the last activation, and I found no statement by the chain operator. Second, a copy shares the record of its code hash. One keepalive extends the original and every copy, and a copy deployed late has only the time the original has left. Third, I checked the 26 program addresses on Robinhood Chain. None answers balanceOf(PoolManager) as a token would: 25 revert, and 0xd6cf26df204184fc9c3f2c47c36b04eb631ecf1f returns 64 bytes of hash output for any input and appears in no Initialize event as a currency between block 77,000,000 and the head. The low bits of 16 of the 26 addresses pass isValidHookAddress. The hook is not an indexed field of Initialize, so I did not establish whether a pool uses one of them, a copy, or an EVM contract that forwards to one. Fourth, the finding lists Hooks.sol:194-245 for liquidity changes. The same failure blocks swaps and donations for hooks with those flags, which the mechanism text implies and the references omit.

findings.title: xStocks tokens multiply every balance by a figure the issuer schedules, and the 8 for 1 split of SNDKx raised the PoolManager balance eightfold on Ethereum and X Layer with no transfer
findings.difference: The Robinhood stock tokens cleared in an earlier cycle keep balanceOf fixed and change a display multiplier. The xStocks tokens (symbols ending in x, one implementation behind every proxy) do the opposite: balanceOf is shares times a multiplier, and the multiplier changes at a time the issuer sets. The PoolManager holds them on Ethereum (5 tokens in the window), BNB Smart Chain (42), Monad (4) and X Layer (7 over 6.9 days).
findings.mechanism: 1. BackedAutoFeeTokenImplementation.balanceOf returns shares times getCurrentMultiplier() (lines 254 to 259). getCurrentMultiplier returns lastMultiplier until newMultiplierActivationTime and newMultiplier from that second on, reduced by feePerPeriod for each period that has passed (lines 265 to 283). Only the multiplier updater may schedule a change (lines 445 to 452) and only the owner may set feePerPeriod (lines 392 to 397). 2. SNDKx 0xb63efbc28860c8097e341de1fcf59456161e9d98 has a stored update from 1e18 to 8e18 with activation time 1795167000 (20 November 2026) on Ethereum and on X Layer. On X Layer the block with that timestamp is 76,397,964. The token emitted no log in that block, and balanceOf(PoolManager) went from 137,059,273,049,122,723 to 1,096,474,184,392,981,784 base units, a factor of exactly 8. 3. Pool accounting did not change (src/PoolManager.sol never reads a balance outside sync and settle), so seven eighths of the SNDKx the PoolManager now holds belong to no pool. A provider who had put in one token before the split can take out one token, which is worth one eighth. 4. A pool that still held liquidity at its old price after the activation time would quote eight times the market value for each token sold into it, and any account could sell new tokens there and take the other currency. I did not observe this: the pool that traded SNDKx before the split on X Layer had 1.04 SNDKx removed 21,405 seconds before activation, and later swaps went through another pool at about 26 units of the 6 decimal quote token per SNDKx, against about 267 before. 5. Dividends use the same path in small steps: STRCx has 26 stored updates and a multiplier of 1.1058, and each step raises the PoolManager balance without a transfer. feePerPeriod is 0 on the six token contracts I read on four networks; a value above 0 would lower every balance each period, which would leave pools short. 6. Transfers convert amounts to shares and back, which explains differences of 1 to 8 base units between Transfer logs and balances.
findings.impact: Every pool in an xStocks token on the four networks. Balances today: 569.57 STRCx, 17.34 NVDAx and 1.40 SNDKx on Ethereum; 1.88 SNDKx on X Layer; 42 tokens of up to 9.96 units each on BNB Smart Chain; a few thousand base units on Monad, where 14,932 NVDAx transfers passed through in a day. A split strands the added tokens in the PoolManager and cuts the value of the token side of each position by the split ratio. Each dividend strands the dividend. The other currency of the pool is exposed to whoever trades first after an activation time that is public in advance. I did not measure what share of the 569.57 STRCx is already unaccounted.
findings.preconditions: The issuer schedules a multiplier change, which is a routine corporate action for these tokens, and liquidity stays in the pool past the activation time. An ordinary account cannot bracket the change with sync and settle or with take and repay, because the change happens at a timestamp or inside the updater's own transaction. The arbitrage in step 4 is my reading of the pool mechanics and was not seen on chain.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers must remove liquidity before every scheduled activation and should prefer a wrapped form with a fixed balance. Interfaces should read newMultiplierActivationTime and multiplierUpdates and warn when a change is pending. A hook cannot recover the stranded tokens, because core has no payout for an unaccounted balance.

verification.factCheck: Sourcify reports an exact match for BackedAutoFeeTokenImplementation at 0x65c40d624af3b18c109fbf87b7deff34cdc5f19b on Ethereum (solc 0.8.9). balanceOf returns shares times getCurrentMultiplier() (lines 254 to 259). getCurrentMultiplier returns lastMultiplier while block.timestamp is below newMultiplierActivationTime and newMultiplier afterwards, reduced per period when feePerPeriod is above zero (lines 265 to 283). updateMultiplierValue is limited to the multiplier updater (lines 445 to 452) and updateFeePerPeriod to the owner (lines 392 to 397). _transfer converts the amount to shares with the same getCurrentMultiplier() (lines 543 to 554), so a transfer and a balance read agree inside one transaction. On X Layer the SNDKx proxy 0xb63efbc28860c8097e341de1fcf59456161e9d98 points to that implementation address, and the code there has the same hash as on Ethereum. Block 76,397,963 has timestamp 1795166999 and block 76,397,964 has 1795167000. balanceOf(PoolManager) is 137,059,273,049,122,723 at the first and 1,096,474,184,392,981,784 at the second, sharesOf(PoolManager) is 137,059,273,049,122,723 at both, and eth_getLogs for the token over the two blocks is empty. multiplierUpdates(1) returns 1e18, 8e18 and 1795167000 on X Layer and on Ethereum, and getCurrentMultiplier returns 8e18 on Ethereum, X Layer, BNB Smart Chain and Monad. feePerPeriod is 0 on X Layer. On Ethereum STRCx returns a multiplier of 1.1057749 and 26 stored updates. I did not recount the 42 tokens on BNB Smart Chain and did not look for a pool that kept liquidity through the activation.
verification.codeCheck: Pool accounting holds amounts and never reads a balance. The only balance reads are in sync and _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:285, 359), and both fall in one transaction with one timestamp, so the timestamp switch cannot fall between them. The tokens added by the multiplier therefore reach no delta and no function pays them out: take debits the full amount (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and fee collection is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). On a take the token moves floor(amount times 1e18 divided by multiplier) shares, so the PoolManager balance falls by at most the debited amount. I confirmed this by simulation on Monad for QQQx and NVDAx, where a transfer of a third of a holder's balance lowered that balance by the amount or by one base unit less. A multiplier that goes down would leave the balance below the accounted amounts and the last take would revert in Currency.transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86).
verification.corrections: The actor value issuer is right: only the multiplier updater 0x5f7a4c11bde4f218f0025ef444c369d838ffa2ad or the owner can change the figure, and no ordinary account can place the change between a sync and a settle. Two details need correction. First, the sentence that one implementation sits behind every proxy does not hold on Monad: the SNDKx proxy there points to 0xd865ce1b07540b5ede20e8298f48da69770fe22e, 14,411 bytes, with no Sourcify match and no multiplierUpdates getter. I tested it from the PoolManager's own balance of 8 base units and 1 share: a transfer of 8 or 9 moves the one share, a transfer of 7 moves nothing and a transfer of 16 reverts, so its transfer uses the 8e18 multiplier as balanceOf does. SPYx, QQQx and NVDAx on Monad use the common implementation. Second, the downward case is wider than feePerPeriod. _updateMultiplier requires only a nonzero value (line 684), so the updater can lower the multiplier, for example for a reverse split, at once or at a set time, and the PoolManager would then hold less than pools record. The STRCx balance on Ethereum was 567.49 at my read. The arbitrage in step 4 remains unobserved, as the finding says.

findings.title: Jenner client source and the Chapel testnet show how a CAS20 issuer can block or seize the PoolManager balance, and seizure needs one more step than first recorded
findings.difference: BNB Smart Chain activates Jenner at timestamp 1796697000 (2026-12-08 02:30 UTC). The client then runs CAS20 tokens as native code behind addresses that start with 0xCA52. Each token carries roles for mint, burn, seize, pause and metadata, a pause mask per feature, and six policy lanes that point at shared allowlists and blocklists in a policy registry. The standard is live on the Chapel testnet since 2026-10-29. Ethereum has no token logic in the client.
findings.mechanism: 1. transfer checks the pause bit, then the sender policy and the receiver policy, then debits the sender and credits the recipient by the amount and returns a 32 byte true (core/vm/cas20_token.go lines 175 to 189 and 239 to 269). The PoolManager accepts that answer (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74). 2. A policy that does not authorize the sender makes transfer revert with PolicyForbids for every amount, zero included. On Chapel the token 0xca52000000000000000001217954ab5467577565 has sender policy 0x0100000000000007, and transfer of 0 and of 1 from an unlisted contract address both reverted with selector 0xa43fec12. If the token admin binds TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY to a list that leaves the PoolManager out, if the admin of that list removes the PoolManager, or if PAUSE_ROLE pauses the transfer feature, then every take and every protocol fee collection in that token reverts (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). 3. A receiver policy that leaves the PoolManager out makes every payment to it revert, so settle credits nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). The transfer reverts and the amount is not diverted to another account. 4. seizeWithMemo needs SEIZE_ROLE and an unpaused seize feature, and it refuses a source that the SEIZE_EXEMPT policy authorizes (core/vm/cas20_admin.go lines 507 to 553). The default policy id 0 authorizes every account, so with default settings no account can be seized. The admin must first bind SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY to a list that leaves the PoolManager out. After that an account with SEIZE_ROLE can move the PoolManager balance to any allowed receiver without a take, and the pools still record the old amounts. The earlier text of this finding named a scope SEIZE_HOLDER_POLICY and a blocklist that contains the PoolManager. The client names the scopes SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY and SEIZE_RECEIVER_POLICY, and the test is the inverse: exemption must be withdrawn. 5. balanceOf returns the raw balance. The Asset multiplier is applied only by the UI selectors, so it causes no rebase at the PoolManager. A call that cannot pay for a storage read ends with an out of gas error and does not return a zero balance (core/vm/cas20_errors.go lines 55 to 63), so sync cannot record a false zero. 6. Token creation and policy creation are closed until an administrator appointed through GovHub 0x1007 activates them (core/vm/cas20_activation.go). On Chapel all three features are active.
findings.impact: All reserves, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees that the PoolManager holds in an affected CAS20 token. A policy change or a pause freezes them until the issuer reverses it. A seizure after the exemption is withdrawn is a loss for the liquidity providers of those pools. None of this applies today on mainnet because no CAS20 token can exist before the fork and before activation.
findings.preconditions: Jenner activates, the activation administrator opens token creation on mainnet, a CAS20 token is created and pooled, and the roles of that token act as described. An ordinary account can do this only with a token it issued itself, which harms only those who pool that token.
findings.mitigations: Before a CAS20 token is listed, read policyId for the six scopes, isPaused for the four features, and the holders of SEIZE_ROLE, PAUSE_ROLE and the admin role. A token whose sender or receiver policy is an allowlist cannot be pooled unless the PoolManager and the routers are on it. Prefer tokens whose SEIZE_EXEMPT policy is the default and whose admin role was renounced. After 2026-12-08 repeat the Chapel checks of this cycle on mainnet.

verification.factCheck: I fetched the client files from the master branch of bnb-chain/bsc. CHANGELOG.md schedules mainnet Jenner in v1.8.2 for 2026-12-08 02:30:00 UTC and lists pull 3829, the rename of the seizure exemption policy, under v1.8.1. params/config.go sets JennerTime to 1796697000 for mainnet and 1793241000 for Chapel. core/vm/evm.go resolves the token range and three singleton addresses to native code once IsJenner is true. core/vm/cas20_token.go lines 175 to 189: transfer rejects a read only frame, reverts with ContractPaused when the transfer bit is set, calls move, emits the log and returns a 32 byte true. Lines 239 to 269: move checks the sender policy and then the receiver policy before it reads the balance, so a policy failure reverts for every amount including zero, and on success it writes the source slot and the recipient slot and nothing else. core/vm/cas20_admin.go lines 507 to 553: seizeWithMemo needs SEIZE_ROLE and an unpaused seize feature, reverts with AccountNotSeizable when the SEIZE_EXEMPT policy authorizes the source, and policy id 0 authorizes every account, so a token with default settings has no seizable account. updatePolicy at line 579 needs the default admin role. core/vm/cas20_asset.go does not override balanceOf, and the multiplier appears only in scaledBalanceOf, balanceOfUI, totalSupplyUI and the conversion views. core/vm/cas20_activation.go: activate and deactivate need the registry admin, and the admin is set only by a caller equal to the GovHub address. core/vm/cas20_errors.go lines 55 to 63 and core/vm/contracts_stateful.go lines 113 to 124: the out of gas flag is sticky and every exit of a token call returns ErrOutOfGas when it is set. On Chapel (Geth v1.8.1, block 144,390,653, timestamp 1795430470, after the Chapel fork time) the factory 0xCA5F000000000000000000000000000000000000 has emitted 33 CAS20Created logs. isActivated returns true for bsc.cas20_asset, bsc.cas20_stablecoin and bsc.policy_registry. Token 0xca52000000000000000001217954ab5467577565 reports policy 0x0100000000000007 for TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY, and transfer of 0 and of 1 from an unlisted address both revert with 0xa43fec12, the selector of PolicyForbids(bytes32,uint64), followed by the scope hash and that policy id. The same token already has SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY bound to 0x0100000000000001, so issuers on the testnet do configure the seizure lane. For 18 tokens with default transfer policies, a transfer from a holder with Multicall3 code placed at the holder address returned a 32 byte true and moved exactly the amount, a zero amount returned true, and an amount above the balance reverted with 0xdb42144d (InsufficientBalance). A call with value reverted with 0x6fb1b0e9 (NonPayable). A gas sweep of balanceOf for a holder of 15 tokens of 0xca5200000000000000000069e5bbadfec8b9075a, from 22,100 gas, just above the intrinsic floor, to 23,700 gas in steps of 25, gave out of gas for every value below the full cost and the correct balance above it, and never a successful zero. On mainnet (Geth v1.8.2, block 135,257,313, timestamp 1795430720, 14.7 days before the fork) the token range, the factory, both registries, 0x2007 and 0x70 hold no code, answer transfer and balanceOf with success and empty data, and sync on the deployed PoolManager reverts for each of them. No pool, claim or fee can therefore exist under these ids before the fork. Not confirmable today: mainnet behaviour after activation, whether the administrator opens token creation, and which tokens will be pooled.
verification.codeCheck: Currency.transfer accepts a call that does not revert and returns 32 bytes holding 1 (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), which is what a CAS20 transfer returns. A revert from the token reaches src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, so take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56) revert when the pause bit is set or a transfer policy leaves the PoolManager out. A closed receiver policy makes every payment to the PoolManager revert, and settle then credits nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). balanceOf is a high level static call (src/types/Currency.sol:94), so a failed or empty answer reverts sync and cannot store a false reserve. A seizure lowers the token balance of the PoolManager and writes no delta. src/ has no function that reconciles pool records with the real balance, so later takes fail with InsufficientBalance once the requests exceed what is left, and a seizure between a sync and its settle makes the subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 revert. initialize makes no call to either currency (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142), so a pool can be created for any created CAS20 address. I found no entry point in the token code that an account without a role can use to change the balance of another holder: transferFrom and its memo variants need an allowance of the source, and permit needs an ECDSA signature of the owner with no contract signature path.
verification.corrections: The actor value issuer is right, and an ordinary account can reach this only with a token it created itself. The correction to the earlier text of F-007 is accurate: the scopes are SEIZE_EXEMPT_POLICY and SEIZE_RECEIVER_POLICY, and an account is seizable only after the admin binds the exemption lane to a policy that does not authorize it. Small differences in my repeat: I tested 18 tokens where the finding names 12, and the Chapel token with the sender policy also has its seizure exemption lane bound. None of this applies on mainnet before 2026-12-08 and before the administrator opens token creation.

findings.title: Token contracts have burned or moved the PoolManager's balance of their own token on six networks, and hookless pools with active liquidity now record tokens the PoolManager does not hold
findings.difference: The cause is token code written by the token's author, on the networks where pool creation is cheapest and most used. These tokens can change balanceOf(PoolManager) without any call from the PoolManager: a transferFrom that skips the allowance for chosen senders, an allowance from the PoolManager that the token writes by itself, a controller contract that rewrites balances, or an owner burn. F-069 recorded tokens whose balance falls with time. These fall in one transaction, to zero in 20 of the 53 confirmed cases on Ethereum.
findings.mechanism: 1. The PoolManager can only call transfer and balanceOf on a currency (src/types/Currency.sol:60-73, 94). It never approves anyone. A fall of its balance in a transaction where it emits no log is therefore the token's own doing. 2. Search: every ERC-20 Transfer log with the PoolManager as sender and the zero address, 0x...dEaD, 0xdead000000000000000042069420694206942069 or address 1 as recipient, over the block ranges in the sources. For each token, receipts of up to six such transactions were read, and for tokens with a hit where the PoolManager emitted no log, every hit. Each flagged token was then checked by balanceOf(PoolManager) one block before and at the block of one example. 3. Results. Ethereum: %s rows over %s tokens, %s tokens flagged, %s confirmed by a balance fall and %s that only emit a log (spoof tokens). BNB Smart Chain: %s rows, %s tokens, %s flagged, %s confirmed. Polygon: 5 flagged, 4 confirmed, of which PolySata and SNI have pools and two are spam tokens without a pool. Unichain: 13 flagged, 1 confirmed (ELX), 12 spoof. Elysium: 3 flagged and confirmed (CLU, EMBR, BLOB). Arbitrum One: 5 flagged and confirmed, one of them the issuer burn of PUSD that is filed as its own finding. 4. Forms seen. (a) A helper contract reads balanceOf(PoolManager) and calls transferFrom(PoolManager, 0xdead, amount) on the token; the token logs Approval(PoolManager, helper, 0) afterwards, so it had written an allowance in the PoolManager's name. Ethereum helper 0xd8e11826e82619bf49c58c05f26c8e00b0b64ea4 with selector 0x73ed6b13 did this for %s of the confirmed tokens, and the same selector appears for %s confirmed tokens on BNB Smart Chain (15 of them through 0xa25c886dced0e8fc0129082bf597381ea073c925). (b) An externally owned account calls transferFrom(PoolManager, 0xdead, amount) on the token directly. For CLU on Elysium I read the runtime bytecode: after the balance update the transfer routine loads a flag for tx.origin and, when it is set, returns true at once, which skips the allowance spending in transferFrom. A read-only transferFrom(PoolManager, other, 1000) reverts with ERC20InsufficientAllowance from an unrelated address and succeeds from the original sender 0xd27d278469aa24b5e8ed3af8675d5f6c2548f884. (c) TRUMP MAGA on Ethereum (verified source): transfer() only calls _beforeTokenTransfer, which emits the log and forwards to an unverified controller (lines 505 to 508 and 652), and cap() lets that controller emit any Transfer log (lines 680 to 688). In transaction 0xa6ce9d53504d62a54600498895c8671eb13fb8f312cdbb9d3a4fa345f0d89003 a holder's transfer of 90,100 MAGA made the controller call token function 0x20bd4fca, and the PoolManager's balance went from 776,894.03 MAGA to 0. Nine such events since block 21,818,333 removed 25,231,970 MAGA. (d) Owner functions such as burn(address,uint256) and burnFrom(address,uint256). 5. Effect in core: take pays out with transfer and reverts when the balance is too low (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-86). A holder of a positive delta in that token can still close it with mint or clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329), so a removal of liquidity can succeed when the caller gives up or defers the token side.
findings.impact: Pools that still have active liquidity while the PoolManager holds none of the token: TRUMP MAGA on Ethereum (balance 0; pools 0x4686f189f970... with liquidity 52,818,877,641,898,785 and 0x03762bf00ac1... with 1,320,363,208,123,135,774, both paired with ETH and without a hook), MEME 0x05f226755b11cb3666340551ebbaa615cdfefdd6 and BITCOIN 0x37d299d9900209c3566254cfe59bfe6ff8f8c295 on Ethereum, ELX 0x6836567f23a137f2ed07576826b0d2579b416b6d on Unichain, and SNI 0xdc685acc53ca2a760029cab2f6a587482aa9cf57 on Polygon with a balance of 1 base unit. For the other confirmed tokens I checked the balance fall and not the pools. Buyers of such a token cannot be paid, and liquidity providers cannot take the token side. Whoever holds the token outside the PoolManager can still sell it into the pool for the other currency. The amounts are in tokens without a price source, so I did not value them. The shortfall stays inside each token's own currency id; pools of other tokens are not affected. The victims chose a pool with a token written by the party that gains.
findings.preconditions: A pool in a token whose author kept a path to the PoolManager's balance. The actor is the token author or an account the token treats as privileged. For form (c) the trigger was an ordinary holder's transfer, and the rule sits in a controller whose code is not public. On BNB Smart Chain the Initialize query failed (limit exceeded), so the number of pools per token is not known there. The Base, World Chain and Robinhood Chain searches cover recent windows only (blocks from 57,500,000, 34,000,000 and 109,000,000) and X Layer 400,000 blocks. Monad, OP Mainnet, Avalanche, Ink, Celo, Arc, Soneium, Zora, MegaETH, Tempo and HyperEVM were searched over the whole history and have no confirmed case. The search sees burns only. A forced transfer to an ordinary recipient shows up only in the census windows of this unit (0.5 to 30 days per network), where none was found.
findings.mitigations: Core cannot stop a token from changing its own ledger. Interfaces and routers can flag a token when balanceOf(PoolManager) falls in a transaction without a PoolManager log, which the scripts scan_burns.py, classify_burns.py and validate_burns.py in the work directory detect. Liquidity providers in such a pool can still recover the other currency with a router that closes the token side by mint or clear. A deployer who wants a hard guarantee needs per currency reserve accounting, which this code does not have.

verification.factCheck: I re-ran one case of each form and the pool state behind the impact text. Ethereum, TRUMP MAGA 0xf211b655431c10e72c1caeae37688ae9f7f7a549: transaction 0xa6ce9d53504d62a54600498895c8671eb13fb8f312cdbb9d3a4fa345f0d89003 (block 26,465,460) is a transfer call by a holder, has two logs, none from the PoolManager, and one of them is Transfer(PoolManager, 0xdead, 776,894.03 MAGA). balanceOf(PoolManager) is 776,894.0285837858 one block earlier and 0 at the block and today. The Sourcify record (status match) shows transfer() calling only _beforeTokenTransfer (lines 505 to 508), which emits the log and calls the controller with selector 0x2bfad8d5 (line 652), and cap() emitting Transfer logs for the controller (lines 680 to 688). The source goes further than the finding says: balanceOf itself returns the controller's answer when that answer is below the maximum (line 493), so the PoolManager's MAGA balance is whatever the unverified controller reports. debug_traceTransaction on https://eth.drpc.org shows the token calling controller 0xa8b0cdcb011c82ca0b3c981868d78f84f06e0c65, which calls token function 0x20bd4fca. StateView and PositionManager.poolKeys confirm that pools 0x4686f189f97040979482293941fa47fb9d4379de767e25518dd90dd26a1a4baf (fee 1 percent, liquidity 52,818,877,641,898,785) and 0x03762bf00ac14b0110e854caa875d620cae2a843525c566a8964a4ad33054b62 (fee 70 percent, liquidity 1,320,363,208,123,135,774) pair ETH with MAGA and have no hook. Ethereum helper: transaction 0xb8a295249493a05eb8b86202111683ad838bbd1a32b970fcfa7629394155d9ef calls 0xd8e11826e82619bf49c58c05f26c8e00b0b64ea4 with selector 0x73ed6b13 and holds no PoolManager log. Elysium, CLU 0x13c83fd2df0ae8c7b462d344a458275d1f6b5b82: transaction 0x0d470f854fb59f4ad2b4c8bcb8dfcafc55a63bcd3f6083cbaf983209d48ed41d (block 4,589,428) is transferFrom sent by 0xd27d278469aa24b5e8ed3af8675d5f6c2548f884 and moves 30,639,051.89 CLU from the PoolManager to 0xdead; the balance is 30,639,996.93 one block earlier and 945.04 at the block. Today a read-only transferFrom(PoolManager, other, 1000) reverts with ERC20InsufficientAllowance (0xfb8f41b2) from an unrelated address and returns true from 0xd27d2784 while allowance(PoolManager, 0xd27d2784) is 0. The PoolManager holds 644,887,349.55 CLU today, so that account can move all of it now. Unichain, ELX 0x6836567f23a137f2ed07576826b0d2579b416b6d: transaction 0xe276007551f292449d6db401530312f9fc55143bf84228ece62ca57ffe4f10dc (block 10,638,254) moves 2,253,186,633,332 base units from the PoolManager to 0xdead with no PoolManager log, and the balance goes to 0. Polygon, SNI: balanceOf(PoolManager) is 1 base unit. Counts: I did not repeat the log search. The researcher's result files hold 54,048 rows and 78 flagged tokens on Ethereum (53 with a balance fall, 20 of them to zero, 25 spoof) and 29,326 rows and 97 flagged tokens on BNB Smart Chain (91 with a balance fall).
verification.codeCheck: The PoolManager makes two kinds of call to a currency: transfer(address,uint256) in Currency.transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:60-74, reached from take at src/PoolManager.sol:295 and from collectProtocolFees at src/ProtocolFees.sol:56) and balanceOf in balanceOfSelf (src/types/Currency.sol:94, reached from src/PoolManager.sol:285 and 359). A search of src/ outside src/test finds no approve and no transferFrom on a currency. A fall of the PoolManager's balance in a transaction without one of its transfers is therefore the token's own doing. take reverts when the token transfer fails (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). mint and clear close a positive delta without a token transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329), so a caller can leave with the other currency and a claim or nothing for the token side. If such a token lowers the balance between sync and settle, the subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 is checked arithmetic and reverts, so the author gains no credit from a fall. The shortfall stays in the token's own currency id because deltas are stored per target and currency (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16).
verification.corrections: Actor pool-creator is right: in every case I checked the balance moved through a path the token's author built (a controller that answers balanceOf, a transferFrom that skips the allowance for one account, a helper with a self-written allowance). The mechanism text was published with unfilled placeholders (%s) in the Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain counts. The values in the researcher's files are: Ethereum 54,048 rows over 1,277 tokens, 78 flagged, 53 with a balance fall and 25 spoof; BNB Smart Chain 29,326 rows over 1,801 tokens, 97 flagged, 91 with a balance fall; helper 0xd8e11826e82619bf49c58c05f26c8e00b0b64ea4 for 12 Ethereum tokens (selector 0x73ed6b13 for 18 through four helpers); selector 0x73ed6b13 for 18 BNB Smart Chain tokens, 15 of them through 0xa25c886dced0e8fc0129082bf597381ea073c925. The MAGA record on Sourcify is a match and not an exact match. For CLU the read-only test sets the caller and the origin to the same address, so it cannot tell whether the flag is read for tx.origin or for msg.sender; the finding's reading of the bytecode on that point is unconfirmed. Two of the four Polygon tokens and one of the five Arbitrum One tokens have no pool, so they show the token behaviour and no pool loss. Who loses is narrower than the text suggests: after such a burn a purchase of the token reverts, holders can still sell into the pool, and the party short of tokens is whoever provided liquidity, which for these tokens is often the author. Medium is the upper bound.

findings.title: The owner of Pleasing USD burned 41,000 PUSD out of the Arbitrum One PoolManager balance with an owner only burnFrom
findings.difference: F-036 and F-028 record that an issuer can block or burn the single address that holds every pool's balance. This is a case where an issuer did it. PUSD at 0xc8fb643d18f1e53698cfda5c8fdf0cdc03c1dbec on Arbitrum One is an upgradeable token whose owner can call burnFrom(address,uint256) on any holder.
findings.mechanism: 1. On 23 April 2026 the owner 0x43f285d7d53cc3e7bd4914d3e57ec90f58f510ff sent burnFrom(PoolManager, 40,000 PUSD) in block 455,597,235 (transaction 0x077516739f49e38972552537bbc49fe61e542dd6ca0b3d4d0ada8c3cf1de8fe6) and burnFrom(PoolManager, 1,000 PUSD) in block 455,604,741 (transaction 0x86afa98aa0369719d0faeda5dce5a1708fd6acc0e054b75f4287523b4f54e8c9). The PoolManager's balance went from 44,024.91 to 4,024.91 PUSD and from 1,509.05 to 509.05 PUSD. 2. The PoolManager emitted no log in either transaction. Pool state was not changed, so pools kept recording the burned tokens. 3. A read-only burnFrom(PoolManager, 1) from an unrelated address reverts with the text Ownable: caller is not the owner. From the owner it reverts today with the text blacklist, so the burn needs the target on a list that the owner controls. 4. Thirteen pools name PUSD, ten of them created between blocks 455,516,336 and 455,554,073, in the hours before the burns, with fees of 9 to 80 percent. Eight still show liquidity. The PoolManager holds 14.14 PUSD today.
findings.impact: 41,000 PUSD of the PoolManager's balance was destroyed. The first burn took 40,000 of the 44,024.91 PUSD it held. I did not establish who the liquidity providers were or why the owner acted, and I found no price source. Whoever held a position or a claim in PUSD at that time could no longer be paid in full by take. The other currencies of those pools were not touched by the burn.
findings.preconditions: Control of the token owner account, and the PoolManager on the token's blacklist at the time of the call. The implementation behind the proxy was not read; the statements about the owner check and the blacklist rest on the revert texts of two eth_call tests and on the two transactions.
findings.mitigations: None in core. Pool creators and liquidity providers should treat an owner burn function as a risk to every pool of that token, and interfaces can show it. The search of this unit lists such burns after the fact.

Transaction 0x86afa98aa0369719d0faeda5dce5a1708fd6acc0e054b75f4287523b4f54e8c9 (block 455,604,741, timestamp 1776972143) burns 1,000 PUSD the same way; the balance goes from 1,509.05 to 509.05. owner() returns 0x43f285d7, name() returns Pleasing USD, the proxy implementation slot holds 0x89ec479a783ff3747f2f0d3c2a292c5986cec099, and the owner account carries an EIP-7702 delegation to 0x63c0c19a282a1b52b07dd5a65b58948a07dae32b. burnFrom(PoolManager, 1) from an unrelated address reverts with Ownable: caller is not the owner. The finding's reading of the blacklist is wrong, and what I found instead makes the case worse. blackList(PoolManager) returns 0 at blocks 455,597,234, 455,597,235, 455,604,740 and 455,604,741, and a read-only burnFrom(PoolManager, 1) from the owner at block 455,597,234 succeeds. The burn therefore needed the owner and nothing else. A search by halving finds that blackList(PoolManager) turns to 1 at block 455,607,037 (timestamp 1776972718, ten minutes after the second burn), in transaction 0x3c0ba45ad6ef5aac6a362f71172134e54f76db41536343e12600db9f174f10c1 from the owner with selector 0x85c1e21d. It is still 1 today. Today a read-only transfer of PUSD from the PoolManager reverts with the text blacklist, and so does a transfer from the owner to the PoolManager. The owner's burnFrom reverts today for the same reason. Since 23 April 2026 the Arbitrum One PoolManager can neither pay out nor receive PUSD. It holds 14.14 PUSD. The pool file is consistent with chain data where I sampled it: thirteen pools, twelve without a hook, eight with liquidity, ten created between blocks 455,516,336 and 455,554,073 with fees of 9 to 80 percent.
verification.codeCheck: take pays PUSD with a token transfer and reverts when the token call reverts (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:64-74, 82-86), so every swap that buys PUSD and every removal that takes PUSD has reverted since the blacklist entry, whatever the balance. A payment of PUSD into the PoolManager also reverts in the token, so no settle of PUSD can be funded (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365). Holders of positions can still close the PUSD side with mint or clear (src/PoolManager.sol:310-329) and take the other currency, if the router they use offers those actions. The burns themselves bypass the PoolManager: balances are read only in sync and _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:285, 359) and nothing in core compares the token balance with what pools record. The loss cannot spread to other currencies because deltas are per currency (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16).
verification.corrections: Actor issuer is right. Preconditions: the sentence that the burn needs the PoolManager on the token's blacklist is wrong; the PoolManager was not on the list at either burn and was put on it ten minutes after the second one. Effect should be both: 41,000 PUSD of the PoolManager's balance were destroyed, and the PUSD side of every pool has been frozen since block 455,607,037 because the token rejects transfers from and to the PoolManager. This is a live freeze of the kind recorded in F-036 and F-056 and belongs in the table of pooled tokens that reject PoolManager transfers today. The finding says eight pools still show liquidity; none of them can pay PUSD out. The pools created in the hours before the burns carry fees of 9 to 80 percent and two older ones 88 and 95 percent, which suggests the owner acted against these pools; I did not establish who provided their liquidity. Medium stands for a token with a supply of 644,376 PUSD.

findings.title: The restrictor of HOLD has restricted the PoolManager address on BNB Smart Chain, so 140,774.9 HOLD held for pools cannot leave, and 448 more of the newly listed BNB Smart Chain currencies refuse every transfer from the PoolManager
findings.difference: HOLD 0xff583dc5ddc7c0bb3625fff39a587a2000e78888 has a restrictor role that can stop any address from sending. One entry for the PoolManager address stops every pool of the token, because all pools share that address.
findings.mechanism: 1. isRestricted(PoolManager) returns true. Every transfer from the PoolManager reverts with ACCOUNT_IS_RESTRICTED, for one base unit as for the whole balance. restrict(address) from an ordinary account reverts with ONLY_RESTRICTER. 2. take pays with transfer and reverts when the token refuses (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:60-80), so no pool can pay HOLD out. 3. The full balance transfer test ran on the 68,701 BNB Smart Chain currencies that cycle 5 had not tested. 517 refuse the full balance. For those I repeated the transfer with one base unit, 1 percent, one half and a second recipient: 449 refuse even one unit, 44 accept a smaller amount (transfer or wallet limits) and 24 passed on the second run. The frozen ones with a price are HOLD, LN (325 USD), STBU (218 USD, text Address: should be allowed), BSU (43 USD, paused) and GBCK (8 USD, text Sender is blacklisted). 4. X Layer: 21 of 2,051 refuse the full balance and 16 of those refuse one unit, none with a price. Base: 3,474 of 54,674 tested currencies refuse the full balance. In a random sample of 240 of them, 206 accept a smaller amount, 28 refuse one unit and 6 passed on the second run. None has a price at coins.llama.fi.
findings.impact: 140,774.905 HOLD, 15,626 USD at the coins.llama.fi price, is the largest priced balance among the frozen ones. The other priced ones sum to less than 600 USD. The liquidity providers of those pools cannot withdraw that side while the restriction stands. The other currency of each pool is not affected.
findings.preconditions: A token with a per address stop and a role holder who applies it to the PoolManager. For HOLD this has happened.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces should test a one unit transfer from the PoolManager address by eth_call before they show a pool. Liquidity providers cannot undo the restriction.
