findings.title: A delegated session credential with a TIP-20 spending limit on Tempo can move the account's ERC-6909 claims and pool positions without limit
findings.difference: Tempo accounts can authorise additional signers in the AccountKeychain precompile, with an expiry, optional call scopes and a spending limit per TIP-20 token. A transaction signed by such a signer runs with the account as msg.sender. The limit is enforced inside the TIP-20 precompile and only when the address that moves or approves tokens is tx.origin. Tempo's documentation states that assets other than TIP-20 tokens do not count and that a signer without scopes can call any contract. Ethereum has no protocol-level delegated signer.
findings.mechanism: 1. A user holds ERC-6909 claims in the PoolManager, or liquidity positions through a periphery contract, and authorises a session signer for an application or agent with a limit such as 100 OUSD per day and no call scopes. 2. The holder of that signer sends a transaction as the user that calls transfer(receiver, id, amount) or setOperator(operator, true) on the PoolManager (src/ERC6909.sol:25-33 and 58-64). The PoolManager sees the user as msg.sender. No TIP-20 leaves the user's account, so AccountKeychain.authorize_transfer is never reached for the user. 3. The receiver or operator opens an unlock, burns the claims (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22) and takes the tokens (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The TIP-20 transfer has the PoolManager as from address, and authorize_transfer returns early because that address is not tx.origin. 4. The spending limit is never charged for any of these steps.
findings.impact: All ERC-6909 claims of that user in the PoolManager, and positions the user holds through contracts the signer may call, can be moved by a signer whose TIP-20 limit suggested a small bound. On 22 November 2026 the PoolManager held about 426,000 USD of TIP-20 tokens for all users together. Other users are not affected.
findings.preconditions: The victim must have authorised a session signer without call scopes, or with scopes that include the PoolManager or a position contract, and the attacker must control that signer. The actor value is the nearest category: the attacker holds no chain role and needs a credential the victim chose to grant, comparable to a hook the victim chose to use. I confirmed the rule in the precompile source and the documentation and did not send a transaction.
findings.mitigations: Users who keep claims or positions should give session signers explicit call scopes that exclude the PoolManager and position contracts. Wallets on Tempo can warn that a spending limit does not cover claims and positions.

verification.factCheck: account_keychain/mod.rs at commit 697ea97: authorize_transfer reads the transaction signer id from transient storage and returns Ok when it is zero (root signer), then returns Ok when the account argument differs from tx_origin, and only after both tests calls verify_and_update_spending. authorize_approve has the same two early returns. tip20/mod.rs: transfer, transferWithMemo and the allowance-free pull call check_and_update_spending_limit(from, amount), which is authorize_transfer(from, token, amount), and transferFrom consumes the allowance without that call. validate_call_scope_for_transaction returns Ok for a signer whose is_scoped flag is unset, so such a signer may call any contract. handler.rs: execute_batch runs every call of the transaction with the account as caller and as origin and checks the call scopes of the signer before execution. The documentation page on spending limits says 'Assets other than TIP-20 tokens, such as NFTs, don't count' and that a transferFrom that spends an allowance the account already granted does not count. The page on scopes says a signer without scopes can call anything and that a call outside the scopes reverts with CallNotAllowed. On 22 November 2026 the PoolManager held 404,991.600244 OUSD and 19,683.832162 pathUSD.
verification.codeCheck: ERC-6909 transfer and setOperator act on msg.sender with no further check (src/ERC6909.sol:25-33 and 58-64). burn lets an operator or an approved spender burn the owner's claim and credits the burner's delta (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22), and take pays that delta out with the PoolManager as the sending address of the TIP-20 transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). The PoolManager is never tx.origin, so the spending limit of the victim's signer is not charged at any step. Core has no notion of the signer behind msg.sender and cannot add such a check.
verification.corrections: No actor value in the schema fits exactly. pool-creator is the nearest, because the victim must have granted the credential to the attacker, and the item is out of scope for the unprivileged goal. The 426,000 USD figure is the whole PoolManager balance and is an upper bound. I did not establish whether any account on Tempo holds ERC-6909 claims. The behaviour is documented by Tempo and is a property of its delegated credentials, which the PoolManager code cannot change. The same documentation sentence means that an allowance given to Permit2 before the credential was issued is also outside the limit.

findings.title: Arc keeps a denylist contract whose owner can keep transactions that name a listed sender or target out of the mempool
findings.difference: Besides the USDC blocklist, Arc has a Denylist system contract at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000004. Every node's transaction pool rejects a transaction whose sender, to address or EIP-7702 authority is flagged there. The client makes the check mandatory and derives the contract address from the chain specification. Ethereum has no protocol-defined admission list.
findings.mechanism: 1. The owner of the Denylist proxy (0x49ec36db19623e4dadc1aa821cba2d1476f8e859) flags an address. 2. If the address is a user's account, that user's transactions are no longer admitted by nodes that run the stock client, so the user cannot call unlock, burn claims or remove liquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114 and 145-184). 3. If the address is the PoolManager, a router or the PositionManager, transactions sent directly to it are refused. A call that reaches the same contract from inside another contract is not checked, because the list is read at admission only and the execution layer has no denylist check. 4. Arc has no forced inclusion path, so a listed account depends on a validator that includes its transaction outside the public mempool.
findings.impact: A listed user loses access to funds held in the PoolManager for as long as the entry stands. A listed router or PositionManager can no longer be the target of a transaction, so its users must reach it through another contract that they deploy or approve. No funds move.
findings.preconditions: The Denylist owner must act. The denylist slots of the PoolManager, the PositionManager, both Universal Routers, Permit2 and the fee adapter were zero at block 32,584,426. I read the admission rule in the arc-node main branch and could not confirm which release mainnet validators run.
findings.mitigations: Users can hold positions directly or through contracts they control, so a listing of one shared periphery contract does not strand them. Deployers should monitor the Denylist contract for entries that touch the deployment.

verification.factCheck: validator.rs on arc-node main: check_for_denylisted_addresses collects the sender, the to address and every recoverable EIP-7702 authority and returns the first one for which is_denylisted is true, and the caller rejects the transaction with DenylistedAddressError. chainspec.rs sets DENYLIST_ADDRESS_MAINNET to 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000004 and its comment states that no node runs without the denylist. The changelog lists for v0.8.0 that denylist checks are mandatory and chain-derived. evm.rs, handler.rs and opcode.rs contain no reference to the denylist, and issue 513 (open, filed 13 November 2026) states that mempool admission is the only caller of is_denylisted and that a transaction already pooled still executes. On chain the address holds 1,494 bytes of code, owner() returns 0x49ec36db19623e4dadc1aa821cba2d1476f8e859 and isDenylisted(PoolManager) returns false. The RPC reports the client string arc/v1, so I could not confirm which release mainnet validators run. That part rests on the main branch and on the contract being live at the address the source names.
verification.codeCheck: Core has no admission logic of its own. A listed account cannot have its transactions admitted, so it cannot call unlock, burn or modifyLiquidity (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 145-184, 332-336) from that account. Positions are bound to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161), so a listed owner contract can still be driven by another account that is allowed to call it, since only the transaction's sender and to address are tested. A listing of the PoolManager address stops direct transactions to it and leaves calls that arrive through a router untouched. No funds move and no core guard is involved.
verification.corrections: The actor governance is right for the owner of the Denylist proxy. The severity low is consistent with the scale because the list acts on single accounts at admission, is not enforced during execution and moves no funds.

findings.title: Two pooled tokens make their transfer rules depend on the PoolManager address: ELO on Elysium needs a budget set by its hook, and v4CRCL on X Layer pays out only to permitted recipients
findings.difference: No chain rule is involved. These are token designs that exist on these two networks among the tokens the PoolManager holds. ELO at 0xe107e5d99910f544f88ef961e3ca6d88f06f29dd on Elysium stores the PoolManager address and has functions poolManagerGateEnabled, poolManagerTransferBudget, authorizePoolManagerTransfer, setPoolManagerGate, setHook and setBlockedVenue. v4CRCL at 0xd4f64a67b2c1295bd6c25b3a306b2a049e392397 on X Layer has POOL_MANAGER, PERMISSIONED_TOKEN, allowListChecker, allowedHooks, allowedWrappers, wrapToPoolManager and swappingEnabled, which is the shape of a wrapper for a permissioned token.
findings.mechanism: 1. take(X, to, amount) debits the caller and makes the PoolManager call X.transfer(to, amount) (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-75). 2. ELO: a transfer of zero from the PoolManager succeeds. A transfer of 1 base unit or of 10^18 reverts with UnauthorizedPoolManagerTransfer(bool,uint256,uint256). authorizePoolManagerTransfer succeeds when called from the address returned by hook() and reverts for any other caller, including the PoolManager. Both budgets read zero outside a transaction and the bytecode contains TLOAD and TSTORE, so the budget appears to live in transient storage. ELO can therefore leave the PoolManager only in a transaction in which its hook has authorized the amount. A pool that names ELO with another hook or with no hook can receive ELO and can never pay it out, and an ERC-6909 claim on ELO can be burned for a take only when the hook takes part (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). The owner of ELO can switch the gate and replace the hook. 3. v4CRCL: every transfer from the PoolManager to the four recipients I tried reverts with TRANSFER_FAILED, for a zero amount as well, and transfers by other senders revert with a custom error. Payouts depend on a permission list kept outside core. 4. In both cases the failed transfer makes take revert with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86), and the same holds for collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). I found no way for an ordinary account to use these rules against another currency: the checks act on the token's own balance, a zero amount poke changes nothing, and each take is debited in full.
findings.impact: The PoolManager holds 60,839 ELO on Elysium (about 46,000 USD of pool reserves on the tracker) and 65.98 v4CRCL on X Layer (about 1,800 USD). Holders of these tokens through pools or claims depend on the token owner and on the hook or permission list for every payout. Other currencies and other pools are not affected.
findings.preconditions: A user must hold liquidity or claims in one of these tokens. The token owner, the hook or the permission list must refuse or stop authorizing. I could not obtain verified source for either token, so the function names come from the public signature database and the behaviour from read only calls.
findings.mitigations: Front ends can flag currencies whose transfer from the PoolManager fails in simulation for a plain recipient. Liquidity providers should treat such a token like a hook that can block removal, which the state already records for all chains.

findings.title: Tokens whose balance falls with time leave the PoolManager short of what pools record: TURING on Ethereum has lost 73 percent of its pooled balance in 263 days
findings.difference: These are token designs with a balance that decays by a time formula. Nobody has to send a transaction for the balance to fall, and no Transfer log is emitted.
findings.mechanism: 1. Pool accounting records amounts and never reads balanceOf again. take pays out recorded amounts with a plain transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:40-87). 2. Thirteen tokens named TURING on Ethereum lost 0.5 percent of their PoolManager balance in the one day window with no log. For 0x11fb7c5e6fe7e42fb9e28929b673d3eee20048d4 getDecayInfo(PoolManager) returns a stored amount of 999,999,999.99 tokens, a current balance of 267,590,219.70 and 263 days of decay. The contract has checkIn(uint256,bytes), lastCheckIn and hook() among its selectors, so holders who check in keep their balance and the PoolManager cannot. 3. Once withdrawals and swaps have paid out the 267.6 million that exist, every later take of this token reverts in the transfer, and the last positions cannot be closed in that currency. 4. On Robinhood Chain three tokens named PYRE fell 5.3 to 5.6 percent in the window and SMK2 fell 0.39 percent. On Arbitrum One DDL fell 3.7 percent. All without logs.
findings.impact: Each TURING token has a supply of 1,000,000,000 and the PoolManager holds about 26.8 percent of it after decay, 5.3 percent for two of them. The stored amount for the token I read equals almost the whole supply, so the liquidity is the deployer's own. The other balances are small: 9.34 PYRE, 2.12 SMK2, 3.34 DDL. I found no third party funds at risk today. The pattern matters for any future pool in a token with demurrage.
findings.preconditions: A pool in a token whose balance decays. No attacker is needed. The TURING source is not verified; I read selectors from bytecode and state through its getters. I did not read the pool positions, so the split between the deployer and others is inferred from the stored amount.
findings.mitigations: Do not pool tokens with a decaying balance unless the token exempts the PoolManager address. Interfaces can detect them with the reconcile script.

sources.supports: take debits the caller and transfers before anything is paid in.
The payout is a transfer call that reverts with ERC20TransferFailed when the token refuses it.

findings.title: The X Layer PoolManager is enrolled in USDG payout group 2, so every USDG transfer runs reward share accounting for it and the rewards go to a third address
findings.difference: USDG is the Paxos reward token. Each account slot packs balance, shares, payout group id and last update time. On X Layer payoutGroupIdOf(PoolManager) returns 2. The claimer and the destination of group 2 are 0xb1b3d51e4be3fe55006d1ae4bc252dc6aa00fa72 and the group holds 23.18 million USDG in total. On Robinhood Chain, Ink, Arbitrum One and Ethereum the same call returns 0 for the PoolManager. A cleared item of cycle 3 states that enrolment needs the registrar role or the consent of the account. The PoolManager cannot give consent, so a role holder enrolled it on X Layer. I did not re-read the enrolment functions.
findings.mechanism: 1. A take or a payment of USDG on X Layer runs _updateWalletWithPayoutGroup for the PoolManager: it recomputes the shares of the PoolManager with reward preservation, writes the timestamp and applies a share delta to the totals of group 2 (ClaimableRewardsBase.sol lines 572 to 619). On the other chains the transfer takes the short path that writes two balances. 2. I traced a full round trip on X Layer. The only slot that differed afterwards was the PoolManager slot, where the timestamp field moved from 0x6b03bb26 to 0x6b03bb81 and balance, shares and group id were unchanged. Twenty five round trips in one call all succeeded and left the balance unchanged. 3. Rounding in calcShares is downward on each step, so a round trip can cost the PoolManager slot up to a few share units of one millionth of a USDG. That reduces rewards of the group destination and does not touch the balance. 4. _applyDelta saturates at zero when it subtracts and the additions are bounded by 64 bit balances, so I found no revert that a caller can cause. 5. The rewards that accrue on the USDG that pools hold are paid to the destination of group 2 by claim. balanceOf(PoolManager) does not rise, so sync and settle cannot book them (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364). 6. The enrolment adds one revert path that the other chains do not have: _getMultiplierAtTime reverts with MultiplierIndexNotFound when the multiplier record of the group is empty. I did not establish whether an administrator can delete a multiplier that a live group still uses.
findings.impact: Liquidity providers of USDG pools on X Layer (385,837 USDG at the PoolManager at block 76,638,290) keep their principal. The reward on that balance accrues to 0xb1b3d51e4be3fe55006d1ae4bc252dc6aa00fa72. Transfers cost more gas than on the other chains. A fault in the multiplier configuration of group 2 would stop every USDG take and payment at the PoolManager, which adds to the issuer powers recorded in F-057.
findings.preconditions: None for the reward routing, which is in place. The revert path needs an issuer side change of the multiplier of group 2, and that part is unconfirmed.
findings.mitigations: Liquidity providers should know that USDG rewards on pooled balances on X Layer go to the group destination. The deployer can ask Paxos and the X Layer operator who controls group 2 and whether the PoolManager should stay enrolled.

I computed that selector locally as registrarRegisterRewardAddressBatch(uint32,address[]). PayoutGroupFacet.sol restricts that function to the payout group registrar role, so a role holder enrolled the PoolManager four days before this review. Source, fetched from the Paxos repository: _transfer takes the two word path only when both group ids are 0 and otherwise runs _updateWalletWithPayoutGroup, which recomputes shares, writes the time and applies deltas to the group (ClaimableRewardsBase.sol lines 473 to 619). _getMultiplierAtTime reverts with MultiplierIndexNotFound when switchTimeMultiplier is 0 (lines 257 to 264). balanceOf reads the stored balance field, and rewards leave the claim source by claim functions. Not confirmed: whether the deployed code equals the repository source (it answers the same selectors), and whether a multiplier in use can be deleted, which the finding also leaves open.
verification.codeCheck: take and the payment before settle reach the token only through transfer and balanceOf (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 349-364, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75, 90-96). Rewards do not raise balanceOf(PoolManager), so sync and settle have nothing to credit (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-360), and core has no call that could claim or register. The three registration paths in the token need the registrar role, a call of acceptRegisterRewardAddress by the account itself, or a signature checked with SignatureChecker. The PoolManager sends only transfer, balanceOf, the IHooks selectors, unlockCallback and empty calldata, and it has no isValidSignature function and no fallback, so it cannot consent. A revert in the group accounting would surface as ERC20TransferFailed on every take of USDG (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86).
verification.corrections: The actor value issuer and the severity low stand. Additions. The enrolment happened on 2026-11-19 through the registrar batch function, which confirms the inference in the finding. The reward amount is close to nothing at the time of my query: getPayoutGroupAvailableRewards(2) returned 2,797 base units, 0.002797 USDG, on a group balance of 23.18 million, and availableRewardsOf(PoolManager) returned 0. The shares of the PoolManager are lower than its balance, so the multiplier has grown since enrolment, and the low figure fits a recent claim for the whole group. I did not find the claim event because the public endpoints limit eth_getLogs to 100 blocks. The statement that _applyDelta saturates is right for subtraction only. The addition is a checked uint64 addition and would revert above 18.4 trillion USDG, which the total supply of 1.0987 billion cannot reach. The comparison with Arbitrum One was not reproduced by me.

findings.title: More pooled tokens gate their own transfers on the PoolManager address: AGL on eight networks, PLAYR, MOON, INFX, A3K, LFNX, FIN and four more Securitize wrappers
findings.difference: No chain rule is involved. These tokens store the PoolManager address and allow a transfer to or from it only inside an operation of their own hook or for permitted parties. AGL (AgroLastro, 0x0000000000109de411eabc9f04906d79f06fda0e, the same address on Ethereum, OP Mainnet, BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, Base, Arbitrum One, Avalanche and Celo) calls its hook contract PoolAGL on every transfer that touches the PoolManager, and the hook keeps a signed quota in transient storage that only its afterSwap and its own fee collection open. PLAYR on Robinhood Chain reverts with V4NotAuthorized. MOON on Elysium reverts with selector 0x971d2ee1 and the PoolManager address for every nonzero amount. INFX on Avalanche accepts transfers into the PoolManager only up to an allowance that its tax hooks credit in the same transaction. A3K on OP Mainnet marks limited accounts, which receive only with an exception that its own contracts grant, and a transfer back to the PoolManager reverts with AccountIsLimited. LFNX on OP Mainnet and FIN on Polygon revert with the same selector on the return leg, and I did not read their source. v4MSTR, v4COIN, v4HOOD and v4VOLOROST2 on X Layer have the selector set of v4CRCL, which F-059 describes.
findings.mechanism: 1. take(X, to, amount) and a payment before settle both end in X.transfer or X.transferFrom with the PoolManager as one party (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297 and 349-364, src/types/Currency.sol:60-75). 2. AGL: _update calls pool.consumirSaida(amount) when the sender is the PoolManager and pool.consumirEntrada(amount) when the recipient is. Both revert with ForaDaCota(amount, quota) unless the quota that afterSwap opened in this transaction covers the amount. From the PoolManager address a transfer of 1 AGL reverts with ForaDaCota(1e9, 0) on Ethereum, Base, Polygon and Celo, and cota() reads 0. The PoolManager holds between 99.9999 and 100 percent of the 1e21 AGL minted on each of the eight networks. 3. A take of AGL therefore works only in a transaction that also swaps in the official pool, and an ERC-6909 claim on AGL can be burned for a take only then (src/PoolManager.sol:331-336). The free round trip of this unit is not available for these tokens, because the return leg is refused. 4. The quota of AGL is one transient value for the whole transaction. It stays set when an unlock ends with claims minted in place of a take. I did not test what a later user of the same transaction meets, which belongs to the unit on shared transactions. 5. For the other tokens the failed transfer makes take revert with ERC20TransferFailed (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86) in the same way.
findings.impact: Holders of ERC-6909 claims and any pool that names one of these tokens without the hook the token expects cannot pay the token out. For AGL the liquidity belongs to the issuer and third party liquidity is refused by the hook, so the exposed parties are claim holders and integrators. No path for an ordinary account to block other users was found.
findings.preconditions: A user holds a claim or a position in such a token outside the flow the token author intended. The token author or hook author sets the rules.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces should not offer ERC-6909 claims or hookless pools for tokens that read the PoolManager address in their transfer logic. Pool creators should simulate a transfer from the PoolManager address before pairing a token.

verification.factCheck: AGL: I fetched the verified sources of AGL and PoolAGL from Celo Blockscout. AGL._update calls pool.consumirEntrada when the recipient is the PoolManager and pool.consumirSaida when the sender is. PoolAGL keeps one signed value in transient storage, adds the negated AGL delta of each swap in afterSwap, and both consume functions revert with ForaDaCota(uint256,int256) outside that value. beforeInitialize and beforeAddLiquidity revert for every caller other than the hook itself. On the eight networks (chain ids 1, 10, 56, 137, 8453, 42161, 43114, 42220, latest blocks of 2026-11-23) eth_getCode of 0x0000000000109de411eabc9f04906d79f06fda0e has 15,125 bytes, poolManager() equals the PoolManager of networks.json, balanceOf(PoolManager) is between 99.99999999999 and 100 percent of the supply of 1e30 base units, and cota() on 0x0000000456b76bc801253ef2366664750f602840 returns 0. A transfer of 1e9 base units from the PoolManager address reverts on all eight with 0x7c467237 followed by 1e9 and 0, and a transfer of the same amount from the hook to the PoolManager reverts the same way. I computed 0x7c467237 locally from ForaDaCota(uint256,int256). PLAYR: the Sourcify record of 0x775fd5a987bf3ff5e205deabde6634ddcee3a3fc on chain id 4663 is an exact match. _enforceTradeGates reverts with V4NotAuthorized when the PoolManager is a party and a transient flag is not set. A transfer from the PoolManager address reverts with 0x19e7dcd0, which I computed as V4NotAuthorized(). INFX: the Routescan source of 0xda7ad1b3423713dc9b4275a00d59b82024b3eb0c shows that a transfer to the PoolManager must fit a transient allowance and otherwise reverts with NoHookAllowance(uint256,uint256). A transfer out of the PoolManager address returned true in my call, which agrees with the finding, since it describes a limit on transfers in. A3K: the verified IndexTokenV4 source declares error AccountIsLimited(), whose selector I computed as 0xb8b82b49, the value the finding reports for A3K, LFNX and FIN. Not reproduced: MOON on Elysium, LFNX, FIN, the four Securitize wrappers on X Layer and the on-chain behaviour of A3K and INFX on the return leg. The finding gives no address for these tokens.
verification.codeCheck: take ends in currency.transfer and a revert there reverts the take with ERC20TransferFailed (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:55-86). burn followed by take is the only way to turn an ERC-6909 claim into tokens (src/PoolManager.sol:332-336). A payment in is a token transfer by the payer before settle (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). core has no bypass for a token that refuses these transfers, and it has no code size or allow list check that would keep such a token out of a pool (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). The gates of these tokens open only inside their own hook operations in the same transaction, and their state is transient, so nothing carries over to a later transaction of another user. PoolAGL comments state the known limit that deltas netted inside one unlock and ERC-6909 claims move AGL between pools without a physical transfer, which matches mint and burn in core (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336).
verification.corrections: Actor pool-creator and severity low stand. The statement that no ordinary account can block other users holds across transactions, because every gate is transient. Inside one transaction the AGL value is shared: a buyer who ends an unlock with claims leaves a negative value, and a later sale of AGL in the same transaction then fails consumirEntrada, which requires a value that is at least the amount. The research file records this as a lead for the shared transaction unit. The entries for MOON, LFNX, FIN and the four X Layer wrappers rest on the researcher's calls alone.

findings.title: Monerium EURe sits in the Polygon PoolManager under two currency ids that share one balance, and the issuer can retire the legacy address
findings.difference: On Polygon the e-money token EURe answers at two addresses that share one ledger. The V2 token is an ERC-1967 proxy at 0xE0aEa583266584DafBB3f9C3211d5588c73fEa8d. The V1 address 0x18ec0A6E18E5bc3784fDd3a3634b31245ab704F6 (name Monerium EUR emoney) has forwarded transfer, transferFrom, approve and balanceOf to V2 since the upgrade of 2024-08-18 at block 60,733,237. Both addresses report the same balance for every holder, and a transfer through either one lowers the balance read at both. The same pair exists on Ethereum (V1 0x3231Cb76718CDeF2155FC47b5286d82e6eDA273f, V2 0x39b8B6385416f4cA36a20319F70D28621895279D). The PoolManager code treats every address as a separate currency with a separate balance.
findings.mechanism: 1. A currency id is the token address, and deltas, ERC-6909 claims and accrued protocol fees are recorded per address (src/types/Currency.sol:110-118, src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41, src/ProtocolFees.sol:21). 2. On Polygon 27 pools were initialized with the V2 address and 21 pools with the V1 address. At block 97,808,450 fourteen of the V2 pools and two of the V1 pools had active liquidity, the PoolManager held one balance of 62,752.2 EURe, and protocolFeesAccrued was 77.59 EURe under the V2 id and 2.27 EURe under the V1 id. 3. Walk of the ordinary caller across the two ids. sync stores one currency and one reserve figure (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32), so two snapshots cannot be open at once. A payment between sync and settle is credited once, to the id that is synced at that moment (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365). A take debits its own id and lowers the shared balance (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). Example: take 100 EURe under the V1 id, sync the V2 id, send the 100 EURe back, settle. The caller now holds a credit of 100 under the V2 id and still owes 100 under the V1 id, so the sum of credits equals the sum paid in. A take or a fee collection under one id between sync and settle of the other id lowers the measured rise, which under-credits the settling caller or reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:360. mint and burn use separate ids (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336). No order of sync, settle, take, mint and burn credits one payment twice, so the two ledgers stay jointly covered by the one balance. 4. The hazard sits with the issuer. The V1 address and the V2 proxy have the same owner, 0x8001ea269cb9715bf7acff89c664ffc134a519ec. getController() on the V1 address returns the V2 address, and the V1 bytecode holds the selector of setController(address). If Monerium disconnects the V1 address, points it at another controller or changes how V2 serves its frontend, transfer and balanceOf at the V1 address fail or stop following the shared ledger. take for the V1 id then reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, and sync for the V1 id fails or reads another figure. The tokens stay in the PoolManager and remain payable only under the V2 id, to parties that hold V2 deltas. Core has no function that converts a pool balance or a claim from one currency id to another. 5. The guard in collectProtocolFees compares addresses (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52), so it does not stop a collection of V2 fees while the V1 id is synced. The fee controller on Polygon lets any account trigger collection. The effect stays inside the transaction of the party that is settling and costs that party the collected amount or a revert.
findings.impact: Funds owed under the V1 id: an unknown share of about 62,750 EURe, in 21 pools of which two have active liquidity, plus 2.27 EURe of accrued protocol fees. If the V1 address stops working these funds cannot leave the PoolManager until the issuer restores it. Liquidity providers could still remove liquidity and hold ERC-6909 claims of the V1 id, which have no payout path. Indexers and risk tools that read balanceOf per currency id count this balance twice. No funds of other pools are affected and no ordinary account gains anything.
findings.preconditions: Monerium, through the owner account of both contracts, must change or disconnect the V1 address or upgrade V2. Monerium states that V1 continues to be supported and that it works with protocols to move liquidity to V2. No ordinary account can trigger the freeze. The split of the balance between the two ids was not computed.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces, routers and token lists on Polygon should offer only the V2 address 0xE0aEa583266584DafBB3f9C3211d5588c73fEa8d and warn on pools that use 0x18ec0A6E18E5bc3784fDd3a3634b31245ab704F6. Liquidity providers in V1 pools can move to V2 pools while both addresses work. Indexers should treat the two ids as one balance. The deployment notes for Polygon and Ethereum should name both pairs.

verification.factCheck: I repeated the chain queries on Polygon. At block 97,816,436 balanceOf(PoolManager) returned 74,818.963182106767473444 EURe at 0x18ec0A6E18E5bc3784fDd3a3634b31245ab704F6 (V1) and the same figure at 0xE0aEa583266584DafBB3f9C3211d5588c73fEa8d (V2). With Multicall3 code placed at the PoolManager address by state override, a transfer of 1 EURe through V2 and a transfer of 3 EURe through V1 each returned a 32 byte true and each lowered the reading at both addresses by the amount. getController() on V1 returns the V2 address, getFrontend() on V2 returns the V1 address, and owner() returns 0x8001ea269cb9715bf7acff89c664ffc134a519ec on both. V2 is a 170 byte ERC-1967 proxy whose implementation slot holds 0xd1cfa02a1785f3ca0a5602b18649b7ca5439681b. I read the verified sources on Sourcify, which the finding did not cite. V1 (contract PolygonPosEUR, file TokenFrontend.sol) forwards transfer, transferFrom, approve, balanceOf and totalSupply to the controller, and setController is restricted to the owner and requires that the new controller names this frontend and has the same ticker. The V2 implementation (PolygonControllerToken) hard codes the V1 address as frontend for ticker EUR, accepts the forwarded calls only from that frontend, and can be replaced by the owner through upgradeToAndCall. So the issuer can end the shared ledger from either side, as the finding says. The Initialize logs of the PoolManager name the V1 address in 21 pools and the V2 address in 27 pools. StateView reports active liquidity in 2 of the 21 and in 14 of the 27. protocolFeesAccrued is 2.2750 EURe under the V1 id and 81.11 EURe under the V2 id. An eth_call of collect((address,uint256)[]) on the fee controller 0x59e84309afa65f084f9c03668583d231afb12cc6 from an arbitrary sender succeeded for both ids, and the controller's TOKEN_JAR is 0xc6ae6373cecc9e595a6c8b9fe581925a8c84f70a. The Monerium notice in the CryptoCompare copy states that V1 keeps its address and operates with the V2 contracts behind it, lists the Polygon, Gnosis and Ethereum address pairs, and dates the Polygon upgrade to 18 August 2024. The Monerium help article says both versions coexist for now. On Ethereum the PoolManager holds 4,188.4737 EURe, read identically at both Ethereum addresses. I measured what the finding left open. The 207 ModifyLiquidity logs of the 21 V1 pools leave three open ranges, which at current prices are owed about 1.53 EURe in total. No ERC-6909 Transfer event with the V1 id was ever emitted, so no claim exists under that id. Together with the 2.27 EURe of fees, the funds recorded under the V1 id are about 4 EURe plus uncollected position fees. Not confirmed by me: the upgrade block height 60,733,237, and the whitepaper sentences about delegated state and the audit note, because my fetch of that page returned only its first parts.
verification.codeCheck: A currency is its address. Deltas are stored per target and currency address (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16), claims use uint160 of the address as id (src/types/Currency.sol:110-118, src/PoolManager.sol:322-336) and protocol fees are a mapping per currency (src/ProtocolFees.sol:21). sync stores one currency and one reserve figure (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32), and a second sync replaces the first. _settle credits the synced currency with balance now minus the stored reserve, with a checked subtraction, and then clears the synced currency (src/PoolManager.sol:358-361). take records the debit before it transfers (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295). unlock reverts while any delta is non-zero (src/PoolManager.sol:112). I walked the two ids looking for a double credit. A credit under either id needs a rise of the shared balance inside that id's own sync window, and every such rise is counted once because only one window can be open. A take under one id followed by a settle under the other leaves the first debit standing, and the unlock check forces the caller to pay it. A take or a fee collection under the other id between sync and settle lowers the measured rise, so the settling caller is credited less or the subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 reverts. mint and burn only move a delta of their own id into or out of a claim. I found no order that credits one payment twice or pays out an amount that was not debited. The guard in collectProtocolFees compares the synced currency with the collected currency by address (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52), so it does not cover the other face. The collection can only shorten the settle of the party that synced, and a payer who syncs, pays and settles with no call to foreign code in between cannot be interleaved. The EURe token calls only the Monerium validator during a transfer. If V1 stopped forwarding, Currency.transfer would revert at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86 for the V1 id and balanceOf at src/types/Currency.sol:94 would fail or read another ledger. src/ has no function that moves a pool balance, a claim or accrued fees from one currency id to another. I found no guard that the finding missed.
verification.corrections: The actor value issuer is right. Severity should be low. The impact text speaks of an unknown share of about 62,750 EURe, and the measured share under the V1 id is about 4 EURe (1.53 EURe in three open ranges, 2.27 EURe of protocol fees, no ERC-6909 claims). The PoolManager balance has since grown to about 75,886 EURe and the V2 fees to 81.11 EURe. The same address pair exists on Ethereum, so the hazard is a property of the token and does not follow from a Polygon network difference. The Polygon specific part is that V1 is also a PoS bridge child token with deposit for the depositor role and withdraw for the holder, and neither can be used against the PoolManager by an ordinary account. The lead that asks for the split of the balance between the two ids is answered by these figures.

findings.title: A pool id that resembles another pool's id can be mined through the hooks field of the PoolKey, and core gives a reader nothing to tell the two pools apart (Trail of Bits finding 6, unresolved)
findings.difference: None found. The report's method places a hook at a mined address with CREATE2. An account with a mined address and an EIP-7702 delegation serves the same purpose where delegation is live, which the ledger records as F-013.
findings.mechanism: 1. The pool id is the keccak256 hash of the five words of the PoolKey (src/types/PoolId.sol:11-15) and the hooks address is the fifth word (src/types/PoolKey.sol:11-22). 2. initialize constrains the hook address only through its low 14 bits and the dynamic fee rule (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127, src/PoolManager.sol:126), so 146 bits of the address are free to vary while currencies, fee and tick spacing equal those of a known pool. 3. Core stores every pool under its full 32 byte id (src/PoolManager.sol:93), so two pools never share state. The hazard is in displays that shorten the id: a mined id can match the first and last characters of the known pool's id. 4. The attacker's pool carries the attacker's hook, which has the powers listed in the hook permissions note of this repository. 5. The fix review marks the finding unresolved, and nothing in src addresses it.
findings.impact: A user who picks a pool by a shortened id, or an integration that matches pools by a prefix, can be led into a pool whose hook takes the swap input or blocks removal. Funds in the original pool are not touched.
findings.preconditions: The victim must choose the attacker's pool. The attacker must author the hook.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces should show and compare the full PoolKey with the hook address. Integrations should match pools by the full 32 byte id.

The report itself says the issue does not affect the protocol and concerns third party integrators. The finding claims no chain fact beyond the reference to F-013, which I did not test again.
verification.codeCheck: The pool id is keccak256 over 0xa0 bytes of the PoolKey in memory (src/types/PoolId.sol:11-15) and hooks is the fifth word (src/types/PoolKey.sol:11-22). initialize checks tick spacing, currency order and isValidHookAddress and nothing else about the hook (src/PoolManager.sol:119-126). isValidHookAddress reads the low 14 bits and the dynamic fee flag only (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127), so the upper 146 bits of the hook address are free. Pool state is stored under the full 32 byte id (src/PoolManager.sol:93, 151, 194, 262), so two pools with similar ids share nothing in core. The attacker's pool runs the attacker's hook with the powers that finding 4 of this file lists.

findings.title: Ten unpriced pooled tokens on Ethereum charge the sender on top of every transfer, so each take lowers the PoolManager balance by more than the caller is debited
findings.difference: This is a token behaviour that the existing mainnet PoolManager meets today. WHITE on Ethereum and ARGUS on Arc (F-092, F-109) charge the sender only when the recipient is a listed pair. The ten tokens of this finding charge the sender on a transfer to any recipient, and none of them has a price at coins.llama.fi, which is why the priced sweep of cycle 7 did not list them. They were present in the stored data of the one third transfer sweep of cycle 5 and were not written up.
findings.mechanism: 1. take debits the caller by amount and then calls transfer(to, amount) on the token (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The transfer routine accepts the call when it does not revert and returns nothing or true (src/types/Currency.sol:60-80). No statement compares the fall of the PoolManager balance with the amount. 2. Simulation at block 26,480,246 with a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address and an unrelated transaction origin. The stub sends one third of the balance to an ordinary account A and the balances are read before and after. The PoolManager balance falls by 150 percent of the amount for SFC, 102 percent for XIN, 101 percent for YZNC, 100.5025 percent for NoMM and Novium, 100.5 percent for Novium+ and NOMM, 100.3003 percent for USDX, 100.1001 percent for MOOP and 100.1 percent for EURX. A receives the full amount in nine cases and 98 percent for XIN. Example: the PoolManager holds 501,793.14 NoMM, sends 167,264.38 and its balance falls by 168,104.90. 3. So every payout of such a token by take, which is how a swap output, a liquidity withdrawal, a claim redemption and a protocol fee collection are paid (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56 uses the same transfer), removes the charge from the shared balance in addition to the amount. Pools and claims keep recording the old amounts. 4. Second simulation: A sends 90 percent of what it received back to the PoolManager. A is charged at the same rate (its balance falls by the same percentage of the amount) and the PoolManager receives the amount sent, or 98 percent of it for XIN. A caller who takes and returns a token in one unlock therefore pays the same charge that the PoolManager pays. The statement of lead L-331 that a caller could grind the balance down at no cost does not hold for these tokens. For SFC the return failed, because the account cannot cover 150 percent of the amount.
findings.impact: Liquidity providers and claim holders of the pools of these ten tokens. The PoolManager balance of the token ends below the sum that pools, claims and protocol fees record, and the last withdrawals of that token revert in the transfer. Other currencies are not touched, because each token has its own balance. Balances at the PoolManager at block 26,480,246: 600 SFC, 2,084.19 XIN, 2.14 YZNC, 501,793.14 NoMM, 4.75e12 Novium, 9,942.19 Novium+, 1,402,836.84 NOMM, 8,155.51 USDX, 22.30 MOOP and 2,083.67 EURX. None has a price at coins.llama.fi, so I cannot state a value and I expect it to be small. The tokens sit in 23 pools, all without a hook, 14 of them with active liquidity.
findings.preconditions: A pool of such a token. Any swap, withdrawal or take of the token triggers the shortfall, with no role and no hook. A caller who wants to enlarge the shortfall on purpose pays the same charge on the way back. I did not read the source of the ten tokens, so whether the rate can be changed by an owner, and whether some senders are exempt, is not confirmed. The same stored sweep lists six tokens on Polygon and one on Arbitrum One with a sender charge of 0.2 to 98 percent, which I did not retest.
findings.mitigations: Core cannot detect the charge, because take does not read the balance after the transfer. Interfaces and routers should not list pools of tokens whose sender pays on top. LPs should avoid such pools or expect that the last units cannot be withdrawn. A periphery check that compares balanceOf before and after a payout would show the difference.

The ERC-20 branch of transfer accepts no return data or the word 1 and never reads the balance (src/types/Currency.sol:55-79). findings.title: Celo's public endpoint routes a minority of requests to an op-geth build that Celo no longer supports and that has no Karst rules
findings.difference: forno.celo.org load balances celo-reth and Geth/v0.1.0-untagged-c7ed55b8-20260817/linux-amd64/go1.24.13. Celo ended op-geth support on mainnet on 22 July 2026, and the op-geth fork's chain configuration has no Karst field. Today both backends are on the canonical chain and give identical results.
findings.mechanism: Wallets, routers and quoters that simulate a PoolManager call through forno get an answer from whichever backend serves the request. Today the two backends agree on every opcode vector and every PoolManager script tried this cycle and on block hash and state root. After Celo activates Karst, the Geth backend cannot apply the new rules and stops following the canonical chain, or applies the old rules to new blocks. A share of eth_call and eth_estimateGas requests (14 of 60 in one sample) would then run against stale state or old rules, so a quote, a minimum output computed from it, or a gas estimate for a long swap could be wrong. The PoolManager itself executes in blocks built by celo-reth and is not affected.
findings.impact: No loss of pool funds. Users who set slippage bounds from a stale quote may get a worse fill or a revert, and an estimate from the wrong rules can make a removal fail for lack of gas and need a retry.
findings.preconditions: Celo activates Karst, which has no date, while the forno operator still serves the op-geth backend.
findings.mitigations: The forno operator removes the op-geth backend before Karst. Integrators simulate against a celo-reth endpoint and check web3_clientVersion. Slippage bounds remain the user's protection.

findings.title: Polygon's Salvador hardfork rewrites the code of five accounts at block 98,688,600 through BlockAlloc, a mechanism that can give any address new code outside a transaction
findings.difference: Bor applies a per-block code table (BlockAlloc) during block finalisation. For every listed address it calls SetCode and keeps the storage, and it sets the balance only when the balance is zero. Ethereum has no rule that replaces an account's code. Polygon has used the table on 0x1001 and 0x1010, and at block 62,278,656 on WPOL (0x0d500B1d8E8eF31E21C99d1Db9A6444d3ADf1270), a token that was deployed by an ordinary transaction and that the PoolManager holds. Salvador, scheduled for 2026-12-08, applies it to five more ordinary accounts.
findings.mechanism: At block 98,688,600 the five Polymarket and Binance accounts get a 344 byte sweeper. A call with value reverts, and sweep() sends the native balance to a fixed recovery Safe. For the PoolManager, an address that changes code under BlockAlloc behaves differently through each of the calls it makes. A native take to that address (src/types/Currency.sol:44-52) reverts afterwards. A token take or sync on it (src/types/Currency.sol:53-80 and 90-95) calls code the pool creator never saw. A hook at that address (Hooks.sol permission bits at src/libraries/Hooks.sol:29) answers with other code. The PoolManager's own code could be replaced the same way, and noDelegateCall (src/NoDelegateCall.sol:19-25) does not detect that. The five Salvador targets hold no ERC-6909 claims at the PoolManager in currency 0 (native), USDC, USDC.e, WPOL, USDT or WETH, and no PositionManager position (eth_call at block 97,906,958), so the scheduled rewrite touches no PoolManager funds.
findings.impact: None for the Salvador entries as scheduled. In general, a BlockAlloc entry for a pooled token, a hook or the PoolManager would decide every pool that uses that address. On 2026-11-24 the PoolManager holds 3,211,373 POL and 7,903 WPOL.
findings.preconditions: A bor release with a BlockAlloc entry, adopted by the validator set through Polygon governance (a PIP and a coordinated release). No ordinary account can add an entry.
findings.mitigations: At each bor release, read params/config.go BlockAlloc for the PoolManager, PositionManager and pooled currencies and hooks. After block 98,688,600, compare the code at the five addresses with the table.

findings.title: BNB Smart Chain runs a call from the system address with its stated value and moves no balance, and no ordinary sender can be that address
findings.difference: On Ethereum as the PoolManager code models it, a frame that reports CALLVALUE v exists only after v was moved from the caller to the callee. The BNB Smart Chain client treats the caller 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe as a system call: EVM.Call skips the balance check and skips the transfer for that caller, and still builds the callee frame with the stated value (core/vm/evm.go lines 311 to 316 and 342 to 347 on master). The same text is in go-ethereum master (lines 288 to 309), in op-geth on the optimism branch (lines 268 to 303) and in the head of the Celo fork of op-geth (lines 285 to 321). Bor, the Nitro fork of go-ethereum, libevm (Avalanche), revm and the Monad client perform the check and the transfer for every caller. A read-only probe on the 21 public endpoints showed the rule active on BNB Smart Chain only: a call from that address with value 7 and an overridden balance of 1000 left the sender at 1000 and the target at its old balance, while the target frame read CALLVALUE 7. The other 20 endpoints moved the 7 wei or rejected the transaction.
findings.mechanism: 1. settle and settleFor credit msg.value as paid when no ERC-20 is synced and read no balance (src/PoolManager.sol:300-307 and 352-354). 2. A frame entered from the system address on BNB Smart Chain reports a value that nobody paid. If such a frame reached settleFor(recipient) while the manager is unlocked, the recipient would hold a native credit backed by nothing and could take the PoolManager's BNB (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). 3. The client itself calls with that caller in three places, the beacon root call, the parent hash call and the request queue call, each with value zero and a fixed target (core/state_processor.go lines 353 to 429). Parlia system transactions use the block's coinbase as sender (consensus/parlia/parlia.go lines 1389, 2069, 2096, 2110, 2131 and 2137), so they pay value from a real balance. 4. A signed transaction or an EIP-7702 authorization from that address needs a signature for an address with no known signing secret. 5. A system call starts a new transaction context, so the manager is locked. A probe call of settle() and settleFor(address) with value 1 from the system address returned ManagerLocked (0x54e3ca0d) on all 21 networks. 6. A contract that the system address calls sees the value but receives no balance, so it cannot pass the value on to the PoolManager. No step lets an ordinary account produce the frame.
findings.impact: None today. The PoolManager on BNB Smart Chain holds about 3,794 BNB plus the tokens of every pool that has BNB on one side. Those funds would be exposed only if a later client release or hard fork added a system call that carries value into contract code chosen by users, or let a public transaction type run with the system address as caller.
findings.preconditions: A consensus rule change on BNB Smart Chain (or on a network whose client carries the same rule) that makes the system address the caller of user-chosen code with nonzero value while the PoolManager is unlocked. Client developers and the validator set must act. No ordinary account can meet this.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can keep this rule on the checklist for every BNB Smart Chain hard fork, starting with Jenner on 2026-12-08, and rerun the probe from this finding after each one. A core change that removes the dependency would have sync(address(0)) record address(this).balance and have the native branch of _settle credit the smaller of msg.value and the balance rise. LPs and pool creators cannot act on this.

findings.title: No test fails when the unsettled delta check of unlock is removed, and under the --isolate flag of the CI no test pins the lock close or the reset of the synced currency; the source has all three statements
findings.difference: None. This is a property of the repository's tests and it is the same on every network. The network features that each unpinned statement stands against are named in the mechanism field.
findings.mechanism: I read every guard and accounting statement in the assigned lines together with every test under test/ and every helper under src/test, and asked which test fails when the statement is removed or its condition is inverted. Nothing could be compiled, so the answer comes from reading. Three statements carry the whole custody model and are weakly pinned. First, src/PoolManager.sol:112 reverts with CurrencyNotSettled when the count of nonzero deltas is not zero at the end of unlock. No file under test/ names CurrencyNotSettled. Outside the interface and PoolManager.sol the name occurs only in the copy of unlock at src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:66. Every expectRevert that is reached through a router expects another error, and the bare expectRevert at test/PoolManager.t.sol:917-922 is satisfied by the failing token transfer. Inverting the condition fails every test that completes an unlock. Removing the line fails no test. The line is what makes take, mint and a swap output a loan that must be repaid (A5), and it reads a transient counter (A1). Second, src/PoolManager.sol:113 closes the lock. Without --isolate the second unlock of one test transaction would revert with AlreadyUnlocked, for example in the setup helper at test/utils/Deployers.sol:199-211, which adds liquidity twice. The CI runs forge test --isolate (.github/workflows/tests-pr.yml:37, .github/workflows/tests-merge.yml:31), and in that mode every top level call of a test is its own transaction, so transient storage is empty at the next call and no test notices a lock that stays open. I found no test that performs two unlocks inside one top level call and no assertion that the manager is locked after an unlock returns. Third, src/PoolManager.sol:361 resets the synced currency after a token settle. Without the reset a second settle would credit the same balance rise again, because the stored reserves are not updated. test_settle_twice_doesNotApplyDelta (test/Sync.t.sol:341-374) does not detect that: it takes the credited amount between the two settles, so the balance equals the stored reserves again and the second settle pays zero with or without the reset, and its last assertion reads the delta of address(0), which is zero in both cases. Without --isolate the reset is pinned by the setup helper, where a token settle is followed by a native settle with value in the same transaction and a stale token sync would raise NonzeroNativeValue (test/utils/Deployers.sol:203-206, src/PoolManager.sol:356). With --isolate nothing pins it. Further statements that no test pins in either mode: the onlyWhenUnlocked modifier on settleFor and on clear (src/PoolManager.sol:305, 310; the locked tests cover take, settle, mint and burn at test/PoolManager.t.sol:962-999); the toInt128 limit as applied in take, clear, mint, burn and _settle (src/PoolManager.sol:294, 313, 326, 334, 364; the library function is pinned by test/libraries/SafeCast.t.sol:85-99, and no manager test uses an amount of 2^127 or more); the use of _burnFrom with its allowance and operator check in burn (src/PoolManager.sol:335; the check is pinned on the mock at test/ERC6909Claims.t.sol:15-48, and every manager test sets the router as operator before it burns); the truncation of the id in mint and burn (src/PoolManager.sol:324, 333); the checked subtraction for a balance that fell between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:360); the acceptance of empty return data, the minimum of 32 bytes for a returned value and the absence of a code check in the token transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74; the tests use tokens that return true, a token that returns false and a contract that reverts); the amount of gas forwarded with a native payout (src/types/Currency.sol:48); the minimum of 32 bytes for a hook answer and the exact 64 bytes for a hook that returns a delta (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152, 166; the mock hooks always return full words); and the absence of a lock check in collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57, recorded in F-006 and F-014). For the increment branch at src/PoolManager.sol:375 I found no test that moves one delta from a nonzero value to another nonzero value and then asserts the count; I did not trace every hook test for that case. I then read each of these statements as if it were the only changed line. Each does what its comment, its error name and the surrounding tests require: line 112 reads NonzeroDeltaCount and runs before the lock is closed; line 113 writes false to the lock slot; line 361 writes zero to the currency slot after the balance was read and before the delta is booked; take, mint and clear negate a value that toInt128 has limited to 2^127 - 1 and book it to msg.sender; burn credits msg.sender and burns from the named account through _burnFrom; settleFor credits the recipient. The deployed PoolManagers are other bytecode than a build of this checkout, so a read-only test of them says how each network executes these paths and nothing about this build. With that limit, three eth_call probes with a forwarder stub placed by state override gave the same words on all 21 networks, the Unichain predeploy included: a callback that only mints leaves the unlock reverting with 0x5212cba1 (CurrencyNotSettled); the lock slot reads zero and a take reverts with ManagerLocked right after unlock returns in the same call; the currency slot reads the synced address before settle and zero after it; settleFor, clear, settle, take, mint and burn revert with ManagerLocked outside an unlock; amounts of 2^127 revert with SafeCastOverflow in mint, take and burn; a burn of claims that another address holds does not credit the caller.
findings.impact: No funds are at risk from the source as it is written. The observation matters for the review method: a build in which line 112 is missing would let any account take every token without paying, a build without line 113 would let any call that follows an unlock in the same transaction take without an end check, and a build without line 361 would let one payment be credited twice, and the repository's tests as the CI runs them would pass in all three cases. Earlier cycles relied on the tests to confirm the source. For these statements the confirmation comes from reading the text and, for the deployed contracts only, from the probes.
findings.preconditions: None for the observation itself. A loss would need a build in which one of the listed statements is missing or changed. The text of this checkout shows each statement in place, and nobody in this review could compile it.
findings.mitigations: Before deployment, compile this checkout and run the three probes in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-test-pins.work against the built bytecode placed at a test address by state override on each network, or add tests: an unlock whose callback leaves a debt must revert with CurrencyNotSettled; a take right after an unlock in the same call must revert with ManagerLocked; two settles in a row after one payment must credit once; settleFor and clear must revert while locked; a burn by an account without approval must revert at the manager.

verification.factCheck: The finding states no chain fact and says so in its difference field. Its claims concern this repository, the Foundry test runner and the behaviour of the contracts deployed today, and I checked each. Repository. A search of the checkout finds the name CurrencyNotSettled at src/PoolManager.sol:112, src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:66 and src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:18 and in no file under test/. 187 lines under test/ and src/test mention expectRevert and 38 of them are bare calls. Of the bare ones only test/PoolManager.t.sol:920 reaches an unlock, and there the take of 100 units from a fresh manager fails in the token transfer before the callback returns (src/test/PoolTakeTest.sol:44, src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). The five bare ones in test/utils/SwapHelper.t.sol (lines 70, 113, 119, 125, 131) stand in front of router calls and fail earlier, in require statements of the helper itself (test/utils/Deployers.sol:220 and 266). The others sit in library, type and mock token tests. No named expectation is CurrencyNotSettled. So no test fails when line 112 is removed, as the finding says. The CI runs forge test --isolate (.github/workflows/tests-pr.yml:37, tests-merge.yml:31) with Foundry v1.3.6 (tests-pr.yml:23-25), and the justfile does the same (justfile:8). Foundry. I fetched crates/cli/src/opts/evm.rs from the master branch: lines 146 to 151 say that in isolation mode all top level calls are executed as a separate transaction in a separate EVM context, which is the sentence the finding quotes. The same file now has a no_isolate option at lines 153 to 156, and crates/config/src/lib.rs line 3301 sets isolate: true in the default configuration. Tests under isolation. The repository's own noIsolate modifier (test/utils/Deployers.sol:78-85) shows the authors rely on that rule: it re-enters the test through one call so that the body runs as one transaction. Three tests use it (test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001 and 1010, test/Sync.t.sol:36). None of them settles, and none makes two unlocks. Every router and helper makes one unlock per external call (src/test/ActionsRouter.sol:92, PoolSwapTest.sol:41, PoolModifyLiquidityTest.sol:49, PoolDonateTest.sol:33, PoolTakeTest.sol:25, PoolClaimsTest.sol:27 and 32), and the nested unlock tests expect AlreadyUnlocked inside the callback (src/test/PoolNestedActionsTest.sol:60 and 113). I found no assertion that the manager is locked after unlock returns. test_settle_twice_doesNotApplyDelta (test/Sync.t.sol:341-374) takes the credited amount between its two settles, so the balance equals the stored reserves again and the second settle credits zero with or without the reset at line 361. Its last assertion reads the delta of address(0). In a run where setUp is one transaction, test/utils/Deployers.sol:203-206 adds token liquidity and then native liquidity with value, which would hit AlreadyUnlocked without line 113 and NonzeroNativeValue without line 361. Under isolation these are separate transactions. The smaller items also hold: locked tests exist for take, settle, mint and burn only (test/PoolManager.t.sol:962-999), SETTLE_FOR appears once and inside an unlock (test/Sync.t.sol:151), clear is called only through ActionsRouter inside an unlock, SafeCastOverflow is expected only in library tests, and the allowance check of _burnFrom is tested on the mock (test/ERC6909Claims.t.sol:15-48). Deployed contracts. I reran the researcher's three probe sequences with my own driver and decoding on all 21 RPC endpoints of state/networks.json on 2026-11-23 (eth_call, forwarder stub placed by state override, no transaction). Every network gave the same words: a callback that only mints ends in 0x5212cba1 (CurrencyNotSettled); mint then burn by the stub succeeds; a burn of claims minted to a third address gives the unapproved stub no credit; take, settleFor and clear from an outside sender revert with 0x54e3ca0d (ManagerLocked); inside the callback the lock slot reads 1, the currency slot reads the stub address after sync and 0 after settle; after unlock returns in the same call the lock slot reads 0 and take reverts with ManagerLocked; mint, take and burn of 2^127 revert with 0x93dafdf1; clear of 1 on a zero delta reverts with 0xbda73abf; a zero take of an address without code succeeds; sync of that address reverts without data; a nested unlock reverts with 0x5090d6c6. Blocks: Ethereum 26478528 and 26478550, Unichain 64696932 and 64697193, Celo 83544535, X Layer 76676261, Tempo 50444717, Arc 32750975, HyperEVM 52041427, and the latest block of each other network. On Arbitrum One two calls of the first run were answered with unsupported block number and gave the same words on the rerun at block 526836202. I recomputed the eight error selectors and the four slot constants with a Keccak routine of my own. Not confirmed: nothing was compiled, so no test was run, and the statement that the deployed PoolManagers are other bytecode than a build of this checkout was tested by nobody. It rests on the brief, which says this build is still to be deployed.
verification.codeCheck: I read the cited lines and the whole of src/PoolManager.sol, src/types/Currency.sol, src/ProtocolFees.sol, src/ERC6909.sol, src/ERC6909Claims.sol, src/libraries/Hooks.sol, Lock.sol, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol, CurrencyReserves.sol, CurrencyDelta.sol, SafeCast.sol, CustomRevert.sol and ParseBytes.sol. The three statements the finding centres on are in place. src/PoolManager.sol:112 reverts with CurrencyNotSettled when NonzeroDeltaCount.read() is not zero, after the callback at line 110 and before Lock.lock() at line 113. The counter is maintained only by _accountDelta (lines 368-378): a zero delta returns early, a result of zero decrements, and a start from zero increments. Lock.lock writes 0 to the slot that the modifier at lines 96-99 and the check at line 105 read (src/libraries/Lock.sol:10-27). In _settle the token branch rejects msg.value at line 356, reads the reserves slot and the live balance, subtracts with checked arithmetic at line 360 and calls resetCurrency at line 361, which writes 0 to the currency slot only (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-25). The credit at line 364 goes to the recipient in the synced currency through toInt128, which rejects 2^127 and above (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). I looked for guards the finding might have missed and found none that changes its statements. settleFor and clear carry onlyWhenUnlocked (lines 305, 310). take, mint and clear negate a value that toInt128 has limited and book it to msg.sender (lines 294, 317, 326). The unchecked blocks cover the negation only, since called functions keep their own checked arithmetic. burn credits msg.sender and burns from the named account through _burnFrom, which lowers a finite allowance unless the caller is the holder or an operator (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). collectProtocolFees checks the caller and the synced token and not the lock (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52). The token transfer accepts empty return data or a 32 byte word equal to 1 and has no code check (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), and the native payout forwards all gas (line 48). callHook rejects an answer shorter than 32 bytes or with another first word, and a hook that returns a delta must answer with exactly 64 bytes (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152, 166). The four slot constants equal keccak256 of Unlocked, NonzeroDeltaCount, ReservesOf and Currency minus one, all four differ, every address mask in these files has 40 hex digits, and all four libraries use TSTORE and TLOAD only. Each statement does what its comment and error name say. I agree with the finding that the source gives an ordinary account no path here and that the observation is about how far the tests can vouch for a build. The finding's own open point on line 375 stays open: in the routers, the nested executor and the hook doubles I read, every delta returns to zero in one step, so I also found no test for a move between two nonzero values.
verification.corrections: actor: governance. The finding names no step that an ordinary account can take against the source as written. The loss it describes needs a build that lacks one of the statements, and only the party that compiles and deploys the PoolManager can bring that about. It is a confirmed info item and it is outside the unprivileged scope. Second, the wording on --isolate is dated. On the Foundry master branch the default configuration has isolate: true and a --no-isolate flag exists, so with a current forge a plain forge test also runs every top level call as its own transaction. Lines 113 and 361 are then pinned by no test in any default run, and the setup helper pins them only with --no-isolate or with an older forge that does not isolate by default. I did not check the default of v1.3.6, the version the CI installs. Third, the finding names one bare expectRevert in front of a router call. Five more are in test/utils/SwapHelper.t.sol. They fail in the helper's require statements before any router is called, so the conclusion stands. Fourth, the impact field says earlier cycles relied on the tests to confirm the source. 37 of the 598 items in state/cleared.json cite a test file, and I found none that rests on a test for line 112, 113 or 361. Those items cite the source text. Fifth, the sentence that the deployed PoolManagers are other bytecode than a build of this checkout is an assumption taken from the brief. Nobody compiled the checkout. The consequence the finding draws from it is the safe one: the on-chain probes describe the networks and the contracts deployed today and say nothing about this build.

findings.title: Six go-ethereum family nodes run a Go toolchain with a published silent dead store miscompile, and no function on the opcode or state path has the triggering shape
findings.difference: Go issue 81863: from Go 1.26.0 through go1.26.10 and from Go 1.27.0 through go1.27.3, the dead auto elimination pass attributes a CondSelect of two local addresses to its first operand only, so a store through a pointer that a branch chose between two non-escaping locals is deleted when the first local is never read, even if the other one is. It applies on every architecture whose compiler emits CondSelect (amd64, arm64, ppc64le, loong64, wasm). The fix is go1.26.11 and go1.27.4, released 2026-11-10. Today Arbitrum One answers as nitro v3.13.0-rc.9 linux-arm64 go1.27.3, Robinhood Chain as the same release on linux-arm64 and linux-amd64 with go1.27.3, Polygon (publicnode) as five bor v2.11.1-private builds with go1.26.10, BNB Smart Chain as Geth/v1.8.2 linux-amd64 go1.26.10, and Avalanche as avalanchego 1.15.3 go=1.26.10. Elysium reports go1.25.12 and the Celo op-geth backend go1.24.13, which predate the faulty pass order. Cycle 17 addition, Ethereum: the official geth v1.17.9 and v1.17.10 builds pin Go 1.27.2 and 1.27.3, both inside the range of the same issue. These releases also run every untraced execution (eth_call, block import, block building) through a new generated switch, execUntraced, while traced calls still use the old table loop, so a step trace no longer shows the loop that produces blocks.
findings.mechanism: The miscompile needs four things in one function after inlining: two stack allocated locals whose address is taken, a pointer that a side effect free if or if-else picks between their addresses, a store, zeroing or copy through that pointer and no load through it (branchelim refuses a CondSelect whose result feeds a load address), and a later direct read of the second local. A scan of holiman/uint256 v1.3.2 and v1.2.4 (all of uint256.go, mod.go, div.go, conversion.go, decimal.go) and of core/vm instructions.go, interpreter.go, stack.go, memory.go, evm.go, eips.go and core/state journal.go, transient_storage.go, statedb.go, state_object.go, access_list.go of the nitro fork 0e44603, bsc v1.8.2, bor v2.11.1 and libevm d398bc4dbe41 found no such function. The only branch selected pointers are: uint256 AddMod (x = &tmpX, y = &tmpY, v1.3.2 lines 240-245), where one operand is the caller's pointer, the pointers are only loaded from, and branchelim therefore keeps the Phi; SMod and SDiv, where the branch calls Neg and so is not side effect free and the pointer is only passed to Mod or Div; DivMod (m = new(Int).Set(m)) with a side effect in the branch; bor's interrupt flag in Run, loaded atomically and passed to runSwitch; the jump table choice in evm.go, which takes addresses of globals; and journal mutation state, which is heap memory. Sqrt in v1.2.4 swaps two pointers in a loop, which branchelim does not touch, and no opcode calls Sqrt. A dropped store in these functions would change the ADDMOD, SDIV or SMOD result, so those operands were run: 6,000 ADDMOD vectors with a modulus of at least 2^192 and each operand above, equal to or below the modulus, 6,112 SDIV and SMOD vectors over all sign pairs, plus the 99,985 battery and 85,544 targeted vectors. On each of the five networks every request was a JSON-RPC batch of web3_clientVersion and eth_call. There was no mismatch on any build. The PoolManager reaches SDIV and SMOD in TickBitmap.compress and Pool.tickSpacingToMaxLiquidityPerTick and MULMOD in FullMath and SqrtPriceMath; ADDMOD appears only in the compiler's metadata trailer. Cycle 17 addition, Ethereum: a scan of geth v1.17.9 core/vm and core/state finds no function with the triggering shape, and the generated loop calls the same handler functions as the table loop. The battery, the targeted vectors and 232 PUSH, DUP and SWAP programs give the specified words on geth v1.17.9 built with go1.27.2 (blockpi endpoint). The verifier corrected two points: the fault also reaches go1.26 releases before its 1.26 backport, and the runs reported for a go1.25.14 build went through a gateway that answered only from reth and erigon in 30 samples, so only one geth toolchain has been tested. Whether go1.26.10, which bor, BNB Chain geth and avalanchego use, holds the backport is lead L-838.
findings.impact: No path by which an ordinary account takes or freezes funds was found. If an unread function of the node held the shape, a node built with an affected toolchain would compute another state than one built with a fixed toolchain, which is a consensus fault of the operators and not something an attacker can aim at a pool through the PoolManager.
findings.preconditions: Block producers would have to run an affected build and some function on the state transition path outside the files read would have to contain the shape. Neither is shown. The sequencer and validator builds are not published.
findings.mitigations: Ask the Arbitrum, Robinhood Chain, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche operators to rebuild with go1.26.11 or go1.27.4 or later. Rerun paired.py after their next release.

verification.factCheck: The Go fix commit 00ba484 on go.googlesource.com is titled 'cmd/compile: teach deadstore about CondSelect', says CondSelect could not reach deadstore before CL 685676 and CL 715044, and says 'Fixes #81863'. deadstore.go at go1.27.3 line 333 keeps autos that reach OpPhi only; at go1.27.4 lines 332-333 the condition adds OpCondSelect with a comment naming issue 81863. compile.go at go1.25.12 lists 'dead auto elim' at line 477 before 'branchelim' at line 480, while go1.26.10 (479, 481) and go1.27.3 (480, 482) run branchelim first, so go1.25.12 is outside the faulty pass order. branchelim.go at go1.27.3 lines 28-41 and 72-83 collects every value used in a load address and refuses to turn it into a CondSelect, which supports the claim that pointers only loaded from keep their Phi. go.dev/doc/devel/release lists go1.26.10 and go1.27.3 on 2026-10-19 and go1.26.11 and go1.27.4 on 2026-11-10. My own web3_clientVersion calls on 2026-11-24 returned nitro/v3.13.0-rc.9 linux-arm64 go1.27.3 for Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain, bor v2.11.1-private linux-amd64 go1.26.10 from publicnode, Geth/v1.8.2 linux-amd64 go1.26.10 from bsc-dataseed1 and avalanchego 1.15.3 go=1.26.10. uint256 v1.3.2 AddMod (lines 215-266) selects x between the caller's pointer and &tmpX and y between the caller's pointer and &tmpY, and reads through them only, as the finding says. The Go issue page on github.com did not load through the proxy, so the issue text itself was not read; the fix commit and the tagged sources carry the same facts.
verification.codeCheck: The cited sites use the opcodes said: TickBitmap.sol:20-27 uses signextend, sdiv and smod for compress; Pool.sol:576-578 uses sdiv and smod in tickSpacingToMaxLiquidityPerTick; FullMath.sol:24 uses mulmod with not(0); SqrtPriceMath.sol:252 uses mulmod for round up. grep finds no addmod in src/. Since every vector against those opcodes matched on the affected builds and no node function with the shape was found, no line of src/ computes a different value. The finding claims no attacker path, and I found none.
