findings.title: MegaETH blocks are executed by a closed JIT executor that no public RPC node re-executes, so eth_call evidence speaks for a different EVM than the one that writes PoolManager state
findings.difference: On Ethereum every node re-executes every block with an interpreter whose source is public. On MegaETH the sequencer runs a parallel, JIT-compiled executor whose source is not published. The default RPC nodes are replicas that apply the sequencer's results without re-execution. Only stateless validators, full nodes and provers re-execute, and the public stateless validator does so with the stock revm 40.0.3 interpreter, mega-evm v1.7.3 and ruint 1.17.2.
findings.mechanism: 1. The stateless-validator README says the validator uses a single-threaded executor based on the vanilla revm interpreter, and that, together with the K-semantics executor and the JIT-compiled executor on sequencer nodes, this makes three MegaETH client implementations. 2. The architecture page says replica nodes receive blocks and execution results from the sequencer and apply them without re-execution, and that this is the default RPC mode. eth_call and debug_traceTransaction on such a node therefore run that node's local EVM on state that the sequencer wrote. 3. The only public compiler from megaeth-labs is the evmone-compiler prototype. Its PUSHnJUMPI tests the whole 256 bit condition through intx's explicit operator bool and falls through when the word is zero (evmone_aot_compiler.hpp lines 84-96, intx v0.10.1 line 997). It checks gas only before jumps, but a frame that ends out of gas is undone as a whole, so the late check changes gas use and not state. Nothing ties this prototype to the production build. 4. If the production executor computed MULMOD, a shift, a comparison or a jump differently from the specification, every pool's swap and liquidity amounts in src/libraries (FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, TickMath, TickBitmap) would differ in blocks only. A replica would store the wrong result. A stateless validator would see a state root mismatch. 5. This cycle found no such divergence. 2,885 mined swaps that crossed initialized ticks or took several steps reproduce to the unit. 53,811 mined swaps satisfy the tick relation. For 7,627 mined PoolManager transactions, the receipts the sequencer wrote equal the replica's re-execution in status and in every surviving log.
findings.impact: None found. The record exists so that deployers know where the assurance comes from. A fault in the closed executor would hit every pool, an ordinary transaction could trigger it, and the only checks are the stateless validators and the fault proof path.
findings.preconditions: A fault in the closed production executor or in a future release of it. No fault is known.
findings.mitigations: Run the public stateless validator against MegaETH blocks that contain PoolManager transactions, and rerun tools/opdiff/swaps.py, replay.py and this unit's frames.py after each mega-reth release.

findings.title: Arbitrum family validators compute the settled state with a go1.25.9 WebAssembly build that public endpoints do not run
findings.difference: On Ethereum the client that answers eth_call also produces the state. On these three chains the state that the parent chain accepts, and so the state behind every withdrawal, is defined by the replay binary compiled by go1.25.9 to WebAssembly (GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm) and published as WAVM machine consensus-v61. The public endpoints and, as far as anyone can see, the sequencers run a native arm64 or amd64 build of nitro v3.13.0-rc.9 made with go1.27.3. The two paths compile the same go-ethereum fork and holiman/uint256 v1.3.2 with different Go releases and different code generators.
findings.mechanism: Every opcode test in this review, including the 185,529 vectors, the 550 scripts and the reruns of this cycle, ran on the native build. If the WebAssembly build of uint256 or core/vm computed one MULMOD in FullMath.sol:24 or 48, one SDIV in TickBitmap, or one JUMPI differently, a swap would produce one state on the sequencer and another in the replay. The sequencer's state is what users see and what the next transactions build on; the replay's state is what an honest validator asserts on the parent chain. An ordinary account cannot cause such a split unless a codegen difference exists, and none is known. The comparison of confirmed assertions with node block hashes over 31 assertions on Arbitrum One, 57 on Robinhood Chain and 6 on Elysium found no split, which covers every PoolManager transaction in those ranges.
findings.impact: No loss path. A split would stall confirmations and withdrawals to the parent chain for all users until the operators reconciled the two paths, and pool funds would stay where they are.
findings.preconditions: A difference between the go1.25.9 WebAssembly build and the go1.27.3 native build on an instruction the PoolManager uses. None is known.
findings.mitigations: Deployers can watch confirmed assertions against their own node, as done here. Operators can build the native node with the Go release of the consensus machine.

findings.title: No public client checks the storage that the closed HyperEVM validator writes, because block headers carry a zero state root and nanoreth compares its own root as zero
findings.difference: On Ethereum every full node recomputes the state root of each block and rejects a block whose root differs. HyperEVM blocks are produced by the closed hl-node validator, and the headers it publishes have stateRoot 0x00..00. The public archive client nanoreth (the build served at rpc.purroofgroup.com reports reth/v0.1.0-f0cad31) replaces its computed state root with B256::ZERO before the comparison with the header, so the comparison always passes. hyper-evm-sync computes a private blake3 hash of its state for snapshots and compares it with nothing. Both clients do re-execute every transaction and stop on a different receipt: nanoreth checks gas used, the receipts root and the logs bloom against the header, and hyper-evm-sync asserts that its computed receipts equal the validator's receipts.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager keeps pool state, positions, ERC-6909 balances and protocol fees in persistent storage (src/libraries/Pool.sol, src/libraries/Position.sol, src/ERC6909.sol, src/ProtocolFees.sol). A state root would commit to exactly those slots. Transient storage is cleared at the end of each transaction and is in no state root on any network, so the missing check has no bearing on it. A validator fault that changed a persistent storage write without changing gas, status or logs of that transaction would not stop either public client. It would show up only once a later transaction reads the slot and its receipt differs, and then the client halts instead of correcting anything. The validator's receipts are therefore checked publicly, its storage writes only indirectly. This needs a fault or a deliberate change in the validator, which only its operator controls. No mismatch was observed: 2,762 mined PoolManager transactions over the whole history agree in status and logs with nanoreth's re-execution, 485 storage slots from prestateTracer agree with nanoreth's state at the block, and 222 touched PoolManager slots read at latest agree between the official endpoint and nanoreth.
findings.impact: No loss path for an ordinary account. The hazard is on evidence: clearances of HyperEVM that rest on storage, as opposed to receipts, are backed by nanoreth's own state and by the official endpoint, not by a check against the validator's commitment.
findings.preconditions: A fault or change in the closed hl-node validator that alters a storage write but not the receipt of the same transaction. Only the validator operator can cause it.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can run nanoreth or hyper-evm-sync and keep it at head, since a later receipt mismatch halts it, and can compare PoolManager slots between the official endpoint and nanoreth at regular intervals with eth_getStorageAt.

findings.title: BNB Chain's own RPC nodes run a geth build whose commit is not in the public repository
findings.difference: bsc-dataseed1.bnbchain.org and bsc-dataseed2.bnbchain.org answer web3_clientVersion with Geth/v1.8.2-4e1c8247-20261104. The v1.8.2 tag is commit 54afaff4 of 2026-11-03. GitHub returns not found for the compare view v1.8.2...4e1c8247 and HTTP 422 for the commit, while the tag commit and the later pre-release commit 4bd1c730 resolve. The geth version string appends the first 8 characters of the build commit and the build date, so the official endpoints run code built one day after the release from a commit the public repository does not hold.
findings.mechanism: Every BSC reading of cycles 8 to 12 (interpreter, jump destination cache, keccak opcode, state) used the public v1.8.2 tag. A build from an unpublished commit can differ in any of these. The vectors and scripts of this cycle ran against that build and gave the specified results, so whatever differs is outside what 185,529 opcode vectors, 8,415 MULMOD sequence vectors and the PoolManager scripts reach. The most likely explanation is a private security or operational patch on top of v1.8.2, as BNB Chain has shipped before, which nobody outside can read.
findings.impact: No loss path. The difference is that the code serving BNB Chain's own endpoints, and possibly its validators, cannot be read, so the source readings of this review cover the public release only.
findings.preconditions: None for the fact. A harmful difference would need BNB Chain or a validator to run a faulty private build.
findings.mitigations: Ask BNB Chain which commit 4e1c8247 is and whether validators run it, and rerun the vector and script sets after Jenner on 2026-12-08 against both dataseed and reth-bsc.

findings.title: Withdrawals on OP Mainnet, Unichain and Ink now settle against kona-client on the Cannon MIPS64 machine, a Rust build that no RPC endpoint runs
findings.difference: On Ethereum the client that answers eth_call also produces the state that matters. On these three chains the state that L1 accepts for withdrawals is fixed by the respected game type of the AnchorStateRegistry. A read on Ethereum at block 26,486,262 returns respectedGameType 9 on all three, which the OP contracts name SUPER_CANNON_KONA. The game implementation 0x19af533c... (SuperFaultDisputeGame 0.8.0) carries absolutePrestate 0x03e5a548...37c9 and the MIPS64 VM 0xacc005dc... version 1.10.1. The superchain registry lists that prestate as the cannon64-kona-interop build of release 1.9.0. The monorepo tag kona-client/v1.9.0 pins revm 43.0.2, revm-interpreter 43.0.1, op-revm 20.0.0, ruint 1.20.0 and alloy-primitives 1.7.3, compiled with Rust 1.95 for the big-endian MIPS64 target of Cannon. The nodes behind the public endpoints are op-reth builds on x86-64 or arm64. Cycle 7 cleared the kona proof issues on the ground that no chain used kona as its respected proof; that ground no longer holds for these three chains.
findings.mechanism: If the MIPS64 build of revm computed one opcode differently from the x86 node for some input, a transaction hitting that input would give one post-state on L2 and another in the proof program. The PoolManager paths where such an input could arise are mulmod(a, b, not(0)) and mulmod(a, b, denominator) in src/libraries/FullMath.sol:24 and :48, the sar and signextend in src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:38, the shifts and byte lookups of src/libraries/BitMath.sol:16-22 and :40-45, div(not(0), price) in src/libraries/TickMath.sol:104 and the rounding mulmod in src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:252. Any account could then disprove the honest output root by running the public program, so proposals covering that block would lose and L1 withdrawals of every user would stall until governance changed the prestate. Pool balances inside L2 would not move. This review found no such opcode difference. ruint 1.20.0 has one architecture-specific path, the borrow chain behind limb comparison (src/algorithms/mod.rs:144-185), with a portable fallback of two overflowing_sub calls (src/algorithms/add.rs:24-35). Its division uses the MG10 reciprocal on u64 and u128 products, and u128 products on MIPS64 lower to DMULTU, whose on-chain semantics in MIPS64Instructions.sol:794-798 are the exact 128-bit product. The same targeted vectors were run through a transcription of the Go library that World Chain's program uses with DMULTU as the multiplier and gave no mismatch (see cleared). The Rust path itself was read, not executed.
findings.impact: No loss path found. A divergence would freeze L1 withdrawals of all users of the three chains, including withdrawals of tokens taken out of the PoolManager, until operators replaced the prestate. Funds held by the PoolManager on L2 stay where they are.
findings.preconditions: An opcode result that differs between revm 43 on x86-64 and the same code compiled for Cannon MIPS64. None is known. Matching the prestate hash to the kona-client/v1.9.0 tag rests on the registry entry; the build was not reproduced.
findings.mitigations: Deployers can run kona-client from the same prestate against blocks that contain PoolManager transactions, or watch for output roots that a SUPER_CANNON_KONA game rejects. Operators can add the opcode battery of this review to the kona test suite on the MIPS64 target.

findings.title: Zora, World Chain and Soneium settle withdrawals on a permissioned proposer, and Zora and Soneium name no proof program at all
findings.difference: Zora and World Chain respect game type 1 (PERMISSIONED_CANNON). Zora's implementation args carry the absolute prestate 0xdead0000...0000, so no step can ever be proven and the outcome rests on the permissioned proposer and challenger. World Chain's carries 0x033c0009...4dbb6e, the cannon64 build of op-program 1.9.0 (op-geth v1.101604.0 pseudo-version of 2025-12-08, holiman/uint256 v1.3.2, Go 1.24.10, GOARCH=mips64 GOMIPS64=softfloat). Soneium respects type 5 (SUPER_PERMISSIONED): the newest game 0xfe326897... was created and resolved DEFENDER_WINS in the same second by proposer 0x49cc743a..., and absolutePrestate() and vm() revert on it.
findings.mechanism: For these chains the state behind a withdrawal is what the operator's proposer asserts. An ordinary account cannot make that assertion differ from the L2 state that the PoolManager's users see, because no proof program is consulted on Zora and Soneium, and on World Chain only the permissioned challenger can play the program. A wrong opcode in the proof build therefore cannot be turned against users by an unprivileged party on these three chains. It also means no program checks the operator's state root.
findings.impact: No loss path for an unprivileged account. A dishonest or faulty proposer could finalise any state, which is an operator risk to every bridged asset, including tokens withdrawn from the PoolManager.
findings.preconditions: Operator action only.
findings.mitigations: Deployers should list these chains as operator-settled in the deployment checklist.

findings.title: Arc nodes from v0.8.0 to v0.8.4 could read stale storage of an account without code that a block deleted and created again, which cannot reach PoolManager storage
findings.difference: Arc v0.8.0 to v0.8.4 build on reth v2.2.0, whose execution cache handled an account without code that a block destroyed and created again by removing the account entry and keeping its cached storage words. A later block on that node read the old words. v0.8.5 moved to circlefin/arc-reth v2.2.0-arc.2 with the upstream fix (reth pull request 28148). The v0.8.4 release fixed a separate state root computation fault of the same base.
findings.mechanism: 1. The cache code runs after each block. For an account marked destroyed it checks whether the account had code at the start of the block. With code it clears the whole cache, which is safe. Without code it removed only the account entry and continued, so storage words cached for that address before the block stayed in the cache. 2. Any account can reach the second branch. The v0.8.5 release note names the trigger: a block deletes an empty account under EIP-161 and a later transaction of the same block creates it again and writes storage. A contract destroyed in its own creation transaction and created again in the same block is marked destroyed in the same way. On a node with the fault, a later read of such a word returns the value from before the block, and that node computes a different result from nodes with the fix. 3. The PoolManager has had code since deployment, so a block that touched it in this way would take the first branch and clear the cache. Its slots are keyed by its own address (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364 and the transient libraries such as src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:21-39 index slots under the PoolManager address), so no stale word of another address is read as PoolManager state. 4. Tokens and hooks of pools that do not use attacker-made contracts also have code at the start of any such block. The only contracts whose reads could go stale are contracts created in that pattern, which are attacker-made by construction, and such a contract can return any value to the PoolManager anyway (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-160, src/types/Currency.sol:40-95).
findings.impact: No PoolManager funds move. On a lagging node, a block that uses the pattern makes that node disagree with the rest, which is a liveness and consistency matter for that node's operator and its RPC users. The official endpoint reports v0.8.6-rc1 and publicnode v0.8.5, both with the fix.
findings.preconditions: A validator or RPC node running arc-node v0.8.0 to v0.8.4. Which releases the validators run is not public.
findings.mitigations: Before deployment, confirm with Circle that every validator runs v0.8.5 or later. Integrations that read PoolManager state through RPC should use an endpoint whose arc_getVersion reports v0.8.5 or later.

findings.title: The LLVM MIPS shift lowering that kona-client 1.9.0 was compiled with miscompiles 128 bit shifts by 64 to 127 under some constant folds, and a scan of the respected prestate finds no bad shape on any fall-through path
findings.difference: OP Mainnet, Unichain and Ink settle withdrawals on kona-client 1.9.0 compiled by Rust nightly-2026-08-22 for the big-endian mips64 target with cpu mips64 (no R6). LLVM issue 235261 (opened 2026-10-24, label miscompilation) shows that MipsTargetLowering::lowerShiftLeftParts and lowerShiftRightParts use (shamt AND 64) as an ISD::SELECT condition although MIPS booleans are 0 or 1, so a DAG fold such as select(c, 0, 1) into xor(c, 1) returns 65 instead of 0 for 128 bit shifts on MIPS64. The fix, commit 0212d77 of 2026-11-14, is on LLVM main only: the MipsISelLowering.cpp of llvmorg-21.1.8, llvmorg-22.1.0, llvmorg-22.1.8, llvmorg-23.1.0 and the release/22.x and release/23.x branches all still use the bare AND, so every Rust toolchain of 2026 including the kona one carries the fault. ruint 1.20.0 implements U256 wrapping_shl and wrapping_shr on two u128 halves with unbounded_shl and unbounded_shr (bits.rs:463-520 and 604-641 of the crate), so every EVM SHL, SHR and SAR and the masks of SIGNEXTEND go through exactly this lowering. On x86 and arm64 nodes the lowering is not used.
findings.mechanism: A shift amount in [64, 127] sets the AND result to 64. Where LLVM folded the select into arithmetic, the MIPS build would return a different word from the node for those amounts. In this bytecode BitMath.mostSignificantBit shifts by the running result r, which reaches 64 to 127 for every input of 64 bits or more, TickBitmap flips a bit with shl(and(tick, 0xff), 1), and the TickMath logarithm shifts by f and by 127 and 128. A changed word there changes the tick, the price or the bitmap slot that a swap writes, so the proof program would compute a different post-state root from the one the op-reth nodes report. The games of type 9 are permissionless, so an ordinary account could post one swap that hits the input and then win the dispute with the program's root against the honest root, delaying withdrawals, or defend a root in which its own withdrawal is larger. Three checks say this does not happen with the present build. First, the revm-interpreter 43.0.1 handlers over ruint 1.20.0 were compiled with rustc 1.97.0 (LLVM 22.1.6, which also lacks the fix) for kona's own mips64-unknown-none target spec, with -mno-check-zero-division and opt-level 3, and run instruction by instruction in an emulator of Cannon's MIPS64Instructions.sol semantics: all 85,544 targeted and 96,876 battery vectors, EXP included, give the specified word, and 3,794 mulDiv and bit scan cases and 2,283 ticks of the price functions match. Second, a planted fault that makes MOVN test bit 0 only, which is the effect the bad fold has, is caught by 624 of 4,278 sampled targeted vectors. Third, the 4,928,204 byte text segment of the respected prestate 0x03e5a548...37c9 itself, rebuilt from the published state file, holds 66 instructions of the form andi rX, rY, 0x40; every later read of rX before it is redefined is the condition of a MOVN or MOVZ (124), a comparison with zero in a branch (10), or one srl by 6 that turns it into 0 or 1. None feeds xori, ori, addu or a store, which is the shape of the miscompile.
findings.impact: None with the respected prestate as built. A future prestate built with a toolchain older than LLVM commit 0212d77 can contain the shape, and would then let an unprivileged account make the proof disagree with the nodes on the price, tick and bitmap arithmetic of every pool on these three chains. The scan follows straight-line code for at most 47 instructions after each site and does not follow branch targets, so a bad shape on a taken branch is not excluded.
findings.preconditions: Governance adopts a new absolute prestate whose code folds the shift-parts select into arithmetic. The present prestate does not.
findings.mitigations: Build future kona prestates with a toolchain that contains LLVM commit 0212d77, or rerun scan_prestate.py of the work directory on each new prestate before it is adopted, and rerun the vector set through the MIPS build.

No xori, ori, addu or store reads the masked value. The run log shows 0 mismatches on 85,544 targeted and 96,876 battery vectors and 624, 895 and 1,797 targeted mismatches for the three planted faults.

findings.title: Nitro's Stylus and JIT compilers use a Cranelift release inside the range of two October 2026 miscompile advisories, and no unprivileged account can reach either fault
findings.difference: Nitro runs Stylus programs as native code compiled on each node, and its JIT validator runs the WebAssembly replay machine through wasmer. Both compile with cranelift-codegen 0.129.1, which is the wasmtime 42 line. Wasmtime's advisories of October 2026 report that Cranelift before 43 can miscompile functions with more than 2^24 values (CVE-2026-115889, any architecture) and that aarch64 code with a br_table of more than about 256,000 targets jumps to the wrong place (CVE-2026-115893). The public Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain endpoints run linux-arm64 builds.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager is EVM bytecode and never runs through Cranelift: the interpreter loop of the fork sends only code with the Stylus prefix to ExecuteWASM (core/vm/interpreter.go lines 168-172 at 0e44603). A miscompile could only touch the PoolManager's funds indirectly, through a Stylus program that calls it, or through a validator that computes a different settled state. A Stylus program would need one function with more than 16.7 million SSA values or a branch table with more than about 262,144 targets. The 256 KB limit on a decompressed program rules out the first; it does not rule out the second, since a branch table with one byte targets can come within a few dozen entries of that count. What closes the hazard is that new programs cannot be activated at all: activationGas is 2^64-1 on all three chains. The replay machine that the JIT compiles is fixed by the consensus-v61 root, chosen by governance, and the one-step prover, which interprets WAVM without Cranelift, decides disputes.
findings.impact: None today. If governance reopens activation with a larger size limit, or ships a consensus machine with a function large enough to hit the overflow, nodes compiling with different backends could disagree on a Stylus call's result, which halts or splits the chain without taking any PoolManager funds by itself.
findings.preconditions: Chain governance raising the Stylus size limit or reopening activation, and a crafted program; or a governance-chosen replay machine with an oversized function.
findings.mitigations: Offchain Labs can move wasmer's Cranelift to 0.130 or later (wasmtime 43 and up, or a 48.0.7, 49.0.4 or 50.0.0 line for the aarch64 issue) before Stylus activation reopens. The deployer needs no action.

findings.title: The released reth binary carries an LLVM compiler for EVM code that validates and builds Ethereum blocks when an operator enables it, and no simulated call can reach it
findings.difference: reth v2.11.0, the client behind the endpoint in networks.json, links the evm2 JIT and its LLVM backend by default. With --jit, a contract that has been looked up 8 times is compiled to native code with no size limit, and that native code then runs inside payload building and payload validation. eth_call, eth_estimateGas and debug_traceCall run the interpreter. On Ethereum a block is accepted only if the execution clients of a supermajority of validators agree, and reth is a small minority client on every published census.
findings.mechanism: The PoolManager is called in many blocks, so on a reth node with --jit it becomes resident compiled code within minutes. From then on every swap that node executes runs FullMath.mulDiv (MULMOD with modulus 2^256 - 1 and with the pool denominator), the SAR and SIGNEXTEND unpacking of Slot0 and BalanceDelta, the BYTE and shift lookups of BitMath and the signed division of TickBitmap.compress in code generated by LLVM. If that code computed one of these differently, the reth node would compute a different post-state root for the block. As a builder it would publish a block that geth, Nethermind, Besu and Erigon reject. As a validator it would reject the canonical block and fall off the chain. Neither outcome changes the balances that the canonical chain records for LPs, swappers or claim holders, because the majority clients decide the canonical state. An ordinary account cannot switch the compiler on, cannot choose which node builds its block, and gains nothing from a divergence on a minority client. The vectors, scripts and mined swap checks of this review never reach this path: simulated calls do not use it, and mined swaps are the output of whichever client built the block, which was rechecked here against the source on 30,321 swaps of blocks 26,485,859 to 26,487,858 without a mismatch.
findings.impact: No loss to users of the canonical chain. A reth operator who enables --jit risks missed slots or rejected blocks if the compiler is wrong. Only if reth with --jit came to build and attest for a supermajority could a compiler fault reach canonical pool state.
findings.preconditions: A node operator starts reth v2.11.0 or later with --jit, and the generated code for one of the opcodes above differs from the specification for an input the pool math produces.
findings.mitigations: Track client share and the --jit flag in reth releases. Before relying on reth block production, read or test the JIT code generation for MULMOD, SAR, SIGNEXTEND, BYTE, SDIV and SMOD, as was done for Monad. The deployer needs no change to the PoolManager.

findings.title: Monad nodes that serve call traces execute blocks with the interpreter only, so no public data shows compiled execution of the PoolManager
findings.difference: Monad v0.16.7 runs two execution engines. The execution daemon builds its VM as InterpreterOnly when it is started with --trace-calls and as Dual (interpreter plus native x86 compiler) otherwise (cmd/monad/main.cpp lines 146, 214 and 484-488). Call frames are recorded and committed only when tracing is enabled (runloop_monad.cpp lines 233-245 and 330-337). Every RPC method that executes code uses a second, InterpreterOnly VM (rpc/monad_executor.cpp lines 1306-1309, used at 1525, 1547, 1824 and 1969; monad-rpc debug_replay.rs lines 61-64 and 236-237). Ethereum has one execution semantics per client and every serving node runs it.
findings.mechanism: Every public Monad endpoint that answers debug_traceTransaction with the call tracer (rpc.monad.xyz, rpc1, rpc2 via eRPC, rpc-mainnet.monadinfra.com, monad-mainnet.gateway.tatum.io) returns stored frames, so those nodes ran their block execution with --trace-calls and therefore with the interpreter. Their receipts and logs, among them every Swap and ModifyLiquidity event earlier cycles and this unit checked, are interpreter output. The only link between those nodes and validators that may run compiled code is the delayed merkle root of the state, checked D = 3 blocks later. On chain this is visible: in blocks 125,115,001 to 125,118,000 all 689 out-of-gas frames of 1,582 failed transactions, 19 of them PoolManager frames (swap with 94,784 gas, take with 1,844 to 18,922 gas), carry status 3 "out of gas", which is what the interpreter writes (interpreter/stack.hpp line 44); compiled code would end a static gas shortfall through error_label_ with StatusCode::Error (emitter.cpp lines 636, 679, 1054-1069), which debug.rs lines 381-388 map to "error". A compiled-only fault in a PoolManager branch that no block has taken yet (the overflow fallback of src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:52, the amount above 2^160 branch at src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:97 and 105, the 512 bit branch of the Q128 mulDiv at src/libraries/Position.sol:94-96) could be triggered by an ordinary swap or removal, and nobody can test it in advance through RPC. If two thirds of validators ran such a build, the canonical PoolManager state would follow the compiled result and the tracing RPC fleet would fall out of consensus. No such fault was found: the compiled paths for MULMOD, shifts, comparisons, sign extension and jumps were transcribed in cycles 9 to 13 without a mismatch, and the state roots of the tracing nodes agree with consensus at the finalized tip (block 125,124,132 on 2026-11-24).
findings.impact: No loss path was found. The finding corrects the evidence base: OPCODES.md says the Monad mined swaps "ran as compiled code", and cycle 11 says call frames are what block execution recorded. Both are true only of an interpreter run on the tracing node. Compiled execution is covered by reading and by state root agreement, not by any served receipt, log or frame.
findings.preconditions: A fault in the native compiler of the release that validators run, on an input that no mined block has produced yet. It needs no role from the attacker, but it needs a client defect that no reading has found.
findings.mitigations: Before liquidity arrives, run one non-tracing Dual mode node (a local monad build replaying mainnet blocks without --trace-calls) and compare its receipts with a tracing node for transactions that take each untaken branch. Ask Monad which execution mode validators run. Treat Monad state root agreement, not RPC answers, as the producer evidence.

findings.title: The LLVM MIPS shift lowering fault does not reach any path of the respected kona prestate, which the control flow scan and a run of its own shift handlers both show
findings.difference: OP Mainnet, Unichain and Ink settle withdrawals on permissionless games of type 9 whose program is kona-client 1.9.0 for MIPS64. Its toolchain predates LLVM fix 0212d77 for issue 235261, in which MipsTargetLowering uses (shamt AND 64) as a select condition and a later fold can treat that 0-or-64 value as a 0-or-1 boolean. eth_call on Ethereum (kona/prestate_now.json, Ethereum block 26,488,182) shows all three portals' AnchorStateRegistry return respectedGameType 9, the factories return implementation 0x19af533c (version 0.8.0) whose gameArgs start with absolute prestate 0x03e5a548...37c9, and the newest game of each chain (indexes 21571, 17871 and 2655) returns the same absolutePrestate().
findings.mechanism: If a fold had turned the condition into arithmetic, an EVM SHL, SHR or SAR with an amount between 64 and 127 would give the proof program another word than the op-reth nodes. BitMath.mostSignificantBit shifts by amounts in that range, TickBitmap.position and flipTick shift by the low 8 bits of a tick, and TickMath.getTickAtSqrtPrice shifts by 127 and 128, so the post-state root of a swap would differ and an ordinary account could contest an honest root. Two new checks rule this out for the respected prestate. First, kona/cfg_scan.py follows every one of the 66 `andi rX, rY, 0x40` sites of the 4,928,204 byte text segment through fall-through, branch targets, delay slots, j and jal targets and returns, with copies and stack spills tracked, until the value is overwritten on every path (up to 11,034 instructions from one site, nested calls to depth 8, no budget exhausted). The value is read 136 times: 135 as the condition of MOVN or MOVZ or a branch compared with zero, and once by srl 6. No path reads it in xori, ori, addu, daddu, sltu, a multiply, a shift amount or a store. The paths still open end in three ways that read nothing: one return with the value left in $3 by a function that returns through memory, where all 8 jal callers overwrite $3 within 8 instructions (kona/ret_callers.json); 36 indirect calls where the value is a stale $8 to $11 and the caller writes only $4 to $6 for that call (kona/jalr_args.json); and direct calls past depth 8 with no read. Second, kona/run_real.py runs the SHL, SHR and SAR handlers of the prestate image itself, located at 0x12006b1a8, 0x12006b328 and 0x12006ad70 by their stack and spec-byte accesses and identified by their results, in the cycle 13 Cannon-semantics emulator. They return the specified word on all 11,316 targeted, 23,763 battery and 57,792 further vectors (every amount 0 to 300 on 64 values for each opcode). The same harness with a planted MOVN fault that tests bit 0 only (the effect of the bad fold) gives 636 mismatches in 1,132 sampled targeted vectors, and a 5 bit DSLLV mask gives 403.
findings.impact: None with the prestate that all three chains respect today. A later prestate built with a toolchain older than LLVM 0212d77 needs the same two checks, since the fault depends on how the code is folded.
findings.preconditions: Governance adopts a new absolute prestate whose code folds the shift-parts condition into arithmetic. The present prestate does not, on any path.
findings.mitigations: Before a new kona prestate is adopted, run kona/cfg_scan.py and kona/run_real.py of the work directory on its state file, or build it with a toolchain that contains LLVM 0212d77.

TickBitmap.flipTick at src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:73 runs shl(and(tick, 0xff), 1), and TickMath.getTickAtSqrtPrice at src/libraries/TickMath.sol:142-151 runs shr(127, ...), shr(128, r) and shr(f, r). Every one of these goes through the interpreter's SHL, SHR or SAR handler, so the right check is the one the finding makes on the image. I reran cfg_scan.py on the work directory's text.bin into my scratchpad. The output is identical to cfg_scan.json: 66 sites, 135 zero tests, 1 srl by 6 (which maps 64 to 1), no budget exhausted, and 162 flags that are 161 tainted-argument jalr records and 1 return in $3. The classifier at cfg_scan.py:88-98 marks any other read as FLAG, including xori, ori, addu, sltu, multiplies, shift amounts, stores and register compares, so it errs toward flagging. One gap remained. The scan stops passing taint into direct calls past depth 8 (142 depth-limit events at sites 0x1201322d8 and 0x1201322f8), so 'no read' past that depth had not been shown. Up to depth 20 the only reads are 2 and 4 zero tests, and the other events are stale $8 to $11 passed on to calls, with no arithmetic, store or shift-amount read. I also reran run_real.py on the published image with the cycle 13 emulator. The handlers identify as SAR 0x12006ad70, SHL 0x12006b1a8 and SHR 0x12006b328, and 11,316 targeted, 23,763 battery and 57,792 amount 0 to 300 runs give 0 mismatches and 0 emulator faults, as stated.

My rerun to depth 20 found no read on them, but the static scan is still bounded and assumes the n64 calling convention for jalr callees. The shift handlers were found by pattern and identified by their results, and the dispatch table entry that selects them was not read. The static scan of all 66 sites covers any other handler. findings.title: Base and Celo block builders read through the reth execution cache that still has the stale branch for a destroyed account without code, when the operator enables cache sharing
findings.difference: Celo's endpoint still reports reth/v2.2.0-74cc8bb, the celo-org/reth revision with the old insert_state branch for a destroyed account whose original info had no code. The block builder reads through the execution cache only when the engine is started with --engine.share-execution-cache-with-payload-builder, whose default is false.
findings.mechanism: 1. Nothing about the code path changed since cycle 14: the endpoint reports the same build and celo-reth v1.0.10 only patched tracing. 2. The public node setup that Celo publishes starts celo-reth without the sharing flag, so follower and RPC nodes built from it never hand the cache to a builder. The sequencer's own start parameters are not published. 3. The PoolManager's storage is never on the faulty branch, because it has code from deployment and cannot be destroyed, and transient storage (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:21-39, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:17-36) is not cached across transactions. Only a contract created in the block that destroyed its codeless address can read a stale word, so only an attacker-made token or hook could be affected, and such a contract can misreport balances to sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364) without any cache fault.
findings.impact: No funds held by the PoolManager for other users move. If the flag is on at the sequencer and the trigger works, unsafe blocks could be published with a state that followers reject, and swaps and liquidity changes in them would be re-executed after the reorg.
findings.preconditions: The Celo sequencer operator runs with cache sharing enabled, and some read in an ordinary block caches a word for a codeless address that a later transaction in the block destroys and re-creates. Neither link is confirmed.
findings.mitigations: Celo upgrades celo-org/reth to a revision with the reth pull request 28148 fix, or keeps sharing off. Integrators wait for safe or finalized blocks before treating a fill as final.

In the same revision crates/node/core/src/args/engine.rs line 289 and crates/engine/primitives/src/config.rs line 238 set share_execution_cache_with_payload_builder to false by default. celo-kona tag celo/reth-v1.0.10 exists, its Cargo.lock pins reth-engine-tree 2.2.0 from celo-org/reth 74cc8bb and revm-interpreter 35.0.1, and tag celo/reth-v1.0.11 returns 404. The published start-op-reth.sh runs celo-reth node without --engine.share-execution-cache-with-payload-builder (its exec command, lines 98-127, has no such flag). The sequencer's own flags are not public, so the trigger condition stays unconfirmed, as the finding says.
verification.codeCheck: The PoolManager has no SELFDESTRUCT or CREATE in src/ (grep over src/ finds none) and has code from deployment, so its account never takes the destroyed branch. Deltas and synced reserves live in transient storage (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:21-39 uses tload and tstore), which is not part of the cross-block cache. sync reads the token balance through balanceOfSelf (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288) and _settle compares it with the synced reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364), so a stale word can only change what PoolManager sees from a contract whose address was destroyed and re-created in the block, which is a new contract made by the attacker. Tokens and hooks of victim pools had code before and cannot be destroyed under EIP-6780. No path to other users' funds follows.
verification.corrections: The title still names Base, while this unit's entry lists only chain 42220; the Base half is held by the existing ledger entry. The follower validation path, which an unprivileged account could reach without the operator flag, is a separate existing finding (theme-reth-cache-drift, actor operator, severity info) and is not covered here.

findings.title: Nodes on seven networks are built with Go releases that are out of support or carry prove pass faults (issues 79874, 80517, 82839), and no EVM result was found to depend on them
findings.difference: The Elysium endpoint reports nitro/vlocal+unknown-unknown/linux-amd64/go1.25.12. Go 1.25 left support when go1.27.0 shipped on 2026-08-19. go1.25.13 fixed, among others, issue 79874, where the prove pass emits a 32 bit slice mask for a 64 bit slice operation on targets that sign-extend 32 bit constants (amd64 named), so a slice with a start index of 2^32 or more advances too little, and issue 80517, where prove applies a fact before the point where it holds and drops a bounds check, shown on amd64 as a call through an out-of-range function table entry. Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain run go1.27.3, which is inside the range of the separate F-117 fault. Cycle 17 additions. (1) BNB Chain: 48 Club, a validator group and block builder, answers at rpc-bsc.48.club from two unpublished geth commits (132104cd and 9b93ce23), both built on 2026-11-16 with go1.25.5, a release line out of support since 2026-08-19 and missing the compiler fixes of go1.25.6 to go1.25.13. (2) Go issue 82839, opened 2026-11-03 and still open: the prove pass carries a fact through a sign extension of a narrow integer compared with a constant that does not fit the narrow type, and takes a branch that cannot be taken. The report names go1.26.6 to go1.26.10, go1.27.3 and master, and a variant from go1.24.13. Inside that range: bor v2.11.1 (go1.26.10), BNB Chain geth v1.8.2 (go1.26.10), avalanchego 1.15.3 (go1.26.10), Celo's op-geth backend (go1.24.13), Nitro on Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain (go1.27.3) and Elysium (go1.25.12).
findings.mechanism: Both faults change behaviour only on unusual shapes. Issue 79874 needs a slice start of 2^32 or more that the compiler has proved in bounds. The interpreter never slices calldata, code, memory or return data with such an index: a copy or load with a larger offset is clamped to the data length or charged for memory expansion first, and a zero-length copy or hash at a large offset touches no slice. The new offsets.py vectors aim at exactly that region (offsets from 2^31 to 2^256-1 for CALLDATALOAD, CALLDATACOPY, CODECOPY, KECCAK256, MCOPY and RETURNDATACOPY) and Elysium returns the specified word or failure on every one. Issue 80517 removes a bounds check whose failure would otherwise panic; on a correct program the check never fires, so it can only turn an existing out-of-range bug of the node into a silent read. The PoolManager paths that depend on these copies are the hook result copy (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:148), the revert bubbling copy (src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:109), and the arithmetic in src/libraries/FullMath.sol:21-54; all match on the battery, the targeted set, the script sets and 3,515 mined swaps. The settled state is computed by the consensus-v61 WebAssembly machine built with go1.25.9 (F-119), which predates both fixes as well but runs on a different target. Cycle 17 additions: the EVM paths the PoolManager depends on work on 64 bit words in holiman/uint256 and the interpreter, and no comparison of the issue 82839 shape was located there, though the source was not searched systematically (lead L-839) and no binary was decompiled. The answers were tested instead on 2026-11-25: the battery (99,985 vectors), the targeted set (85,544) and the large-offset vectors match the specification on Polygon, BNB Chain, Avalanche and Celo (Celo pinned to its op-geth backend), and on the 48 Club endpoint the battery, the targeted set, the call semantics words, the slot reads and the script sets match too. Which of the two 48 Club builds answered each batch is not known (lead L-844). bor, BNB Chain geth and avalanchego at go1.26.10 already contain the fixes for issues 79874 and 80517.
findings.impact: None found. A miscompiled routine in one operator's build would make that node disagree with the others, which shows up as a missed or reorganised block. On Elysium, with one whitelisted validator, the operator would be agreeing with itself.
findings.preconditions: An operator keeps building from an affected or unsupported Go release, and some function on the interpreter or state path has one of the faulty shapes. No such shape was found. The Elysium, 48 Club and Nitro rc.9 builds are private, so those checks are by their answers.
findings.mitigations: The deployer can ask the operators (Kinetiq for Elysium, 48 Club, and the client teams of bor, BNB Chain geth, avalanchego, Celo op-geth and Nitro) to build with a supported Go release that holds the fixes, and to publish the version and commit of each build. LPs need do nothing.

verification.factCheck: web3_clientVersion queried on 2026-11-25 returns nitro/vlocal+unknown-unknown/linux-amd64/go1.25.12 on https://rpc.elysium.kinetiq.xyz, nitro/v3.13.0-rc.9+b72783f-20261116T155937Z/linux-arm64/go1.27.3 on https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc and the same version on linux-amd64 on https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com. The Go release history page lists go1.25.12 on 2026-07-07, go1.25.13 on 2026-08-13 with compiler and runtime fixes, go1.25.14 on 2026-08-19 and go1.27.0 on 2026-08-19. Issue 79874 describes the slicemask fold that emits a Const32 mask for a 64 bit slice operation and needs a reslice index of 2^32 or more; its 1.25 backport 79875 is listed closed in the Go1.25.13 compiler/runtime milestone. Issue 80517 describes a prove fault that drops a bounds check and makes an indirect call through an out of range table entry on amd64; the 1.25 backport 80618 was merged to release-branch.go1.25 on 2026-08-05 (commit f59f3cc) and says the tests of CL 807182 fail on 1.26 and 1.25. The other compiler fixes in that milestone are for mips, mips64le, riscv64, js/wasm, darwin and arm64 or are compile-time errors, so the two amd64 items are the ones that apply to this build. My own eth_call with a state override on Elysium and Arbitrum One ran CALLDATALOAD at offset 2^64-1, a zero-length MCOPY at offset 2^255 and a zero-length KECCAK256 at offset 2^200; both returned a zero word and the empty-input hash c5d24601...a470, as specified. offsets.log in the work directory records 200 vectors per chain with no mismatch.
verification.codeCheck: The PoolManager paths named do not use large offsets. src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-153 calls the hook with output size 0, then copies return data from offset 0 for returndatasize bytes into freshly allocated memory and checks length >= 32 and the selector. src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:91-117 copies return data from offset 0 for returndatasize bytes. src/types/Currency.sol:44-75 calls with fixed calldata of 68 bytes and copies at most 32 bytes of return data to offset 0. Any large offset would come from a memory expansion that gas makes impossible before a Go slice is formed. I found no path in src/ that reaches the slice shape of issue 79874, and issue 80517 can only turn an existing out of range access in the node into a silent read. No PoolManager result was found to depend on either fault.
verification.corrections: go1.25.12 is two point releases behind, since go1.25.14 also shipped on 2026-08-19; the security fixes in go1.25.13 (crypto/tls, net/http, net/url and others) are an additional operational reason to rebuild, not an EVM result. The reporter of issue 80517 says it does not reproduce on 1.26.5; the exposure of 1.25 rests on the backport note in issue 80618 that the root cause is older and the new tests fail on 1.25. Issue 79874 says the upper half of the mask register is zeroed on amd64, so on amd64 the effect is truncation of the index to 32 bits.
